en: Preface to the Comprehensive Discourse on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is the great gateway of dhāraṇī and the secret heart-seal of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas. It universally encompasses the teachings of the entire Great Canon across the five periods and three vehicles;
it subsumes the holy and the mundane, the true and the false, delusion and enlightenment, cause and effect, and the inclusion of all phenomena without exception. Regarding its cultivation...
The distinctions between the false and the correct, and the deluded conditions of saṃsāra, are clearly perceived before one’s eyes as if observing fruit in the palm of the hand.
It may be said that there is nothing like this sutra, which is so vast and complete, for it penetrates the source of the One Mind and encompasses the ultimate principle of all phenomena.
It was for this single great cause and condition that the Tathāgata appeared in the world; apart from this, he had no other means to open [the way].
It is indeed a guidance. Therefore, for those who judge the teachings by confining them to a single period or a single doctrine—is this not like peering through a tube or measuring with a ladle?

Since these teachings entered the Middle Kingdom, there have been some ten or more schools of interpretation. Beyond the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Commentary), in recent times, both monastics and laypeople have each produced their own insights and perspectives, and those who have propagated and mastered them are not few.
Veneration has reached its peak and diligent effort has become profound; yet, as one examines the texts and provides explanations...
There is no principle that has not been scrutinized and refined with precision, leaving no further depths to be exhausted. What need is there, then, for this superfluous "snake's foot"?
However, upon surveying various expositions, I found only one point unsatisfactory: the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*) had not yet been fully integrated.

Consequently, while the phrasing was clear, the great purport remained unelucidated; thus, students could not help but sigh over it like those who "feel the elephant by its parts. In the past, when I resided at Mount Wutai...
While investigating the ultimate path amidst ice and snow, he used this sutra as a seal of verification. With a firm and concentrated mind, he contemplated it until he attained sudden enlightenment.
Later, after sitting in meditation by the Eastern Sea for three years, he happened to read this sutra one night;

at the moment when the sea was profoundly still, the sky was clear, and the moonlight mingled with the snow, he experienced a great awakening. Suddenly, his body, mind, and the world—*dharmadhātu*—were [realized] in that very instant.
It settled calmly like the reflection of a flower in the sky falling away. That night, holding a candle, he composed the *Xuanjing* (The Suspended Mirror) in one scroll.

This work fuses the entire sutra according to the threefold contemplation of the One Mind; it establishes the main framework by asserting that delusion and enlightenment do not transcend the One Mind and ultimately do not depart from the threefold contemplation.
However, it takes rational contemplation as its primary focus, thus being concise regarding the literal text, much like the arrangement of the *Avataṃsaka*’s Dharma-realm.

The intent lies in attaining the meaning, so that the words may be forgotten. Commentators, moreover, take the written text to be an obstacle and are unable to integrate it with contemplation of the mind;
this is because their minds remain deficient. For over twenty years, I have harbored within my breast a critical assessment of this state of affairs.
Even while drifting through the pestilential seas during times of famine and disaster, I did not forget this for a single thought. This reached the year Wanyili Jia-yin (1614).
Having retired in old age to the South Peak, I resided at the Wansheng Hermitage on Linghu. During the summer retreat, my disciple Chaoyi attended me for the longest time;
he shared in my hardships, illnesses, and adversities without exception. Moved by his sincerity, I [honored him].

Because he entered the room to seek further instruction, the *Xuánjìng* (The Suspended Mirror) triggered his prior realization. He subsequently composed this work directly with the brush, forming it into a volume.

Although it is more extensive than the *Xuánjìng*, it does nothing but broadly expound the principle of the three contemplations within the one mind; however, there was no leisure to provide detailed explanations in the text.

It is titled *Tōngyì* (Comprehensive Discourse), taking its meaning from the *Chūnqiū*: "the laws of the former kings for governing the world were discussed but not adjudicated. This is what is meant by "discourse" (*yì*).
To organize its categories and penetrate its great framework is truly superfluous for the path that transcends all.
For those of beginner's capacity, it is like taking a single drop from the ocean to swallow the flavor of a hundred rivers. Someone asked:
"Can the inconceivable Dharma of the Buddha be discussed? He replied: "No. The Dharma is fundamentally beyond words; yet people stubbornly cling [to them]."
Those with false views are not those whose words cannot be refuted. The Buddha taught that *upadeśa* is called "discourse" for the purpose of breaking the banners of false pride.
Indeed, this sutra destroys the evil blades of the nine realms and dismantles the defensive fortresses of attachment held by both the holy and the mundane;
there is nothing that is not fully revealed from the tip of his broad and long tongue. All manner of solid walls are pierced by a single arrowhead, directly causing wisdom—

Only after one has exhausted their worldly attachments and withered the pride of the descending mind so as to submit in devotion may they cease. For it is through the exhaustion of the sutras that their true nature is revealed.

If one does not deliberate upon and clarify the Correct Commandment, there will be no means to purify the demonic vapors of the Dharma-realm or to manifest the Great Transformation of the Awakened Sovereign. How can this be described merely by means of written words? To grasp the meaning and leave behind the traces lies within the Golden [Sutra].
Written by the Chan practitioner Deqing, the Hermit of Mount Han,
on the Dragon Boat Festival of the Ding-si year of the Wanli era (1617), at the Baye Studio in Wumen.
Preface to the Re-engraved *Tongyi* on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:

How great is the Teaching! The truthful words from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata, elucidated through the compassionate heart of the Patriarchs—when seeking that which is wondrous for entering and easy for awakening to its depths, none surpasses the commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* composed by the Great Master Hanshan.

This is a comprehensive treatise. Its essential purport is clearly manifest, and its language is concise and precise. It does not depart from the written text to reveal the subtle, nor does it become mired in phrases to discuss the mysterious.

It harmonizes the two schools of Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang), penetrates the single mind and the three contemplations (san guan), accords with the established tenets, and leaves nothing out, even down to the finest detail.
From beginning to end it is perfectly integrated, and from root to branch it is consistently unified. It is truly the compass for the garden of the teachings and the true eye of the Chan school.
(Interlude) Having first donned the black robes on Mount Yunshan, I subsequently obtained a fragmentary manuscript of the *Dream Journey* (Mengyou).

As I contemplated its profound instructions and the teachings of the Dharma, I was moved by a sense of universal sincerity and awe. Upon reaching the lectures on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I examined the commentaries of various masters;

only then did I learn that the Great Master [Zhiyi] had also produced an elucidation of this scripture titled the *Tongyi*. Thereupon, I engraved these words into the depths of my five internal organs. Not yet...

I encountered this once and from that point on, throughout more than ten years, there was not a single thought-moment that did not dwell upon this book. In the spring of the Jia-wu year, I traveled as a wandering monk to Mount Tai;
my former aspiration was thus fulfilled, and in a single moment the feverish afflictions of my mind were dispelled, while in an instant the ice-like stiffness of my breast was melted away.

Having happened upon this by chance, I was filled with joy beyond the ordinary. Consequently, unable to remain idle like one waiting for a rabbit at a tree stump, I have initiated the effort to carve the woodblocks for publication.
My true intention is to share this with my fellow practitioners; I do not yet dare to claim it as the direct lineage of Master Zhuan Shun’s Dharma stream.
Written on the first month of winter in the twentieth year of the Guangxu era by Tian-tai descendant Yun-shui Shan-ren Di-xian.
General Discourse on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause, Cultivation, and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume One.
At the Scripture Library of Longhua Temple on the River Shen.
The Prefatory Judgment, composed by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Shi Deqing of Nanyue, states: "In the past,
whenever masters who expounded the scriptures interpreted this particular sutra, they invariably first established a preliminary judgment through ten topical gates."
This is intended to let students know that throughout the forty-nine years of my appearance in the world, the Tathāgata has expounded the Great Canon of Teachings,
which from beginning to end is distinguished by five periods and five teachings— namely, the Hīnayāna, Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect—
each differing in its depth and sequence. It is necessary to identify precisely which period and which teaching a specific sūtra belongs to.
This is the standard for commentaries; from the time of Master Xianshou and Master Qingliang onwards, all have followed this tradition without exception.

Yet, regarding this single sutra alone, there have been more than ten schools of interpretation over its history. Each relies on its own particular view, resulting in differing dates assigned to the events;
consequently, many disputes have arisen, making it difficult to resolve the doubts of the multitude. I have previously observed that...
The original separate title is also known as having been extracted for independent circulation from within the *Abhiṣeka-varga*.

Because I have carefully examined this scripture, I find no definitive evidence that it was taught all at once. Having seen the version of the text with Changshui’s commentary, the separate title reads:
*The Scripture of the Great Maṇḍala of Nālandā in Central India, Extracted from the Abhiṣeka-varga*.
[The text continues with] "Practice. Master Xuán judges that the Buddha did not preach this sutra all at once; rather, it was necessarily taught in successive stages.
Thus we know that the compiler arranged it into a single volume according to its categories. Taking this as the standard, one may believe it with confidence and without doubt.
However, if one examines the title "Mantra of Consecration" (*abhiṣeka-pada*) within the sutra itself, the compiler’s method of categorization becomes clear. Please allow me to explain this briefly.
However, the Guanding (Consecration) Section consists of the teachings spoken by me, Vairocana Buddha of the Center.
Since Vairocana is the Dharmakāya Buddha, he is called Rocana when manifesting from the Dharma. Seated at the site of enlightenment, he expounded the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra;
this is termed the Fundamental Wheel of Dharma, which was intended solely for sentient beings of a single class possessing great faculties.

Yet those of inferior faculties are like the blind and the deaf. Therefore, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni entered the Samādhi of the Limit of the Kṣaṇa, manifesting both [the Dharma and Transformation] bodies;
he appeared as a Transformation Body, demonstrating birth within the triple world under the name Śākyamuni.

Beginning from his descent from Tuṣita to the royal palace, his entry into the womb, his emergence from the womb, and his departure for home, he underwent ascetic practices and perfected the eight phases of enlightenment.
The Way began with the preaching of the Dharma at the Deer Park and proceeded through the Vaipulya, Prajñāpāramitā, and Lotus Sūtras over forty-nine years until the entry into Great Nirvāṇa.
From beginning to end, it did not depart from the Samādhi of the Limit of a Single Instant (*kṣaṇa*).

The entire Great Canon of teachings thus spoken is called the "Dharma Wheel that Subsumes the Branches and Returns to the Root," and is also termed the "Teaching of Inductive Guidance. It is intended to guide those of the five natures and the three vehicles.
To "gather and return to the single vehicle’s ground of tranquil extinction" refers specifically to the *Avataṃsaka* as the ocean of wondrous adornment—the destination to which one returns.
It is like the home of a destitute son; the sublime gateway of the three contemplations is the path by which one returns home.

This is what is called the "Single Path to the Gate of Nirvana. Now, observing that this sutra begins with [the Buddha] manifesting his descent into a chamber of debauchery, this is precisely the period of the Āgamas.
Its examination of the mind serves to shatter attachment to the body and the view of permanence;

its address to King Bimbisāra serves to shatter the view of annihilation—this is the teaching of the Āgamas. Its discernment of false views serves to reveal true vision and to destroy the essence of [deluded] seeing.

In manifesting original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), its meaning is simultaneous with that of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*. When the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the three categories (*triskandha*) are seen to converge in the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, it is identical to the true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; furthermore, this spans the interval between those two periods.

As for the seven elements (*saptadhātu*) being all-pervasive and their nature being truly interfused, it is indeed equal to the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena (*dharmārtha-avyāghāta*) within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Furthermore, in the fourth fascicle it says: "One is immeasurable, and the immeasurable is one. Within the small appears the large, and within the large appears the small.
Upon the tip of a single hair, a Jewel-King Buddha-land is manifested; seated within a minute speck of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel."

This briefly elucidates the *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*) in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; it is precisely the Ocean of Wondrous Adornments to which one returns.
This is called the ultimate place of rest and peace. It is here that the three bodies as a single essence (*trikāya-ekasvabhāva*) are fully revealed.
Śākyamuni’s fundamental intention in appearing in the world—to teach and transform sentient beings—was necessarily to lead them to this very state before his work was complete.
Thus we know that this sutra encompasses all teachings without exception and gathers in all capacities without exclusion; how could it be restricted to a single period?
Indeed, it is the Seal of the One True Aspect held by Śākyamuni Buddha, which is called the subtle and secret Single Mind.
Furthermore, the dharma-gate of the three contemplations—emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way—is the sharp instrument for destroying delusions. Thus says the World-Honored One.

The World-Honored One desired that sentient beings realize this single mind. However, as the afflictions and defilements of sentient beings were heavy, he did not dare to reveal this mind all at once.
Thus, during the assembly of the *Āgamas*, he provisionally taught the ten wholesome paths of human and celestial beings to prevent them from falling into the three miserable realms;

he further taught impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and the Twelve [Links of Dependent Origination].
The Dharma of causes and conditions enables all sentient beings to temporarily emerge from the triple world and escape birth and death.

The nirvāṇa they realize is termed "partial emptiness" (*prādeśika-śūnyatā*). Because they cling to emptiness and are unable to perceive existence, and because the followers of the Hīnayāna do not penetrate the principle of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only), the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* was taught to establish the doctrine of the nine consciousnesses, based upon which the eight consciousnesses arise and transform.

Regarding the sense organs, the body, and the objective world, one must realize that these delusive appearances are all transformations of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and that their characteristics are fundamentally empty.
Next, Prajñāpāramitā was taught to reveal true emptiness and illusory existence, thereby shattering the Small Vehicle’s attachment to partial emptiness.
This occurred forty years after the *Āgamas*. Upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there was a discussion solely of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), directly pointing to the single mind.
This reveals the Middle Way; Nirvāṇa clarifies the equality of Buddha-nature, wherein the three vehicles converge and the five natures enter together.
All who possess a mind shall attain Buddhahood, thereby fulfilling the World-Honored One’s original intent for appearing in the world.
Yet, the principle of perfect interfusion has not yet been fully revealed in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Now, by applying the general purport of the principles elucidated in this present sutra:
It is certain that the teachings of a single lifetime encompass all phenomena without exception.

Moreover, since the teachings beginning from the *Āgamas* and ending with the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* are still the Dharma spoken by the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha, whereas the principle of perfect interfusion belongs to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as spoken by the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha, how can one limit them to a single period? If one considers the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharmadhātu...
If one illuminates this, it becomes clear that Śākyamuni’s forty-nine years of preaching the Dharma never departed from the samādhi of the limit of a single kṣaṇa from beginning to end.
This is because kalpas and moments are gathered together; in the time that is timeless, there is truly no before or after.

Nevertheless, within the gate of expedient transformation, as the capacities of sentient beings vary—being either mature or immature—there is no lack of sequential order from the shallow to the deep, by means of the dharma-gate of the one mind.

All Buddhas realize this in common; the three contemplations constitute the essential core for awakening to the mind. Because [the Buddha] traversed five periods according to the differing capacities of sentient beings, he dispersed these teachings throughout his lifetime.
Each teaching was tailored to the specific needs of those present, universally encompassing the three faculties of the audience. Thus, their sequential arrangement also differs.

Therefore, the compilers of the canon, fearing that practitioners of future ages would possess limited understanding and that the vast ocean of the teachings would be difficult to fathom in its ultimate destination,
selected from among the two types of Dharma wheels— the wheel of provisional transformation and the wheel of ultimate reality taught by the two Buddhas—

those that proceed from the source to the branches and return from the branches to the source. From within the entirety of the teachings throughout his lifetime, they extracted the "One Mind" to manifest it preeminently.
Sentient beings proceed from awakening to delusion, reaching the extreme states of ascent and descent within the seven realms of existence.

By returning to the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) and refuting the two attachments (*dvividha-grāha*), one reveals the fifty-five stages of progress—from delusion to awakening—distinguished by their varying depths of realization.

These stages are unified throughout the entire path from beginning to end as a single continuity, all of which is subsumed within the One Mind. From the ordinary person to the sage, it is a direct [path].

Entering the ocean of fruition, one does not encounter byways or branches; it allows the practitioner to see everything at a single glance without remainder, like a mirror of wisdom suspended before one’s eyes.
Thus one understands the path for returning home, which is what is called "the single path, the gate of nirvana. How could this be restricted to a single moment?
If one does not employ principle to harmonize and seal it in accordance with the Buddha-mind, then to fixate upon it as a mere instant—
At such a time, what benefit would there be in the Dharma? Therefore, those who propagate [the teachings] value attaining the fundamental source rather than being mired in the traces.
*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause for the Realization and Proof of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*.
The commentary states: Regarding the title of this sutra, the World-Honored One himself spoke of five names within the text;

the present title may be understood as one that preserves these meanings in an implicit manner. Although this title consists of nineteen characters, its primary emphasis rests solely upon the three characters "Śūraṅgama.
The preceding sixteen characters are all explanatory of its meaning. [Now follows] the explanation of Śūraṅgama.
This is called "The Ultimate Solidity of All Affairs. It is the general name for the Great Samādhi and is a synonym for the One Mind.
It possesses both its formal essence (*dharma*) and its meaning (*artha*). To summarize, the substance of this samādhi is the One Mind;

to distinguish it, it consists of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). Nevertheless, these three contemplations are all established based upon the One Mind. As the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "The True Mind..."
That which is "suchness" (tathatā) is the essence of the great universal-dharma-gate of the single dharma-realm; it is what is called the pure true mind of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Based on this essential mind, there are three designations: first, the empty Tathāgatagarbha; second, the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha;
and third, the empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha. This refers to the fact that the essence of this mind is originally pure.
Because not a single dharma is established, it is called "empty. Because it possesses merits equal in number to the sands of the Ganges that accord with its nature, it is called "not empty.

Regarding these three—emptiness and non-emptiness—their two essences are in fact but one mind. Stillness and illumination are simultaneous: because it is still, it is empty; because it illuminates, it is not empty.
The unimpeded coexistence of presence and disappearance is called "empty and not empty. It is based on this meaning that [the teaching is so named].
One establishes the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). By means of these three contemplations, one returns to realize the single mind (*ekacitta*);
therefore, it is called the general name for the Great Samādhi (*mahāsamādhi*). This is what is meant by "this is called the Dharma.

The sixteen characters above constitute its meaning, as this single mind possesses the three great meanings of essence (*svabhāva*), attributes (*lakṣaṇa*), and function (*vṛtti*). First is the greatness of essence; second is the greatness of attributes; third is the greatness of function.

The title, "The Great Buddha-Crown," and so forth, indicates the three meanings of "greatness. That which is called "Great" refers to the essence of this mind, which is vast and expansive, encompassing the entire dharma-realm;
it is great without exterior and its substance transcends all names and words, yet it is forcibly designated as "Great.
"Buddha-Crown" (Buddhoṣṇīṣa) is used metaphorically to clarify the greatness of its characteristics; that is, the Buddha represents the ultimate limit.
The "Holy Crown" (*ārya-uṣṇīṣa*) is the most honored and unsurpassed crown. Among the Buddha’s marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*), it is called the "Crown Mark Invisible to Sight.
Thus it is said: "At birth, he was held and gazed upon by his parents, yet they could not see the crown of his head.
This supreme, signless (*animitta*) crown is used as a metaphor for the vast and boundless mind. Being signless, it cannot be seen even with sight; therefore, it is [the uṣṇīṣa].
The "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refer to the Greatness [of the Mind]. The passage beginning with "The secret cause of the Tathāgata" clarifies the Greatness of Function (prayojana).

This means that all Buddhas rely upon this single mind to ascend to the ultimate fruit, reaching it exhaustively without remainder; therefore, it is called the "definitive meaning" (nītārtha). All Bodhisattvas rely upon this single mind to reach the stage of the Tathāgata;
therefore, it is called the "ten thousand practices" (sarvacaryā). It is because this single mind possesses the three aforementioned [greatnesses]...

This is the meaning; therefore, it serves as the general name for the Great Samādhi. Below this, Ānanda requests the three contemplations based on their meanings, and the Buddha’s response directly points to the one mind.

Thus, we know that all that is expounded throughout the entire sūtra regarding the causes and fruits of cultivation and realization does not, in total, go beyond the three contemplations, and ultimately does not depart from the one mind. If one uses this mind to illuminate the myriad dharmas, then every dharma...

It is entirely true. Therefore, it is said that "all matters are ultimately firm and solid. If one understands this single title, more than half the purport of the entire scripture will have been grasped.
It is also known as *The Scripture of the Great Site of Nālandā in Central India*, excerpted from the *Abhiṣeka* section and circulated separately.
The commentary states: This is an alternative name. In India, it is fully called Indraka; here it is translated as "Moon Country.
There are five regions of India, and this is one of them. It is a great kingdom of the Western Regions. Nālandā means "Insatiable Giver" (or "Never-Tiring in Giving"), which is the name of a dragon.
The *Record of the Western Regions* says: "In the country of Āmra, there is a pond, and within the pond there is a dragon."

It is named "Giver Without Weariness" (*Anikṣiptadhura*), having been given this name because the monastery is situated near that pond. As for the "Great Mahāmaṇḍala," among all the monasteries of the Western Regions, this one alone is the largest;
it is venerated by the kings of the five regions of India, and eminent *śramaṇas* who are masters of both the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics) and *Yogācāra* (Nature) schools reside there.
A great deal of the Buddha-dharma is accumulated here. Formerly, when Xuanzang first arrived in the Western Regions...
This is the very place where [the Master] previously came to this monastery to study the Yogācāra school under the preceptor Śīlabhadra.

Regarding the *Abhiṣeka-varga* (Consecration Section), within the realm of the *Avataṃsaka*, there are five sections of teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the Five Directions, each constituting a distinct division.
The teaching spoken by Vairocana Buddha, who presides as the central figure, is named the *Abhiṣeka-varga*. This scripture reveals that...
It is titled as such because it generally reports what was spoken by the Buddha. Since it is designated as the *Nalanda Great Maṇḍala Sūtra*, the compiler can be known [from this].
According to Changshui’s commentary, this title is preserved, and it is also stated that this sūtra was not taught at a single time.
The Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra from Central India translated [this] at the Zhizhi Daochang in Guangzhou.
Regarding the commentary: this is the name of the translator. "Tianzhu" is also called "Qiandzhu," also called "Shendu," and also called "Yindu.
These are names for a country in the Western Regions; they differ only in the dialects of the Sanskrit language. "Pralamiti" (般剌密諦) is translated here as "Ultimate Measure" (Jiliang).
This is the name of the translator. This sutra was most highly treasured by the kings of the Western Regions, who strictly prohibited it from leaving their territory.
When the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñācakra wished to transmit it to China, he repeatedly stole it away; however, each time he was captured and sent back, and it seemed impossible to obtain.
Later, he wrote it upon fine, delicate silk, then broke his own arm to conceal it within his flesh, and finally set sail.

He traveled by sea and arrived at Guangzhou. On the twenty-third day of the fifth month of the first year of the Shenlong era of the Tang dynasty (the year of Yichou), he happened to encounter the Chancellor Fang Rong, who was presiding over the Southern Selection Office in Guangzhou.

At that time, the Tripiṭaka Master was staying at Zhiyi Temple to translate this scripture, and [the author] served as the scribe for the oral transmission. Such was the difficulty with which this scripture arrived. Shortly after the translation was completed, the Tripiṭaka Master...
He arrived in secret. His country’s borders were subjected to interrogation, and as the Tripitaka Master sought to resolve this difficulty, he returned home.
When Lord Fang submitted his memorial, he encountered the early reign of Emperor Zhongzong; as the state was preoccupied with many affairs, there was no leisure to promulgate [the teachings].

At that time, Chan Master Shenxiu entered the Inner Court and, upon seeing them, transcribed them, whereby they subsequently circulated in the northern regions. Daotong remained within the palace, personally...
When the *Yuzou jing* (Sutra of the Imperial Edict) was presented, it was further transcribed and brought back to Du-men Temple in Jingzhou.
The śramaṇa Hui-zhen of Sha-tao in Northern Wei constantly yearned for this sutra and obtained it at Du-men Temple.

Later, Master Jue obtained its translated version from the home of the former Chancellor Fang Rong, and thus it was transmitted. Such was the difficulty in the circulation of this sutra. Formerly, at Tiantai...
When the Great Master Zhiwei was completing his *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation), he encountered a Brahmin master who showed him the principles of *zhi guan*.
The Brahmin said, "This is essentially identical to the three contemplations (*san guan*) in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* of the Western Regions.
The Great Master gazed toward the west day and night, bowing and praying for a vision of it, yet he did not see it; this illustrates the difficulty of encountering this sutra. Now, fortunately...

Throughout antiquity and the present, more than ten schools of commentators have produced exegetical works that have almost entirely elucidated its profound mysteries and revealed its hidden meanings.

Today, there are no few among the monastics and laypeople who have entered this Dharma gate; yet students generally regard it as something ordinary. How could they know how difficult it is to encounter the Buddha-dharma?
The Śramaṇa Mīghaśikṣa from the kingdom of Udyāna provides the following commentary on the translation:
"Udyāna" means "Garden" (vana) in this language; it is the name of the country. "Mīghaśikṣa" means "One Capable of Subduing."
Because it translates from Sanskrit into Chinese, it is called "translation" (yi-yu).

It was transcribed by the Bodhisattva-precept disciple Fang Rong, Formerly Grand Master for Regular Counsel, concurrently Minister of the Department of State Affairs and Director of the Secretariat, of Qinghe.
The commentary states: A "disciple who has received the Bodhisattva precepts" refers to a high official who has received the Mahayana Bodhisattva precepts.

This is the convergence of seeing back into the mind. Below, the text correctly clarifies the overturning of delusions to destroy the arising [of false views].

The Death-Mind. It is verified that the six consciousnesses falsely grasp the five aggregates—the body and mind—as a self, calculating them as either permanent or impermanent, thereby giving rise to inverted views;
that is to say, ordinary beings falsely grasp the five aggregates—the body and mind—as permanent, reckoning the impermanent to be permanent.
The followers of the Two Vehicles do not realize that body and mind are fundamentally true and eternal; they falsely reckon them to be impermanent, and thus it is said they are "inverted.
This precisely belongs to the doctrinal meaning of the *Āgama* teachings. Those who dare to interpret it in this way [should consider that] the subsequent passage on inversion states:
"Thus you shall know that your body and the pure *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas are revealed through comparison. The body of a Tathāgata is named..."

"O Samyaksaṃbuddhas, your bodies are designated as having inverted natures. Therefore, we know that the preceding passage refers to the deluded and discriminative mind arising from the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi)."
◎ Part Three: Showing Those Who Are Deluded, divided into two sections. [□@(?(○/(○*○))] First, the Request:
Although Ānanda had heard these words, he and the great assembly remained silent with their mouths, yet their minds were not yet awakened.
I still hope that the Tathāgata will graciously proclaim his voice and provide instruction. With palms joined and a pure mind, I await the Buddha’s compassionate teaching.
The discussion states: The false mind that Ānanda clung to has already been refuted as having its basis in the two aggregates of form and feeling;
now, when he turns to seek refuge in the mind itself, it is utterly devoid of a place of return. Thus, not knowing what to request, he remained silent.
However, my mind has not yet attained awakening; I merely await the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.
Next, the response is divided into six parts. First, the delusions of ordinary beings are shown.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his hand, which was marked by webbed fingers like fine cotton-wool and radiated light, and opened his five wheel-like fingers.

He instructed Ānanda and the great assembly: "When I first attained the Way, in the Deer Park, for the sake of the five bhikṣus including Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya and you fourfold assembly, I declared that all sentient beings fail to achieve Bodhi or Arhatship solely because of adventitious [defilements]."
"Deceived by the dust-like afflictions, how did you all attain awakening at that time to now achieve the fruit of sainthood?
At that moment, Kauṇḍinya rose and addressed the Buddha: "I am now the elder among this great assembly and alone have earned the name 'The Liberated.

It was through awakening to the two characters 'guest' and 'dust' that I achieved this fruit. World-Honored One, it is like a traveler who stays at an inn, either lodging there or eating; having lodged..."
When the meal is finished, one packs for the journey ahead and finds no leisure to remain. If the true host were present, there would be no need to depart.
Reflecting thus, "not remaining" is designated as the guest, while "remaining" is designated as the host; therefore, the state of not remaining is defined by the meaning of being a guest.

Furthermore, it is like after a fresh clearing of the sky, when the bright sun ascends and its light enters through a crack in a wall, revealing the various forms of dust suspended in the air. These dust motes...
The substance is in motion, while empty space is tranquil. Reflecting in this way, that which is clear and still is called "space," and that which is in motion is called "dust.
For that which is in motion is given the meaning of "dust. The Buddha said: "It is so."

The commentary states: This is to shatter the inverted views of ordinary beings in order to reveal their delusion. At the very beginning of shattering these views, the Buddha suddenly questions them regarding "adventitious dust" (*āgantuka-rajas*).
This is because ordinary beings falsely cling to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—the body and mind—as permanent, thereby giving rise to the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

The Tathāgata employs the metaphor of adventitious dust to refute this; for just as a traveler stays at an inn only for food and lodging before departing, so too are these defilements merely temporary visitors.

The true master has no place of departure; this is a metaphor for sentient beings who are like travelers lodging within the three realms, subject to the impermanence of birth and death—how could they be reckoned as permanent?
When clear sunlight rises into the sky, dust may stir, yet the essence of space remains tranquil;
this is a metaphor for the impermanence of arising and ceasing. How could such impermanence be falsely reckoned as permanence? This is precisely...
Ordinary worldlings are inverted.
[△@○] Second, showing the inversion of the two vehicles, which has two parts. [?╳] First, showing their delusion:
At that time, the Tathāgata, in the midst of the great assembly, bent his five fingers; having bent them, he opened them again; having opened them, he bent them once more.
He said to Ānanda, "What do you see now? Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata’s palms, adorned with the hundred jewels, opening and closing amidst the assembly.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Regarding what you see as my hands opening and closing amidst the assembly:
is it that my hands themselves open and close, or is it that your vision perceives them as opening and closing? Ānanda replied, "World-Honored One, it is the precious hands amidst the assembly..."
"Opening and closing. I see the Tathāgata’s hand opening and closing by itself; it is not that the nature of my seeing has opening and closing.
The Buddha asked, "What moves and what is still? Ānanda said, "The Buddha’s hand does not remain still, but as for my nature of seeing, it is not even still;
how could it be 'not remaining'? The Buddha said, "It is so. Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted a single jewel-light from his palm, which flew away—
To Ānanda’s right, the Buddha immediately turned his head to look to the right. Again, he emitted a ray of light to Ānanda’s left;
Ānanda then turned his head to look to the left. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Why is your head shaking today?
Ānanda replied, "I see the Tathāgata emitting wondrous jewel-rays coming from my left and right; therefore, as I looked left and right, my head moved of its own accord."
“Ānanda, when you shake your head while gazing at the Buddha’s light, does it move because your head moves, or does it move because your vision moves?
“World-Honored One, it is my head that moves; as for my nature of seeing, it has no stillness—so who could cause it to shake? The Buddha said, “It is so.”
The commentary states: This passage refutes the inverted views of the two vehicles to reveal their delusion.

When the Tathāgata bent his fingers and projected light to test that the seeing-nature was immovable, it was because the followers of the two vehicles falsely reckoned the five aggregates—the body and mind—to be impermanent, thereby giving rise to revulsion and detachment.
Because they did not understand that sentient beings are suchness, the Tathāgata first bent his fingers and projected light in order to shatter their false views.
This was verified by means of light. Since Ānanda knew that while the head moved, the vision remained unmoving, he thereby realized that the body and its objects are fundamentally unmoving.
Why, then, do you calculate them to be impermanent? This has already subtly revealed true permanence.
That the flying dust and the drifting light are all sealed with this truth means that what Ānanda perceived was not erroneous.
[?×] Next, regarding reprimand:
thereupon the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly, saying, "Furthermore, if sentient beings name that which is agitated as 'dust' (rajas), [it is so]."
That which does not abide is called a guest. Observe Ānanda: your head moves to and fro, yet you see nothing that moves.
Again, observe my hand: it opens and closes, yet you see nothing that expands or contracts. Why, then, do you now take that which moves to be the body?
Taking movement as their object, from beginning to end they undergo birth and extinction in every thought-moment. They lose the true nature and act with inverted views;
their fundamental mind loses its truth, and they mistake external objects for themselves. Thus they transmigrate within this cycle, taking upon themselves the process of wandering.
The commentary states: This is a general reprimand of the two delusions, a strategy for driving away both ordinary beings and sages.
The intent is that once sentient beings know that movement is called "dust," it is clear that arising and ceasing are not permanent. How could one reckon this arising and ceasing as being permanent?
If those of the Two Vehicles know that while the head moves, the nature of seeing remains unmoving, then it is clear that the fundamental source is inherently true and constant.
How can it be reckoned as impermanent? Since you already know the meaning of permanence and impermanence, what is it that you take movement to be the body and movement to be the environment?
These two lines of the sutra contain two meanings; therein, truth and falsehood drive each other along.
The meaning is this: how could an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) possibly recognize this impermanent body and its objects as permanent?
This rebukes the ordinary person. This illusory and false body and its objects are, in their original nature, truly eternal.

How could a follower of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha) recognize this phantom-like empty body as impermanent? The intent is to rebuke the followers of the Two Vehicles. From this delusion...
To calculate from beginning to end how, moment by moment, arising and ceasing, one has lost the true nature and acted in delusion—
losing the fundamental mind-nature that was originally present, and instead identifying external objects as the self— one thus undergoes the cycle of rebirth within this state of inversion,
taking the flow of transmigration upon oneself. This is a comprehensive indictment of such delusion.
