[△@○] Part Three: Showing the Perverse View of Annihilationism held by Non-Buddhists.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, felt their bodies and minds become serene and at ease.

They reflected that since beginningless time they had lost their original mind, mistakenly identifying with the delusive reflections of discriminating thoughts regarding conditioned objects. Today they have attained awakening, like a child who has lost its mother suddenly encountering her again.
Joining their palms and bowing to the Buddha, they wished to hear the Tathāgata reveal the truth and falsehood, the reality and unreality of body and mind.
The manifestation of arising and ceasing, and non-arising and non-ceasing—these two clarify the nature of the mind. At that time, King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha:

"In the past, before I had received the instructions of the Buddhas, I encountered Kātyāyana and Ajita Keśakambalin, both of whom told me that the annihilation of this body after death is called Nirvana. Although I have now met the Buddha, I still harbor doubts. How can this be?"
He manifested and certified that this mind is the ground of neither-arising-nor-ceasing. Now, all those in this great assembly who still possess outflows (āsrava) wish to hear it.
The commentary says: This emerges from the doubt of the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Having heard the previous instruction on the guest-dust and the flying light, Ānanda...

By demonstrating that while the objects of the body’s realm move, there is that which is unmoving, one comes to know the principle that within birth and death there is that which is neither born nor extinguished.
Although you have already attained this realization, you have consistently and erroneously identified the mind of discursive differentiation regarding conditioned objects as the true mind;
thus, you have not yet seen the nature that is neither born nor extinguished. Therefore, I pray that the World-Honored One will, right before me, demonstrate what is the reality and what is not.
This would be false and delusory. What, then, is arising and ceasing? What is non-arising and non-ceasing?

Only when the two natures of reality and delusion are made clearly distinct can one gain self-confidence and be free from doubt. This was precisely the aspiration of Ānanda’s heart, yet he had not yet resolved it.
Therefore, King Ajātaśatru used this as a pretext to request [the Buddha's presence]. Previously, King Ajātaśatru had served non-Buddhist teachers;
one was of the Kātyāyana clan, named Kakuda Kātyāyana, who maintained that all phenomena both exist and do not exist.
Another non-Buddhist teacher was Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra—the name "Vairaṭī" being his mother’s name, hence he is called her "son"—who maintained that all phenomena...
It is natural. Although there are many non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika) in the Western Regions, their philosophical calculations do not go beyond the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.

Regarding these two, King Ajātaśatru has already followed the doctrine of annihilationism; therefore, even upon seeing the Buddha, he still clung to his old habits, knowing only that after death there is total cessation.
Now, hearing that this mind possesses a nature that is neither born nor extinguished, he still harbors doubts.
Therefore, I pray that you will expound upon this; may the great assembly listen with aspiration.

If one awakens to the mind that is neither born nor extinguished, then Ānanda’s deluded attachments will naturally subside, and the nature of true permanence will naturally manifest. However, the view that [the self] is annihilated after death is not unique to the Western Regions;
it is also prevalent here in this land. It is said that when a person dies, the pure qi returns to heaven and the turbid qi returns to earth.
That the single spiritual true nature returns to the Great Void—this is the view of annihilationism.
If it were indeed to return to the Great Void, then cause and effect would be severed. How unfortunate this would be!
The Buddha said to the Great King: "Your body exists now. I ask you again: does this body of yours remain eternally indestructible like a diamond, or does it eventually perish?
"World-Honored One," [the King replied], "this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and destruction. The Buddha said:
"Great King, since you have not yet perished, how do you know that it will perish? "World-Honored One," [the King replied], "this body of mine is impermanent and subject to transformation and decay."

"Although it has not yet been extinguished, I observe that before my eyes, every thought-moment (kṣaṇa) shifts and passes away; new and new states do not abide, like fire turning to ash, gradually wasting away and perishing.
As this process of decay continues without ceasing, I know for certain that this body must eventually come to total extinction.
The Buddha said, "It is so, Great King. Your current age has already reached senility. How does your appearance compare to when you were a youth? "World-Honored One," [the King replied].
In my past childhood, my skin and flesh were moist and lustrous; as I reached adulthood, my blood and qi were full and robust. Now, in this declining age, I am pressed by senility;
my physical form is withered and haggard, my spirit is dark and obscured, my hair is white and my face is wrinkled, and it will not be long before my end.
"How can I see that it has become so full and flourishing? The Buddha said, "Great King, your physical form should not have suddenly decayed.
The King replied, "World-Honored One, change and transformation move secretly; I truly did not perceive it. As the cold and heat shifted and flowed, I gradually reached this state."
Why is this? Although I am twenty years old and thus called young, my countenance is already aged compared to when I was ten.
At thirty, one declines further than at twenty; now that I am sixty-two, looking back at the time I was fifty, I appear as robust and vigorous as ever.
World-Honored One, I observe this subtle shifting: although such decay occurs, the transition between these stages is limited to ten-year intervals.
Years. If I were to reflect further upon this with subtle discernment, would its transformation be merely one or two *jī*?

In truth, it is the transformation of years; yet how could it be only the transformation of years? It is also accompanied by the changes of months. Not only does it change with the months, but it also shifts with each day.

Upon deep reflection and careful observation, one finds that between every *kṣaṇa* and every moment of thought, there is no staying still. Therefore, we know that my body ultimately follows this transformation.
"It ceases. The Buddha said to the Great King, "You see that transformations and changes ceaselessly proceed; you have realized and known this cessation.
At the moment of cessation, do you know that within your body there is something that does not cease? King Prasenajit joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, "I truly do not know.
The Buddha said, "I shall now show you the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. Great King, at what age did you first see the Ganges?"
[He pointed to] water. The King said, "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother took me to visit the deity Jīva.
As we passed by this stream, I immediately recognized it as the waters of the Ganges. The Buddha said, "Great King, as you have said, at twenty one is decrepit compared to ten;
even by sixty, the days, months, years, and seasons shift and change from moment to moment. Thus, what you saw at three..."
"When this river reached the age of thirteen, what was its water like? The King replied, "It was exactly as it was at the age of three, without any difference;
even until now, at the age of sixty-two, there has been no change. The Buddha said, "Now you see for yourself that your hair is white and your face is wrinkled.
Your face must certainly be more wrinkled than it was in your youth. Thus, when you now observe this Ganges River,"
"In the past, when you were a child, did the vision you had of the river change as you grew from childhood to old age? The King replied, "No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face has wrinkled, the essence of this seeing-nature has never wrinkled.

That which wrinkles is subject to change; that which does not wrinkle is not subject to change. That which changes undergoes extinction. That which is unchanging is fundamentally without birth or death. How could it within that [unchanging nature] undergo what you call 'birth'?"
"Even though he has died, he still cites that Makkhali Gosāla and others who claim that after the death of this body there is total extinction.

Upon hearing these words, the King came to know with conviction that after casting off this life one proceeds to another birth; together with the great assembly, he leaped for joy and rejoiced at this unprecedented occurrence.

The commentary states: This passage refutes the nihilistic view of the non-Buddhists. Ānanda wished for the Buddha to point out the nature that is neither arising nor ceasing within his very own present body and mind;
however, this principle is extremely difficult to manifest, and thus he used King Bimbisāra as a pretext to reveal it.
Yet, King Bimbisāra not only failed to understand that what arises and ceases is itself eternal, but moreover clung to the notion of annihilation after death.
If one knows that the source of extinction does not itself extinguish, then one knows that the origin of birth is fundamentally without birth. The meaning of true permanence is thus revealed.
While the nature that does not extinguish is difficult to clarify after death, it can be known by examining it within one's present body and mind.
Therefore, he asked King Nimi: "Is this physical body of yours as eternal and indestructible as a diamond, or is it subject to decay?
This question was intended to lead [the king] toward the realization that it ultimately undergoes transformation and extinction.

If one examines the reality of the physical frame, its actual nature is one of constant flux and change: from birth to childhood, from childhood to youth, and from youth to old age, it gradually [transforms].

Gradually they become different; until one reaches old age and decay, one ultimately returns to death. If one observes their actual state over the course of years and months, they flow and shift without ceasing:
the seasons change as the years pass, and the months change as the days shift.

Examining them closely, it is not merely that time passes, but that every moment (*kṣaṇa*) and every thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) does not abide. All of this constitutes the arising and ceasing of body and mind.
"All things are impermanent. Yet within this very process of arising and ceasing, there exists a true, eternal nature that neither arises nor ceases.
How can this be seen? Therefore, the World-Honored One questioned the nature of the vision used to observe the river to provide verification.
From the age of three until old age, though the physical body has changed, the seeing-nature that perceives the water remains unchanged. This is precisely that which does not change."
This nature is the true nature. This sufficiently proves that it is the changing [aspect] that undergoes extinction;
how then could the unchanging nature undergo your birth and death? Although this body perishes, the true nature eternally persists.
How can you cite the likes of Maskarī Gośālīputra to claim that after death there is total annihilation? This eternally abiding nature is precisely within this very body.
Thus it becomes manifest. Upon hearing these words, the King came to believe that when the body dies, one does not enter into annihilation.
This concludes the refutation of the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists. [△@○] Fourth, showing the nature of perversion.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and knelt on his right knee to address the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, if this seeing and hearing are indeed neither produced nor extinguished, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and engage in inverted actions?"
"I pray that you will arouse compassion and wash away my defilements. At once, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm, pointing downward with his wheel-marked hand, and said to Ānanda:
"Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted? Ānanda replied:
"The sentient beings of the world consider this to be inverted; yet I do not know who is upright and who is inverted. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If..."
The people of the world consider this to be inverted. What, then, do these worldly people take to be upright?
Ānanda said, "If the Tathāgata were to extend his arm—his hand as soft as *tūla* cotton—and point it upward toward the sky, that would be called upright.

The Buddha then extended his arm and told Ānanda, "If this inversion were such that head and tail were swapped, and all the people of the world looked at it with double the intensity, then you would know..."
I shall now clarify this by comparing your body with the pure *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas.
The body of a Tathāgata is called "Right Universal Knowledge" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), whereas your bodies are designated as "inverted in nature.

As you observe carefully, if both your body and the Buddha’s body are termed "inverted," then in what respect is the name itself designated as inverted? At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly stared blankly.
Gazing at the Buddha’s eyes without blinking, they were unaware of where their own bodies,
minds, and delusions lay. [△@○] Fifth, the Buddha,
out of compassion and pity for Ānanda and the great assembly, issued a voice like the tide, proclaiming it throughout the gathering.
"Sons of good family, I have always said that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and the objects of perception, are manifested solely by the mind.
Your bodies and your minds are both things manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence of the wondrous mind."
"How is it that you have lost your original, wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind, and your precious, brilliant, and wondrous nature, such that you recognize delusion within awakening?
Ānanda said: "I have heard the Buddha’s instruction that within the arising and ceasing of the perception of the river, there is that which neither arises nor ceases."
Thus, the seeing that previously perceived the fist is precisely this seeing-nature. One can truly know that the true nature has never been lost.
Why, then, does the World-Honored One grant special permission to King Bimbisāra while saying to us that we have lost our true nature?
Since we are fundamentally not inverted, why do you reproach us for acting with inverted conduct? In truth, Ānanda, you have not yet seen the Real.
By nature, one mistakes the false for the true and fails to recognize where the inversion lies. Therefore, the World-Honored One pointed downward with his hand to demonstrate this.

While his hand was naturally pointing downward, people took it to be inverted; this is just as the body and its environment are fundamentally true and eternal, yet one instead gives rise to aversion and detachment.
This is the inversion of the followers of the Two Vehicles and the externalists. Pointing the arm upward is the inversion.
Yet they return to regarding it as correct. This is to mistakenly reckon that which is subject to arising and ceasing, and is impermanent, as being permanent;

this is the inversion of ordinary beings. However, there is only my single arm; fundamentally, there is neither correctness nor inversion. It is merely because the head and tail have been exchanged that false discrimination arises.
A certain class of people in the world view things in this way, and they are even more like [ordinary] types. Thus says the Tathāgata.
The Dharma-body and your physical bodies are, in truth, one and the same body. To illustrate this through analogy:
the body of the Tathāgata is called "Right Universal Knowledge," whereas your bodies are designated as "inverted nature.

This is because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is tranquil and sovereign, while your bodies are characterized by the false conceptualization of annihilationism and eternalism; it is for this reason that they are termed "inverted. Worldly...
The World-Honored One’s intention was to lead Ānanda to realize the Dharma-body through his very physical body.
Therefore, He asked Ānanda, "Follow your own careful observation: where in your body and the Buddha's body do you find what is called 'inversion'?

Previously, because Ānanda and the great assembly were mired in delusion, they were bewildered and did not know where this inversion lay. The Buddha, arising in compassion, addressed the entire assembly, saying:
I have often said that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors (*caitta*) and all objects of cognition, are manifested solely by the mind.

"Form" refers to the eleven types of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). "Mind" refers to the four aggregates (*skandha*) and the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). "Conditions" refer to the sense objects and sense organs.
"Mental factors" refer to the fifty-one mental concomitants. "All objects of cognition" refers to the entire universe of the physical body, the environment, and the world of vessels.

This is the Dharma. All things are manifested solely by the mind. Observing this, you can sufficiently know that your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously bright, true essence of the wondrous mind.

Why then do you merely recognize the illusory and false body and mind, thereby losing the fundamental, wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind—the precious, brilliant, and wondrous nature—and instead recognize delusion within enlightenment? Because of your original...
There is no delusion. Because you recognize the false and lose the true, this is what is called "delusion within awakening. This is precisely where the inversion lies.
[△@○] Sixth, showing that delusion and awakening share the same source.

Obscuration and darkness constitute emptiness (*ākāśa*). Within this darkened emptiness, the accumulation of darkness forms matter (*rūpa*). Matter mixed with deluded thoughts, and the conceptualization of these thoughts, form the body.
As it gathers conditions within and stirs, it rushes outward in flight; this state of murky agitation is taken as the nature of the mind.

Once deluded, one takes this as the mind and becomes firmly convinced that it resides within the physical body, unaware that it extends beyond the body to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth.

All these are things within the wondrously luminous true mind. It is like discarding the clear, vast ocean of hundreds of thousands of miles and instead recognizing only the substance of a single bubble, calling that the entirety of the tide and exhausting the whole expanse of the sea. You all are people who are doubly deluded.
"Just as my hanging down of the hand is without distinction," the Tathāgata says, "those who [fail to realize this] are to be pitied.

The commentary states: Because it was feared that the teaching that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone would be difficult for those suited to the teaching to awaken to, he traced back the origin of delusion to demonstrate that the source of both delusion and awakening is the same—the principle of Mind-only—in order to shatter their inverted views.

This is the deluded mind and deluded vision. [The Master] feared that [the student] might further calculate that since all dharmas and this body and mind are both manifestations of Mind-only, how then could one become deluded?
Therefore, he traced the origin of delusive error to clarify it. To examine its source:
the One True Dharma-realm, the Tathāgata-garbha, the pure true mind, originally has no body or mind, nor does it have a world.

This is the characteristic of the realms (*dhātu*). It is simply that from within the truly pure realm, a single thought of deluded movement gives rise to the ignorance of non-awakening (*abodha-moha*).
Because this ignorance covers and obscures the true mind, it transforms the vacuous, penetrating, and numinous emptiness into a dull and insentient void;
thus it is said, "Obscuration and gloom become space. Relying upon this inert void, [the subsequent stages arise].
Because ignorance coagulates and transforms into the illusory forms of the four great elements, it is said that "darkness binds and becomes form.
Once the true mind is deluded, its originally inherent wisdom-light is transformed into false perception.

When this false perception confronts those illusory forms, and after they have coexisted for a long time, it grasps a small portion of the four great elements and merges with them through false perception.
Because one takes the body and mind of the five aggregates as oneself, it is said: "Form is mixed with deluded thoughts; the grasping at these marks constitutes the body.

By clinging to this deluded body, one consequently loses the originally inherent true nature. One merely recognizes the gathering of conditions, the internal agitation, and the state of turbid confusion as one's own mind-nature.
This is what is meant by the loss of the true nature of the mind. Once lost in this vast delusion...
By clinging to this deluded mind and relying upon this insignificant, illusory body and mind, you have certainly come to mistake [the mind] for being within the physical body.
You do not realize that this physical body, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, are all things manifested within the wondrously luminous true mind.
It is like abandoning the great ocean to identify with a single bubble; this is already...
You are deluded. Furthermore, to take a single bubble for the entirety of the tide is even more delusion.
Therefore, you all are those who are doubly deluded; this is precisely the state of inverted perception. It is no different from my hanging down my hand.
Thus, the Tathāgata calls you merely "those to be pitied."

From the preceding two types of fundamental [ignorance] onwards, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been refuted and the extinction of the first six consciousnesses explained; thus, the first section on inversion is concluded.

[Section Three: Distinguishing False Views to Refute the Aggregate of Volitional Formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and Clarify that the Seven Consciousnesses Lack Substantiality, divided into two parts.
The first section, "Refuting Delusion," is divided into five parts.
◎ First, the section "Investigating and Refuting the Lack of Substance in Discriminative Delusive Views" is divided into four parts. [□@(?(○/(○*○)))] First, presenting the delusive view.
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, wept and joined his palms, addressing the Buddha:

"Although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha and have awakened to the wondrous, luminous mind—the originally perfect and eternally abiding ground of the heart—I nevertheless perceive the Buddha’s present preaching of the Dharma with my conditioned mind (yuanxin), which I currently rely upon for my veneration. I have merely attained this mind, yet I do not yet dare to recognize it as such."
This is the fundamental source-ground of the mind. I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim the perfect sound to uproot my doubts and lead me back to the Unsurpassed Way.
The commentary states: From here below, the second type of perversion is clarified. Previously, Ānanda identified this momentary, deluded, and inverted mind as his true mind;
now, having received the Buddha’s instruction on the wondrously luminous, vast, and great True Mind, he truly finds it beyond his [prior] comprehension.

Upon hearing this, I was moved to tears of gratitude. Yet, because I have awakened to this wondrous mind as fundamentally perfect through receiving the Buddha’s sublime voice, this awakening has occurred by means of the causal mind triggered by the sound of the Dharma; it is not yet direct realization.
I do not yet dare to claim it as my own original, fundamental ground of mind. Pray, pull out the root of my doubt. The ancients attained thorough conviction in their own minds directly...
Only upon reaching the stage of non-doubt can one achieve true realization. What Ānanda realized was merely the mind that discriminates based on sound;

it is the arising and ceasing of the mind conditioned by sensory objects. Therefore, it belongs to the faculty of the intellect (*manas*). This is what is meant by "recognizing the conditions and losing the truth."
[□@(?(○/(○*○)))] Second, distinguishing that false conditions are unreal. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You all still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind; this Dharma is also a condition and does not constitute the attainment of the Dharma-nature."
It is like a person pointing out the moon with their finger to another. That person, because of the finger, should look at the moon.
If they instead gaze at the finger, taking it to be the substance of the moon, would this person not only lose sight of the lunar disc, but also lose the finger itself?

Why is this? Because they have taken the finger used as a pointer to be the bright moon. Would they not only lose the finger, but also fail to distinguish between light and darkness? How much more so...
For this reason, since the substance of the finger itself cannot be identified as having the dual natures of brightness and darkness that constitute the nature of moonlight, you are likewise so.
If you take the conceptualization of my voice as teaching the Dharma to be your own mind, then this mind should inherently possess a conceptualizing nature even apart from the conceptualized sound.
It would be like a traveler lodging at an inn who stays only briefly before departing; it never...
It is eternally abiding. Yet, among those who manage the pavilion, there is no one who actually departs; thus he is called the "pavilion master.
This case is also like this. [Symbol] (3) It is shown that both the sense organs and consciousness are false.
If it were truly your own mind, it would have nowhere to go. How could it be that, apart from sound, there is a nature free from discrimination (as the preceding six consciousnesses lack substance)?
This is not merely the case for the discriminating mind regarding sound; even when discriminating my own appearance, there is a nature free from discrimination apart from all forms and marks.

(Lower section: Indicating that the eight consciousnesses are not the ultimate reality) Thus it continues until, when all discrimination has ceased, there is neither form nor emptiness; those such as Kuśarī and others mistakenly take this state to be the "Primal Darkness" (Tamas).
[□@(?(○/(○*○)))] Fourth, it is shown that what can be returned is not the true reality.

When one is free from the conditions of all phenomena and possesses a non-conceptual nature, then the various objects to which your mind-nature returns will each have their own place of return; how then can it be considered the master?

The commentary states: This clarifies the second root; thus, by borrowing the "seeing-essence" (*jijing*) to refute that the seven consciousnesses lack substance, it intends to reveal the essence of consciousness (*shijing*) as the substance of *nirvāṇa*.

Since the seven consciousnesses are the roots of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and constitute the nature of discrimination, they merely rely upon the discrimination of the six consciousnesses to manifest their function;
they are collectively comprised within the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses.
That which conditions both the internal and external is also called the "conditioning mind. Now, if it is separated from the external objects, it has no substance;

therefore, [the teaching] refutes [this view] by means of the conditioned objects. The World-Honored One said: "If you listen to the Dharma with a conditioning mind, this Dharma belongs merely to the arising and ceasing of the mind that takes objects as its condition;
it does not attain the essence of the Dharma that transcends words. However, the Dharma I preach is like..."
Pointing at the moon to show it to others, the finger is not the moon. Only by letting go of the finger can one perceive the moon.
If one were to take the finger for the moon, then both the moon and the finger would lose their distinct natures, and the two qualities of light and darkness could no longer be discerned.
If you take the sound of the Dharma as your own mind, this mind ought to have an essence independent of sound, like a traveler staying overnight.
When guests depart from a roadside inn, the innkeeper remains; if this discrimination were your true mind, it should likewise remain constant.
Why then does it lack substance when separated from sound? In this way, not only would this mind lack substance, but so too would everything else.
One then discerns that even apart from all phenomenal forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), the self has no substance.

This collectively reveals that the discriminating mind of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) lacks substance. Since the six consciousnesses possess discrimination only by depending upon this seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*), now that discrimination is shown to be without substance, it is revealed that this [seventh] consciousness is likewise illusory. Not only is discrimination not real, but even if—

Discrimination is entirely non-existent; it is neither form nor emptiness. Because the seven consciousnesses take internal objects and are detached from the external five sense-objects, they are not form.
Because they grasp at the internal as a self, they are not emptiness. This very essence of the eight consciousnesses, being dark and obscure, is still not the true mind.
The Kauśikas and others mistake this for the "Dark Principle" (tamas-tattva); yet even this is not true, let alone those who engage in conceptual discrimination based on external objects.
Those who discriminate based on external objects do so because the seven consciousnesses take the manas as their root and thus possess such discrimination.

If they are separated from external objects and have no external conditions, they then internally take the eight consciousnesses as their own internal self. Therefore, the non-Buddhists reckon this [internal self] to be...
The *puruṣa* (spiritual self). This is established as the primordial principle (*ādi-pradhāna*), which they reckon to be eternal. Based upon this, twenty-five principles arise;
this is the doctrine of the Kauśika heretics. By refuting the seven consciousnesses, it is revealed that the eighth consciousness, which is grasped as the self, is likewise not real.
If one is separated from objective conditions and abides in non-conceptual nature, that is your own mind-nature.
Each has its own point of return; how can one be considered the master? This section concludes the preceding discussion and introduces the subsequent one.
The intent is to establish the Non-returner as the master, thereby revealing the true mind.
◎ Second, borrowing the "seeing-essence" (*jiejing*) to distinguish it from the objects of perception, divided into two parts. [□@(?(○/(○*○)))] First, the request.
Ānanda said, "If my mind-nature has various things to which it returns, then why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, luminous, original mind has nothing to which it returns?
I pray that you will deign to show me compassion and explain this for me."
[□@(?(○/(○*○)))] Next, the response is divided into three parts. [△@○] First, establishing the essence of seeing.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, as for your seeing me—this clarity of the faculty of sight, though it is not the wondrous, supremely clear mind, is like a second moon rather than a reflection of the moon.
You should listen attentively; I shall now show you the ground from which there is nothing to be returned."
[△@○] Second, distinguishing the objects of perception:
Ānanda, this great lecture hall opens wide toward the east. When the sun rises in the sky, there is bright radiance;

at midnight, during the dark fortnight, when clouds and mist obscure the light, it becomes dark and gloomy again. Through the openings of doors and windows, one perceives penetration; yet through walls and buildings...
In the intervals between them, one again perceives obstructions; in the places of differentiation, one again sees conditions. Within the stubborn void, there is everywhere the nature of emptiness;
when the appearance of dense clouds arises, turbid dust swirls about. When the sky clears and the mists subside, one again perceives purity. Ānanda!
"You all observe these various manifested forms. I shall now each return them to their original causes. What are these original causes? Ānanda, these various manifestations:
clarity returns to the sun; why is this? Without the sun there would be no clarity, and since clarity is dependent upon the sun, it returns to the sun.
Darkness returns to the dark moon; penetration returns to doors and windows; obstruction returns to walls and buildings; and conditions return to the divisions [of space]."

They are distinct. When the stubborn void returns to emptiness, when the dense clouds return to dust, and when the clear brightness returns to a cloudless sky, then all that exists within the world does not transcend these categories.
As for the eight kinds of seeing you perceive—the luminous nature of your faculty of vision—toward what would you wish to return it? Why is this so?

If one returns to the state of light, then when it is not light, one no longer perceives darkness. Although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, the seeing itself is seen to be without distinction.
[△@○] Third, the demonstration of the nature of seeing.

All things that can be returned are naturally not you; as for that which cannot be returned by you, if it is not you, who else could it be? Thus you know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure.
Yet, through your own confusion and delusion, you have lost your fundamental nature and undergone the cycle of rebirth, constantly drifting and drowning within birth and death.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called "the one who is to be pitied.
The commentary states: Ānanda, hearing it said that he could return, realized he was not the master; thus, he requested the true mind that does not return.
Because the true mind is difficult to clarify, I shall temporarily borrow the "essence of seeing" to dispel this confusion.

Since "seeing" is mixed among the various conditioned objects (*ālambana*), whereas the essence of the eight consciousnesses is a brilliant clarity that does not belong to these conditioned objects, it is called the "bright source of the essence of seeing."

Although this is not the ultimate reality, because it originally depends on the transformation of True Suchness (tathatā) and is already closely proximate to the Real, it is like a second moon that does not depart from the substance of the moon;
it is not a reflection in water. If one awakens to this seeing-essence so that it does not revert [to the objects], then one can realize the True Mind.
As stated previously, because one recognizes conditions and loses the Reality, the selection was made in terms of conditioned objects.
This demonstrates the stage of Non-returning. If all conditions are purified and exhausted, the true nature will manifest of itself.
Furthermore, that which you perceive as objects does not exceed eight conditions: light and darkness, openness and obstruction, emptiness and dust, and clear skies.

Now, each of these eight conditions has something to which it returns; but as for the luminous essence of your seeing-nature within these eight kinds of objects—to whom or what would it return? All...
It is evident that those who can return are not your true mind. As for those who do not return, could they be anything other than your true nature?
Thus, this true nature resides within you, inherently wondrous and luminous. Yet, now you are deluded and distressed, failing to awaken;
you have lost what was originally possessed and undergo birth and death. For this reason, the Tathāgata says you are to be pitied.

This is all there is to it. ◎ Third, demonstrating that the nature of seeing is independent of conditions in order to reveal the essence of seeing, which is divided into four parts. [□@(?(○/(○*○)))] First, the request not to return.
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no place to return, how can I know that it is my true nature?
The commentary states: Ānanda’s intention was that he already knew this nature which does not return;
however, he did not know how this nature could be his own true nature. This was not a presentation of realization, but rather a statement of his lack of realization.
It is the mind. For although this seeing has been refuted, it is the refined radiance of these eight consciousnesses that responds to the five sense organs to discern objects;
therefore, for the time being, we borrow the essence of seeing as the subject. We first eliminate external conditions and objects to refute it.
Once the objects vanish, this seeing will also subside. Thus, we first establish the measure of seeing, eliminate the conditioned objects, and only then proceed with the refutation.
[□@(?(○/(○*○)))] Second, the determination through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"I now ask you: although you have not yet attained the untainted purity (*anāsrava-viśuddhi*), by relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power (*buddhānubhāva*), you see the first dhyāna without obstruction. Yet, Anuruddha sees Jambudvīpa as if looking at the palm of his hand."
The *āmalaka* fruit [is seen by those with ordinary vision]. The various bodhisattvas see hundreds of thousands of worlds.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions behold all pure lands as numerous as atoms, leaving nothing unseen. As for sentient beings, their clear vision does not extend beyond a mere inch.

[□@(?(○/(○*○)))] Third, examining the objects of perception: Ānanda, let us observe together the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings dwell. Surveying thoroughly all that moves upon water, on land, and through the air, we see various forms, whether obscured or luminous;
yet none of them are anything other than the obstructions left behind by the discrimination of external objects. You should...
In this state, you distinguish between self and other; now I shall lead you to discern within your vision: what is the essence of the self, and what are external objects?
Ānanda, exhaust the source of your vision. From the palaces of the sun and moon—these are objects and not you—to the Seven Golden Mountains, observe them thoroughly all around.
Though they possess various kinds of light, these too are objects and not you. Gradually, observe further the rising clouds and the flying birds.
When the wind moves and dust rises, the trees, mountains, rivers, grasses, shrubs, humans, and livestock—all these things are not you.
[This concludes the third illustration. Fourth, the demonstration of the essence of seeing.
Ānanda, although these various phenomena, whether near or far, differ in their natures, they are all equally beheld by your faculty of vision, which is pure and clear.

Thus, while the various categories of objects possess their own distinctions, the nature of seeing is without difference. This subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence is truly your own nature of seeing.

The commentary says: This precisely demonstrates the fundamental essence of the clarity of seeing. Since "seeing" is the refined radiance of the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), which perceives objects by reflecting upon the five sensory realms, it is called "the seeing that conditions the dust.
If one refers to the very first moment of illuminating an object, it is termed "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*);
this properly belongs to the essence of the eighth consciousness's refined clarity. However, if a second thought arises to engage in conceptual discrimination, then—

This is called *anumāna* (inference), which belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The previous section refuted it by means of the "eight returns," thereby destroying the views that differentiate based on objective conditions;
these still belong to inference. Now, by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the essence of seeing is revealed; therefore, the commentary states: "Refuting by means of direct measurement.
Furthermore, although Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, Buddhas, and sentient beings are each distinct as holy or ordinary, yet...
The function of illuminating objects varies in its breadth and narrowness, yet all are what is beheld by the seeing-essence of the eighth consciousness through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Although heaven, earth, empty space, and the myriad things are presented in a complex array, a single vision illuminates them all at once; thus one knows that while the objects differ, the vision does not.
This non-differentiating vision, which is not mixed with objects, is this subtle, wondrous, and luminous essence—truly your own vision.
This is the nature (*prakṛti*). If one knows this nature, one may transcend and awaken to the true nature.
◎ Fourth, the refutation of the further calculation that the essence of vision is a material object, divided into two parts. [□@(?(○/(○*○)))] First, the refutation of the further calculation.
If you see this object, then you can also see my seeing. If you see it as I do, that is called "seeing me.
When I am not seeing, why do you not see the place where I am not seeing? If you see that non-seeing, then it is naturally not the characteristic of that non-seeing.
If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, then it is naturally not a material thing. How could it not be yours?
Furthermore, at the very moment you see an object, if you have seen the object and the object has also seen you, their essential natures would become confused and intermingled;
consequently, you, I, and all the world would fail to be established as distinct entities.
[□@(?(○/(○*○)))] Second, demonstrating the true vision: "Ānanda, when you see, it is you who see and not I.
Since the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, if it is not you, then who is?
Why do you doubt your own true nature, claiming that your nature is not real and seeking reality from me?"
The commentary says: This refutes a shifting argument. Previously, he pointed to the myriad things to demonstrate the essence of seeing;
this was done because he feared that Ānanda might mistake the seeing for an object. Therefore, he specifically showed him, saying:

"The myriad things are the objects of what is seen, but the essence of seeing that perceives those things—how could that be an object? If seeing were itself an object, then the seeing of you and me...

All these are objects. Yet you can also see my seeing. If you mistakenly insist that seeing the same object as I do constitutes seeing my seeing, then when I am separated from the object, why do you not see the place where I do not see?
Even if you were to grant that you could see the place where I do not see, this would merely be...
Your deluded vision is naturally not that state of non-seeing; the character "that" (*bi*) refers back to the Buddha himself—view it as the word "I.
If you do not see me, the ground of my non-seeing, you will know for certain that both your vision and my vision are not material objects.
Is this very vision, which is detached from objects, not your own seeing-nature? If you must insist...
If seeing this object meant that all objects possessed seeing, then self and other would see one another, and the distinction between person and thing would not be established.
This seeing that is apart from objects reunites with the aspect of seeing and returns to the essence of consciousness.
By knowing this, one may gradually perceive the true nature. Therefore, it is specifically pointed out that when you see an object, it is your own—
That which you see yet do not include within yourself—that which you perceive as the object, perfect and all-pervading—is it not your own true nature?
Who else could it be? Furthermore, your seeing-nature is perfectly clear and lucid; why do you harbor doubts about it instead of awakening to it?
This nature is inherently possessed by you, yet you do not regard it as real, instead taking my words as the standard.
To claim this is "real" would it not be an error?
◎ Part Five: Correctly Refuting the Valid Cognition of Views (*dṛṣṭipramāṇa*) to Reveal the True Mind. This section is divided into two parts. [□] First, establishing the formal argument (*prayoga*).

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing is necessarily mine and not that of others, then when I and the Tathāgata were observing the magnificent treasure-palace of the Four Heavenly Kings and residing in the palaces of the sun and moon, this seeing was all-encompassing, pervading the Sahā world.
Yet, upon returning to the Jetavana Vihāra, I saw only the monastery; entering the hall of the purified mind, I beheld only the corridors. World-Honored One, this seeing is like..."
"It is so. Its substance is originally all-pervasive throughout the entire realm; yet now, being within this room, it fills only the room.
Does this vision contract from great to small, or is it that the walls and roof have constricted it and severed it? I do not know where the truth of this matter lies.
I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and explain it for me."

[□@(?(○/(○*○)))] Next is the formal refutation. The Buddha told Ānanda: "All worldly activities, whether great or small, internal or external, each belong to their respective objective fields (*viṣaya*)."
One should not say that there is expansion and contraction to be seen. It is like seeing the space within a square vessel as being square. I ask you again:
Is this square space seen within the square vessel definitely square, or is it not definitely square?

If it were definitely square, then when a round vessel is placed elsewhere, its space should not be round. If it were not definitely square, then there should be no square space within the square vessel.
You say that you do not know where this principle resides. Since the nature of the principle is such as this, how could it have a location?
Ānanda, if one wishes to cause [the space] to enter [a vessel] without its being square or round, one need only remove the squareness of the vessel; the substance of space itself has no directions.

One should not say that there is a further location for the directional characteristics of the void to be removed. If it were as you ask—when entering a room, the vision contracts and becomes small, and when looking up at the sky...

If you say that at times you can pull back your vision so that it is level with the surface of the sun, yet when building walls or houses your vision is cut off by them, and even when you pierce small holes, why is there no trace of continuity? This argument is not tenable.
Second, revealing the truth:
All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded regarding themselves as external objects; they have lost their original mind and have been turned about by those objects.
Therefore, within this state, one contemplates the great through the small. If one can master all things, then one is identical to the Tathāgata.
With body and mind perfectly luminous and unmoving at the site of enlightenment, one is able to universally contain the lands of the ten directions within the tip of a single hair.
The commentary states: This precisely refutes the "measuring consciousness" (*dṛṣṭi-pramāṇa*). Through delusion regarding the true mind, the *ālayavijñāna* is formed.

This consciousness possesses three divisions: first, the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*); second, the seeing division (*darśanabhāga*); and third, the perceived division (*nimittabhāga*).
Because the power of ignorance has coagulated for a long time, it eventually solidifies into a stubbornly insentient void, thereby forming the illusion of the four great elements.

Form exists because of this, giving rise to deluded views. By grasping the four great elements, one becomes a sentient being; thus, the physical body, the vessel-world, and all myriad phenomena arise from this.
Now, in order to shatter delusion and reveal the True, we first eliminate the "object-aspect" (nimitta-bhāga) of what is perceived.
This is done provisionally to demonstrate that the nature of seeing is independent of conditions; once the engagement with sense-objects has ceased, the capacity to see [the nature] is revealed.
It is also extinguished. This is what is meant by "converging deluded vision to return to the essence of seeing.

Now that the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) has been extinguished and the essence of seeing alone remains, because the eight consciousnesses have not yet been shattered, this consciousness—though its direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) can fully manifest the sense organs, the body, and the physical world—still retains limitations.
It cannot yet universally illumine the Dharma-realm; therefore, there still exist distinctions of internal and external, large and small.

This separation is a view that suspects a partition or interruption. If this measure of the faculty is once shattered, then both the sense organ and its object vanish, and the perfect clarity shines universally throughout the ten directions.
Ānanda’s intent in his question can be understood from the scriptural text. However, the doctrine of shattering the measure of the seeing-faculty has not been articulated previously.
If it were not so, how could the mere shattering of this single seeing enable [the realization of] a single hair?
"Does it encompass the lands of the ten directions? The World-Honored One’s response, intended to dismantle [the notion of the world] by means of the vessel, is as follows:
This perfectly luminous and wondrous mind is currently within delusion, constrained and obstructed by the sense organs, the physical body, and the vessel-world.
If one can internally detach from the body and mind and externally relinquish the world, then this perfectly luminous and wondrous essence will manifest immediately before one. Therefore, remove...

A vessel is square, yet the essence of emptiness is fundamentally neither square nor round. Not eliminating the square characteristics of empty space is what the ancients meant by "not seeking truth through effort, but only requiring the cessation of views.
If the measure of seeing (*dṛṣṭi-pramāṇa*) is entirely extinguished, then the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) suddenly vanishes.
This is what is meant by "if one can master objects, one is identical to the Tathāgata," with body and mind perfectly luminous and unmoving.
The site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is that which can universally contain the lands of the ten directions within a single hair-tip.

Originally, because one was deluded regarding the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the one mind, it transformed into delusive appearances. Now, by transforming these delusive appearances back into the one mind, one becomes identical to the Tathāgata.
Only through such profound contemplation does one perceive the subtlety of the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma; for [the path] proceeds from awakening to delusion, and from...
From the subtle to the coarse, phenomena naturally possess the characteristics of three subtleties and six coarsenesses.
Now, to shatter the false and reveal the true, one must proceed from the coarse to the subtle, gradually reaching the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is clearly stated in the treatise.
When the treatise is compared with the sūtra, there is not even the discrepancy of a single hair; it is no mere fallacious discourse. I ask that the wise contemplate this deeply.

Since Ānanda previously received the Buddha’s compassionate salvation, he has refuted false views by breaking down the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) and extinguishing the functioning of the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*), thereby revealing the truth of the partial seeing; thus ends the second section on inversion.
[□@○] Part Four: The Path of Correct Practice for Destroying the Aggregate of Consciousness and Extirpating the Eighth Consciousness by Refuting the Essence of Views.
This section is divided into three parts. [?︽] First, destroying the grasping at a self to reveal the One True Reality, which is further divided into three.
① First, the interlocutor presents his calculation.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if this essence of vision is necessarily my wondrous nature, then this wondrous nature is now present before me.
(He calculates that form itself is the self. If seeing is necessarily my true self, then what are my current body and mind? (He calculates that it must be apart from form.)"

I now perceive that my body and mind are distinct and real. Yet, in that vision, there is no differentiation; I conceive of my own body as having both large and small forms, with the "I" residing within them.

If it were truly my mind that enables me to see, and if the nature of seeing were truly the self while the body were not the self, how would this differ from what the Tathāgata previously refuted—the notion that an object can see the self, or that the material form is large while the self is small and resides within the form? I pray that you will bestow great compassion and explain this.

Fawei remarked: "The following section refutes the self-attesting portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses. It implicitly refutes the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) to reveal the single reality (*eka-tattva*).

It is the true self of nirvāṇa. Because non-Buddhists cling to this as a *puruṣa* (ātman), they claim that the self pervades the ten directions and so forth.
Therefore it is said: "The ādāna-vijñāna is profound and subtle; the habitual tendencies and seeds form a torrential stream.
I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, fearing that they would conceptually grasp it as a self. Regarding this consciousness, the World-Honored One has never treated it lightly.

This is the reason for what was discussed. Upon hearing the Buddha’s instruction that if one can transform objects, one is identical to the Tathāgata, Ānanda subsequently gave rise to the doubt that grasping at objects constitutes the view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*).
