Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, although the World-Honored One has for our sakes expounded upon the characteristics of both causal conditions and spontaneity—both those that are harmonious and those that are not—my mind has still not yet attained clarity. Now, however, I have again heard and seen..."

Seeing what is not seeing, our confusion and distress increase all the more. We humbly pray that your vast compassion will bestow upon us the eye of great wisdom, revealing to us the clarity and purity of the awakened mind.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with tears of sorrow and received the holy instructions.

The commentary states: Now, at the beginning of the refutation of the attachment to dharmas, Ānanda had merely heard the preceding discussion on causes and conditions being either spontaneous (*svabhāva*) or conditioned;
yet he still did not understand their conjunction and non-conjunction, which is why it is said that "his mind was as yet not opened.

This is because the previous teaching—that the five aggregates do not belong to either causes and conditions or spontaneity—merely refuted conventional designations while actual dharmas (*dharmatā*) still remained; thus, he had not yet reached the fundamental [reality].
Because [the mind] is empty, the heart has not yet opened. Now, hearing that even the view of the five aggregates is not a view, one’s confusion and distress increase all the more;

this is precisely because, although the self-attachment (*ātma-grāha*) of the two vehicles is empty, their attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) has not yet been forgotten, and they still falsely perceive the existence of body, mind, and the world.
Therefore, the awakened mind is not yet pure, which is why he requests further instruction.
The response below generally reveals that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are unreal, thereby illustrating that the world is fundamentally empty.
This section on the World-Honored One’s permission to speak is divided into two parts: first, the permission to speak and the exhortation to listen.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly, and wishing to expound upon the path of sublime practice consisting of the various samādhis of the Great Dhāraṇī, addressed Ānanda, saying: "Although you possess a powerful memory, this merely increases your learning."
Regarding śamatha, your subtle and secret contemplation has not yet reached full realization. Listen attentively now;
I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so that all future beings subject to outflows may likewise attain the fruit of Bodhi.
[?︽] Second, the correct demonstration of the two types of delusion is divided into two parts. ◎ First, the general demonstration:
Ānanda, all sentient beings revolve in the world due to the false perception of inverted discrimination;
it arises from its own locus and revolves according to its own karma. What are these two perceptions? The first is the false perception of the individual karma of sentient beings. The second is...
Sentient beings share this same deluded vision.
◎ Second, the detailed exposition of the individual [karmas] is divided into three parts. [□@(?(○/(○*○)))] First, the deluded vision of individual karma.
What is meant by "delusive vision caused by individual karma"? Ānanda, it is like a person in the world whose eyes have a cataract of redness.
At night, they see a circular shadow with five overlapping colors appearing beside the light of a lamp. What do you think?

Is this circular light manifested by the lamp at night the color of the lamp, or is it the color of the vision? Ānanda, if this were the color of the lamp, then it would not be seen by one who has the cataract.
Why is it that, while the views differ, this circular shadow is seen only by those with cataracts?
If it were the seeing of color, then once the seeing has become color, what would you call that person with cataracts who sees the circular shadow?

Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular shadow existed separately from the lamp, then when one looks sideways at a screen, a curtain, or a table, a circular shadow should likewise appear; yet it exists separately from the seeing.
It should not be within the range of visual sight. How then can a person with cataracts see a circular shadow? Therefore, one should know that the color actually resides in the lamp;

it is the defect of vision that perceives it as a shadow. Both the shadow and the perception of it are defects of vision. While perceiving the defect is itself a disorder, the perception of that disorder is not a disorder. Ultimately, one should never say that this is the lamp or that this is the vision.
Within this, there is that which is neither lamp nor vision, just as a second moon is neither a substantial entity nor a reflection. Why is this?

Because the perception of a second moon is produced by pressing [the eye]. A person of wisdom should not say that the source of this pressing of the organ is either a shape or no shape, or something apart from vision or non-vision;
this [second moon] is likewise produced by an ocular ailment (*taimirika*). Now, whom do you wish to name as its [true] subject?
The lamp is seeing; how much more so the conceptualization of that which is neither lamp nor seeing?
[This concludes] the second section on the deluded vision of the homogeneous class (sabhāga).
What is meant by "common delusive vision"? Ānanda, in this Jambudvīpa, excluding the great oceans, there are three thousand islands amidst the level lands.
In the central great island, encompassing the large nations from east to west, there are two thousand three hundred;
as for the other small islands within the various seas, among them there may be two or three hundred nations, or perhaps only one.

Or two, up to three, four, five, or ten. Ānanda, if within this there is a small continent containing only two kingdoms, and the people of that single kingdom collectively experience adverse conditions, then the sentient beings of that land on that small continent will behold all manner of inauspicious omens;
they may see two suns, or they may see two moons, and so forth, even unto...
Halos, sunspots, pearls, jade pendants, comets, meteors, flying stars, "burdened ears," rainbows, and halos—various such evil omens are seen only in this country;
the sentient beings of that country have neither seen nor heard of them.
[□@(?(○/(○*○)))] Third, the combined clarification of advancing and retreating is divided into three parts. [△@○] First, the specific examples of advancing are the same as before.
Ānanda, I shall now clarify these two matters for you by examining them from both their progressive and regressive aspects.

Ānanda, it is like those sentient beings who, due to the deluded vision of their individual karma, perceive a circular shadow appearing within a lamp’s light. Although it appears to be an external object, it is ultimately produced by the visual impairment of the observer.
This impairment is simply the fatigue of seeing and is not created by the color itself. Yet, one who perceives this impairment never incurs the fault of seeing.
For example, today as you observe with your eyes the mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings, these are all produced by the disease of vision that has existed since beginningless time.
The vision and its conditions appear as present objects; fundamentally, they are the optical aberrations of my enlightened awareness as it perceives its objects.

To perceive [the cataract] is itself the disease; the originally enlightened, luminous mind perceiving its conditions is not the disease. The perception of that which is perceived is the disease, but the perceiver is not within the disease.
This is truly the seeing of seeing. Why, then, would you further call it "awakening," "hearing," "knowing," or "seeing"? Therefore, you now see me and yourself.
Together with all the ten classes of sentient beings in the world, they all see the optical aberration, yet they are not those who see the aberration.
Because that which sees the true essence of nature is not itself an aberration, it is not called "seeing."
[△@○] Second, the analogy between collective and individual cases of regression.
Ānanda, just as those sentient beings share a commonality in their deluded vision, so too is the case of that single person with a distinct karmic destiny who possesses a deluded vision.
[△@○] Third, advancing and retreating to clarify the point together:
First, the person with diseased eyes perceives the same circular shadow as that one man in the country; this is produced by the delusion of a visual ailment (*taimira*).

What these members of the same class of beings perceive as an inauspicious sign arises from the miasma of evil karma shared among those who see alike. Both are produced by beginningless delusions of vision.
For example, within the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa, including the four great oceans, as well as the Sahā world and all impure realms throughout the ten directions,
along with all sentient beings therein— these are all, by nature, the pure, untainted, wondrous mind of enlightened awareness. Yet,
through the conditions of false sicknesses involving seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they falsely give rise to union and falsely undergo death through union.

The preceding section concludes the manifestation of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā). Third, it manifests that fundamental awakening (mūlajñāna) is free from conditions in order to demonstrate that suchness (tathatā) emerges from its entanglements.
If one can remain far removed from all conditions of conjunction as well as non-conjunction, then one will further extinguish and eliminate all causes of birth and death.
The nature of perfect enlightenment is neither arising nor ceasing; the pure fundamental mind is the eternally abiding original awakening.
The commentary states: This uses the five aggregates as an analogy to deconstruct the world, thereby breaking through attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

Regarding the statement that one is about to break through attachment to phenomena and will "expound the great *dhāraṇī*s, various *samādhi*s, and the sublime paths of practice": [this refers to] the *dhāraṇī*...

*Ni* (尼) here means "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*). Previously, when it was exhorted that one must not grow weary on the wondrous path to Bodhi, this merely demonstrated the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) without yet revealing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); thus, it still belonged to what is termed "mere emptiness.

Because attachment to phenomena had not yet been relinquished, [the teaching] now intends to demonstrate the essence of the perfectly interfused contemplation of emptiness, wherein taking up one is immediately three, and speaking of three is immediately one; hence it says "all... [諸].
Samādhi. Now, with the single attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha) shattered, the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha is suddenly revealed as emptiness.
Furthermore, this empty treasury is the essence of perfect interfusion; it universally encompasses all existence and harmoniously returns to the one mind.
Therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Universal Retention (dhāraṇī). This is why it serves as the wondrous path of cultivation for all samādhis. Its meaning reveals that true emptiness is...

The emptiness of the provisional is not merely emptiness. Therefore, the Buddha rebuked Ānanda for his strong memory and extensive learning, noting that regarding *śamatha* and subtle, secret contemplation, his mind had not yet opened.

This specifically points to his failure to realize the principle that [all things] are neither caused nor spontaneous, and his failure to reach the realization of the emptiness of the provisional. Thus, he now provides a further explanation. However, as for attachment to dharmas...
In essence, these are merely two kinds of substantial dharmas: the internal five aggregates of body and mind, and the external mountains, rivers, great earth, and the world of empty space.
As previously stated: "Your body and mind, extending outward to empty space, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are objects manifested within the wondrously bright, true, and subtle mind.
This is like discarding the hundreds of thousands of great oceans and instead recognizing...

To regard a single bubble as the entirety of the tide is a perversion. Now, in order to shatter these two delusions, I first inform Ānanda that all sentient beings transmigrate through the world due to the false discrimination arising from two perversions of vision.
Furthermore, these two delusions arise from within the single realm of True Suchness at that very place. Since these delusory afflictions have arisen, there must necessarily be delusory karma;
that is to say, movement immediately entails suffering, and thus one undergoes the circulation of karmic retribution. What are the two views?
The first is the delusive vision of individual karma; the second is the delusive vision of shared karma.
Individual karma refers to the bodies and minds of sentient beings as their primary retribution—the five aggregates of each person—which are evoked by the individual karma of each.
Shared karma refers to the world as the secondary retribution of sentient beings, which is evoked by the collective karma of all. These two delusions are the fundamental basis.
That they do not exist inherently is truly because a single thought of deluded movement within the true, pure, and wondrously luminous mind gives rise to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Consequently, the true mind transforms into the *ālaya-vijñāna*, whereby the two divisions of subject (*darśana-bhāga*) and object (*nimitta-bhāga*) come into being. The subject is the deluded mind;
the object is the deluded realm. Through the opposition of mind and realm, one gives rise to delusions and creates karma, revolving through birth and death; thus, these two are indeed real.
This is the fault of delusion. What is called the seer and the objects of seeing, along with the characteristics of what is conceived, are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.
Thus, the true mind is like healthy eyes; the deluded mind is like an eye ailment (cataract); the five aggregates and the body-mind are like the circular shadow on a lamp;
the four elements, mountains, and rivers are like the frantic flowers in the sky. If one understands this eye ailment...
Thus, the two delusions are fundamentally empty. Therefore, he uses the example of an eye affliction to refute them. What is meant by "delusive vision as distinct karma"?
"Distinct karma" refers to the body and mind—the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)—which constitute the primary retribution of individual sentient beings.

This is intended to reveal that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty and exist only based on the delusion of seeing. Thus, it is likened to having a red film over the eye and seeing a lamp at night.

The five-colored light and the circular shadow, along with the fine eye and the lamp’s radiance, collectively metaphorize the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). The eye ailment (*taimirya*) metaphorizes deluded vision; the shadow metaphorizes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Therefore, one distinguishes between them by identifying them as being both identical to and separate from the lamp. Since they fundamentally do not exist, how can they be discussed in terms of "is" or "is not"?
The fact that the color actually resides in the lamp metaphorizes that delusion does not depart from the true. That the visual affliction constitutes the shadow metaphorizes the causal condition.
Delusion constitutes the false; the metaphor of "seeing shadows" together with the eye disease illustrates that both mind and objects are deluded.

Because awakening brings the cessation of delusion, one realizes that seeing the eye disease was not an illness. Furthermore, it is like the second moon: one clearly knows there is no characteristic of right or wrong.
If you know that the second moon is produced by the distortion of the eyes, then you will know that the seeing of the shadow is the fault of a cataract in the eye.
Why, then, would you give rise to the deluded calculation of right and wrong regarding the lamp? By understanding this, one knows that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally empty;
thus, the doubts concerning causes and conditions versus spontaneity can be resolved. What is meant by "commonality of perception" (*sabhāgatā-viparyaya-darśana*)? Commonality...
This refers to the world as the common environment experienced by sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

To demonstrate that this world does not have an original basis but is produced from the delusions of one's own perceptions, [the text] clarifies this through the diverse calamities and blessings occurring across the many large and small nations of Jambudvīpa in the south.
However, when the people of a single nation collectively experience adverse conditions, they will all perceive them together.

Xiang: That those who are without evil have never seen or heard of such things shows that the sentient beings of the defiled land are moved by their own evil karma, whereas the people of the Pure Land fundamentally do not see or hear it. As it is said:
"When the great fires burn, my land remains peaceful and secure," because they fundamentally do not perceive any filth or evil. I now advance these two points.

This concludes the combined explanation through progression and regression. That is to say, one progresses by using individual karma as an analogy for the common lot (*sabhāgatā*), and regresses by using the common lot as an analogy for individual karma.

This is because the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are fundamentally empty and thus easy to realize, whereas the non-existence of the world is difficult to clarify. Therefore, these two matters are combined through progression and regression to illuminate the truth.
Thus, the illusory perception of the five aggregates—the body and mind—of those sentient beings due to their individual karma is like seeing a lamp.
The circular shadow manifested by the light: although this shadow appears to exist, it is ultimately produced by a cataract in the eye and does not inherently belong to the lamp.
If one knows it is a cataract, then the disease of seeing ceases.
By this analogy, you should understand that your perception of mountains, rivers, the lands, and all sentient beings is entirely produced by the disease of seeing caused by beginningless ignorance.

Hear me. That which is seen and the conditions for seeing appear as if they were present objects before one, yet fundamentally they do not truly exist. They are originally the ignorance within my own enlightened awareness;
thus, it is merely a cataract of false seeing that perceives the existence of objects. Consequently, both the faculty of cognition and the act of seeing are themselves the cataract.
Only the fundamentally enlightened, luminous mind that clearly perceives all conditions is not the cataract. However, when one awakens to this...
That which is perceived is the eye-disease; this is true awakening (*tathatā-jñāna*). How could true awakening fall into the midst of deluded perception?

Therefore it is said: "Awakening is not within the eye-disease. This is truly the seeing of seeing. Because Ānanda had previously said, "Now that I hear of the seeing of seeing, my confusion increases all the more," the Buddha used the phrase "awakening perceives the eye-disease of what is perceived" and "awakening is not within the eye-disease" to explain the seeing of seeing.
This is a doubt. To establish this through proof: the vision above is true awakening; the vision below is a cataract of the eye.

A cataract is a deluded vision, which specifically refers to the consciousness-essence of ignorance (*avidyā-vijñāna-dhātu*). This is the Tathāgata’s own explanation; the clear text is manifest, so there is no need for alternative interpretations.
Furthermore, the consciousness-essence is the essence of seeing; even when viewed with true wisdom, it is still but a cataract.
Delusion! How could awakening, hearing, knowing, and seeing ever reach it? This is what is meant by "even seeing is already detached from seeing;
seeing cannot reach it. You should know that within the single true realm, both Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent.
That you now perceive there to be Buddhas and sentient beings is entirely the cataract of deluded vision; it is not the vision of the cataract itself. That wondrous vision is the truth.
The fact that the essential nature of the faculty is not a cataract means that because it is far removed from all delusions, it is simply not called "seeing.
By advancing this specific karmic activity (*bhinnakarma*) as an analogy for the shared portion (*sabhāgatā*), and observing them together, one can know that the world is fundamentally empty.

Therefore, by again withdrawing the analogy of the shared portion to illustrate specific karma—that is, by taking the deluded seeing of the shared portion of these sentient beings as an illustration of that specific karma—one understands its nature.
One sees a person with a diseased eye whose vision of circular shadows is produced by the delusion of the cataract;
this serves as an analogy for the inauspicious sights seen throughout that entire land, which likewise arise from evil karma.
Furthermore, this realm is entirely born of beginningless false perceptions. Taking this one land as an example, it applies to Jambudvīpa and all beyond.
All the realms of outflows and all sentient beings throughout the ten directions are, in essence, this enlightened, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
It is only because of ignorance that they are deluded regarding this untainted, wondrous mind, falsely giving rise to the sickness of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Through the conjunction of the false faculties, objects, and conditions, they undergo false birth and false death. Viewed from this perspective, [it is clear that...]
If one acts thus, the five aggregates, the body and mind, as well as external space, mountains, rivers, and the great earth, will instantly vanish and leave nothing to rely upon.
Therefore, know that this serves as an analogy for destroying the two kinds of worlds to reveal the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*).

Once these two attachments are destroyed, initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) becomes effective and fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is revealed. In summary, fundamental awakening is shown to be free from conditions to demonstrate the Truth.

It is like emerging from bondage; therefore it is said: "If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction and non-conjunction, then one further eliminates the causes of birth and death, perfects the nature of bodhi which is neither arising nor ceasing, and the pure fundamental mind—the original enlightenment—will abide eternally.
From the previous inquiry into the mind and the examination of vision, he has extensively revealed the teachings to shatter delusion and manifest the truth.
True. At this point, once these two attachments have been refuted, the original awakened true mind (*mūla-bodhi-citta*) is revealed.
However, this still involves refuting the synthetic consciousness (*saṃvṛti-vijñāna*) to reveal the original awakening; it does not yet reach the source of the one mind.
Below, the conceptualization of the synthesis of the beginning and the origin is further refuted, only then returning to the nature of the treasury (*tathatā-garbha*).
The preceding section has concluded by revealing that original enlightenment is free from conditions, thereby demonstrating that True Suchness transcends entanglement.
[△@△] Fourth, the elimination of traces to enter the profound, demonstrating that True Suchness is beyond all relativity, divided into two parts.
[□@○] First, the World-Honored One specifically instructed:
"Ānanda, although you have previously realized that the wondrously luminous nature of original enlightenment is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously,
you have not yet clarified that this source of awakening is neither born from conjunction nor from non-conjunction."
[□@○] Second, the twofold refutation of false conceptualization is divided into two parts.
[?︽] First, the refutation of conjunction. Ānanda, I shall now again question you regarding external objects.

You still harbor doubts based on the nature of all worldly false conceptualizations and the conjunction of various causes and conditions, thinking that the mind of Bodhi arises through conjunction. Thus, your...
Now, does this wondrous, pure essence of seeing blend with light? Does it blend with darkness? Does it blend with openness? Or does it blend with obstruction?
If it blends with light, then when you observe light as it appears before you, where does it mingle with seeing?

Can the characteristics of seeing be distinguished from it, and what form would that mixture take? If it were not seeing itself, how could it see the light? If it were identical to seeing, how could it...?

Regarding the seeing of seeing: if the seeing were necessarily complete, with what would the clarity harmonize? If the clarity were complete, it could not harmonize with the seeing. The seeing must then be distinct from the clarity.
If they were mixed, the names "nature" and "clarity" of that [seeing] would be lost. To lose the nature and clarity is contrary to the meaning.
It is the same for darkness, openness, and all various obstructions. Furthermore, Ānanda, as for your current state of wondrous purity...
Does this seeing-essence unite with light? Does it unite with darkness? Does it unite with openness? Or does it unite with obstruction?
If it unites with light, then when darkness arrives and the characteristic of light has already ceased, this seeing would not be united with the various forms of darkness;
how then could it see darkness? If, when seeing darkness, it is not united with darkness but is instead united with light, then it should not be seeing the light. Since this is not the case...
Seeing light, one understands that light is conjoined with clarity and is not darkness. It is the same for darkness, penetration, and all various obstructions.
[This constitutes] the second: the non-conjunction of breaking.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, as I contemplate it, is this wondrous source of awakening not in a state of non-conjunction with the various objective conditions and the mind’s thoughts?
The Buddha said, "You now say again that awakening is not in a state of conjunction. I shall ask you further:

regarding this wondrous essence of seeing which is not in a state of conjunction—is it because it does not conjoin with light? Or is it because it does not conjoin with darkness? Or is it because it does not conjoin with openness?"
Harmony. This is not a harmony that obstructs; it is a harmony that clarifies. If this were not a harmony that clarifies, then between vision and light there would necessarily be boundaries.
You should carefully observe: where is the light? Where is the vision? Within vision and within light, what constitutes their boundary?
Ānanda, if within the limit of light there were no vision, they would not reach one another; one would not know the location of the limit of the light's own appearance.
How is this established? It is the same for that darkness, the openings, and all the various obstructions. Furthermore, as for this wondrous seeing-essence, which is not a product of combination:
does it not combine with light, or does it not combine with darkness, or does it not combine with openness, or does it not combine with obstruction?
If it did not combine with light, then the nature of seeing and the nature of light would be mutually contradictory, just as the ear and light do not touch one another at all. Seeing—
Furthermore, since one does not know where the characteristic of light resides, how can one distinguish between what is reasonable and what is unreasonable?
It is the same with darkness, openness, and all various obstructions.

The commentary states: "As previously revealed, it is through the efficacy of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) that fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) becomes manifest; this is what is called *bodhi*."
The arising and ceasing of the mind, and even the cessation of the mind, still belong to the realm of arising and ceasing, for they involve mutual opposition.

Ānanda’s previous question did not clarify the meaning of "harmony" (saṃghāta). Previously, it was stated that the union of initial awakening (ādikṣānti-bodhi) with fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) is called ultimate awakening (atyanta-bodhi).
One might suppose that the fundamentally enlightened true mind also arises through combination;

therefore, this section again brushes away such false conceptualization to reveal that the true mind is beyond all relativity, where both contemplation and wisdom are extinguished. Only then can one wondrously accord with the One Mind.

Thus, the title of this section is "Brushing Away Traces to Enter the Mysterious. It should be understood that the "combination" mentioned here is used to distinguish initial enlightenment from the true mind.
Therefore, this is not the same as the previous refutation of the "synthesized consciousness" (*saṃghāta-vijñāna*), which was intended to exclude false conceptualization.
Because Ānanda had previously stated that his mind was still not yet clear, [the Buddha] did not wait for a question but told him:

"Although you have already realized that the wondrously luminous nature of fundamental awakening is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously, you have still not clarified that this source of awakening is not a synthesized entity."

Regarding "arising through conjunction and non-conjunction": that which does not arise through conjunction refers to the innate, wondrous nature (*prakṛti*), which is neither produced through cultivation nor born from conjunction.
Furthermore, "not non-conjunction" means that while its essence is utterly free from delusive conditions, it does not conjoin with various conditions, yet never departs from them.
However, because the essence of awakening is luminous and pure, it is difficult to apply the mind to it.
Therefore, I borrow the delusions regarding external objects to clarify this for you. I shall now ask you again about those external objects.

You still take the nature of all worldly delusions, which are a combination of various causes and conditions, and designate the substance of the eight consciousnesses as the "consciousness of combination.
Thus, you harbor doubts within yourself, claiming that the mind which realizes Bodhi arises from a combination [of factors]. It is said:
You still rely on long-standing habitual delusions to falsely claim that the awakened mind of bodhi also arises from a combination of conditions.
You should now examine this with your wondrously pure faculty of seeing: does it combine with the preceding objects—light and darkness, or penetration and obstruction?
What is meant by "combining" (he) is like the blending of water and milk; what is meant by "uniting" (he) is like the fitting together of a box and its lid. What...
To speak of "harmony" (he) means the sense of being mixed and undifferentiated. Furthermore, when you observe light, where do you see this mixing?
[If you say it is] below, that is immediately refuted. If light is not seeing, then since light is not seeing, it ought not to be seen by seeing.
This separation is untenable. If clarity were itself seeing, then clarity would already constitute seeing and should not need to see further;
this too is untenable. Therefore it is asked: "How can seeing see? This follows with the refutation of identity and difference.
If seeing were one, then seeing would already be complete; where else, then, could it combine with clarity? If clarity were one, then clarity—
Since [the nature of] seeing has already been established as complete, it should not be further combined with illumination. The meaning is that two things must be intermingled to be called "combined.
This is the first impossibility. If seeing were necessarily distinct from illumination and yet one spoke of their combination, they would be so mixed as to be indistinguishable;
thus, both seeing and illumination would be lost. How could one then speak of "seeing-illumination"? This is the second impossibility.
This is not possible. Since you have already confused [the faculties] and lost their distinct natures, to further claim that clarity is "harmonized" with them is contrary to reason.
If clarity is not harmonized with them, then it can be inferred by analogy that darkness, as well as openness and obstruction, are likewise not harmonized.

Furthermore, how could your present wondrous, pure faculty of vision be combined with light, darkness, openness, and obstruction? If it were combined with light, then when the light ceases, [vision] would no longer exist.

When one perceives darkness, it is because the perception of light has ceased; if one were conjoined with darkness, then as darkness subsides, one would not perceive light, for the perception [of light] follows the subsiding of darkness.
Since the nature of perceiving light is thus, the principles regarding darkness, penetration, and obstruction can be understood by analogy.
Having received this instruction on the meaning of non-conjunction, Ānanda again shifted his calculation, saying: "As for me..."
One might reflect: "Is this wondrous source of awakening fundamentally not a combination, being non-combined with the various objective conditions, sensory objects, and mental deliberations?
The World-Honored One refutes this, saying: "If it were not a combination with light, then vision and light would each have their own distinct boundaries."
If they were not joined by clarity, then seeing and clarity would be two things at odds with one another, unable to reach each other. How can one know whether they are joined or not?

By inferring from this, it is sufficient to know that the wondrous, pure essence of seeing and the various conditioned objects—whether one says they are in union or not in union—neither can be established. Even the essence of seeing transcends such categories of "is" and "is not."
How much less can the wondrously enlightened true mind be reckoned through the conjunction of "is" and "is not"?

This is because the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing conjoin to form the eight consciousnesses; therefore, when the conjunctive consciousness is now破除 (shattered), all delusions are exhausted.

Through the initial enlightenment (śikṣābodhi) merging with the original enlightenment (mūlabodhi), both contemplation and wisdom vanish together, leaving no room for the sentiments of "is" and "is not."
[The term] "forgetting" is used to reveal that True Suchness is beyond all dependence; thus, the single mind of quiescent extinction is herein manifested.
This concludes the section on the gate of arising and ceasing, which determines the distinction between the real and the false to reveal the true mind of original enlightenment.

[□@◇] Second, regarding the convergence of the delusive toward the true by means of non-arising and non-ceasing to reveal the nature of the True Emptiness Tathāgatagarbha, this section is divided into two.
[○@◇] First, the direct pointing to the One Mind.
Ānanda, you have not yet clearly understood that all these floating, ephemeral, illusory, and transformative phenomena arise at the very place they appear and perish at the very place they exist.
They are called "phenomena" because they are illusory and false; their true nature, however, is the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity.

This is true even for the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), and from the twelve bases (*āyatana*) up to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is a false arising; through causes and conditions...

The separation and the false are called "extinction. Yet they are utterly unable to know that birth and extinction, going and coming, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness.
Within this true and eternal nature, one seeks in vain for going and coming, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death;
nothing at all can be found.
The commentary states: This directly points to the true source of the one mind—the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, which is neither arising nor ceasing—in order to harmonize and integrate all phenomena.
Through delusion regarding this one mind that is neither arising nor ceasing, it combines with the process of arising and ceasing to form the *ālayavijñāna*.
This gives rise to the two divisions of the perceived (*nimitta*) and the perceiving (*darśana*), constituting the two dharmas of matter and mind, and internally forming the five [aggregates].
Within the aggregates of sentient beings and externally within the world of empty space, all objects of perception appear therein.
It is precisely because sentient beings fail to awaken and, by clinging to conditions, lose their true nature that they undergo the cycle of rebirth.

Ānanda, the manifestation of great compassion through the pretext of falling into a chamber of lust was entirely due to the error of falsely identifying with the five aggregates of body and mind. Therefore...
I specifically requested that the World-Honored One reveal the initial expedient means for the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to attain the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* of Bodhi.
Therefore, the World-Honored One first dismantled the five aggregates and pointed to the mind and eyes as the source of fault.
From the initial inquiry into the mind and the discernment of vision, he has been entirely refuting the deluded mind and deluded vision. Thus, it is said:

The "mind-seeing" (*xinjian*) is the seeing-part (*jianfen*) of the eight consciousnesses; the "various conditions" (*zhuyuan*) are the appearance-part (*xiangfen*) of the eight consciousnesses. This constitutes fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).

Because of this ignorance, one fails to realize that all appearances are fundamentally empty. Consequently, one gradually discriminates from before that the objects of the conditions are non-existent, falsely perceiving that the seeing itself is originally non-existent.
One merges the seeing and the appearances to return to the essence of consciousness (*shijing*), and then breaks through the essence of consciousness to return [to the source].
Initial Awakening (shijue): By bringing initial awakening back to the one mind, the essence of the empty Tathāgatagarbha is thereby revealed.
That which was previously termed "emptiness" as revealed through the destruction of delusion is merely a state of voidness; because it is empty and incapable of existence, it is not true emptiness.
Now, by bringing together the five aggregates, the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses, as well as the seven great elements, they are seen to be fundamentally suchness.
The wondrous true suchness-nature of the ālayavijñāna is what constitutes emptiness within existence, termed the "emptiness of the true mark" (lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā).
Only then does one fully exhaust the essence of the Mahāyāna’s perfectly interfused treasury of emptiness. This is not something known by those of the two vehicles;
therefore, the World-Honored One specifically told Ānanda: "You have not yet understood that all these floating dust-like, illusory, and transformative appearances arise in their very place."

They cease and vanish wherever they arise. If one realizes that dependent origination is like an illusion, fundamentally unborn from the start, being merely a phantom and delusion designated as "phenomena," then their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity. Thus, every dharma is entirely true;
how could there be a single dharma with a false appearance? In this way, one knows that the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and so on, up to the twelve entrances...

The eighteen realms: these various delusive appearances merely arise falsely through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and they are called "extinction" falsely when causes and conditions separate.

You perceive only the delusive appearances of arising and ceasing, yet you are utterly unable to know that the one who undergoes arising, ceasing, departing, and coming is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha—eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, all-pervading, and the wondrous reality.

It is like the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Once one has thoroughly understood the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, how could there be any illusory delusions of arising and ceasing, or coming and going?
If one observes with deluded thought, it appears as if there are signs of birth and death, or coming and going;
yet if one observes with correct wisdom, seeking within the true permanence of the nature, one finds absolutely nothing regarding coming and going, delusion and awakening, or birth and death. This...
This specifically reveals the true source of the one mind; that which was manifested through the prior refutation of delusion reaches its ultimate subtlety here.
Below this, as each of the five aggregates, the three categories, and the seven elements is shown to converge back into the nature of the treasury, the substance of true emptiness is fully exhausted.
The direct pointing to the one mind is concluded above.
[○@◇] Second, the section on the sudden integration of the myriad dharmas, divided into three parts.
[△@△] First, the reconciliation of the three categories to reveal that phenomena are identical to principle, divided into four sections.
[□@○] First Assembly: The Five Aggregates. [?︽] First: The Aggregate of Form.
Ānanda, how is it that the five aggregates are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness?
Ānanda, suppose there is a person who, with clear eyes, gazes at a bright, cloudless sky. It is a single expanse of clear void, vast and empty of anything whatsoever. That person, for no reason...

By fixing one's gaze without moving the pupils until they become fatigued, one perceives illusory flowers in the empty space; furthermore, there appear all manner of other chaotic, non-existent forms.
You should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exactly like this, Ānanda. These illusory flowers do not come from the empty space, nor do they emerge from the eyes.
If, Ānanda, they were to come from the empty space, then having come from the space, they would have to return to it.
It enters into space. If there were actually entering and exiting, it would not be empty space.

If space were not truly empty, it could not accommodate the arising and ceasing of these floral manifestations, just as Ānanda’s body cannot accommodate Ānanda himself. If [the flowers] emerged from the eyes, then since they emerge from the eyes, they must also enter through the eyes;
and because these flowers originate from the eyes, they ought to possess the faculty of vision. If they possessed vision, then upon departing...
When the flowers in the sky revolve and merge back [into space], one sees the eyes. If there were no seeing, then as they emerge to obscure the sky, they would likewise obscure the eyes.

Furthermore, when seeing the flowers, the eyes should be free of obscuration; why then is the clear sky called "clear and bright eyes"? Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is empty and false;
it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This assembly concerns the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). The clear and pure eye is a metaphor for true wisdom; the bright and clear sky is a metaphor for true reality (*tattva*);
the fixed stare is a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*); the fatigue is a metaphor for deluded vision; and the floating flowers are metaphors for deluded appearances—this is the aggregate of form.
By means of the empty eye, one discerns their lack of intrinsic substance. If one realizes that the floating flowers do not come from the sky nor emerge from the eye, then one knows.
The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is fundamentally non-existent; it is entirely and uniformly a false illusion.
Second, regarding the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*):
Ānanda, suppose there is a person whose hands and feet are at ease and whose entire body is in harmony, yet suddenly they forget their very existence and lack a sense of self.
Regarding compliance and resistance: suppose a person, for no apparent reason, rubs his two palms together in the air;
within his hands, various illusory sensations of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat falsely arise. You should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exactly like this, Ānanda.
These illusory tactile sensations do not come from the air, nor do they emerge from the palms. If they were to come from the air, Ānanda, since they can touch the palms...
Why does it not touch the body? It cannot be space, for you have chosen to say it comes and touches. If it were to emerge from the palm, it would not depend upon the joining [of hands].

Furthermore, because it emerges from the palm, when the hands join, the palm should perceive it; when they separate, the contact should enter [the body], and the arm, wrist, bones, and marrow should likewise perceive the traces of its entry.
There must be a conscious mind that perceives its emergence and its entry; there must be a distinct entity that moves back and forth within the body.

What need is there to wait for the conjunction of cognition and name to be called "contact"? Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary says: This section addresses the aggregate of sensation. Serene peace and harmonious adjustment are, in their essence, the absence of both opposition and compliance within all sensations. (2)

When the hands rub against each other, the sensations of cold and warmth appear; this is discerned by reference to the empty palms. These sensations do not come from the void, nor do they emerge from the palms.
Thus one knows that touch and feeling have no substance; the aggregate of feeling is fundamentally non-existent, being entirely a single delusion.
[3] Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Ānanda, it is like a person who, upon speaking of sour plums, has saliva flow from their mouth; or one who, thinking of treading on a precipice, has their feet tingle with acid pain.
You should know that the aggregate of perception is also like this. Ānanda, such talk of sourness does not arise from the plum itself.
"It does not enter through the mouth. It is thus, Ānanda: if the plum were to speak, it ought to speak of itself; why wait for someone else to say it?
If it entered through the mouth, one ought to hear it with the mouth; why wait for the ears? If it were heard by the ears alone, why would this water not emerge from within the ears?
To imagine [the water] treading on a precipice is similar to what you have said. Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is empty and false."
"It is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). When one speaks of sour plums, saliva flows; when one thinks of treading upon a precipice, the feet feel a tingling numbness.

These describe the state of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). By taking the mouth [watering] at the mention of plums as an illustration, one discerns that the aggregate of perception is devoid of intrinsic reality.
[The Master] said: "The substance [of saliva]. Thus, what you have called 'sour' should rather be called 'saliva. Now, this saliva exists because of the mention of the plum.
If this saliva were produced from the plum itself, then the plum ought to speak for itself; in that case, the water would reside in the plum and not in the mouth.
If it emerges from the mouth, yet does so only because of hearing the mention of the plum, then it must be the mouth that hears."
Wait and listen. If water were to flow solely because one hears talk of plums with the ears, then this water ought to emerge from the ears rather than the mouth.
This is analogous to the case of the cliff-treading. By investigating in this manner, one sees that thought has no substantial reality;
thus, one can know that the aggregate of thought (saṃjñā-skandha) fundamentally possesses nothing at all and is entirely a false fabrication.
[4] Fourth, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Ānanda, it is like a violent torrent where waves succeed one another, such that the preceding and succeeding limits do not overlap.
You should know that the aggregate of formations is also like this. Ānanda, the nature of this flow does not arise because of space, nor does it exist because of water.

Nor is it of the nature of water, yet it is not separate from space and water. Thus, Ānanda, if it were produced because of space, then the inexhaustible spaces of the ten directions would become an inexhaustible flow, and all worlds would naturally be submerged and drowned. If it existed because of water, [the same fault would follow].
In that case, this nature of turbulence would not be water; whatever characteristics it possesses must now be manifest.

If it were simply the nature of water, then when it is clear and still, it would not be the substance of water. If it were separate from space and water, then space would not exist, nor would there be external water or external flow.
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is empty and false, fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor arising spontaneously.
The commentary states: This section concerns the aggregate of formations. The metaphor of the violent torrent continuing in succession illustrates the characteristic of the aggregate of formations.

This is analyzed through four points to demonstrate its lack of substantiality: namely, [the water] depends on emptiness and depends on water; yet the nature of water is distinct from both emptiness and water. That is to say:
If this flow were produced from space, then the empty space of the ten directions would become an inexhaustible flow.
In that case, the flow would pervade wherever space extends, and all worlds would be submerged; how could such a principle exist?
If it were produced from water, then the nature of this flow should exist outside of the water, because it is something possessed by the water.
Therefore, if there were any characteristic of existence, one would now have to stop the water so that its flowing nature could be pointed out.
If the flow were the nature of the water, then the flowing part would be water, while the clear and still part would not be water.

If one separates the empty space from the water, yet that space is not external to the water, then outside the water there is no flow. Thus, through such investigation, this process of shifting and flowing—
When the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has thus come to an end, what could possibly exist? This is sufficient to know that it is entirely and uniformly a false illusion.
5. Discourse on the Aggregate of Consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Ānanda, it is like a person who takes a *piṅgala* bottle, plugs both its openings, fills it with empty space, and carries it for a thousand li.
When one travels afar, one uses provisions to sustain oneself in another land; you should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exactly like this.
Ānanda, just as this empty space does not come from that place nor enter into this place, so it is, Ānanda.

If it were to come from that place, then since the space already contained within the original flask has departed, there should be less empty space in the location of that original flask. If it were to enter into this place, then when the opening is uncovered and the flask is overturned...

One should see that it emerges from emptiness. Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This section discusses the aggregate of consciousness. The jar is a metaphor for the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*). Emptiness is a metaphor for consciousness. The two holes are metaphors for seeing and hearing.

Because seeing and hearing are stifled when a person dies, they are metaphorically described as being blocked. Because consciousness is dragged away by karma, it is metaphorically described as going to another country.

If one maintains that consciousness travels with the body, such that it ceases in this place and arises in that place—just as a vessel filled with the space of this region might be sent to another country—then the original location of the vessel should have less space, and when the vessel is overturned there, one should see space emerge.
Therefore, one knows that space is immobile; likewise, consciousness has no coming or going. And...
To reckon that consciousness follows along with birth and death as it goes and comes is an error; this arises from failing to realize that the essence of consciousness is fundamentally empty.

Alas! The Tathāgata’s wondrous eloquence exhaustively investigates and fully elucidates this principle, collectively revealing that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally one illusory fabrication and utterly devoid of substantial reality.
If one knows that the five skandhas have been non-existent from the beginning, then the nature of true emptiness will manifest. [The Three Categories]...
The same applies to each of the seven elements.

[□@○] Second, the assembly on the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). [?︽] First, the assembly on the eye base.
Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the six sense bases that are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of *tathatā*?

Ānanda, that very act of the eyes staring fixedly until they become fatigued—both the eyes and the fatigue are, in truth, the appearance of fatigue produced by the fixed staring of Bodhi. Because of this...
The two kinds of delusive objects—light and darkness—arouse the faculty of vision which dwells between them. To absorb these objective images is called the nature of seeing.
Yet this seeing has no ultimate substance apart from those two objects, light and darkness. Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this seeing does not come from light or darkness;
it does not emerge from the sense organ; nor is it produced from empty space. Why is this? If it were to come from light, it would necessarily follow darkness.
It ceases. If it were not seeing darkness, then when it follows [the light] from darkness into brightness, it should cease;

thus there would be no seeing of brightness. If it were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be neither brightness nor darkness. Thus, the essence of seeing originally has no self-nature.

If it emerged from space, then when one first gazes at external objects, upon returning, one should see the sense organ. Furthermore, if space were observing itself, what would it have to do with your faculty? Therefore, you should know that the eye-faculty is empty.
"Delusion. Originally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
The commentary states: This is a general inquiry into the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as being fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.

Exponents generally take the six sense bases to be the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), asserting that the organs are the locations where the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) enter. However, upon carefully examining the meaning of the sutra, this is not so; for it clarifies...
When it speaks of the essence of seeing, the nature of hearing, and so forth, how could these possibly be compared to the physical sense organs (*bu-chén-gēn*)? The Sūtra states:

"Originally, the one luminous spirit was divided into six harmonious combinations. Here, the specific mention of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is intended to trace back to the source of the six divisions from the profound stillness.
The meaning is that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is solely the single, firm, and dense body, entirely devoid of [dualistic] capacity.
Originally, it was impossible to enter [the state of delusion]. This is truly because a single thought of false movement gave rise to ignorance (*avidyā*).
One becomes deluded regarding this true mind and it manifests as the eight consciousnesses—namely, the essence of consciousness which is fundamentally luminous.

Because this consciousness possesses the three divisions of self-validation, seeing, and appearance, through the mutual dependence of the seeing and appearing aspects, it draws in and stores the phenomenal marks of the sensory objects within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). By drawing them in...
Therefore, it is called "entry. It initiates seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognition as the source of the six functions;

the essence of profound stillness is thereby divided, and the six faculties of sensory reception are established upon it. It is by means of this that they become the points of entry for the six sense objects.

This does not refer to the physical, superficial organs (the *phu-ch'en ken*), but rather to those very eyes which, when stared at fixedly, give rise to fatigue—referring to both the eyes and [their underlying faculty].

"Exhaustion (*láo*) is likewise the appearance of exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi. This says that the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) share the same source. "The eyes" refers to the faculty;

it is the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which belong to the objective portion (*nimittabhāga*) and constitute the root of the six faculties. "Exhaustion" points to the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*), which constitutes the root of the seventh consciousness.
"Bodhi staring and producing exhaustion" refers to the ignorance of the phase of arising (*utpattilakṣaṇa-avidyā*), which is [the nature of] the self.

The Section on Realization clarifies that the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) are identical within the self-realized aspect (*svasaṃvitti*). Thus, the sense organs and consciousnesses are one and the same as the essence of the fundamental, original clarity of consciousness.
It is only because of the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā*) that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing arise, serving as the source of the six functions.

Therefore, we know that the metaphor of "staring" represents ignorance, and "fatigue" represents the perceived and perceiving aspects; both are the result of the fundamental enlightenment manifesting fatigue through staring.
Aspects. Thus, it is solely due to the power of ignorance perfuming True Suchness that the eight consciousnesses and their three divisions arise.

Inferring from this, if one realizes that these three divisions have no substance and are fundamentally the one true mind, then the three—sense organs, objects, and consciousness—are entirely devoid of self-nature.
Therefore, they belong neither to causes and conditions nor to spontaneity; they are all the wondrous nature of True Suchness, the Tathāgatagarbha.
...Thus it is. Second, the entry through the ear.
Ānanda, suppose there is a person who tightly blocks their ears with two fingers; because the faculty of the ear is strained, within the head—
The production of sound, together with the ear and the state of exhaustion, are all the signs of the eye of enlightenment (bodhi) manifesting as exhaustion.
Because of the two kinds of false objects—motion and stillness—the faculty of hearing arises in the midst of them; it draws in these objective images, which is called the nature of listening.

This hearing has no ultimate substance apart from those two objects of motion and stillness. Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this hearing does not come from motion or stillness, nor does it reside within them.

It does not arise from the sense organs, nor is it produced from empty space. Why is this? If it were to come from stillness, then movement would cause it to cease immediately; thus, one should not perceive movement.

If it were to come from movement, then stillness would cause it to cease immediately; thus, there would be no perception of stillness. If it were to arise from the sense organs, there would necessarily be neither movement nor stillness.
Thus, the essence of hearing fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature. If it were to emerge from empty space and possess the nature of hearing, it would not be void.

"Empty. Furthermore, since emptiness hears itself, what concern is that with your ear-faculty? Therefore, you should know that the ear-faculty is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This section discusses the ear-faculty. It says that the nature of hearing is called the "hearing-nature" (*śrotra-bhāva*) to distinguish it from the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇa-āyatana*). This clarifies [the distinction].
It is the Tathāgatagarbha, which is originally without self-nature.
Third, the assembly on the faculty of the nose:
Ānanda, it is like a person who forcefully pinches their nose; after pinching for a long time, they become fatigued, and then within the nose they perceive a sound.
The sensation of cold. By means of contact, one discriminates between the open and the obstructed, the empty and the solid. Thus it extends even to various fragrant and foul odors;

together with the nose and its fatigue, these are all the signs of the labor-induced delusion arising from Bodhi. Because of the two kinds of false objects—the open and the obstructed—a sense of hearing arises within, inhaling these objective phenomena;
this is called the nature of smelling and hearing. This hearing is ultimately independent of those two objects, the open and the obstructed.
It has no substance; you should know that this hearing does not come from openness or obstruction, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced in space.

Why is this? If it came from openness, then when there is obstruction, hearing would cease; how then could one perceive obstruction? If it were due to obstruction that openness exists, then there would be no hearing;

how then could it manifest the perception of fragrance, stench, and so forth, as well as tactile objects? If it were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be no openness or obstruction; such is the nature of hearing.
The faculty is fundamentally without self-nature. If it were to emerge from space, then as it hears, it would naturally turn back to smell its own nose.

Since space itself possesses the capacity for hearing, what concern is this with your sense-faculty? Therefore, you should know that the olfactory faculty is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This assembly concerns the faculty of the nose. It is also called the "nature of hearing" (*śrotra-svabhāva*) or the "mechanism of hearing" (*śrotra-karaṇa*), and its meaning is identical to that of the ear.

When it resides in the ear, it is called "hearing"; when it resides in the nose, it is called "smelling. Their substance is the same, yet their functions differ; this is what is meant by the saying, "They know one another within the nature, yet they oppose one another within their functions."
[The Buddha said: "Ānanda, there are four ways the tongue-sphere is experienced.
For example, suppose a person licks their lips with their tongue; as it becomes thoroughly sweet, it causes fatigue. If that person is ill, they perceive a bitter taste;
if the person is healthy, they experience a slight sensation of sweetness. Through this contrast between sweetness and bitterness, the immobility of this tongue-faculty is revealed."
At that time, the nature of neutrality remains constant. Furthermore, the tongue and weariness are both manifestations of the state of *bodhi* arising from the exhaustion of staring.
Because of the two kinds of false objects—sweetness and bitterness—the faculty of cognition arises within them; it absorbs these objective images and is called the "nature of knowing taste.
This nature of knowing taste has no ultimate substance apart from those three objects: sweetness, bitterness, and neutrality. Thus, Ānanda, you should know this.

In this way, one knows bitterness and sweetness through tasting. It does not come from sweetness or bitterness, nor does it exist because of sweetness or bitterness; furthermore, it does not emerge from the tongue, nor is it produced from space. Why is this?

If bitterness or sweetness were to come [to the tongue], then the knowledge of sweetness would cease; how then could one know sweetness? If [the taste] were to emerge from sweetness, then the knowledge of bitterness would perish;
how then could one know the two characteristics of bitterness and sweetness? If [taste) were produced from the tongue, there would necessarily be no sweetness.

Regarding the flavors of blandness and bitterness, one knows that these tastes fundamentally lack intrinsic nature. If they were to emerge from space, then their own flavor would belong to space and could not be known by your mouth.
Furthermore, if space knew it itself, what would that have to do with your sense-faculty? Therefore, you should know that the tongue-faculty is illusory;
it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
The commentary states: This assembly concerns the sense-base of the tongue (*jihvā-āyatana*). To apply the tongue against an object is called "licking. The "kiss" refers to the lips.
To speak of "knowing the nature of taste" and further of "knowing the faculty of taste" indicates that the faculty and its nature share a single source.
[?︽] Fifth, the entry into the body through assemblies.
Ānanda, it is like a person who touches one warm hand with another cold hand. If the power of the cold is greater, the warm hand follows the cold;
if the efficacy of the heat is superior, it becomes warm. In this way, the touch of this combined sensation is manifested.
Detached cognition. When it encounters conditions and arises from the contact of toil, both the body and toil are equally the signs of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi.
Depending on the two kinds of false objects—separation and union—the faculty of awareness abides in the midst and absorbs these objective images; this is called the nature of cognitive awareness.
Yet this essence of cognitive awareness has no ultimate substance apart from those objects of separation and union, or of opposition and compliance. Thus it is.

Ānanda, you should know that this perception does not come from union or separation; it does not exist through opposition or compliance; it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it born from space. Why is this?
If it came when there is union, it would have already ceased when there is separation; how then could one perceive separation? The two characteristics of opposition and compliance are likewise so.
If it emerged from the sense organs, it would necessarily lack the four characteristics of union, separation, opposition, and compliance. Thus, your body...
Knowing that there is fundamentally no self-nature, one must realize emptiness within emptiness through one's own self-awakening; what concern is this for your entry?
Therefore, you should know that the body and its sense-bases are illusory, being neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The commentary says: This assembly concerns the entrance of the body. When it resides in the body, it is called "awareness," which is the nature of cognitive awareness.
[Next,] the sixth assembly concerns the entrance of the mind.
Ānanda, it is like a person who, when weary, falls asleep; having slept soundly, he awakens. Upon encountering sensory objects, he recollects them; yet when he loses his memory...

This is forgetfulness. It is the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of inversion that is absorbed within the habitual tendencies; they do not transcend one another. This is called the faculty of mental cognition (*manas*).
Both the mind and its toil are equally the signs of exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi.

Because of the two kinds of false objects—arising and ceasing—the faculty of cognition gathers and dwells in their midst, absorbing and grasping internal objects. When seeing and hearing flow against the current so that the current cannot reach them, this is called "awakening" (*jue*).
This nature of awareness—this faculty of cognition—is ultimately without substance apart from the two objects of waking and sleeping, or arising and ceasing.
Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this root of cognitive awareness does not come from waking, nor does it exist through arising and ceasing;
it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it produced from space. Why is this? If it came from waking, it would cease upon falling asleep; what then would [the self] rely upon?
When asleep, there must be birth; yet if there were cessation at the time of waking, it would be identical to non-existence—what then would undergo cessation?

If birth arises from cessation, then cessation itself is non-existent; pray tell, who is it that gives rise to birth? If these two states of waking and sleeping emerge from the sense organs, they merely follow the body’s opening and closing.

Apart from these two physical forms, this cognizing subject is like the cognition of flowers in the sky—it ultimately lacks any inherent nature. If it were born from space, it would simply be space itself.

"Know that this has nothing to do with your entry [into consciousness]. Therefore, you should know that the faculty of mind (manāyatana) is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This section concerns the faculty of mind. When one sleeps, there is forgetting; when one awakens, there is recollection. As for Zhuangzi’s "sleeping... [the text here refers to his state of profound repose].

When forms intersect, their perception awakens as the forms open; hence it is called "opening and closing. To remember is birth; to forget is cessation. The brief suspension of these phenomena of birth is called duration (*sthiti*).

That duration does not remain long is called change (*anyathātva*). Thus, inhaling and grasping these phenomena of birth, duration, change, and cessation constitutes the internal sense-object (*dharmaviṣaya*).
This is compared to the previous instance where one blocks the ears and hears a sound, or suddenly pinches the nose and experiences a sensation of coldness.
The tongue tastes bitterness and sweetness upon licking the lips, and the hands perceive cold and warmth through mutual friction; thus one knows that objects do not come from without.

This reveals that the three—sense organs, objects, and consciousness—are merely transformations of consciousness alone. Furthermore, since the mind draws in the arising and ceasing [of phenomena] to constitute objects, how could there be any real dharmas?
As for "seeing and hearing flowing against the current, where the flow cannot reach," this refers to the five [senses], such as seeing and hearing.
The faculties flow outward in accordance with their nature, taking the five sensory objects as conditions;

now, they do not take external objects as conditions but only internally take the shadows of the five sensory objects that have fallen away, arising and ceasing without pause—hence it is called "flowing against the current.

Because these dharmas of arising and ceasing belong only to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), while the fundamental substance of the eight consciousnesses is beyond the reach of seeing and hearing, it is said that "the flow does not reach this ground," which is termed "knowing" (*jñāna*).
The nature of awakening encompasses the six sense faculties, yet is described simply as seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
When each of these is analyzed to reveal their lack of substantiality, they are all fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
[□@○] The Third Assembly: The Twelve Bases. [?︽] The First Base: The Base of Form.
Furthermore, Ānanda, what are the twelve bases that are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of True Suchness?
Ānanda, you should observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds. What do you think? Are these forms...

The arising of the eye sees. The eye gives rise to the appearance of form. Ānanda, if it were the visual faculty that gives rise to the appearance of form, then when seeing empty space—which is not form—the nature of form should dissolve.
Once dissolved, everything would be revealed as utterly non-existent. If the appearance of form is already absent, who would perceive the substance of emptiness?

It is the same with emptiness. Furthermore, if it were the object of form that gives rise to the seeing of the eye, then when observing empty space—which is not form—that seeing would immediately dissolve.
They are non-existent. Since they are non-existent, who can clarify the emptiness of form? Therefore, one should know that both vision and the emptiness of form have no location;
thus, form and vision are both illusory in their respective locations. Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This is a general inquiry into the twelve bases (*āyatana*). Initially, by correlating the sense-object of form (*rūpa*) with the sense-organ of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*), it reveals the falsity of the twelve bases consisting of organs and objects.
Commentators claim that the primary refutation regarding the twelve bases lies in form;
yet the sutra clearly states that both form and seeing (*darśana*) are false. How could this refer to the bases alone? Now, it is clear that all of them lack intrinsic substance.
This is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha.
Second, regarding the sense-field of sound:
Ānanda, listen further to this Jeta Grove: when the meal is prepared, the drum is struck; when the assembly gathers, the bell is tolled. As for the bell and the drum—
Sounds arise in continuous succession, one after another. What do you think: do these sounds come to the ear, or does the ear go to the place where the sound is?
Ānanda, if this sound were to come to the ear, it would be like my going to the city of Śrāvastī for alms.
In the Jeta Grove, there is no self. This sound must come to Ānanda’s ears;
otherwise, Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it together, let alone the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas who, upon hearing the bell, all came to the place of the meal.
If, on the other hand, your ear traveled to the location of the sound, it would be as if I had gone back to dwell in the Jeta Grove.
In the city of Śrāvastī, there is no "self. When you hear the sound of a drum, your ear has already gone to the place where the drum is struck.
Yet, when the sounds of bells ring out simultaneously, they cannot be heard all at once; how much less so the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within that multitude?
If there is neither coming nor going, there is likewise no hearing. Therefore, one should know that both hearing and sound have no location;
thus, the two locations of hearing and sound are both illusory. Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
The commentary states: This assembly consists of sound and the sense-field of hearing. Sound does not come to the ear, nor does the ear go to the place of sound;

thus, both the audible sound and the nature of hearing are equally quiescent. Yet, one falsely gives rise to discrimination. Since these two delusions have no inherent substance, they are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
[?︽] Third, the place of incense.

Ānanda, you should again smell this sandalwood in the censer. If even one *zhu* of this incense were burned, its fragrance would be smelled simultaneously throughout the forty *li* within the city of Śrāvastī. What do you think? Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood?
Sandalwood grows from your nose, or does it grow from space? Ānanda, if this fragrance were produced from your nose, then as something produced by the nose, it ought to emerge from the nose.
Since the nose is not sandalwood, how could there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose?
You claim that you "smell the fragrance" by means of its entry into the nose. To say that fragrance issues from within the nose and thus one "smells" it is incorrect.
If the fragrance were produced in space, then since space is eternal and constant, the fragrance should be ever-present; why then rely on burning this dry wood in an incense burner?

If the fragrance were produced in the wood, then the substance of the fragrance would become smoke due to the burning. If the nose perceives it through smelling, it ought to be enveloped by the scent of that smoke as the smoke rises into the air.
It has not yet reached a great distance; how is it that within forty li one can already hear it? Therefore, one should know that the nose and its smelling, as well as the hearing, have no location.
Thus, both the act of smelling and the fragrance are in two places that are false; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This assembly is the locus of fragrance. Fragrance has no fixed location; when one hears that both [fragrance and its locus] are fundamentally empty and lack intrinsic substance, this is the original Tathāgatagarbha.
[?︽] Fourth, the meeting with the sense-field of taste.
Ānanda, you constantly carry the alms-bowl among the assembly at two times each day. During that interval, you may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter, which are called the "superior flavors.
What do you think? Does this flavor arise in space, or does it arise within the tongue, or does it arise...?
Ānanda, among these foods, suppose this particular flavor arises on your tongue; while it remains in your mouth, you have but a single tongue.
At that time, your tongue has already become the flavor of ghee; when it encounters black rock sugar, it should not shift.
