If it does not shift, it cannot be said to know the taste. If it does shift, then since the tongue is not a plurality of entities, how can a single tongue perceive multiple flavors?
If it arises from food, since food itself is not conscious, how could it know for itself? Furthermore, if food were to know for itself, that would be identical to the eating of another;
what concern would that have with your own knowledge of names and flavors? If it arose from space, when you consume empty space, what flavor would it have?
If empty space were to possess a salty taste, then since it would salt your tongue, it would also salt your face;

consequently, the people of this world would be like sea fish, constantly experiencing saltiness and never knowing what fresh water is. If they did not recognize fresh water, they would likewise have no perception of saltiness.

Since there is necessarily nothing that can be known, how can there be such things as "taste" and "flavor"? Therefore, one should know that flavor, the tongue, and the act of tasting are all without location;
thus, both tasting and flavor are equally false and illusory. Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This assembly concerns the sense-object of taste (*rasa*). To analyze it by way of taste: if taste were produced within the tongue, then a single tongue could not perceive multiple tastes.
If it were produced within the food, then the food itself would perceive it, leaving the tongue with no involvement.

If one were born within emptiness, then the sense organs and their objects would have no interaction; how, then, could there be the perception of flavor? To know that both are without intrinsic substance is the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha.
(5) The fifth assembly concerns the sphere of touch.
Ānanda, you habitually rub your head with your hand every morning. What do you think? Regarding this sensation known through the rubbing, who is it that performs the touching?
Does the capacity to touch reside in the hand, or does it reside in the head? If it resides in the hand, then the head would have no cognition;
how then could there be contact? If it resides in the head, then the hand would be useless; how then can it be called contact? If each possessed its own [capacity], then for you—
Ānanda, you must have two bodies. If head and hand arise from a single contact, then hand and head should be one entity.
If they were one entity, contact could not be established. If they were two entities, with which would the contact reside? It cannot reside in the agent, nor can it reside in the object.
It is not possible for empty space to enter into contact with you. Therefore, you should know that the perception of contact—

Together with the body, they have no fixed location; thus, both the body and contact are equally illusory. Fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This section concerns the sense-base of contact (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*). It is analyzed by way of contact; for instance, when one rubs the head with the hand, it constitutes the body.
It is contact (*spraṣṭavya*). If contact were in the hand, it should not be perceived [in the head]. If contact were in the head, it would not depend upon the hand’s contact.
If both the head and the hand possessed contact, there would be two cognitions and consequently two bodies.
If the head and the hand were one, contact would not be established. If the head and the hand were two distinct entities, contact would have no fixed location. Thus, one knows that contact and—
The body and [the hand] both have no location; both are empty and false. This uses the touching of the body by one's own hand to distinguish between oneness and duality.
Ultimately, being without substance, it is the primordial Tathāgatagarbha.

[The Buddha said: "Ānanda, regarding the six sense-bases of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), you should constantly consider within your mind how the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—are produced according to their respective laws.
Does this phenomenon arise from the mind itself, or does it exist separately from the mind in some other location? Ānanda, if it were identical to the mind..."

Phenomena (*dharmas*) are not objects (*viṣaya*). (Since phenomena are already the mind, they are not objects; being so,) they are not what the mind takes as its objective support (*ālambana*). How, then, could they constitute a sense-field (*āyatana*)?
If they existed apart from the mind in a separate location, then would the self-nature of phenomena be conscious or unconscious? If it were conscious, it would be called "mind.

If it were different from you yet not an object for you—just like the mental objects of another—it would follow that [if there were consciousness] and it were different from you, it would not be your own dharma-object, but would instead be identical to the mental objects of another. It is simply you, it is simply the mind. (If there were...)
To know is precisely your dust, which is precisely your mind. How could your mind be dualistic toward you?

If it were different from you and not a faculty of knowing, then since this dust is neither form, sound, fragrance, nor flavor, and is apart from contact, cohesion, cold, warmth, and the element of space, where would it reside?

Now, within the emptiness of form, there is no representation whatsoever. It should not be that there is further emptiness outside of the human realm (even if one were to calculate an emptiness outside of it, the mind would have no object of perception;
from what basis could such a location be established?). Therefore, you should know that dharmas and the mind both lack any locus.
Thus, both the mental faculty (*manas*) and dharmas are equally illusory; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
The commentary states: This assembly concerns the realm of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). It is explained by way of the objects of phenomena (*dharmaviṣaya*).
That which arises from the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—as the objective conditions within the mind is termed the object of phenomena.

Since these objects of phenomena are transformed solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one should investigate them by whether they are identical to or distinct from the mind. If these objects of phenomena exist as identical to the mind, then there would be no such thing as "phenomena."
This mind is not the same as the sensory objects. Since they are not dharma-objects, they are not the objects perceived by your mind;
how then could they constitute a sense-field (*āyatana*)? To say that these exist within the mind is false.
If these dharma-objects existed apart from the mind, they would necessarily have a distinct location. If they had a location, then the self-nature of dharmas would possess cognition.
Is this ignorance? If it were knowing, it would not be an external object (*viṣaya*); it should be called your own mind.
If it were knowing yet distinct from you, it would not be your mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*); it would have to be the same as the mental capacity of another person.
Furthermore, if it is distinct from you yet possesses knowing, and you claim it is your object—that is your—[it would follow that]... [it would be your own].
Regarding the statement, "It is the mind," this means that it is you who are the mind. How could this be so? Could your mind be something separate from you?
This would imply that there is a knower distinct from you, which is incorrect. If it were distinct from you yet not a knower, it would be considered a dharma-object (dharmāyatana) for you;
however, since this object is neither form, sound, fragrance, taste, nor the real dharmas of contact, separation, cold, or heat, [it cannot be established].
Furthermore, it is not the same as empty space; after all, where could it possibly be located? To say that this [consciousness] is separate from the mind yet is not the knower is an error.

Now, when we seek it within form and emptiness, there is no indication of its presence at all. It cannot be that there is something further outside of emptiness within the human realm that serves as your "dharma-object" (*dharmāyatana*).
This metaphor implies that there would be a separate dharma existing apart from the five sense-objects.
It is merely dust. Even if one were to grant that there exists a phenomenon outside of phenomena, it would not be an object perceived by your mind;
from what, then, could its locus be established? Viewed in this light, it possesses no substantial reality at all.
Since everything is entirely non-existent, the meaning of the empty *tathāgatagarbha* is thereby revealed.
[□@○] The Four Assemblies and the Eighteen Dhātus. [?︽] The First Assembly: The Dhātu of Eye-Consciousness.
Furthermore, Ānanda, as to how the eighteen dhātus are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness:
Ānanda, according to what you understand, the eye and forms serve as conditions to produce eye-consciousness. Does this consciousness arise because of the eye, or...
The eye is a constituent element (*dhātu*). It arises because of forms and takes form as its constituent element.

Ānanda, if it arises because of the eye, yet there is no form—being empty and without anything to be distinguished—then even if your consciousness were present, what would you have it serve? Furthermore, your seeing is not blue, yellow, red, or white;
since it has nothing to represent, on what basis could a constituent element be established? If it arises because of form, then when form is absent and space is empty, your consciousness ought to...

How can you know that extinction is the nature of space? If, when form undergoes change, you also perceive the shifting and transforming characteristics of that form, then from what could your own unchanging consciousness be established?
If it were to change along with the transformation of form, then the very characteristic of its realm would cease to exist.
If it were unchanging, it would be permanent. Since it arises from form, it should not be able to cognize the location of space.

If both types [of causes] are combined such that the eye and form arise together, then when they meet, there is a separation in the middle; when they separate, the two must meet. Their essential natures would thus be confused and disordered; how could they constitute a sensory realm?
Therefore, one should know that the eye and forms serve as conditions to give rise to the visual consciousness-element, yet these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the eye, forms, and the visual consciousness-element—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This refers to the eighteen *dhātus* (realms). Because consciousness arises within them through the conjunction of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), one examines the organs and objects to demonstrate that consciousness has no intrinsic nature. The preceding and following discussions of phenomena are intended to reveal the meaning of non-arising.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both, nor without a cause. Therefore..."
It speaks of non-arising. Arising from the sense organs is "self-arising. Arising from form is "other-arising. Arising from the conjunction of the organ and the object is "co-arising.
Arising from space is "causeless arising. These four modes of arising appear sequentially and intermittently to collectively reveal the meaning of non-arising;
that which is called the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha.
[2] Second, the Ear-Consciousness Element.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the ear and sound as conditions, ear-consciousness arises.
Does this consciousness arise because of the ear and thus have the ear as its element, or does it arise because of sound and thus have sound as its element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the ear...
Since the two characteristics of motion and stillness do not manifest before it, the faculty cannot constitute cognition; there would necessarily be nothing known.
(Since the object of knowledge does not exist, the faculty that knows it also does not exist. If cognition itself cannot be established, what form could the consciousness produced from it have?

If one were to take "hearing" as the basis, since there is neither motion nor stillness, hearing itself cannot be established. How then can the form of the ear be mixed with the objects of color and touch?

It is called the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*). (Since there is neither movement nor stillness, and furthermore no faculty of hearing,) from whom then could the element of ear-consciousness be established?
If it arises from sound—if consciousness exists because of sound—then it has nothing to do with hearing. If there is no hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound perishes.

If this consciousness arises from sound (if this resultant consciousness arises from sound), and you admit that the characteristic of sound exists because of hearing, (then this consciousness would already have been heard). Hearing should then intervene between [the sound and] the consciousness. (This is not so.)

One hears the sound; one does not hear what is not its sphere. When there is hearing, it is identical to the sound. Once consciousness has already been heard, who knows that consciousness of hearing? If there were no knower, one would ultimately be like grass or wood.

It should not be that the sound and the hearing become mixed to form a middle sphere (the sense-object). [For] if the faculty and the object are already mixed, then a middle sphere cannot be established.

If there is no middle position within the spheres, then from what could the characteristics of "internal" and "external" be established? Therefore, one should know that the ear and the sound arise as conditions.

The auditory consciousness element (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*) is entirely absent in these three locations. Thus, the ear, sound, and the sound element—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.
The commentary states: This section discusses the auditory consciousness element. Because the ear hears the objects of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*), it is analyzed in terms of movement and stillness. If...
The arising of auditory consciousness from the ear is explained by way of its basis. If auditory consciousness arose solely from the ear, what need would there be for movement or stillness?
If there were no movement or stillness, the sense organ would not constitute a "knower," and there would necessarily be no object known, nor any faculty capable of knowing.
Since even the knowing faculty would fail to be established, what form could the resulting consciousness possibly take? If one were to grasp...
Hearing depends on the ear as its root. When there is neither movement nor stillness, hearing itself cannot be established.
If the nature of hearing is not established, how can the physical form of the ear, mingled with the objects of color and touch, constitute the auditory consciousness-element?
Since there is neither movement nor stillness, and no ear-root, from whom could the auditory consciousness-element arise? This calculation that consciousness arises because of the ear is false.
Furthermore, if we examine this from the perspective of the object below the level of sound: if ear-consciousness arises because of sound, then this consciousness exists because of sound.
Since it exists because of sound, it has no relation to your faculty of hearing. If hearing itself were sound, then where there is hearing, there would necessarily be sound;
and where there is no hearing, there would be no locus for the characteristic of sound. If this is indeed the case...
If you claim that consciousness arises from sound and further assert that this sound exists because it is heard, then consciousness itself has already been heard.
Since consciousness has been heard, hearing sound would actually be hearing consciousness rather than hearing sound. If one does not hear consciousness, then it is not the realm of sound.
If one does hear consciousness, then consciousness is identical to sound; and since consciousness is identical to sound...
It has already been heard. Who, then, would know that hearing? If there were no knower, one would ultimately be like grass and wood.
This calculation—that consciousness arises because of sound—is false. It is not possible for the object of sound and the faculty of hearing to coexist and combine to form the intermediate realm.
This refutes the theory of co-arising. When examined from every angle, both the faculties and their objects lack intrinsic substance.
The element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) is thus concluded: from what is it established? Since the element of consciousness is empty, it is fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha*.
[Third Assembly: The Element of Olfactory Consciousness.
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding that which you understand—the nose and fragrance acting as conditions to produce olfactory consciousness—does this consciousness arise because of the nose?

That which arises takes the nose as its element; that which arises because of fragrance takes fragrance as its element. Ānanda, if it arises because of the nose, then within your mind, what constitutes the "nose"?
Is it the physical form of the two nostrils, or is it the nature of olfactory cognition and its movement?
If you take the physical form, then that fleshly substance belongs to the body; since the body perceives it, it is contact (*spraṣṭavya*), and is thus called the body, not the nose.

That which is called "contact" is simply the object-field (viṣaya). (Contact is the object-field of the body; it is not called nose-consciousness. Since even the name "nose" does not exist [independently], how can one establish the [nose] element? If one takes the act of smelling as the cognition, [then the nose is merely that cognition].

(If you take the nature of cognition to be the nose: Furthermore, within your mind, what constitutes this cognition? If you take the flesh to be the cognition, then the cognition of the flesh is fundamentally that of touch and not the nose.
If you take space to be the cognition, then space would cognize itself, and the flesh should lack sensation. If this were so, then empty space would be you and your body would lack cognition;
today, Ānanda, you would have no place to exist. Since the nature of cognition does not even exist, what could serve as the nose? [The faculty of the nose.]
Furthermore, from what could consciousness arise? You take fragrance as the object of cognition; since that cognition belongs to the fragrance itself, what concern is it to you?

If fragrant and foul odors were necessarily produced within your nose, then those two types of flowing air—fragrance and stench—would not exist in the *eranda* (castor-oil plant) or the sandalwood tree.
When these two substances do not come near you and you smell your own nose, is it fragrant or foul? If it is foul, it is not fragrance; if it is fragrant, it should not be [foul].
Foulness. If you were able to smell both fragrance and foulness simultaneously, then you, as a single person, would have to possess two noses.
When I questioned you, there were two Ānandas before me; which of them constitutes your true self? If the nose were one, then fragrance and foulness would not be two distinct things.

If foulness becomes fragrance, and fragrance in turn becomes foulness, then these two natures do not exist. (Since even fragrance has no inherent substance,) from what could the sensory realm be established? If consciousness arises because of fragrance...

Because of fragrance there is [consciousness]. (Fragrance is itself consciousness. Just as the eye has the capacity for seeing yet cannot perceive the eye itself, because [consciousness] exists dependent upon fragrance, it should not know the fragrance.

If it knows [the fragrance], it is not "arisen" [from it]; if it does not know it, it is not "consciousness. (If it does not know the fragrance, it is not nose-consciousness. Since fragrance does not exist through being known, the fragrance-element (*gandhadhātu*) is not established.
If consciousness does not know the fragrance, then the element is not established by means of fragrance. Since there is no intermediate consciousness, it is not established.
The internal and external [factors]—the sense organs and their objects—and that nature of hearing are ultimately and utterly false.

Therefore, one should know that the nose, fragrance, and the olfactory consciousness element produced with them as conditions do not exist in any of these three locations. Thus, the nose, the fragrance, and the olfactory element are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This assembly concerns the element of olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*). While the texts discussing the elements of consciousness generally define them in terms of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), this particular section alone possesses the nature of both smelling and knowing;
thus, it defines the lack of intrinsic substance by treating both the physical form of the nose and the nature of smelling-and-knowing together.
That is to say, when olfactory consciousness arises based on the nose, one first examines what constitutes the "nose":

is it the apprehension of the physical form of the flesh, or is it the apprehension of the nature of smelling? If it were the apprehension of the physical form, then that fleshy substance would simply be the body.
If that which perceives fragrance through the body were called the "body," then it would not be the nose. That which is called "contact" is simply the object of the body;
yet since even the nose has no [independent] name, how could the sense-sphere (dhātu) be established? This calculation that [the nose] arises from the fleshly nose is false.
If you take the nature of that which knows by smelling as the nose, then what within your mind serves as the knower? If you consider the flesh to be the knower—
Thus, it is clear that the cognition of meat is fundamentally a tactile perception of the body and not a nasal consciousness.
If you were to take space as the cognizer, then space would be you, and your body would not be the cognizer; in that case, Ānanda would have no location at all.
Since the nature of cognition itself would then be non-existent, what could possibly serve as the nose? This calculation that takes cognition to be the nose is false. If [you were to argue]...
If the perception of fragrance belongs to the fragrance itself, then that perception pertains to the fragrance; what concern is it to you?
If fragrant and foul odors must arise within your nose, then fragrance and foulness would not exist in the *eranda* and sandalwood trees respectively.

If these two objects do not come to you, then when you smell your own nose, is it fragrant or foul? If both fragrance and foulness were perceived simultaneously, you would have two noses. If the nose is but one...

Fragrance and stench are not two; what is stench becomes fragrance, and fragrance again becomes stench. Since these two natures do not exist, fragrance itself has no substance; from whom, then, could its cognition arise?
If cognition itself has no substance, from where would consciousness be produced? To conceive of fragrance as the knower is an error.
If it is argued that consciousness arises because of fragrance, this is an analysis based on the object. If olfactory consciousness arises because of fragrance, [then fragrance is its cause].

Then this consciousness would also exist because of the fragrance; the fragrance itself would be the consciousness. Just as the eye does not see the eye, since consciousness exists because of the fragrance, consciousness is already the fragrance and should therefore not further cognize the fragrance. If it were to cognize the head [of the nose], it would not have arisen from the fragrance.
If it did not cognize the fragrance, it would not be olfactory consciousness. If the fragrance existed without depending on cognition, [then consciousness would be redundant].

Then the realm of fragrance would not be established. If consciousness does not perceive fragrance but arises because of the element [of fragrance], then it is not established on account of fragrance.
This calculation that consciousness arises from fragrance is false. Since there is no intermediate state, the internal and external are not established.

Yet the consciousness that perceives fragrance is ultimately false and illusory. Since it does not exist in any of the three locations [the nose, the object, or the space between], the consciousness itself lacks intrinsic substance.
The meaning of non-arising is thus revealed herein.
Fourth, the analysis of the tongue-consciousness element.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that tongue-consciousness arises with the tongue and flavors as conditions—does this consciousness arise because of the tongue, taking the tongue as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise because of the flavors, taking the flavors as its constituent element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the tongue...
Then all things in the world—sugarcane, *ume* plums, *hāridrā*, rock salt, *śuṇṭhī*, ginger, and cinnamon—would have no taste at all.

You should taste your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter? If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste the tongue? If the tongue does not taste itself, what could there be that perceives?

Since the nature of the tongue is not bitter, taste does not arise of its own accord; how then can the elements (*dhātu*) be established? If [taste] arises because of the sense-object (taste), [then the sense-faculty must likewise exist].

If consciousness itself were the taste, then, being identical to the tongue faculty, it would not be able to taste itself. How then could consciousness distinguish between what is a taste and what is not?

Furthermore, all tastes do not arise from a single substance; since tastes arise from many sources, consciousness should likewise have multiple entities. If the entity of consciousness were a single entity, then it must be produced by taste;
yet when salty, bland, sweet, and pungent flavors combine and arise together, their various changing characteristics would necessarily become one and the same taste.

It should be without discrimination. Since discrimination is absent, it cannot be called consciousness. How, then, can it be called the element of tongue-consciousness? It is not from empty space that your mind-consciousness arises.
When the tongue and flavors combine (arising together from the sense organ and its object), there is fundamentally no self-nature within them; how, then, could an element arise?
Therefore, you should know that with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the element of tongue-consciousness arises; these three locations [are thus established].
If none of these exist, then the tongue, the object of taste, and the tongue-consciousness-element—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor by spontaneous nature.
The commentary states: This section discusses the element of tongue-consciousness. If this consciousness were produced based on the tongue, it would be analyzed according to its faculty.
If this consciousness were produced because of the tongue, why would it require various flavors to manifest? If there were no various flavors, one should be able to taste the tongue itself.
Whether it be sweet or bitter, if the tongue constitutes the taste, who comes to taste the tongue? The tongue does not taste itself; who, then, is the cognizer?
Since the nature of the tongue is not bitter, the taste does not arise [from it] on its own. Thus, the calculation that consciousness arises from the tongue is false.
If, like the taste, it arises from below, it is distinguished by way of the object. If this consciousness were produced because of the taste, then the consciousness itself would become the taste.
It is the same as with the tongue faculty. Since the tongue does not taste itself, how could it cognize what is flavorful and what is not?

Furthermore, if flavors were not a single entity, then consciousness would have to possess multiple substances. If the substance of consciousness were one while consciousness arose from various flavors, then consciousness being one, multiple flavors would collectively constitute a single flavor, and there would be no differentiation. If there is no differentiation, how can it be called "consciousness"?

Is it tongue-consciousness? This calculation that consciousness arises from flavor is erroneous. Since neither the sense organ nor the object has intrinsic substance, they cannot give rise to your consciousness as if from empty space.
If the tongue and flavor arise together through their conjunction, then within that very process there is fundamentally no self-nature.
To say it arises from the organ is "self-arising"; to say it arises from flavor is "other-arising"; and to say it arises from their conjunction is "co-arising."
It is also produced from emptiness and produced without cause. Throughout the preceding and following sections, this principle is relied upon to manifest non-arising;

yet this particular passage is the most explicit. Through subtle and minute investigation, it is found that across all three locations there is nothing at all; one realizes the absence of self-nature, which is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
[The Fifth Assembly of the Body-Consciousness Element.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: that the body and contact serve as conditions for the arising of body-consciousness—does this consciousness arise because it is produced by the body and thus has the body as its element, or does it arise because it is produced by contact and thus has contact as its element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the body...
If there were necessarily no union or separation, what would the two types of mental application (vitarka and vicāra) perceive regarding the body?

If it arises because of contact, then if your body did not exist, who would possess this union or separation of what is not the body? Ānanda, objects do not perceive through contact; (objects do not have perception because of contact). It is the body that perceives contact;

(the body has contact because it possesses perception). The perception of the body is manifested precisely through contact; (the body's perception is revealed by contact). The perception of contact is precisely the body; (the perception of contact is itself the body).
That the body manifests this [touch] means that body and touch are not separate. If it were identical to touch, it would not be the body; if it were identical to the body, it would not be touch.

The two characteristics of body and touch originally have no location. When joined with the body, it becomes the very nature of the body itself (if touch joins the body, it becomes the body’s own essence and reaches the state of touch).
When separated from the body, it is the characteristic of empty space (if touch separates from the body, it is simply empty space). Thus, there is no distinction between internal and external.

Regarding the establishment of the "middle": if the middle is not further established as having either internal or external nature because it is empty, then from what would your consciousness arise to establish the [six] elements (*dhātu*)?
Therefore, you should know that the body, touch, and the body-consciousness element—these three locations do not exist at all.
Thus, the body, touch, and the body-element—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The commentary says: This refers to the body-consciousness element (*kāya-vijñāna-dhātu*). If it were produced from the body, one would analyze it by way of the sense organ (*indriya*);

yet, if this consciousness were produced from the body, there would necessarily be no two conditions of conjunction or separation—so what would the body cognize? Thus, this consciousness is not produced from the body.
If it were produced from contact (*spraṣṭavya*), one would analyze it by way of the object (*viṣaya*); yet, if this consciousness were caused by the tangible object...
If this were the case, there would be only contact without a body. How could there be cognition of conjunction and separation without a body?
Furthermore, objects do not possess cognition because of contact; rather, the body possesses contact because it possesses cognition.
Cognition of the body is manifested through contact, and cognition of contact is manifested through the body. Thus, the body and contact are inseparable.
If touch were identical to the body, it would not be touch; if the body were identical to touch, it would not be the body.

Thus, the two characteristics of body and touch fundamentally have no location. If touch were to unite with the body, it would become the very substance of the body itself and would no longer be touch.
If contact were to depart from the body, it would be identical to the nature of empty space. Since both internal and external natures are empty, from what could consciousness establish its realms?
Thus, the principle that all things lack intrinsic nature and are without arising is revealed.
[The sixth is the consciousness element.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand—that mental phenomena (*dharma*) serve as conditions for the arising of the mind-consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—does this consciousness arise because it takes the mind as its cause and has the mind as its element, or does it arise because it takes mental phenomena as its cause and has mental phenomena as its element? Ānanda, if it arises because of the mind...
Within your mind, there must be something you are thinking of; clarify this for me. If those preceding dharmas did not exist, no thought would arise in the mind.
Apart from conditions, consciousness has no form—what then would it be used for? Furthermore, is your conscious mind identical to or different from the nature of deliberation and discrimination?
If it were identical to the mind, how could that which is the mind give rise to itself? If it were different from the mind, being distinct from it, it should have no capacity for cognition.
If there is nothing cognized, how can the mind arise? If there is something cognized, how can one cognize the mind?
Since neither identity nor difference can be established, how can the realms be posited? If they arise from dharmas, then all worldly phenomena do not transcend the five sensory objects.
Observe the phenomena of form, as well as those of sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. Their characteristics are distinct and manifest;

they correspond to the five sense organs and are not subsumed by the mind. Your consciousness definitely arises in dependence upon these phenomena. Now, observe closely: what is the nature of these phenomena?
If one is apart from form, emptiness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction, union and separation, and arising and ceasing—transcending all such marks—[what remains?]
In the end, nothing is obtained. When there is birth, form, emptiness, and all dharmas arise together; when there is cessation, form, emptiness, and all dharmas cease together.

Since the cause itself does not exist, what kind of form or characteristic could consciousness—which arises dependent on that cause—possibly have? If its characteristics do not exist, how can the realms (dhātus) arise?

Therefore, you should know that when the mental faculty (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*) serve as conditions for the arising of the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the mental faculty, mental objects, and the mental-consciousness element—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.

The commentary states: This refers to the sphere of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*). Regarding the mental faculty (*manas*), one analyzes the mental consciousness as being without intrinsic substance by means of the objects of thought (*dharmaviṣaya*).
That is to say, if mental consciousness were to arise from the mental faculty, there must necessarily be some object of thought within that faculty.
It is only through the presence of mental objects (*dharmas*) that the faculty of the mind (*manas-indriya*) can manifest its nature.

If there were no mental objects, the faculty of the mind would not even exist, and the consciousness produced from it would necessarily be non-existent. If one is separated from the mental objects that serve as its objective referents (*ālambana*), the faculty itself would have no form.
Even if your consciousness were present, what would it have to function upon? Since there would be nothing to differentiate, this is because both the faculty and the object are absent.
Then consciousness (*vijñāna*) would likewise lack a substantial nature. Below, [the text] uses identity and difference to distinguish between the sense organs (*indriya*) and consciousness.

Furthermore, "your consciousness-mind" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), while "together with the various deliberations" refers to the seventh consciousness, the mind-faculty (*manas*). These two both possess the nature of discernment (*viniścaya*).
Is this consciousness identical to or different from the faculty? If it were identical to the mind, it would simply be the faculty; how then could it [function as consciousness]?

Is it the consciousness that arises [from it]? If it were different from the mental faculty (*manas*), then it would not be logical for there to be a consciousness that knows, as it would not correspond to the mental faculty.
How, then, can it be called "consciousness produced by the mental faculty"? If there were a consciousness that knows while being distinct from the mind, [it would be untenable].
This is precisely what is called the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*). Why is it called the mind-faculty, and yet also the consciousness-faculty?

Furthermore, since both the duality of identity and difference lack any inherent nature, how could the [eighteen] elements (*dhātu*) be established? This calculation that consciousness arises from the faculties is erroneous. Below, this is analyzed in terms of the objects (*viṣaya*).

If this consciousness were to arise because of mental objects (*dharma-viṣaya*), yet the various phenomena of the world— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*
Apart from the five sense-objects, those that clearly correspond to the five faculties all possess distinct characteristics and are not subsumed by the mind-faculty (*manas*).
Now, observe closely: what kind of characteristic does the phenomenon of the dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*) possess?

Since the dharma-object is merely the shadow of the five sense-objects after they have ceased, it is shown to lack substantiality when contrasted with them. The five sense-objects, moreover, encompass both form and emptiness, motion and stillness.
To block, join, separate, arise, or cease is to transcend these various marks; ultimately, nothing can be apprehended.

Thus, arising is merely the simultaneous arising of all dharmas, and ceasing is merely the simultaneous ceasing of all dharmas. Since the dharmas that serve as causes do not exist, what form or characteristic could the consciousness produced by those causes possess?
This calculation that consciousness arises from sense objects is false. Since both the faculties and the objects are empty...
When the realm of consciousness no longer exists, the nature of the treasury of non-arising will immediately manifest.

From the beginning, when Ānanda first requested the wondrous *śamatha*, up to this point, there has been first the refutation of the false to reveal the true, and subsequently the integration of the false back into the true;
the principles thus revealed proceed from the shallow to the deep, encompassing them all in their entirety.

The teachings expounded throughout the four periods are as follows: first, the investigation of the mind and the discernment of views to shatter the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which is the meaning of the *Āgama* teachings;
second, the shattering of views to distinguish the essence of consciousness, which is the meaning of the *Vaipulya* (Mahāyāna) teachings;

third, the convergence of the five aggregates and the three categories back to the hidden nature, wherein the realms of faculties, objects, and consciousness are each fundamentally empty, which is the meaning of the *Prajñā* teachings; and finally, the wondrous reality of the original *Tathāgatagarbha*.
If "nature" (xing) refers to the fact that all phenomena are entirely true and universally return to the true mark (*dharmatā*), this is the meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s ultimate teaching.

If, however, the subsequent passage regarding the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) being omnipresent and each being perfectly interfused throughout the Dharma-realm, then it leads back to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s doctrine of the unobstructed Dharma-realm of principle and phenomena.
In both cases, it collectively reveals the perfect fusion of the three truths and the emptiness of the Tathāgata-garbha nature as emptiness.
As for the essence of contemplation, it is said that one should harmoniously integrate [the mind] into the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornments;
this is the general principle. When reasoned through logic, how could this be restricted by time?
The first section, "Synthesizing the Three Categories to Reveal that Phenomena are Identical to Principle," is concluded.
[△@△] Second, "Synthesizing the Seven Elements to Reveal the Non-obstruction of Phenomena and Principle," which is divided into five parts.
[□@○] First, the disciple’s inquiry based on doubt:
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often taught that all things arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

All the various transformations in the world are manifested through the conjunction of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). How is it, then, that the Tathāgata speaks of both 'causes and conditions' and 'spontaneity' (*svabhāva')?"

Both [positions] have been rejected. I do not now understand to which category this meaning belongs. I only pray that you will take pity on us and reveal to sentient beings the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, and the dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
The commentary states: The Tathāgata’s initial exposition may be said to have reached the ultimate principle where emotions are forgotten;
yet that Ānanda still clung to conventional talk of causes and conditions or spontaneity as a source of doubt—was it that Ānanda was so exceptionally ignorant?

Rather, it is because the principle had not been fully exhausted that the doubt remained unresolved. Thus, he appeared to be one who had not yet awakened, acting as a catalyst for the assembly. By means of this, the opportunity was seized.
The meaning of the Way is to request [instruction]. That this judgment belongs to the *Kongzang* (Emptiness Treasury) means what is called "when one is empty, all is empty":
there is no provisional, no middle, and nothing that is not empty.
[□@○] Second, the permission to speak and the request for attentive listening.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "You previously felt weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
Having resolved to diligently seek unsurpassed bodhi, I now reveal the ultimate truth for your sake.
Why then do you further entangle yourself with the causes and conditions of worldly frivolous discourse and delusive conceptualization? Although you possess much learning...
It is as when a man who knows medicine cannot distinguish a genuine medicine even when it is present before him; the Tathāgata says such a person is truly to be pitied.
Listen attentively now, and I shall analyze and reveal this for you, so that those who practice the Mahāyāna in the future may penetrate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Ānanda silently accepted the Buddha’s holy instruction.

The commentary states: The Buddha told Ānanda that because he was weary of and seeking to leave behind the Lesser Vehicle while diligently seeking the Great Dharma, he had already been shown the First Noble Truth (paramārtha-satya).

Yet, he remained entangled in his own deluded thoughts. This was truly because, though he had long been devoted to extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), he had persistently clung to names and words without yet engaging in genuine cultivation.
He was like a person who knows how to describe medicines but cannot distinguish them when the actual medicine appears before him.
[□@○] Third, a general refutation of false conceptualization:
Ānanda, as you have said, the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world.
Ānanda, if the essential nature of those great elements were not itself a combination, it could not intermingle with the other great elements, just like empty space.

The various forms are not in harmony; if they were to harmonize, they would be like transformations. From beginning to end they mutually constitute one another, and birth and cessation continue in succession.
Birth and death, death and birth, birth and death, death and birth, revolve like a whirling firebrand without ever finding rest.
[□@○] Fourth, specifically demonstrating the single source.
"Ānanda, it is like water forming ice, and ice returning to water. Commentary:
This is the general answer to the question. Ānanda held the view that the world is manifested through the combination of the four great elements.

Regarding these various transformations among the elements, because they do not comprehend the principle that their true nature is perfectly interfused and all-pervading, they falsely conceive of them as being compounded.
The Buddha said: "If the great elements were not in a state of non-compounding, they could not intermingle with one another, just as empty space does not compound with material forms.
If they were to compound, they would be identical to transformations, characterized by the continuous succession of arising and ceasing."
Birth after birth and death after death have never ceased; thus, one cannot speak of them as being either in union or not in union.
If one realizes that the true and the delusive are of one essence—like water forming ice, and ice returning to water—then all false conceptualizations will, in that very moment, be forgotten.
[□@○] Section Five: A Sevenfold Demonstration of the Nature of the Great Elements. [?︽] First, demonstrating the element of earth: Observe the nature of earth;

its coarse form is the great earth, and its subtle form is minute dust. Even down to the *paramāṇu* (the smallest particle), when that ultimate limit of material form is analyzed, it is composed of seven parts.
If one further analyzes the *paramāṇu*, it is simply the true nature of emptiness. Ānanda, if this—
When the atom (*paramāṇu*) is analyzed into space, you should know that space gives rise to material form (*rūpa*).
As for your current question regarding how the various transformations of the world arise through combination: consider this single atom;
by how much space must it combine to exist? It is not possible for atoms to combine to form an atom. Furthermore, when an atom is analyzed and enters into...
Regarding emptiness: by how many material forms (*rūpa*) is space (*ākāśa*) composed? If it were composed of forms, then when combined with form, it would be form and not emptiness;
if it were combined with emptiness, then when combined with emptiness, it would be emptiness and not form. Since form can still be analyzed [into its parts], how could emptiness be so combined?

You fundamentally do not understand that within the Tathāgatagarbha, essential form is true emptiness and essential emptiness is true form—pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, and responding to sentient beings.

The arising of the mind corresponds to the measure of what is known; it manifests in accordance with karma. The ignorant people of the world take delusion as their cause and condition, as well as a nature of spontaneity;
all of these are merely the conceptual calculations of the discerning consciousness. They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
The commentary says: This demonstrates the all-pervasiveness of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). Its intent is to show the reality of its nature by means of the emptiness of its substance.

Furthermore, since this earth element is composed of accumulated atoms (*paramāṇu*), one analyzes these atoms down to the *anu* (subtle particle), and analyzes the *anu* to form empty space (*ākāśa*).
From this, it is known that while empty space gives rise to material forms, the earth element—
Their essence is fundamentally empty. If you say that the great earth is formed through combination, then by how many spaces do these *paramāṇu* (subtle atoms) combine to exist?

Since the *paramāṇu* is the very beginning of the earth-element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), if one were to analyze the *paramāṇu* into space, by how many material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) would one have to combine them to constitute space? If one were to combine material forms...
If it were empty, it would not be form; if it were conjoined with emptiness, it would not be form. Form can be analyzed away, but emptiness cannot be conjoined [with it].

This calculation that the manifestation of light arises from the combination of the four great elements is erroneous. You do not fundamentally understand that this substance of the earth element is discovered through the following of karma within the Tathāgatagarbha;
it does not exist as a result of combination. If you realize that it is discovered through the following of karma, [you will understand its true nature].
Thus, the meaning that the nature [of phenomena] is truly all-pervasive is made manifest.
Second, to demonstrate the fire element:
Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self and depends upon various conditions. Observe, for instance, a household in the city that has not yet eaten and wishes to cook.
When cooking, one holds a sun-glass (*ādityakānta*) before the sun to seek fire.
Ānanda, that which is called "conjunction" is like myself and you, along with these twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, now forming a single assembly. As for this assembly, what constitutes its unity?
If one examines its basis, each individual has their own body, and each possesses a specific birth, clan, and name—such as Śāriputra, who is of Brahmin descent.
The lineage of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, down to the lineage of Ānanda-Gautama.

Ānanda, if this nature of fire exists because of a combination of causes, then when one holds a mirror in the hand and seeks fire from the sun, does this fire emerge from within the mirror, or does it emerge from the tinder, or does it come from the sun? Ānanda, if it comes from the sun, it would naturally burn you yourself.

If the moxa in your hand were truly coming from the forest trees, those trees should all be subject to burning. If it emerges from within a mirror, it should naturally emerge from the mirror and burn the moxa;
why then does the mirror not melt? Since your hand holding it shows no sign of heat, how could it ever be melted or dissolved?
If fire arises from the moxa, why must it depend on the meeting of the sun and the mirror’s light before it can be produced? Furthermore, observe closely:
the mirror is held by the hand, the sun comes from the heavens, and the moxa grows naturally from the earth; from what direction does the fire travel to arrive here?
The sun and its reflection are far apart; they are neither joined nor blended. It cannot be that the light of the fire exists spontaneously without a source.

You still do not understand that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true fire—pure and fundamental by nature, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It accords with the minds of sentient beings and corresponds to the measure of what they know. Ānanda, you should know that when people hold a mirror in one place, fire arises in that one place;
when they hold it throughout the Dharma-realm, it arises filling the entire world. Since it arises pervading the whole world, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.
The ignorant of the world delude themselves regarding causes and conditions as well as the nature of spontaneity; all of these are merely the discriminations of the conscious mind.
[This is] mere conceptualization; there is only verbal expression, but no actual reality.

The commentary says: This demonstrates that the fire-element is all-pervasive. If one holds a mirror in one's hand and seeks fire from the sun, observing closely, this fire does not come from the sun, nor does it emerge from the mirror, nor is it produced from the tinder; furthermore, it does not arise from nowhere of its own accord.

If fire exists [independently], then it is clear that it is not produced through combination. You still do not understand that within the Tathāgata-garbha, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm, the nature of fire is true emptiness and is inherently and universally pervasive. Therefore, if one seeks fire in one place, fire arises in that place;
if one seeks it throughout the realm, it arises filling the world. This is sufficient to know the meaning of "manifesting according to karma."
[3] Third, he demonstrates the water element.
Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing are without constancy.
For instance, the great illusionists of Śrāvastī—such as the sages Kapila, Kāpya, and Padma-Hrasvaja—and others, sought the essence of the great moon to use for their concoctions.
It is like an illusionary drug. These masters, during the daytime of the bright fortnight, hold a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hands to catch the water from the moon.
Does this water emerge from within the pearl? Does it exist of its own accord in the air? Or does it come from the moon? Ānanda, if it comes from the moon, [then...]
Yet it can cause water to emerge from afar, such that all the trees and forests through which it passes must likewise discharge streams. If the flow occurs, why wait for the pearl to appear?
If it does not flow, it is clear that the water does not descend from the moon. If it emerges from the pearl, then this pearl should constantly produce flowing water;
why wait for the middle of the night to receive the white moonlight? If it arises from space, then its arising from space would be boundless.
Water should be boundless; from humans up to the heavens, all would be equally submerged and drowned. How then could there still be those that move on water, land, or through the air?
You should further observe closely: the moon ascends from the sky, the pearl is held in the hand, and the water basin upon which the pearl rests was originally set out by a person.
"From what direction does this water flow here? The moon and the pearl are far apart; they are neither joined nor blended. It cannot be that the water-crystal arose spontaneously from nowhere.
You still do not understand that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water."

It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It responds according to the minds of sentient beings and the capacity of their cognition. If one person grasps at a pearl in one place, water will emerge in that place;
if the entire Dharma-realm grasps at it, water will arise throughout the entire Dharma-realm. When it arises filling the world, how could there be any fixed location?
They manifest according to karma. Those who are ignorant in the world attribute them to causes and conditions, or to a nature of spontaneity;
yet these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating consciousness. They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
The commentary says: This demonstrates the pervasiveness of the water element. The *fangzhu* is a water-crystal bead.
Observe merely how a magician uses the *fangzhu* to seek water; this water does not emerge from the bead, nor does it come from the moon, nor does it issue from space.

Furthermore, it does not arise spontaneously from nothingness. You still do not understand that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of water is empty space, which is fundamentally all-pervasive and originally not a composite.
If one seeks throughout the Dharma-realm for something to fill the Dharma-realm and give rise to it, then it can be known that these manifestations occur according to karma.
[4] Fourth, the demonstration of the wind-element.

Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not fixed. When you regularly adjust your robes upon entering the great assembly, if a corner of your *saṃghāṭī* moves and reaches a person nearby, there will be a slight breeze that brushes against that person’s face. Does this wind emerge from your *kaṣāya*?

The corner of the *kāṣāya* robe arises from empty space and reaches the faces of those people. Ānanda, if this wind were instead to emerge from the corner of my *kāṣāya* robe, you would be wearing the wind;
the robe would flutter and sway, and should thus be separated from your body. Yet now, as I preach the Dharma, the robe hangs down within this assembly.
"Look at my robe; where is the wind? It cannot be that there is a place within the robe where the wind is hidden. If it arises in empty space, why does it not blow when your robe is motionless?
The nature of emptiness is eternally abiding, so the wind should arise constantly. If there were no wind, then empty space would perish.
If the wind could be seen to perish, what would the state of perished emptiness look like? If it possesses arising and ceasing, it cannot be called 'empty space.'"
It is called "empty space. How could wind emerge from it? If the wind were produced spontaneously upon the face that is being brushed by it, then it should brush you as well.
Since you yourself are adjusting your robe, why do you brush it away? You should examine this closely: it is you who are adjusting the robe.
The face belongs to that person; empty space is quiescent and does not participate in movement. From which direction does the wind stir and come here?
The natures of wind and space are distinct; they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that the nature of wind exists spontaneously without a source.

You simply do not realize that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true wind—pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
It accords with the minds of sentient beings and corresponds to the measure of what they know. Ānanda, it is like when you, a single person, slightly move your robe and a subtle breeze arises;
it sweeps throughout the Dharma-realm and fills the lands, pervading the entire world—how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.

Those in the world who lack knowledge delude themselves into thinking this has causes and conditions, or that it is of a spontaneous nature; all such views are merely the discriminations of the conscious mind.
[The opponent] calculates: "There are only words, but no actual meaning. [The Master] comments:

This demonstrates the pervasiveness of the wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*). Because the substance of wind is difficult to describe, he borrows the act of adjusting his robe—whereby the wind brushes against that person's face—to clarify the emptiness of its nature.
This subtle eloquence of the Tathāgata is most worthy of reflection. Because of this adjustment...
As for the *kāṣāya*, a gentle breeze brushes against that person's face. Does this wind emerge from the *kāṣāya*, arise from space, or originate from that person's face?
If it emerged from the *kāṣāya*, then when you put on a garment made of wind, you would surely be blown away by it;
how could there be any place within my robe where wind is stored? If it arises from space... [space]...

If the nature [of space] were permanent and wind were also permanently produced, then when the wind ceases, space should likewise cease. If there were arising and ceasing, it would not be empty space.
Furthermore, if the wind arises spontaneously and brushes against a person's face, since it arises from that face, it should brush against you;
why then does it brush against that other person instead? Since these three locations lack substantiality, how can they constitute a conjunction? You—
It is as if one were unaware that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness, inherently pervasive, and devoid of any fixed location;
it manifests according to karma and cannot be known through the calculations of the conscious mind.
[5] Fifth, the demonstration of the great element of space (*ākāśa*).

Ānanda, the nature of space is formless; it is manifested through form. For example, in a place far from the river in the city of Śrāvastī, where there dwell various Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as Purohitas and Caṇḍālas, who have recently established—
Suppose, Ānanda, one were to dig a well during the summer retreat in search of water. When one foot of earth has been removed, there is one foot of empty space within;
likewise, when ten feet of earth have been removed, there is still ten feet of empty space within. The depth of this empty space corresponds exactly to the amount of earth that has been excavated.
Is this space caused by the removal of the earth, or does it exist because of the act of digging? Or does it arise spontaneously without a cause? Ānanda.
Furthermore, if this emptiness were produced spontaneously without a cause, why was there no obstruction before the earth had been excavated?
Why did we see only the great earth, with no passage or penetration? If it arose because of the earth, then at the time the earth emerged, one should have seen emptiness entering.
If the earth emerged first without emptiness entering, how could empty space have emerged because of the earth? If there is neither entering nor exiting, then space and earth must be identical.
Originally there was no distinct cause. If there were no distinction, they would be identical; if so, when the earth emerges, why does space not emerge as well?

If it emerges due to digging, then the space emerging from digging should not be the same as the earth emerging from digging. If it does not emerge due to digging, yet the digging itself brings forth the earth, how can one perceive space?
Examine this further with the utmost precision and scrutiny: the chisel moves according to the direction of the person’s hand, while the earth shifts because of the ground.
Thus, from what source does this empty space emerge? The chisel and the void are distinct realities that do not function as one; they are neither blended nor joined.

Space cannot emerge from nowhere on its own. If this nature of space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, you should know that the earth, water, fire, and wind manifest before you are likewise called the five great elements.
Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; all are the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction.
Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused, failing to realize that the four elements are originally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should contemplate this.

Is space something that comes out, or goes in, or neither coming nor going? You do not at all understand that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness.
It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to their respective capacities.
Ānanda, it is as if when one well is dug, one empty space arises within that well; the empty space of the ten directions is likewise so.
Pervading the ten directions, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.

That the world lacks knowledge and takes delusion as its causal condition, or that it possesses a nature of spontaneity—all these are merely the conceptual calculations of the discerning mind. They are nothing but words and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
The commentary says: This demonstrates that space is all-pervasive. Space is manifested because of form;

since space is the very substance of form, a well is metaphorically dug to illustrate this point. Space permeates the great earth, yet one perceives only the obstruction of form and does not perceive the space.
Because space is revealed by digging a well, one might mistakenly think that space is not omnipresent.
Therefore it is said: "It is like empty space, which pervades all places, whether material or immaterial. Now, consider the space within a dug well:
it does not arise because of the earth, nor does it arise because of the digging; yet it is not without a cause.

If one realizes that the nature of this empty space is perfectly pervasive, then one will know that the present earth, water, fire, and wind are all equally termed the "five great elements," their natures truly perfect and mutually interfused.
This Tathāgatagarbha manifests according to karma; how could it be reckoned as arising spontaneously through causes and conditions?
This empty space, along with the aforementioned four great elements, are all the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness.
[6] Sixth, demonstrating that seeing is great:
Ānanda, the faculty of seeing is devoid of cognition; it exists because of form and space.

Just as you now, in the Jeta Grove, experience morning brightness and evening darkness, or if it is the middle of the night, there is light during the bright fortnight and darkness during the dark fortnight—thus, brightness and darkness alike depend upon seeing.
Analyze this: does this vision share the same substance as light and darkness, as well as the great empty space; or is it not of one substance?

Is it both the same and not the same, or different and not different? Ānanda, if this vision were fundamentally of one substance with light, darkness, and empty space, then when light and darkness—these two substances—mutually negate each other, there would be no light at the time of darkness.
When there is light, there is no darkness. If light were identical to darkness, then seeing would cease to exist. If they were necessarily one, then at the time of light, darkness should perish;
if it perishes, how can one see light or see darkness? If light and darkness are distinct, then seeing would be without arising or ceasing; how then could they be said to be one?

If this essence of seeing were not of one substance with darkness and light, then when you are separated from light, darkness, and empty space, what form or appearance would you discern as the fundamental source of seeing?
Separated from light, separated from darkness, and separated from empty space, this fundamental seeing would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare.
Since light, darkness, and empty space—these three things—are all distinct, from what could seeing be established? Light and darkness are mutually opposed.
How can they be the same? Apart from these three, there is nothing else; how can they be different? The divisions of space and the divisions of vision originally have no boundaries;
how can they not be the same? Seeing darkness and seeing light—their nature does not change or alter; how can they not be different?

You should examine this further, scrutinizing it with extreme subtlety, with precision, with clarity, and with deep observation: that light comes from the sun, darkness follows the dark moon, and their pervasion belongs to empty space.

It returns to the great earth. In this same way, from what source does the essence of seeing arise? The faculty of seeing and its awareness are empty and inert; they are neither a composite nor a union.

Thus, it cannot be that the essence of seeing arises of itself from nowhere. If the nature of seeing, hearing, and knowing is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unshakable, [how could it arise or cease?]
You should know that the boundless, immovable space, together with the shifting earth, water, fire, and wind, are all collectively termed the "six great elements.
Their nature is truly perfect and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

Ānanda, your nature is submerged in samsara because you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should observe whether this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are produced...
Is it cessation? Is it identity or difference? Is it neither arising nor ceasing? Is it neither identical nor different?

You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of seeing and the clarity of awareness, the essence of awareness and the clarity of seeing, are fundamentally pure and pervade the entire Dharma-realm.

They respond to the minds of sentient beings according to the capacity of their cognition. Just as with the faculty of sight, seeing pervades the Dharma-realm; so too do hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the awareness of touch.
Awakened awareness is wondrously virtuous, radiantly pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm; it fills the ten voids—how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.

Those in the world who lack knowledge take delusion as their cause and condition, or conceive of it as having a spontaneous nature; all such views are merely the conceptual calculations of the conscious mind.
They are nothing but words and have no actual reality.

The commentary states: This demonstrates that seeing is great and all-pervasive. This "great seeing" is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses; it is also termed the "essence of seeing.
Those who lack understanding fail to realize that this source of seeing is fundamentally the light of wondrous clarity, inherently devoid of any opposition.
Now, being deluded, one forms false views; because of confronting the false objects of form and emptiness, consciousness subsequently manifests as discernment.
Since there is originally nothing to be known, [the text] refutes [this view] by means of the identity or difference between light, darkness, and empty space.

If it were one, then since it is one with light, it would not reach darkness; and since it must be one with darkness, it would not reach light. If the two do not reach one another, then [it cannot be one].

It is able to perceive both light and darkness simultaneously. If it were distinct [from these], one would have to seek the form and characteristics of this seeing apart from empty space and from light and darkness, yet it cannot be found.
Apart from these three locations, from what could seeing be established? Furthermore, since light and darkness are mutually opposed, it is difficult to say they are the same;
since there is no substance apart from these three, it is difficult to say they are different; and since space and seeing are not differentiated, [it is difficult to say they are the same].

One cannot say they are the same, for while light and darkness shift, their nature does not change; yet one cannot say they are different, for how could seeing possess cognition while emptiness is inert and devoid of cognition?
Thus, they are not a composite. Furthermore, it is not that they arise from nothingness; since they ultimately lack substantiality, the nature of seeing is fundamentally empty.
If the nature of seeing, hearing, and knowing is perfectly pervasive and inherently unmoving, then one knows it is void.
"Space, together with the four great elements, are by nature truly perfect and harmonious; they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, a nature that is neither born nor extinguished.
You have previously failed to realize that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of seeing and the clarity of awareness are fundamentally pervasive throughout.

They merely manifest in accordance with the mental capacity of sentient beings and follow their karma. How could one possibly calculate them as being either caused by conditions or produced spontaneously?"
[7] Seventh, the Great Element of Consciousness.
Ānanda, the nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of sense organs and their objects.
As you now survey the assembly of holy ones here with your eyes, moving them across the gathering, your eyes look all around like a mirror, without further analysis. Your consciousness—
Within this, he pointed them out in succession: "This is Mañjuśrī; this is Pūrṇa; this is Maudgalyāyana; this is Subhūti;
this is Śāriputra. Then he asked: "Does this consciousness that cognizes arise from the seeing? Does it arise from the forms? Does it arise from empty space?
Or does it emerge suddenly without any cause? Ānanda, if the nature of your consciousness were to arise within the seeing...
Just as with ignorance, darkness, form, and emptiness—these four factors must necessarily not exist for you to have vision.

If the nature of your vision itself does not even exist, from what could consciousness arise? If the nature of your consciousness were produced within the objective phenomena and did not arise from vision, then you would neither see light nor see darkness.
If light and darkness do not impinge upon it, then there is no form or emptiness. Since those phenomena themselves do not exist, from what could consciousness arise?

If it arises in emptiness, it is neither a characteristic (*nimitta*) nor a vision (*darśana*). Without vision, there is no discrimination, and one cannot by oneself know light, darkness, form, or emptiness.

Since it is not a characteristic, the conditions for seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are extinguished and have no place to be established. Abiding in this state where both [vision and characteristic] are absent, emptiness is then identical to non-existence;
there is nothing that is not a non-entity. Even if you were to activate your consciousness, what would you have to discriminate? If it emerges suddenly without any cause, how could it arise?
"Why do you not separately perceive the bright moon at midday? You should examine this more closely and scrutinize it minutely:

when the seeing relies upon your pupils and projects toward external objects, it can be characterized as existing; it cannot be characterized as non-existent. Thus, from what does such consciousness arise as its condition?"
The movement of consciousness and the clarity of vision are neither a blending nor a union. The same applies to hearing, listening, sensing, and knowing.

It should not be that these faculties arise from nothingness through the conditions of consciousness. If this conscious mind has no origin, you should know that the nature which performs discernment, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is perfect, tranquil, and its essence does not derive from external sources.
Together with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are all designated as the seven great elements.
The nature is truly perfect and harmonious; all are the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction. Ānanda, your mind is coarse and restless;
you do not realize that seeing, hearing, and the clarity of conscious cognition are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. You should observe these six consciousnesses of the sense-bases:
are they the same or different? Are they empty or existent? Are they neither the same nor different? Are they neither empty nor existent? You have never known the Tathāgata.
Within the storehouse consciousness, there is the clear knowing and awareness of true consciousness. This wondrous awakening is profoundly still and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm;

it encompasses and emits the ten voids—how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma. Those in the world who lack knowledge delude themselves regarding causes and conditions as well as the nature of spontaneity;
all of these are merely the conceptual calculations of the discriminating mind. They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
The commentary states: This demonstrates that consciousness is all-pervasive. The nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of sense organs and their objects.

Therefore, it is refuted by means of the two divisions of seeing and appearance. The eight consciousnesses take the false aspect of seeing as their basis, and the seventh consciousness serves as their root.
Taking the mutual characteristics of subject and object as its objects, this dualistic discriminative consciousness is fundamentally empty in nature. Therefore, it is asked:
"From where does consciousness arise? If it arises within emptiness, it is neither characteristic nor vision. If it is not vision, it is a state of blinding obscurity without discrimination.
If it were not characterized by marks, there would be no prior conditions, and seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing would have no basis for establishment.
If one says it is empty, it would be identical to nothingness; if one says it exists, yet it is not the same as material objects; nor does it suddenly emerge without cause.
If this consciousness-mind fundamentally has no origin, then one knows that its discernment, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing [arise from such a source].
All are fundamentally without origin. Furthermore, those elements of space, earth, water, fire, and wind are equally termed the "Seven Great Elements. Their nature is truly perfect and interfused;

they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing. You originally did not know that within the Tathāgata-garbha there is the cognitive consciousness, the clear awareness, and the true consciousness of awakening.
This wondrous awakening is profoundly still, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, encompassing and exhaling the ten voids.
These manifest according to karma; they are by no means knowable through the conceptual calculations of the deluded mind.
This concludes the preceding section, which, by means of the non-arising and non-ceasing, brings the delusive back to the true to reveal the nature of the treasury of true emptiness.
