The three preceding sections on the seven elements collectively demonstrate the convergence of delusion into truth to reveal the nature of the treasury of true emptiness (*śūnyatā-garbha*).

Furthermore, the principles thus revealed differ according to their respective gateways. According to the fourfold meaning found in the *Huayan fajie guanmen* (Contemplation of the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka), these are:
first, the convergence of form into emptiness; second, the clarification that emptiness is itself form; third, the non-obstruction of emptiness and form; and fourth...

Completely extinguished and without dependence. Now, the three categories [of the *Śāstra*] converge in the nature of the treasury; this precisely corresponds to the first phrase of the contemplation, which brings form back to emptiness.
This corresponds to the meaning of "emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*) in the treatise.

Now, in each of the passages concerning the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), it is stated that "the true nature is perfectly interfused and manifests according to karma"; this corresponds to the second [section] of the contemplation, which clarifies that emptiness is itself form.
The third is the meaning of the non-obstruction between emptiness and form. This corresponds to the meaning of "not empty according to reality" as presented in the treatise.
The treatise states: "Not empty according to reality means that all objective realms appear within it; they neither emerge nor enter, neither lose nor perish."
Now, regarding the inclusion of the *Amoghasiddhi* (Not-Empty) within the "Empty Treasury" (*Śūnyagarbha*) as the essence of this sūtra:

while the doctrinal tenets of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and other such texts accord with the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*), this sūtra leads one back to the ocean of nature (*dharmadhātu*), manifesting the principle of perfect interpenetration that encompasses the Avataṃsaka’s Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-naya*).
Therefore, by incorporating the "Not-Empty" of those [texts] into this "Empty Treasury," the meaning of the wondrous existence of true emptiness (*bhūtakoṭi*) is revealed.
This is the emptiness of perfect interfusion and non-obstruction; it is not an emptiness that distances itself from all mental objects and phenomenal marks.

This essence of the treasury of emptiness corresponds precisely to the Dharma-realm of Principle in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, wherein the four propositions are fully encompassed and the ten gates are simultaneously realized.

If one considers the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*) in terms of the pervasive and perfectly interfused nature of matter and mind, this already carries the meaning of the first two of the ten gates concerning the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma*) within the contemplation of manifestation.
Because they are identical with reality (*tathatā*), their characteristics are pervasive; because their characteristics are pervasive, they are without obstruction.

Observing it through this lens, it is evident that the principles of this scripture encompass the five teachings (*pañca-śāsana*). Thus, we know that what follows below reveals [the teaching] that is not...
The "Empty Tathāgatagarbha" precedes the eightfold meaning of the *Avataṃsaka*’s Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena;
yet, when it manifests lands upon the tip of a hair and turns the wheel within a single atom, it further brings to light the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.
This reveals that the meaning of this sutra is to serve as a teaching for guidance and inclusion, for it subsumes all causes and effects back into the ocean of fruition.
Please observe the text of the *Fajie Guan*; there shall be no further doubt.
[△@△] Third, the audience attains realization according to their capacity and expresses their sentiments through verses.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, felt their bodies and minds become utterly serene and expansive.
They attained freedom from all hindrances. Each member of this great assembly individually realized that their own minds pervaded the ten directions.

They saw the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as looking at a leaf held in the palm of their hand. They perceived that all things existing within all worlds are none other than the wondrous, luminous, original mind of Bodhi.
This essence of mind is perfectly pervasive and completely encompasses the ten directions. Turning back to examine the body born of one's parents...

It is like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions, appearing and disappearing; or like a single bubble floating on a vast, tranquil ocean, arising and ceasing without a trace.
Thus, one clearly knows for oneself that the fundamental, wondrous mind has been attained, eternally abiding and never extinguished.
Prostrating to the Buddha with palms joined, they attained what they had never experienced before. Before the Tathāgata, they spoke verses in praise of the Buddha.

A commentary states: "This represents the realization of those whose faculties were suited to the teaching. At first, Ānanda and the great assembly merely identified this wretched physical body as the mind, believing it to reside within the body;
now, having received the Tathāgata’s subtle and wonderful instruction, each has come to know the mind for themselves."

It pervades the ten directions. Previously, one took empty space to be vast; now, having realized that the wondrous mind is vast and great, one perceives the emptiness of the ten directions as being like a leaf held in one's hand.
Previously, one took the various objects before one’s eyes to be obstacles, failing to realize they are manifestations of the mind-only;
now, one understands that all things are none other than the wondrously luminous true mind, and this mind is omnipresent.
It encompasses and envelops the ten directions. Previously, you took this body born of your parents to be real and gave rise to attachment;

now, however, you look back upon this body as but a single speck of dust in the void of the ten directions—a bubble floating upon the vast ocean, arising and ceasing from nowhere, ultimately ungraspable.
Thus far, you have been deluded regarding the Truth and have clung only to the false.

He had previously taken the arising and ceasing of thoughts to be the mind; now, having attained clear realization, he knew for himself that he had recovered his original wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and indestructible.
Were it not for the Tathāgata’s great compassion in revealing and instructing him, how could he have suddenly transcended to such an awakening?
Therefore, he spoke these verses to express his feelings and praise the Buddha.
"The Wondrous, Profound, Total-Mastery, Immovable Honored One, the King of Śūraṅgama, rare in the world.
Commentary: The first phrase praises the Buddha. This is a singular praise of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body), yet the three bodies (*trikāya*) are fully present therein;

there is no need for further distinction. Because the pure and wondrous *dharmakāya* responds to all things with profound stillness, it is called "Wondrous and Profound" (*miaozhan*). By means of this Dharma...
As the embodiment of all dharmas, he is fully endowed with the three virtues; therefore, he is called "Dhāraṇī.

The Buddha-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm and manifests universally before all sentient beings. Responding to conditions and meeting with those who seek him, there is nowhere he does not reach, yet he eternally remains upon this seat of Bodhi;
therefore, he is called "Immovable. By manifesting a single body while possessing the three bodies, he is the most honored among the sages.

The reason for praising the Dharmakāya alone is this: when Ānanda first saw the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, his mind was attached to them with fondness, and thus he left the household life to follow the Buddha.
Because the Buddha he perceived was not the true one, the mind he had generated was likewise a false conception.
Now that he has received this instruction and attained wondrous awakening to his own mind, he finally sees the Buddha.
The Dharma-body. Therefore, it is praised specifically here. Regarding this phrase, some correlate it with the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*);
if one speaks of the Dharma-body, there is nothing that is not fully contained within it. The next phrase praises the Dharma. Ānanda first requested the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*.
The Buddha granted his permission, saying: "There is a *samādhi* named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King. From what precedes...
First, by shattering the false to reveal the true, one reaches the ultimate source of the One Mind; this universally reveals the empty essence of Great Samādhi.
The three truths are perfectly interfused, collectively merging into True Emptiness. Having already awakened to the essence of this samādhi, he praises this Dharma as something rare in the world.
"May it eliminate my inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas; may I attain the Dharma-body without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

The commentary states: These two lines generally describe the attainment of benefits. Regarding what was previously cited and refuted, the Buddha rebuked [the disciples], saying that all [errors] arise from grasping at these inverted deluded thoughts and mistaking them for reality. Now, they have all attained full realization and are completely purified.

It eliminates [delusion]. Previously, one merely identified with the illusory and false body and mind; now, by awakening to these very five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one suddenly attains the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
There is no need to pass through further eons (*kalpa*). This demonstrates the swiftness of attaining benefit through the presentation of awakening.

It is precisely as it is said: "The wild mind does not cease; when it ceases, that is *bodhi*. The supremely pure and luminous mind is fundamentally coextensive with the Dharma-realm; it does not originate from others."
It is attained. What need is there for arduous toil or the cultivation and realization of subtle refinements?
May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, returning to deliver as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges. With this profound resolve, I shall serve every atom of every land;
this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
The commentary states: This expresses a vow. Since the first phrase has already awakened to the Dharma-body, Buddhahood is not far off;
by practicing in accordance with this, the fruit of sainthood can be expected. In the Hinayana, there has never been the aspiration for Buddhahood from the outset;
now, having gained confidence in one's own mind, one seeks the fruit of Buddhahood above. The second phrase refers to the downward transformation of sentient beings. In the Hinayana...

Previously, he was unwilling to benefit sentient beings; now, having realized that there are no sentient beings apart from his own mind, he vows to deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Seeking the supreme above and transforming those below is called the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*); with this profound mind, he serves many Buddhas.
Regarding the grace of the Buddha that I have received, there is nothing by which it can be repaid; only this benefiting of living beings may serve as repayment.
I humbly entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness: I vow to enter first into the evil world of the five turbidities.
As long as even a single sentient being has not yet attained Buddhahood, I shall never take *nirvāṇa* here.

The commentary states: This is a request for the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) to fulfill his great vow. It is difficult to enter the evil world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*); now he vows to enter it.
Relying upon the Tathāgata’s empowerment, he hopes to remain far removed from demonic activities; therefore, he requests [the Buddha] as a witness.
His vow to deliver all sentient beings before attaining the path of Buddhahood is the Great Vow. For forty years, he had followed exclusively the Hīnayāna.
I have not yet made this vow: "O Great Hero,
of Great Power and Great Compassion, I pray that you will further examine and eliminate my subtle delusions,
so that I may quickly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment and sit at the site of awakening throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
The commentary states: This is a request for further instruction. Although Ānanda had realized the Dharma-body, he had merely attained the initial vision of the Path;
there still remained subtle, deep-seated, and dense fetters of ignorance that were difficult to sever, which could not be known through his own wisdom alone.
He must rely upon the power of the Buddha’s heroic and compassionate strength to be able to break them apart. Therefore, he requested the Buddha to examine and thoroughly eliminate each one. This...

Once delusion is entirely exhausted, Buddhahood is not far off. Therefore it is said: "One may ascend early with the desire to swiftly realize Bodhi, manifesting as one currently sitting at the site of enlightenment throughout the ten directions.
Even if the nature of Śūnyatā (empty space) should perish, the *śakara* (adamantine) mind remains unmoving and unchanging.
The commentary states: This is the vow of the firm mind of non-retrogression. *Śūnyatā* is translated here as "emptiness" (*ākāśa*).
*Śakara* is translated as "firm. The meaning is that while emptiness is formless and could be made to perish, my power of aspiration and firm mind shall never waver or shift.
Were it not for the power of the Great Samādhi, how could such a vow exist?
How powerful! Having concluded the preceding opening on the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness,

[this is] the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, the definitive meaning of the secret causes for the cultivation and realization of the myriad practices of all bodhisattvas, concerning the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Tathāgata.

[□@◇] First, the inquiry of the primary interlocutor:
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;

he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, you who are well..."

For the sake of sentient beings, you have expounded the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). World-Honored One, you have always ranked me as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
Yet now, hearing the subtle and wondrous sound of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, it is like a deaf person trying to listen for the sound of a mosquito from more than a hundred paces away;
what they could never see, how much less could they hear? Although the Buddha has proclaimed this clearly to remove my delusions, now—

We have not yet fully understood this meaning to the point of reaching a ground free from doubt. World-Honored One, although those like Ānanda have previously attained awakening, their habitual outflows have not yet been eliminated;

and although those among us in this assembly who have ascended to the state of being without outflows have exhausted all such outflows, even now, upon hearing the Dharma-sound preached by the Tathāgata, we still feel constrained by doubt and regret.
The commentary states: To reveal the nature of the non-empty treasury, Pūrṇa manifested doubt to request instruction;

because he sought to thoroughly investigate the causes of the arising [of phenomena], he posed the question regarding their "sudden" emergence. This first section records his doubt. Because Ānanda had failed to achieve merit through his extensive learning, he initiated this teaching.
Having previously received the instructions, he had already attained realization of the Dharma-body and gained self-confidence in his future Buddhahood.
There is no doubt of this. Yet Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was always esteemed as foremost in expounding the Dharma;
since he has not yet reached the stage of being free from doubt despite having heard these instructions, it is evident that this Dharma cannot be entered through mere words or hearing.

"World-Honored One, if all the world’s faculties, objects, aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are the Tathāgata-garbha, pure and fundamental from the beginning, how is it that suddenly the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena arise? Once again:
[②] Second, there is doubt that the four great elements mutually overcome one another.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has said that the fundamental nature of earth, water, fire, and wind is perfectly interfused, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, serene and eternally abiding.
“World-Honored One, if the nature of earth is all-pervasive, how can it accommodate water? If the nature of water is all-pervasive, then fire cannot arise.
Furthermore, how do you explain that the two natures of water and fire both pervade space without one subduing or extinguishing the other? World-Honored One, the nature of earth is obstructive.”
"Emptiness is pervasive and unobstructed; how is it that both are universally present throughout the Dharma-realm? I do not know the direction in which this meaning leads.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will flow forth his great compassion to dispel the clouds of delusion for me and for this great assembly.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, thirsting for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction.

The commentary states: This presents a doubt and poses a question. Pūrṇa, based on what the previous Buddha had taught—that the faculties, objects, consciousnesses, and elements are all the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and fundamentally so—asked how it could be that mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arise.
This was because he did not understand the cause for the arising of worlds and sentient beings. Furthermore, he heard [the teaching] regarding the seven elements.

If earth, water, fire, and wind are all-pervasive and equally pervade the Dharma-realm, yet water and fire mutually overcome one another and earth and space mutually displace one another, how can each be said to be all-pervasive?
This is a failure to realize the principle that the nature is truly perfect and harmonious.
This question probes to the very bottom and exhausts the source; were it not for the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes, how could the origin and beginning be fully investigated?
The Cause. [□@◇] The Three Honored Ones of the Three Times open the void and divide it into five parts. [○@◇] First, the permission to speak and the exhortation to listen.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa and all the Arhats in the assembly who were free from outflows and beyond training.
Today, the Tathāgata has universally proclaimed for this assembly the true nature of the ultimate within the ultimate.

"All shall attain the site of the single vehicle’s quiescent cessation, the true *araṇya* and place of right practice.
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. Pūrṇa and the others, revering the Buddha’s Dharma-voice, listened silently.

The commentary states: This is the position of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. Regarding the nature of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) within the ultimate, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* establishes four types of the ultimate:

first, the conventional ultimate, referring to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); second, the ultimate of reasoning, referring to the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths;
third, the ultimate of realization, referring to the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness; and fourth, the ultimate of ultimates, referring to the single true reality.
The *dharmadhātu*. Hereafter, it correctly exhausts the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, it is said to be the true ultimate nature within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
*Āraṇya* is translated here as "place of quiescence. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* describes the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) as an *āraṇya* place;
this is what is called the site of quiescence of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This is because the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is taken as the fundamental cause for cultivation.
This is the locus of correct practice. Below, it reveals the two kinds of Tathāgatagarbha-nature—emptiness and non-emptiness—and by extension, it reveals the perfectly interfused Dharmadhātu;
therefore, the Buddha permitted this teaching so that there might be a point of ultimate resort.
[○@◇] Part Two: Showing that the False Arises from the True; divided into five sections.
[△@△] First, establishing the One Mind as the root of delusion and enlightenment.
The Buddha said: "Pūrṇa, as you have said, it is fundamentally pure and serene; how then could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?"
“Pṛthivī, have you not always heard the Tathāgata proclaim that the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous, and that fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous?
Pūrṇa replied, “Indeed, World-Honored One, I have always heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning.”
[△@△] The two pairs of interrogations serve as the causes for the subsequent exposition.

The Buddha said: "Regarding what you call 'awakened clarity' (*jue-ming*): does this mean that the nature is inherently luminous and is thus designated as 'awakening'? (This interrogates the *tathatā-gate* of the mind.
"Or does it mean that because the nature is not inherently luminous, it is called 'luminous awakening'? (This interrogates the *utpāda-nirodha-gate* of the mind.)
The commentary states: These two interrogations clarify the source of delusion to demonstrate the manner in which it arises. Pūrṇa asked:
"If the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally pure and inherently so, then it is entirely devoid of all marks.
How can such a thing suddenly arise within the pure realm? "Suddenly arising" means that it emerges where there was previously nothing. This is like pushing a cart against a wall.

It is most difficult to find words to express this. In the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), it is sufficient to use a single blow of the staff or a single shout to thoroughly penetrate the state of doubt.
Now, in this ocean of teachings, if one wishes to exhaust its source, one must trace back to its beginning. Thus, the World-Honored One’s compassionate heart opened the way for instruction;
intending to clarify that delusion arises in dependence upon the True, he first established the source of the Single True Dharma-realm as the foundation.

Regarding the root of delusion and enlightenment, he specifically singles out the two commonly discussed phrases—“the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous” (*xingjue miaoming*) and “fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous” (*benjue mingmiao*)—to simultaneously open two gates for the purpose of interrogating Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. He asks:

when you refer to it as "awareness" (*jue*) and "luminosity" (*ming*), is this because the nature of awareness is inherently luminous and does not require illumination to be called "awareness"? This interrogation concerns the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatāmukha*). Is it because it is awareness...?

If one asks whether the nature is not originally luminous, but must be made luminous by means of illumination—calling this "luminous awareness"—this interrogates the gate of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha*).

This was established by the World-Honored One as a fixed double-gate, intended solely to lead Mañjuśrī and Pūrṇa to clarify that single phrase which serves as the very starting point for the fabrication of delusion.

Buddha-nature is threefold: namely, the direct cause (*dharmatā-hetu*), the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), and the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*). This naturally wondrous nature is fundamentally...
Because it is spontaneously perfected and does not rely on effort or merit, it is called the direct cause (*zhengyin*).

Because it must depend on the conditions of a teacher and spiritual friend for its development—what is known as "the Buddha-seed arising from conditions"—it is called the conditional cause (*yinyin*). Because one awakens through cultivation, it is called the revealing cause (*liaoyin*).

This neutral, intrinsically enlightened, wondrously luminous [nature] is the Buddha-nature of the direct cause (*hetu-bhūta-bīja*). Fundamental enlightenment, which is luminous and wondrous, is the Buddha-nature of the understanding cause (*parijñāna-hetu*).
It manifests its original existence by relying on the efficacy of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaṇika-abhisambodhi*); thus, it belongs to that which is accomplished through cultivation.
Because these two Buddha-natures are collectively unified within the one mind, both are cited together to establish the fundamental tenet.
[△@△] Third, recognizing delusion and losing the truth.
Pūrṇa said: "If this lack of clarity were called awakening, then there would be nothing to clarify."
The commentary states: The Buddha’s intention was to lead Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra to clarify a single phrase in order to initiate the inquiry into delusion and error.

Yet, Pūrṇa indeed identified with the awakening that is subject to arising and ceasing, asserting that if one does not rely on illumination to illuminate this awakening, then there would merely be the act of illuminating without an awakening that is illuminated.
His underlying intent was that there must necessarily be something illuminated for it to constitute [awakening].
This is luminous awareness.
[△@△] Within the gate of arising and ceasing, based on the non-awakening of ignorance, the three subtle states arise.

The Buddha said: "If there were nothing to be illumined, then there would be no 'ignorance' in relation to awakening. To have something is not awakening; to have nothing is not ignorance. This is non-ignorance.

Furthermore, it is not that the nature of profound, lucid awareness is [unaware]; (first, this section refutes potential objections by alternating between affirmation and negation). The nature of awareness is necessarily luminous (the meaning of "awareness").

To falsely conceive of luminosity as an object of awareness (the meaning of "non-awareness")—such that awareness is not itself the object of illumination—is to establish an objective realm based on that luminosity (the *xiang* of manifestation). Once the objective realm has been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises (the *xiang* of transformation).

The commentary says: This demonstrates the beginning of the arising of delusion. "If there were nothing to be enlightened, then there would be no enlightenment" (*wú suǒ míng zé wú míng jué*)—this is an exaggerated expression.
Its intent is to take up the single phrase "nothing to be enlightened" and state that if, in fact, there were nothing to be enlightened, then the delusion of "enlightenment" would not exist.
Is this not a great misfortune? The text then refutes it below, saying: "Alas, since there *is* something [to be enlightened], it is not true enlightenment."

That which is "nothing" is not the same as the absence of false luminosity. If there were absolutely no fundamental luminosity, it would not be the true essence of the nature of awakened, profound luminosity.
"The nature of awakening is necessarily luminous" means that the nature of awakening is inherently and wondrously luminous; it does not require further illumination by means of luminosity.
This is the original Buddha-nature, and it is in this sense that the meaning of "awakening" (jue) should be discussed. "False [conception] acts as luminous awakening" means...
As soon as one stirs a single thought of that which is illuminated, one loses the wondrous clarity of the originally inherent nature of awakening;
this concerns the meaning of non-awakening (*a-vijñapti*). Awakening is not something that can be illuminated; if there were something illuminated, it would belong to ignorance (*avidyā*).

This concerns the karmic marks of the three subtleties (*tri-sūkṣma-karma-lakṣaṇa*), for by means of this delusive illumination of ignorance, one is obscured and cut off from the absolute (*an-apekṣā*).
This true mind thus takes shape as the phenomena of opposition. This single character "one" (一) already portends the characteristics of empty space, the world, and sentient beings.
Therefore it is said: "Because of clarity, the object is established. This refers to the manifestation of appearances.
Once the object of appearance has been falsely established, then opposition takes form. Thus, the originally quiescent, illuminating, and wondrously bright [mind]...
This light of wisdom is transformed into the deluded vision of the subject that perceives; hence it is said: "Since the object has already been falsely established, your deluded subjectivity arises.
This refers to the stage of the transformation of characteristics (*xiang*). Here, the three subtle marks (*san xi*) are clearly revealed.
[△@△] With the five objects as conditions, the six coarse divisions grow and are divided into three. [□@○] First, the six coarsenesses are revealed in general:

within that which is neither identical nor different, a blazing differentiation is established (clarifying how delusion arises entirely from the True). Based on that which is differentiated from what it differs from, identity is established through difference;

because identity and difference manifest, "neither identical nor different" is further established. (The above generally presents the marks of delusion; below, the six coarsenesses are explicitly explained. Such is the turmoil.
Mutual dependence gives rise to weariness (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). Long-standing weariness gives rise to dust (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*). One's own characteristics become turbid (*sva-lakṣaṇa-saṃkīrṇa*).

From this, one is led to give rise to worldly toil and affliction (*kleśa*), initiating karma and the bonds of suffering (*karma-bandhana-duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*); [this concludes the summary of deluded appearances]. When active, they form the world; when still, they become empty space.
Space is considered "same," while the world is considered "different. Yet, in that which is truly conditioned (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there is neither sameness nor difference.

The commentary states: This passage traces the origin of delusion and inversion to reveal the six coarse marks (*ṣaḍ-audārika-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding "within that which is neither identical nor different, there blazes forth the formation of difference":
this means that within the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-tathatā-dharmadhātu*), the eternally abiding true mind (*nitya-sthita-bhūta-citta*), there is fundamentally no mark of identity or difference.
When a single thought stirs delusively, True Suchness (tathatā) follows conditions and undergoes arising and ceasing; thus, it becomes non-enlightenment and forms the ālaya-vijñāna.
From this, there arise the three subtle characteristics, and the six gross characteristics already manifest their signs.
Consequently, the various differentiated phenomena of the world and its sentient beings appear vividly within the storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna). This is then...
Originally there was neither identity nor difference, yet now they exist. Because phenomena naturally manifest in equality, it is called "blazing.

The phrase "different from that which is differentiated" refers to the four subsequent lines; by using the single character "one" (一), it distinguishes between identity and difference within delusion in order to reveal the characteristics of the six coarse states (*ṣaḍ-audārika*).
That which is differentiated is precisely the blazing that constitutes differentiation—namely, ignorance as the differentiator and the world-systems, etc., as the differentiated.

It is that which is distinct from what is to be differentiated. Now, within these distinctions, we select one dharma that differs from the worlds to be differentiated, and that is empty space (*ākāśa*). As it is said: "Due to delusion and confusion, there is empty space.

It is established as "the same" in contrast to the various differences of the worlds, because it is constant and unitary. This is because empty space is still while the world is moving; [the world] moves...
When stillness gives rise to clarity, another dharma is established as being neither identical nor different; this is the sentient being (*sattva*).

Because sentient beings possess physical forms that differ from empty space, and possess cognition that differs from the world, these distinct characteristics of empty space, the world, and sentient beings manifest from within delusion through the three subtle states. This is what is called "relying upon..."
The world stands in emptiness; perception is the sentient being. Because this single thought-moment is perfectly complete, the Buddha himself explains this in the following passage.
Thus, the section beginning with "such disturbances" clarifies the six coarse characteristics (*ṣaḍ-audārika-lakṣaṇa*).

It means that within the wondrously perfect mind of the one true *dharmadhātu*, there is profound stillness and eternal quiescence. Now, having become deluded and false, there exist worlds and sentient beings within this void.

In the midst of space, movement and stillness condition one another, giving rise to agitation and weariness. This weariness gives rise to false discrimination; it corresponds to the characteristic of the wisdom of the coarse and the intermediate.
When this weariness persists for a long time, dust is stirred up. This prolonged weariness corresponds to the characteristic of continuity.

Its own nature becomes turbid—this is what is meant by "the self-mind grasping at the self-mind"—and it corresponds to the characteristic of clinging to names and designations. From this, [the cycle] is further incited.
When the karma of worldly toil and afflictions arises, suffering necessarily follows; this refers to the characteristic of suffering bound by karma.

It is because of the single word "one" (i.e., the grasping at oneness) that, within the fundamentally quiescent and pure realm, the delusory appearances of mountains, rivers, and the great earth—the shifting flux of conditioned phenomena—arise. The phrase "arising as the world" below explains what was stated above.

The reason for the identity and difference within delusion is as follows: regarding the "identity and difference" mentioned above, that which arises and moves is termed the world (*loka*), while that which is singular and still is termed empty space (*ākāśa*).

Fearing that this [distinction] might be confused with the True [Nature], it is pointed out that true conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are sentient beings. This above section generally clarifies how [this state] arose from a single delusion.
Delusion thus gives rise to the three subtle and six coarse states, forming the characteristics of the world, sentient beings, karma, and its fruits.

Below, the meaning of the uninterrupted cycle of saṃsāra is shown; therefore, the causes for the continuity of the three types of succession and the reasons why the four great elements mutually produce one another are explained separately.
[□@○] Second, the specific exposition of the continuity of succession has three parts. [?︽] The succession of the world-systems:
Because the clarity of awakening and the dullness of emptiness interact and become agitated, there is a wind-circle that upholds the world-systems. From emptiness, agitation arises;
from this, solidity and clarity establish obstruction. As for those precious metals, because the clarity of awakening establishes solidity, there is a gold-circle that maintains the lands.

The solidified essence of the jewel-essence produces the shaking wind of luminosity. Because the wind and the gold rub against each other, there is the fire-light, which serves as the nature of transformation.
The moisture produced from the luminous jewel and the steam rising from the fire-light combine to form a water-wheel that contains the worlds of the ten directions.

As the fire ascends and the water descends, they interact to establish solidity; the moist becomes the vast ocean, and the dry becomes the continents and sandbanks. For this reason, within that great ocean...
The fire-light constantly arises. Within the shallows of that continent, rivers and streams flow perpetually. Where the force of the water is weaker than the fire, it solidifies into high mountains;

therefore, when the mountain rocks are struck, they burst into flames, and when melted, they become water. Where the force of the earth is weaker than the water, it is drawn up to form grasses and trees.
Therefore, forests and thickets become soil when encountered by fire and become water when subjected to pressure; these mutual delusions arise and serve as seeds for one another.
By these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.
The commentary states: This clarifies the cause for the continuity of the world. Initially, it spoke of "establishing the basis through the illumination of causes";

here, the word "basis" (*suǒ*) refers to the manifested phenomena, pointing to the world, sentient beings, and so forth. Now it is said that the world is the *xiàng-fen* (objective aspect) transformed by consciousness alone.
It begins with delusion and ignorance, whereby empty space arises; based upon this space, the world is established. Therefore, one traces [the origin] back to the awakening of illumination.
This ignorance, confronting the stubborn void, serves as the fundamental basis for the arising of the world.
Within the darkness of the void, obscurity coagulates into form; this is precisely the beginning of the formation of form.
Since the world consists of the four great elements—which correspond to the five primal elements (wuxing) inferred by the orthodox Confucians—it is said to be produced from ignorance.
As for the world of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), heaven and earth are established by means of them;

from the four great elements arise the five elements (*pañcabhūta*), and because they bring about generation and completion, all things are nurtured by means of them. However, this "world" is none other than the heaven and earth in which we ourselves dwell;
it is not that there exists some separate world. Those who explain this merely rely on the literal words within the scriptures...
I offer this explanation. Since there has never been one who has clarified this before our very eyes, I have therefore established these questions based on the scriptural text to elucidate it.
This shall not only resolve the doubts of the two schools, but our own followers shall also come to understand the essential meaning of Vijñaptimātra.
I trust you will not weary of its prolixity.
Question: How is it that the wind-wheel exists to support the world? Answer: The Sūtra says, "Awakened clarity, emptiness, and darkness," and so forth.
This means that by being deluded regarding the wondrously luminous true mind of the one true Dharma-realm, there arises the ignorance of "awakened clarity."
Thus, the true emptiness of numinous clarity and quiescent extinction was transformed into the dull emptiness of ignorance and obscurity.
As subject and object interacted and light and darkness vied with one another, after a long time, deluded thoughts were formed.

These thoughts stirred the substance of the mind, and as accumulated vacuity became a vital energy (*qi*), it filled the midst of space, thereby giving rise to the appearance of wind. It is like wind arising in an empty room, or again—
Fanning [the air] produces wind; when thoughts accumulate without ceasing, the power of the wind grows ever greater. Therefore it is said that all worlds are sustained by the power of wind.
Furthermore, all realms of the world exist and are maintained based upon the deluded mind of ignorance.
Thus, there is a wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) that upholds the world. This is the great element of wind (*vāyu-mahābhūta*). (The *Laozi* points to the clarity of awakening...)

Ignorance (*avidyā*) constitutes the essence of the Way; thus it is said: "Profound and dark, within it there is a subtle essence. Furthermore, taking the essence of emptiness as the Great Way of Non-being, this wind-element is pointed out as the "pneuma of the profound" (*chong qi*);

hence it is said: "Concentrate the pneuma to achieve suppleness. It is also said: "The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows. This is the source of the Way of the Master of Old (Laozi). The Confucians take the cognitive spirit (*vijñāna*) to be the nature of the mandate of Heaven (*tianming*). They point to the great element of emptiness as the Supreme Ultimate (*taiji*), and they point to this great element of wind as the unified pneuma of the primordial chaos (*hun-yuan yiqi*), from which all things are generated and sustained.

All of these fail to realize that [all phenomena] are transformations of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Thus, in the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate, black and white are intermingled. Yet, white is the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*), while black is ignorance; they are precisely the non-arising and non-ceasing versus the arising and ceasing.

The harmonious synthesis that constitutes the *ālaya-vijñāna* serves as the beginning for the arising of all phenomena; this consciousness possesses three divisions, and the world of space is merely its *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect).
Question: Why is the world said to have gold and jewels as its substance? Answer: The Sūtra says, "Because of emptiness, movement arises," and so forth.

This means that from within the substance of insentient emptiness, the wind of deluded thought and movement arises. This wind blows back upon the insentient [nature] within the substance of the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

Luminous awareness—through the incessant alternation of movement and stillness, arising and ceasing, rubbing and surging against one another—becomes increasingly firm in its luminous essence after a long duration, eventually coagulating into form.
This constitutes the objective portion (nimitta-bhāga), the insentient matter external to awareness; hence it is said that "darkness coagulates into form.
That which is the golden treasure is the solidity produced by luminous awareness; therefore, the treasure possesses radiance.
"Clarity" refers to attaining the nature of firm awakening. For this reason, there is a golden wheel that sustains the land.

This nature, as form, constitutes the earth element (*mahābhūta*); because it refers to its essential substance, it is called "golden treasure. That which lies beneath Mount Sumeru, at the bottom of the earth, is the adamantine limit (*vajratala*).

(This corresponds to what the Confucian school calls "the alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Way," which they regard as the fundamental source for the generation of heaven and earth. Herein lies emptiness and stillness; it is dark and profound.)

Therefore, stillness is Yin; it is quiescence. Awareness is clarity; therefore, it is Yang. Thus it is said: "In movement and stillness there is constancy; thus are hardness and softness determined. This arises from movement and stillness to form the Golden Wheel as the great element of earth—this is the very beginning when heaven and earth first came into being.

Taking movement as the essence of Qian (Heaven) and stillness as the essence of Kun (Earth), that which is above form is Heaven, and that which is below form is Earth. This is what is meant by "Qian and Kun are arrayed, and the *Yi* (Change) stands between them.

This is the so-called *Xiantian Yi* (Primordial Change), wherein Yin and Yang have not yet taken form, yet movement and stillness, as well as hardness and softness, are already fully present. Question: How is it that there is the light of fire, which constitutes transformation?
[Question: Is it the nature [of fire]? [Answer: The Sūtra says, "The precious substance of firm awareness is formed," and so forth.

This means that once the precious substance of prior firm awareness has been formed and the wind of shaking luminosity has emerged, these two interact. As the one is hard and the other is soft, they rub against and stir one another;

thus, there is the light of fire, which constitutes the nature of transformation. This is the great element of fire (*tejo-mahābhūta*). (This corresponds to what is stated in the *Yì* [Book of Changes]: "The hard and the soft rub against each other, thereby producing transformations. Regarding form...

That which exists above, forming images in heaven, becomes the sun; it is the fiery essence of the Great Yang. That which exists below, forming shapes on earth, becomes fire; it is the nature of transformation, meaning the transformation of the raw into the cooked and the transformation of existence into non-existence.

Furthermore, among the Five Elements of the Post-Celestial (Hou Tian) order, Xun represents wind and wood; thus, by drilling wood to produce fire, one obtains the nature of the Pre-Celestial (Xian Tian). This [is the sun within the Four Images]. Question: How can there be a water-wheel that contains the realms of the ten directions?
Answer: The Sūtra says, "Precious clarity gives rise to moisture," and so forth. The wording of this sentence is inverted.
One should say that the fire-light steams upward, causing the brilliance of the jewels to produce moisture.

This means that because the fire-light’s upward flames steam the solidified jewels, the jewels, being steamed by the fire, become moist and water emerges. Thus, there is a water-wheel containing the worlds of the ten directions.
The meaning of this passage in the sutra is extremely difficult to comprehend. Furthermore, if the jewels constitute the substance of the earth, why would fire...

Is it that they are steamed and become the water of rain and dew within space? Taking gold and jewels as the substance of the earth’s body, Mount Sumeru is also called the Diamond Mountain (*vajra-parvata*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Mount Sumeru is composed of four precious substances;
at its summit dwells Śakra, the Lord of the Thirty-three Heavens. Thus, for the upper realms, it is appropriate that diamond constitutes the substance of the earth. Moreover—
Mount Sumeru is shaped like a narrow-sided drum; the ground of the upper realms that covers it below is likewise similar in form.
As the sun and moon travel around its waist, they illuminate the four continents below.

Thus, one can know for certain that what appears as a vast, azure-blue expanse when gazed upon from below is the substance of the precious ground of the upper realms, serving as a support for the sentient beings of the lower world.
Moisture is produced by the steaming of the fires of karma; thus, the rain, dew, frost, and snow in the air are all waters born from the jewels.

This means that sentient beings constantly dwell within the realm of jewels. Since there is water within these jewels, is it not the case that the water-wheel contains the worlds of the ten directions?
(This corresponds to what the *I Ching* calls "that which is above form manifests as images in heaven," being the moon—the essence of the Yin—and the stars.)
The temporal forms manifesting in the downward direction take the shape of rivers, streams, lakes, and oceans as they flow and pour forth; thus, these four images are complete.

Prior to this, because the clarity of awareness and the darkness of emptiness interacted with one another, the two great elements of wind and gold arose. Because the wind and gold rubbed against each other, the great element of fire arose.

Because the fire steamed the moisture within the precious [earth], the great element of water arose. Thus, through the four great elements, heaven and earth, yin and yang, the sun, moon, and stars were formed.

The four images of the seasons. This is precisely what the *Yijing* explains: the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) gives rise to the two polarities (*liangyi*), and the two polarities give rise to the four images, which constitute the substance of the eight trigrams (*bagua*).
Therefore it is said: "Heaven is noble and Earth is base; thus Qian and Kun are determined. The low and high are displayed;
thus the positions of noble and base are established. Movement and stillness have their constants; thus the hard and the soft are distinguished. In heaven they form images; in..."
The earth takes form, and its transformations become visible. This above has merely described the manner in which heaven and earth are generated;

hereafter, I shall explain the origins of the beginning and end of all phenomena. By inferring from this, it is clear and unmistakable that the world arises from the transformation of consciousness through enlightened clarity (*bodhi-vijñapti-mātra*).
In the past, I encountered a foreign monk who told me that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* discusses the five elements.
This subtlety is ultimate and exquisite; therefore, one must strive to investigate it. It is something our fellow students must know. Question:

How is it that there come to be the forms of rivers, streams, lakes, seas, islands, sandbanks, dry lands, and moist lands, as well as the flow and confluence of waters? Answer: The Sūtra says, "Fire ascends and water descends," and so forth.
As previously stated, once heaven and earth were established and yin and yang were differentiated, the positions of heaven and earth were settled.
Thus, from the four great elements arise the five post-heavenly phases (*wǔxíng*) to generate and sustain all things.
This refers to fire and metal producing water, and water and fire producing earth. It is said that as the light of fire rises and steams upward, precious brilliance produces moisture;
thus the fiery light flares upward while the force of water descends, merging within the midst of space. When water and fire are thus brought into equilibrium, they form the earth.
The union of yin and yang gives birth to offspring; thus, when water and fire both become solid and firm, they form a physical shape.
The moisture of their original source flows to become the four great oceans, while the fire of their original source coalesces to form the earth.
That which is large becomes a continent (*dvīpa*), and that which is small becomes an islet (*taraṅga*). Thus, there exist the four great continents and various smaller islands. For this reason:
Water contains the nature of the Father; therefore, the light of fire constantly arises within the ocean. Earth attains the nature of the Mother;

therefore, rivers and streams constantly flow through the continents and sandbanks. Because water and fire are thus the water and fire of the fundamental nature, they form celestial images in the heavens as the sun, moon, and stars, and take physical form on the earth as the four great divisions: rivers, streams, lakes, and seas.

This is the form of the continents; thus it is said that they appear through transformation. Here, the interaction of the establishment of solidity with water and fire being in opposition constitutes the "water and fire already completed" (*ji-ji*), which signifies mutual generation.
Below, because the power of the water is inferior to the fire, there are mountains, rocks, grasses, and trees;
this constitutes mutual overcoming (*xiang-ke*) whereby things are formed. Question: How is it that there are mountains and rivers, with their heights and depths, such that they are not level?

Yes. The Sūtra states that "the power of water is inferior to fire," and so forth. Because the preceding water and fire were in a state of mutual completion (*ji-ji*) with their powers opposing one another, they formed continents and oceans.
Now, because the water and fire have not yet reached such completion, the power of the water is inferior to the power of the fire;

as their powers do not oppose each other, the fire blazes upward, eventually solidifying into high mountains and massive boulders. Because it inherits the nature of its father [fire], the mountains and rocks [are thus formed].
When struck, it becomes flame; because it possesses the nature of its mother-element, when melted, it becomes water.

This can be seen today in stones containing volcanic fire, on mountain peaks possessing water, and in the great moisture found at the roots of rocks. These still belong to the innate, primordial fire;
however, because their natures do not mutually overcome one another, they manifest as tangible mountain rocks. Question: How is it that there are grasses?
"Is it of the category of wood? He replied: "The Sūtra says that the power of earth is inferior to that of water and so forth; thus, among these five elements, water and earth give rise to wood.
Because it receives a portion of its father’s qi, forests and thickets turn into soil when burned.
Because it receives a portion of its mother’s qi, grasses and trees turn into water when twisted. This arises from the two delusions of the clarity of awareness and the obscurity of space."

These become the seeds of the four great elements (mahābhūta), which subsequently give rise to heaven and earth, the sun and moon, the four great continents, rivers, lakes, seas, mountains, rivers, grasses, trees, and all things.

Thus, the single vital energy (qi) circulates, yin and yang interweave, the five phases (wuxing) produce one another, and the eight trigrams (bagua) undergo transformations until they reach sixty-four.
Therefore, the hexagrams of the *Yi* begin with Qian and Kun and conclude with Ji-ji.
This is the state of "Unfinished" (Wei Ji). Therefore it is said: "Mutual delusions arise, successively becoming seeds for one another; by these causes and conditions, the world continues.
In the past, Master Dahui said: "The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* explains the continuity of the world in great detail regarding the five elements.
I cite this to show the assembly, though he did not provide a detailed analysis."
[2] Second, explaining the continuity of sentient beings.

Furthermore, Pūrṇa, the delusion is not caused by another; the fault lies in the fact that the luminous awareness itself becomes deluded. Once the object of delusion is established, the principle of luminosity cannot transcend it.
For this reason, hearing does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not surpass form. Thus, the six objects—form, smell, taste, touch, and so forth—are formed through delusion.
Thus, from this, seeing, cognition, hearing, and knowing become separated. Karmic affinities entwine one another; through union and separation, transformation occurs.

Seeing gives rise to luminosity, and luminous seeing brings about ideation. Divergent views give rise to aversion, while shared ideation gives rise to attraction. This flowing attraction becomes the seed, and the reception of ideation forms the embryo.
Through their mutual encounter, there is generation and attraction of karmic affinities; thus, by means of causes and conditions, the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages arise.

[The four modes of birth,] such as these—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—occur according to what is appropriate for each. Egg-birth arises solely from thought; womb-birth is caused by emotion;

moisture-birth results from a union of desire; and transformation-birth occurs through a response to separation. Emotion, thought, union, and separation mutually transform one another; all karmic retributions follow their respective ascent or descent.
By these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.
The commentary states: This clarifies the cause for the continuous succession of sentient beings. As for the passage beginning with "Clarifying that delusion is none other than...

and ending with "...the union and separation that form transformation," it refers to the causes by which the four modes of birth receive physical forms, and how the body serves as the root of suffering.
Within the pure realm, there are fundamentally no sentient beings; it is only because of a single moment of deluded movement from time immemorial that ignorance arises.

Thus, it becomes the root of all sentient beings. Therefore, it is said: "The delusion of clarity is not from another; the clarity of awareness itself is the fault. "Clarity of awareness" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because of this ignorance, the characteristics of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) take form.
One inhales and gathers these four elements to constitute a body, thereby causing the principle of true clarity to be unable to transcend the physical form. Furthermore, one grasps external forms.
The six sense-objects produced by [the mind] become the objects of experience. For this reason, hearing does not transcend sound and seeing does not surpass form;
because these six kinds of delusive objects—form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—are present, the faculties and objects combine to give rise to the six consciousnesses.
Consequently, the perfectly湛 (pure and still) essence is divided into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing. Thus, the faculties [are established].
With the karma created through the conjunction of the three—the object, the consciousness, and the sense organ—as the cause, the bitter fruits of the four modes of birth accordingly manifest.

Thus, through the mutual entanglement of shared karma, there arise the forms of the womb-born and egg-born; and through the response to the conditions of union and separation, there arise the classes of moisture-born and transformation-born.
These four modes of birth for sentient beings first arise from a single thought of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The passage from "seeing the light and colors emerge" up to "the *arbuda* stage and so forth" describes the process of entering the womb. The ascent and descent within the six realms of existence are not uniform.

This is spoken with reference to the human realm. It means that once sentient beings have created deluded karma and die, they obtain an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*), which is what is called a "wandering soul.
Although ghosts lack physical bodies, they possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Their vision reaches the furthest distances;

because of their habituated tendencies of craving and attachment, they inevitably seek out the objects they love. They pursue these objects to the limits of their vision, even across thousands of *li*.
Externally, the objects that are desirable then manifest; hence it is said, "Seeing clarity, form arises.

Having seen those objects, the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) necessarily moves toward them. Because one clearly sees what is desirable and conceives of its form, it is said, "Clear seeing brings about conception.
At the moment of sexual union between man and woman, the conscious spirit takes hold of it. If [the spirit] was originally male...
Thus, one loves the mother and hates the father; if one were originally female, one would love the father and hate the mother. Therefore it is said:
"Diverse perceptions give rise to hatred, while identical conceptions give rise to love. Riding upon their union, one thirsts for and follows after them.
Inhaling the saliva of craving, one flows into the mother’s womb to become the seed for receiving a physical form. Therefore it is said: "The flow of craving becomes the seed," and "conception..."

One seizes the single point of the parents' vital essence and blood, conceiving it within and thus grasping it as "self. Therefore, it is said that "conceiving [the thought] is the formation of the embryo.
This is the beginning of entering the womb and receiving a physical form; it arises from the act of sexual union.
Furthermore, the distinction between male and female occurs due to the attraction of shared karma through hatred or love. It is by means of the karma of love that...
With craving for objects as the condition, the embryo becomes *kalala* (translated here as "coagulated mucus") after seven days in the womb;

*arbuda* (translated here as "bubble," the state at two weeks); *peśī* (translated here as "soft flesh," the state at three weeks); *ghana* (translated here as "solid flesh," the state at four weeks);

and *praśākhā* (translated here as the "stage of formation," meaning the six sense organs are finally complete, the state at five weeks). The above explains the reason for entering the womb. As for...
The four modes of birth—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—are not uniform; they specifically correspond to the karma created by each being.
This is what is meant by "the transmigration according to one's karma. The egg-born arises solely from thought (*saṃjñā*); the womb-born is due to emotional attachment (*sneha*);

the moisture-born results from a response through union; and the transformation-born occurs through a response to separation. Thought is light and soaring, whereas emotion is heavy and turbid; because craving follows upon thought, [the womb-born arises].
Eggs are primary. Those born by adhering to moisture are called moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*). Those that transform and change their forms are called transformation-born (*upapāduka*).

Because of the union or separation of emotional thoughts, they undergo mutual transformations; according to the causes they invoke, the fruits they receive, and the karma they experience, they follow their respective destinies of flight or descent.
By these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.
[...? Third, regarding the continuity of the karmic results of the three knowledges:
Pūrṇa, when ideation and craving are bound together such that craving cannot be abandoned, then the succession of parents and children throughout the world continues without interruption.
These are rooted in desire and greed. When greed and craving nourish one another such that greed cannot be stilled, then...
In all worlds, those born from eggs, from transformation, from moisture, or from wombs devour one another according to their relative strength and weakness.
These beings take the greed for killing as their foundation. As humans eat sheep, when the sheep die they become humans; when humans die they become sheep.

In this way, even among the ten classes of living beings, death follows birth and birth follows death as they mutually devour one another. This evil karma arises together with them and persists until the end of the future. This is...

These are rooted in theft and greed. You owe me my life; I shall repay you with my debt. Because of these causes and conditions, we remain constantly in birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
You love my heart; I cherish your form. Because of these causes and conditions, we remain constantly bound in entanglement for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—these three are the roots. Because of these causes and conditions, [this is] karma.
"Continuity of the fruit.
The commentary states: This clarifies the cause for the continuity of karmic fruits. Through the joint binding of perception (*saṃjñā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one cannot be separated from craving.
Parents and children are born of one another in an uninterrupted succession. This explains why sentient beings are unable to transcend birth and death.
Furthermore, that which undergoes the bitter fruits of saṃsāra has craving as its root. "Greed and love nourish one another" means that greed cannot be stopped;
it is called "nourishing one another" because one takes the flesh and blood of sentient beings as food to nourish one's own body.
Because one uses strength to oppress the weak and seizes them for food, it is said that killing has greed as its root. Thus...

When a person eats sheep and the like, they act as a thief and a greedy one; because the animals were not given to them yet they took them, forcibly ending their lives to consume their flesh, it constitutes theft.
You owe me my life—this is the greed of killing; I repay your debt to you—this is the greed of theft;
you love my mind and I cherish your form—this is the greed of lust. Thus, throughout successive kalpas, we have been bound together.
The three types of entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) are the root of the three karmas. By these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue in succession.
[The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) reveal the nature of delusion.
Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted continuities are all caused by the nature of the luminous clarity of awareness.
The characteristics of arising are produced from deluded vision. The various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth undergo successive flux;
because of this delusion, they end and then begin again.
The commentary states: This binds together the three kinds of deluded origins. It means that the characteristics of the three kinds of inversion do not exist inherently;
rather, they arise due to ignorance (avidyā) caused by a single moment of deluded movement from time immemorial.

Therefore, it is called "awakened clarity" (jue-ming). From this ignorance arises deluded vision; therefore, it is called the "nature of clear cognitive awareness. Due to ignorance, the object of perception is manifested.
It is from ignorance that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena arise.
Thus we know that the initial statement, "based on luminosity, the object is established," already contains within it the three types of appearances through the single word "object" (*so*).
Because deluded vision is not extinguished, saṃsāra does not cease; therefore, it begins again after having ended.
The preceding section concludes the demonstration of how delusion manifests as the false by relying upon the True.
[○@◇] Third, the demonstration that fundamentally there is no arising or ceasing, divided into two parts. [△@△] First, clinging to the false and doubting the True.

Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally wondrously enlightened and luminous, and neither increases nor decreases compared to the Tathāgata’s mind, then why have the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arisen without cause? Now that the Tathāgata has attained the wondrous, empty, luminous enlightenment..."
"When will the conditioned habitual outflows of the mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever arise again?

He deliberated, saying: "Pūrṇa has already received this instruction that from awakening to delusion, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise through the delusive falsehood of the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind.
He then wondered: 'If the Tathāgata has already realized the wondrous emptiness and luminous awakening, yet the mountains..."
When will the great earth and the rivers ever arise again? This question is raised to clarify that awakening is non-arising and that delusion is fundamentally without birth or extinction.
[△@△] The earth element is fundamentally without birth or extinction.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Suppose a person who is lost mistakes south for north in a certain village.
Does this delusion arise because of delusion, or does it emerge because of awakening? Pūrṇa replied: "Such a lost person does not arise because of delusion, nor does he arise because of awakening.
Why? Because delusion originally has no root; how could it arise because of delusion? Awakening does not give rise to delusion."

"What is meant by awakening through understanding? The Buddha said: 'When that deluded person is in the midst of delusion, suddenly there is an awakened person who points it out and causes him to awaken.
Pūrṇa, what do you think? Even though this person was previously deluded, would he become deluded again regarding this village?
No, World-Honored One. Pūrṇa, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are also like this. This delusion has no fundamental basis.'"

The nature is ultimately empty. Originally there was no delusion, yet it appeared as if there were; through awakening, delusion is extinguished, and once awakened, one no longer gives rise to delusion.
It is like a person with cataracts who sees flowers in the sky: when the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish from the sky.
Suppose a foolish person were to stand upon that very spot where the sky-flowers vanished, waiting for them to reappear. Do you consider such a person to be foolish or wise?
Pūrṇa said: "Empty space originally has no flowers; it is through deluded vision that they arise and perish. To perceive the extinction of the flowers as the emptiness itself is already a perversion.
To command them to appear again is truly madness and folly. How can such a madman be called either ignorant or wise?"

The Buddha said, "It is as you understand it. Why do you ask how the mountains, rivers, and great earth could ever emerge again from the wondrous, enlightened, luminous emptiness of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas?
It is like gold ore mixed with refined gold; once that gold is pure, it can never again become alloyed.
It is like wood turned to ash, which cannot become wood again. The Bodhi and Nirvana of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are likewise."
Thus it was.
The commentary states: Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, this question was intended to reveal that delusion and awakening share the same source and are fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

Therefore, the Tathāgata answered with four successive metaphors. The first metaphor, that of one who has lost his way, was meant to make known that he was originally not deluded and is likewise not deluded now.

Awakening: The single metaphor of flowers in the sky serves to make known that the true source is without delusion, so that awakening does not give rise to confusion. Gold symbolizes the unchanging nature of awareness;
ashes symbolize the non-arising of the fruition of virtue.
The upper [section] answers: "How could they suddenly arise? The lower [section] answers: "The four great elements mutually overcome one another.
[○@◇] Fourth, it reveals the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.
Pūrṇa, furthermore, you asked: "I have doubts regarding the nature of earth, water, fire, and wind, which is perfectly interfused and all-pervading throughout the Dharma-realm."

The natures of water and fire do not mutually overcome or extinguish one another. Furthermore, it is examined that empty space and the great earth both pervade the Dharma-realm, yet they cannot coexist within one another.
Pūrṇa, it is like this: the substance of empty space is not composed of various characteristics, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those various characteristics.
Why is this so? Pūrṇa, when the sun shines upon that great empty space, it becomes bright; when clouds gather, it becomes...

It is dark. When stirred by the wind, it moves; when clear after a rain, it is pure; when the vapors condense, it becomes turbid. When soil accumulates, it forms a haze; when water is still, it forms reflections. What do you think?
Regarding these various conditioned phenomena in different realms, do they arise because of those [conditions], or do they exist independently of them?
If they were produced by those conditions, Pūrṇa, consider this: when the sun shines, that which is bright is already the light of the sun throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
It is the same solar light; why then does one see a round sun within the sky? If this light were the illumination of space itself, space should be able to illuminate itself;

why then does it fail to produce radiance during the midnight hours when shrouded by clouds and mist? One should know that this light is neither the sun nor space, yet it is not distinct from space and the sun.
When examining these appearances, they are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described—just like seeking to gather empty flowers to form empty fruit.
How can one interrogate the meaning of their mutual subjugation and extinction? Contemplate that the fundamental nature is originally true, consisting solely of wondrous, enlightened clarity.
Since this mind of wondrous, enlightened clarity was not water or fire from the outset, why further ask how they cannot coexist? True, wondrous, enlightened clarity is likewise thus.
If you manifest through clarity in emptiness, then emptiness appears. If earth, water, fire, and wind each manifest through their own clarity, then each appears individually.
If they all manifest together, then they all appear together. How do they appear together? Pūrṇa, it is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a single body of water.
If two people look at the sun in the water together and each walks in opposite directions—east and west—the sun follows each of them respectively.
The two depart—one to the east and one to the west—without any prior fixed direction. It should not be difficult to ask:
if this day is one, how can they travel separately? Since each day is dual, how can only one appear? Thus, it is a circular and empty falsehood, with nothing upon which to rely.
The commentary states: The following parable illustrates the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*) to demonstrate the nature of the treasury of non-emptiness.

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra doubted that the natures of water and fire could coexist without one subduing or extinguishing the other, and further doubted that empty space and the great earth could fundamentally accommodate one another.
The Tathāgata raised the analogy of empty space to manifest the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle; hence it is said: "For example, the substance of empty space..."
It is not that it lacks manifold characteristics, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those various characteristics.

This analogy shows that while the wondrous enlightened nature is empty and its essence transcends all delusions, it does not hinder the appearance of phenomena according to karma. Furthermore, although characteristics such as light and darkness within space are fundamentally not space itself, they are not different from space;
thus, one knows that the manifestation of various characteristics by the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind is fundamentally not [the mind].

That wondrous clarity is not different from wondrous clarity; thus, the meaning of "not empty" is made manifest. To observe the characteristics is fundamentally delusory, while to observe the nature is fundamentally true.
It is but the single wondrous mind, which fundamentally is neither water nor fire. Why, then, do you again ask how they can be mutually exclusive?
It is because the truly wondrous awakened mind possesses vast functional activity; thus, it manifests in accordance with karma. And as for earth...
If water, fire, and wind each manifest individually, they appear individually; if they manifest together, they appear all at once.
However, as for their simultaneous appearance—like the reflection of the sun in water which moves east or west according to the person—it cannot be understood as being either one or different.
Once this is known, the doubt regarding the individual pervasiveness of these four great elements will dissolve like ice melting away.
The preceding analogy clarifies the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle.
[○@◇] Fifth, it clarifies that delusion and awakening share the same source, thereby concluding the discussion on the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle:
"Pūrṇa, you have used the characteristics of form and emptiness to oppose and supplant one another within the Tathāgatagarbha; yet the Tathāgatagarbha, in accordance with..."
Because the emptiness of form pervades the entire Dharma-realm, within it there is the movement of wind, the clarity of space, the brightness of the sun, and the darkness of clouds.
Sentient beings, deluded and distressed, turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of sensory objects; thus they give rise to worldly toil and the appearances of the mundane world.

I, however, unite my wondrous clarity—neither extinguished nor born—with the Tathāgata-garbha. And this Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, awakened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm. This is...
Therefore, within this state, the one becomes the immeasurable and the immeasurable becomes the one. The small manifests the large, and the large manifests the small.

Without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one pervades the worlds of the ten directions; the body contains the inexhaustible space of the ten directions. Within the tip of a single hair, one manifests jeweled king-lands;
sitting inside a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel. By extinguishing the dust of delusion and merging with awakening, one gives rise to the wondrous True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the "nature of awakened clarity," the commentary states: This section reveals the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle, while implicitly indicating the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.

That is to say, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally perfect, pervasive, and all-encompassing; yet, if it is confronted by the shifting and displacing of form and emptiness, it follows along with form and emptiness to pervade all dharmas.

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): the pervasiveness of phenomena is itself the pervasiveness of principle. It is only because sentient beings are deluded and distressed, failing to awaken and instead turning their backs on enlightenment to unite with sensory dust, that they give rise to worldly toil and the appearances of the mundane world. This serves to manifest the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle.
I, through my wondrous clarity—neither arising nor ceasing—unify with the Tathāgata-garbha; and this Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating all phenomena.

Because the realms [are thus], the one and the many can contain one another; the small and the large can encompass one another. A world-system appears on the tip of a hair; a wheel-turning monarch moves within a speck of dust.

This is truly because, by extinguishing the dust of phenomena and merging with awakening, the wondrously enlightened nature of true suchness (tathatā) is manifested. This illustrates the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (shishi wuai).
