Ānanda, if, at the causal ground, one takes a mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation, [the result will be that of a śrāvaka].
And to seek the Buddha-vehicle while [clinging to] that which is neither born nor extinguished—such a thing is impossible.

For this reason, you should illuminate how all conditioned phenomena within the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) are subject to transformation and extinction. Ānanda, observe the conditioned phenomena of the world:
what among them is not subject to decay? Yet, one never hears of empty space (ākāśa) rotting or decaying. Why is this? Because space is not something that can be...
It is so because, from beginning to end, there is neither destruction nor cessation.
Second, the section showing the object of contemplation is divided into three parts. First, showing the source of arising and ceasing.
Thus, within your body, that which has the characteristic of solidity is earth; moisture is water; the sensation of warmth is fire; and movement is wind.
Due to these four entanglements, they divide your profoundly still, perfect, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
From beginning to end, the five turbidities are intermingled.
◎ Second, the analogy for the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
What constitutes turbidity? Ānanda, it is like clear water, which is pure by nature; yet when dust, soil, ash, and sand [are cast into it],...
The essential nature of these categories is characterized by obstruction and resistance. Their two natures are such that they do not accord with one another.

Suppose there were a person in the world who took soil-dust from that land and threw it into pure water; the soil would lose its obstructive nature and the water would lose its clarity, their appearances becoming turbid, which is called "turbidity.
Your five layers of turbidity are likewise thus.

The commentary states: From this point downward, the text correctly demonstrates the source of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*). First, it establishes two definitive meanings to inspire the initial resolve for enlightenment.

Intending to demonstrate the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing as the fundamental cause of cultivation, it first presents the characteristics of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) of arising and ceasing.
The underlying purpose is to realize the unarisen within arising and ceasing itself, and to realize the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) themselves.
The reason sentient beings are deluded and inverted is truly because they mistake the One Mind for the karmic consciousness; they rely on the perceived and the perceiver to constitute form and mind;
and they rely on form and mind to give rise to the five aggregates. From this, they falsely differentiate the realms of the sense organs, their objects, and consciousness.

The five aggregates alone constitute the root of birth and death. Now, as one seeks to turn back from delusion and return to truth, there is no ground for cultivation other than these five aggregates of body and mind.
Therefore, contemplating the five aggregates serves as the gateway to entering the Way; it is like rising from the very spot where one fell on the ground.
The previous investigation of the mind and discernment of the faculty of sight were refutations intended to dismantle [false attachments].

These five aggregates (skandhas) of body and mind are merely illusory. Yet, when they are traced back to their ultimate source in the hidden nature (tathāgatagarbha), the five aggregates must be taken as the primary point of departure.

For sentient beings in the continuity of rebirth, the five aggregates constitute the root of suffering. Therefore, in the present practice of cultivation, one must necessarily contemplate the illusory characteristics of the five aggregates to set out upon the path.
Furthermore, the final instruction regarding the demons of the aggregates (skandhamāra) arises precisely from this contemplation of the five aggregates.

Because they do not grasp its subtle essence, they fall under the sway of Māra. This text summarizes and demonstrates the limits of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) so that one may know where to find refuge.
This is the fundamental intent of the Buddha’s appearance in the world and his preaching of the Dharma: specifically to shatter the five-aggregate body and mind of sentient beings.
Since this alone is complete and exhaustive within this sutra, it ensures that those who contemplate it must first attain its essential core.
Thus, both principle and contemplation will each have their point of convergence. At the beginning of the World-Honored One’s permission to speak, he said:
"Regarding the wondrous *samādhi* of the Buddha-Tathāgata, do not give rise to weariness.
This was because he initially permitted that there is a *samādhi* named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King. Now, first admonish [the assembly] not to [be weary of] this great concentration.

It merely gives rise to weariness. Using this as evidence, it is beyond doubt that what was previously revealed as the principle constitutes the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), while what is now explained as the gate of practice constitutes the characteristics of contemplation.
Regarding the "two definitive meanings"—that which is certain and unalterable—they are: first, examining the arousal of the mind in the causal stage;
second, examining the root of afflictions (*kleśa*). The intent is that if one enters illumination through the cessation of arising and ceasing, then...

It is truly eternal in the present moment. If one knows the root of the afflictions, they will be resolved as easily as a blade cutting through wood. There is no essential point for cultivation more urgent than this.
Therefore, it is made necessary to examine carefully whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening of the resultant stage.
The intention is to take the awakening of the resultant stage as the fundamental cause-mind; it is certainly not a mind subject to birth and extinction that can accord with it.
Arising and ceasing are the fruit. Therefore, it causes one to illuminate that all phenomena of arising and ceasing in the world possess a nature of disintegration;
only empty space is indestructible because it is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*). This precisely points to unconditioned wondrous practice as the root.
Furthermore, that which is neither arising nor ceasing is the perfectly湛 (zhàn) [profoundly still], wondrous, pure, and clear true mind. It is solely because of...
The initial moment of deluded movement constitutes ignorance (*avidyā*). This subsequently manifests as the perceived object, forming the false colors of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Thereupon, deluded views arise, and one grasps these four elements to form a body.

Bound by these four entanglements, the perfectly luminous and wondrous mind is divided into seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, thereby becoming a sentient being of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). It is, for example, like this:
When clear, cold water is cast with ashes, sand, dust, or soil, it becomes turbid and undifferentiated.
It is from this that the cause of the impurity of these five aggregates arises.
◎ Third, a specific explanation of arising and ceasing.
Ānanda, you see that empty space pervades the worlds of the ten directions, yet the emptiness and the seeing are not distinguished.

There is emptiness but no substance; there is seeing but no awareness. These interweave to form delusion. This is the first layer, called the *kalpa-turbidity*. Your body is currently composed of the four great elements as its substance;
seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are congested and obstructed, while water, fire, wind, and earth cause these faculties to revolve in their perceptions. These interweave.

These delusions are established; this second layer is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Furthermore, within your mind, memory, cognition, recitation, and study give rise to the nature of knowing and seeing, which allows the six sense objects to appear.
Apart from the objects there are no signs (*nimitta*); apart from perception there is no nature. These signs and perceptions interweave to form delusion;
this third layer is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Moreover, your life arises and ceases incessantly morning and evening; your knowing and seeing are thus constantly retained.
In this world, the course of karma constantly shifts across the lands, interweaving to form delusions; this is the fourth layer, called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
You all see and hear without any difference in fundamental nature, yet various dust-like phenomena obstruct one another, giving rise to unaccountable differences.

Within their nature they recognize one another, yet in their functions they turn away from one another. Standards of identity and difference are lost, as they interweave to form delusions; this is the fifth layer, named...

Regarding the "impurity of lifespan" (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*): The commentary states that the preceding section generally reveals the source of the arising and ceasing of the five impurities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), while the following section specifically demonstrates the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the five impurities.

Now, as for the statement that the five impurities are established based upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the intended meaning is that within the pure realm (*viśuddha-dhātu*), there are fundamentally no sentient beings.
How could there be such things as the kalpa-view afflictions or the turbidity of sentient beings' lives?

It is solely because one is deluded regarding the fundamental original luminosity, binding it into form and mind to become a sentient being of the five aggregates; thus, the true mind becomes thoroughly turbid, and the five kinds of delusive appearances arise.
Regarding the appearance of emptiness woven into the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), this is explained by way of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
This refers to the *kalpa-kāṣāya* (the turbidity of the eon). *Kalpa* is a Sanskrit term; *kāṣāya* translates as "time-period," a designation for a long duration.
Furthermore, to clarify this based on the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), one should speak of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) being mutually entangled.

However, the present explanation is given in terms of the view of emptiness (*ākāśa-dṛṣṭi*), because at the very beginning of delusion, empty space arises as the substance of form, which is what is first grasped by false perception. Therefore...
Due to stubborn emptiness (*ākāśa*), the true mind becomes turbid and gives rise to deluded views. This view absorbs the characteristics of emptiness;
over time, these coalesce into form (*rūpa*), thereby forming both form and mind. Because this obscures the true mind, one explains the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) by means of emptiness.
Regarding the interweaving of these elements, from the perspective of their meaning, it refers simply to a dense entanglement that remains inseparable. This is because...
In terms of the incessant arising and ceasing [of phenomena], there is the sense of being "woven together. This is not like the weaving of warp and weft as understood in the mundane world.

Regarding the phrase "the distinction between emptiness and vision is not made": this refers to delusion. When one mistakes wondrous emptiness for dull emptiness, emptiness is fundamentally pervasive.
When one mistakes wondrous clarity for false vision, vision is likewise pervasive. Because these two delusions merge and become one, it is so stated.
They are not distinguished. Furthermore, emptiness is fundamentally the substantial reality of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and seeing is fundamentally the wondrous awakening of perfect clarity.
Now that these have become confused and merged due to delusion, it is exactly like throwing ash and soil into clear water; thus, both are lost.
Consequently, there is only emptiness without the true substance, and only seeing without true awakening. From these two...
Because the marks of false arising and ceasing entangle one such that matter and mind come into being, this constitutes the beginning of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

It is called the "impurity of the eon" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) because within the originally pure realm there was fundamentally no time; now, from the very moment matter and mind first assemble, it becomes the basis for long duration.
Thus, based on the aggregate of form, it is named the impurity of the eon. Your present body is a composite of the four great elements.
Regarding the statement that "the view-affliction (dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya) refers to the aggregate of sensation," this view is the deluded view grasped by the five consciousnesses.

As for the identification of the four great elements and the six sense organs as the view-affliction, it is because one falsely identifies the four great elements as the characteristics of one's own body;
this constitutes a deluded view. The intent is to say that your physical body is fundamentally non-existent; rather—
Manifestly grasping the four great elements to form a body, you have consequently obstructed the wondrous, luminous mind, causing it to become stagnant and hindered.
This divides it into seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, which become separated and fail to communicate. Furthermore, those four great elements are originally devoid of cognition;

now, by confining the conscious mind within them, you cause that which was originally non-cognitive to appear as if it possessed cognition. Thus, you grasp at and accept it as a self. Because there is no...
Know that cognition is cast within the sphere of cognitive views, while awareness permeates the midst of non-cognition.
Their own characteristics are turbid, and their arising and ceasing never cease. Through deluded vision, one clings to this as the faculty of experience (*upabhoga-indriya*).

Because one falsely perceives these appropriated material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) within the pure mind, it is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) based upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Furthermore, you—
The so-called "turbidity of afflictions" (kleśa-kaṣāya) regarding the mental consciousness and its recitations refers to what is established upon the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
Perception is the deluded conceptualization of the six consciousnesses; the nature of affliction is empty, and this deluded conceptualization is fundamentally non-existent.
However, due to the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of past events that you have constantly recited and familiarized within your mind, they suddenly surge from within.
When one intends to know or perceive an object, it arises from the activation of past habitual tendencies; thus it is said that "nature gives rise to knowledge and vision.
Following these deluded thoughts, the sensory objects being contemplated appear with distinct forms within the deluded mind.
This is what is meant by falsely identifying the shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind; hence it is said that "the six [sense-fields] appear in form."
Dust. Yet this deluded thought exists only by depending on dust; apart from dust, it has no substantial reality. Apart from cognition, it utterly lacks self-nature.

Because this deluded thought arises and ceases without ceasing, it disturbs the pure mind; therefore, based on the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), it is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Furthermore, that which does not cease day or night within your mind is called a sentient being (*sattva*).
"Turbidity" is established based on the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). This means that these sentient beings originally do not exist;
yet, because your deluded thoughts arise and cease without ceasing, and because your perceptions and views constantly desire to remain in the world, you create karma from moment to moment.
Furthermore, the power of good and evil karma flows and transforms from moment to moment within the twelve classes of beings.

Because arising and departing, birth and death constitute the very basis of sentient beings, they turbidify the true mind; therefore, based on the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), this is called the "impurity of beings" (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

When you perceive and hear that there is originally no difference in their nature, this is termed the "impurity of life span" (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*), which is established based on the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). However, this...
The life-faculty has no fundamental existence. This is because your original, single, wondrously perfect true mind fundamentally lacks any characteristics of sameness or difference.

It is simply because the four elements have become obstructed and partitioned that the nature of consciousness is divided into seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; thus, the various sensory objects are separated and distinct, giving rise to unaccountable differences.
Yet, within the essential nature they are originally one body, and therefore they know one another; this is the function of the six sense organs.
Because they are partitioned and separated, they oppose one another; thus, their sameness lacks any fixed sameness, and their difference lacks any distinct difference.

Both lose their standard of reference. This consciousness maintains and sustains matter and mind as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); sameness and difference become turbid and interwoven, falsely forming [existence].
Therefore, based on this aggregate of consciousness, it is called the turbidity of life. To trace these five turbidities back to their source, they originate within the wondrously perfect mind.
In the midst, there is originally nothing at all; it is merely because the true mind is turbid due to the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates that it becomes defiled.
These are all the sources of delusion and falsehood. Therefore, what follows below explains the practice of contemplation by means of returning to the truth from delusion.
[?︽] Third, the section showing the causes of contemplative practice is divided into three parts. ◎ First, clarifying that the cause is true and the fruit is correct:

"Ānanda, if you now wish to cause your seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to reach far in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, you should first select the root of birth and death, and establish yourself upon the nature of the non-arising, non-ceasing, perfect, and profound stillness. By means of this stillness, turn back its false delusions."

Extinguishing birth and subduing [delusion] to return to original enlightenment; attaining the nature of original luminous enlightenment, which is free from arising and ceasing, as the mind for the stage of the cause, and subsequently achieving the full realization of the stage of fruition.
◎ Second, the two analogies for the depth and shallowness of severing delusions, divided into two parts. [□@(?(○/(○*○)))] First, the analogy for gradual severance.

It is like turbid water placed in a clean vessel; when it is still, deep, and unmoving, the sand and soil naturally settle, and the clear water appears before one—this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).
[□@(?(○/(○*○))] The two metaphors for sudden severance: removing the mud so that only pure water remains is called the permanent severance of fundamental ignorance.

When the three fetters are truly exhausted and delusions are eradicated, the luminous signs become pure and refined; all transformations and manifestations no longer constitute afflictions, as they all accord with the wondrous virtue of the purity of nirvana.
The commentary states: This briefly demonstrates the characteristics of contemplative practice (*guanxing*).

The intent is that, wishing to cause turbid awareness to remotely accord with the wondrous virtue of the purity of *nirvāṇa*, one should first select the root of birth and death. "Select" (*zhe*) means to pluck out.
One should rely exclusively upon the nature of non-arising and non-extinction to revolve the arising and extinction. "Revolve" (*xuan*) is like a whirlpool, as in the swirling of water.

"Subduing" (*fu*) means that in every thought-moment one whirls away from delusion to return to the truth. One subdues the returning primordial awakening and takes the primordial luminous awakening as the mind for the causal stage.
Only by doing so can one perfectly accomplish the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage. Thus, it is like settling turbid water until clear water appears;
this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions, which is a gradual severance. When the mud is removed, [the water] is pure.

The water is named "the permanent severance of the root of ignorance," which refers to this sudden cutting off. Upon the final moment of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one is about to enter the Subtle [State].
When reality is fully exhausted and delusions are utterly ended, one then accords with the pure and wondrous virtues of *nirvāṇa*.
This is due to the power of the practice of contemplation based on the mind that is neither arising nor ceasing.
[□@○] Section Two: Examining the Fundamental Intent of Afflictions and Distinguishing the Perfect Faculties, divided into six parts.
[?︽] First, the command to examine in detail.
Second, the meaning: "If you all truly desire to give rise to the bodhicitta, you must generate great courage and resolve toward the Bodhisattva Vehicle."
One must resolutely abandon all conditioned marks (*saṃskṛta-nimitta*). One should carefully examine the root of afflictions (*kleśa-mūla*):
since beginningless time, who has produced karma and moistened rebirth, and who has received [the results]?

Ānanda, if you cultivate Bodhi without carefully observing the root of afflictions, you will not be able to know where the false roots and objects (*viṣaya*) are inverted. If you do not even know their location, how can you...?
Subduing [defilements], one attains the stage of Tathāgata.
Second, directly pointing to the root of the knot:
Ānanda, when you observe a person in the world who unties a knot, if they do not see what was knotted, how could they know how to untie it? You have not heard this.
"Then empty space would be torn asunder by you. Why? Because space has no form or appearance, and thus it is neither bound nor liberated.
Yet your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these six serve as the intermediaries for thieves who plunder the family’s treasures.
Because of this, sentient beings have been entangled in bondage since beginningless time, and thus they are unable to transcend the vessel-world."

The commentary states: This examines the root of afflictions (*kleśa*). The "activation of karma" refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), while the "moistening of rebirth" refers to the two delusions of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).
Birth and death truly exist because of these two; they are collectively termed "afflictions.

However, when these two types are distinguished according to their basis, it means that these two dharmas originally have no substantial reality, but merely depend upon the six consciousnesses as false [constructions].

Perception functions as an instrument; therefore, at the gates of the six sense organs, the apprehension of objects through their corresponding sensory fields is entirely the activity of ignorance, serving to support craving and grasping.

Consequently, in every thought-moment there is craving and grasping, and in every place there is greedy attachment. Birth and death are bound within the interaction of the sense organs and their objects.
Therefore, one must carefully discern where the delusions regarding these false sense organs and objects arise, for it is through the mutual intersection of the organs and objects that they occur.
The place where the knots are tied is the place of perversion; it is the very locus of the root of birth and death. If one wishes to untie the knots, one must untie them at their root.
Therefore, one examines the relative superiority or inferiority of the six faculties, intending to select the faculty that is most perfect, for it is empty and easy to untie.
This is why the selection process is employed. Before selecting the perfect faculty, the relative superiority of the six faculties is first demonstrated.
I merely wish to let those of inferior capacity know what has been selected.
Third, to reveal that the causes of the faculties are woven from delusion:
Ānanda, what is meant by the "world of sentient beings"? "World" refers to the flow of time; "realm" refers to spatial directions. You now—
One should know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the directions (*diś*).

The past, future, and present constitute the time periods (*adhvan*). There are ten spatial orientations and three temporal flows. All sentient beings, through the interweaving of delusive ignorance, construct these realms;
within their bodies, they trade and migrate as worlds intersect one another. Although the nature of these realms is established across the ten directions, its position is fixed.
It should be understood that in the world, there are only the directions of east, west, south, and north; above and below have no fixed positions, and the center has no determinate direction.
These four numbers must be clearly understood as interacting with the world: three times four and four times three result in twelve when turned over.
Flowing and transforming through three cycles—ten, hundred, and thousand—they encompass the beginning and the end. Within each of the six sense organs, there are thus one thousand two hundred merits.
[?︽] Fourth, revealing that the power and function are not equal, divided into six parts. ◎ First, the eye faculty:
Ānanda, you should further determine the relative superiority and inferiority among them. For example, when the eye sees, it is dark behind and bright in front;
the front is entirely bright, while the back is entirely dark; looking to the left and right, it covers two-thirds of the field. If one considers the total merit produced by its function:
It is not complete. Three parts consist of functional merit; one part is devoid of virtue. You should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits.
◎ Second is the faculty of hearing.

Just as the ear listens all around to the ten directions without omission—whether movement is near or far, and in stillness it is boundless—one should contemplate the emptiness of the faculty of hearing.
This fulfills one thousand two hundred merits.
◎ Second is the nose faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*).

Just as the nose smells, its function extends through both inhalation and exhalation; yet while there is out-breathing and in-breathing, the intermediate junction is missing. This is verified by examining the nose faculty.
Lacking one-third, it should be known that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits.
◎ Fourth is the tongue faculty.
Just as the tongue proclaims all mundane and supramundane wisdom, its expression has distinct divisions while its principle is inexhaustible.
One should know that the tongue faculty is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits.
◎ Fifth, the body faculty:
as the body perceives touch, it cognizes what is disagreeable and agreeable; it can perceive when there is contact, but does not know when separated. Separation is single, while contact is dual.
Examining the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it lacks one of its three parts; thus, one should know that the body possesses only eight hundred merits.
◎ Regarding the six mental faculties (*manendriya*):
as with the mind, they silently accommodate all mundane and supramundane phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time, whether pertaining to the noble ones or the ordinary.
There is nothing it does not encompass, reaching to the very limits of all things. You should know that the faculty of mind is perfected with one thousand two hundred merits.
[5] Fifth, the Selection of the Perfect Faculty.

Ānanda, if you now wish to go against the current of the flow of birth and death, to turn back and exhaust the root of that flow until you reach the state of non-arising and non-ceasing, you must examine these six faculties of sensory reception:
which are conjoined and which are separated; which are deep and which are shallow; which constitute perfect penetration and which are not yet complete.
If you can, through this, awaken to the faculty of perfect penetration, you will be able to go against that beginningless flow of deluded karmic activity and follow [the path of liberation].

"O Yuantong, those with non-perfect faculties differ from you by factors of ten million times a kalpa. I have now fully revealed that the quantity of the fundamental merits of the six profound, perfect, and luminous faculties is thus.
Choose from among them according to your own discernment that which you can enter; I shall then clarify it for you so that you may advance."
[?︽] By deeply entering through the single gate of the six *āsras*,
the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all attained the perfect and unsurpassed Bodhi by practicing within each of the eighteen realms (*dhātus*).
Within this, there is neither superiority nor inferiority; it is only that you are of inferior capacity and have not yet attained sovereign wisdom therein.
Therefore, I proclaim this so that you may enter deeply through a single gate; once you have entered one without delusion, those six faculties of cognition will simultaneously become pure.
The commentary states: This demonstrates the relative superiority and inferiority of the six sense faculties.

The preceding passage stated that because sentient beings give rise to entanglements within the world, they are unable to transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). Thus, we know that what is called the "sentient-being world" refers specifically to the body as the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
As for what is termed "world," "world" (*loka*) refers to the shifting flow of deluded thoughts, while "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to a single [unit of existence].

Because the body possesses left, right, front, and back, it constitutes a realm (*dhātu*). As soon as a single thought arises, it naturally flows on, and thus the three periods of time (*adhvan*) emerge.
Although there are ten directions, only the four cardinal directions are mentioned; these three periods and four directions are observed solely with respect to a single body.
Therefore, it is said that within the body there is exchange and transition, for the realms and the periods intersect with one another.

This refers to what is called the mutual formation of the woven delusions. "Three and four, four and three, winding around to twelve" means that within a single thought-moment, the Dharma-nature naturally encompasses all three periods of time and pervades the entirety of the body.
Without departing from the four directions of left, right, front, and back, each direction possesses its own three periods; thus, these "three and four" constitute the twelve. As for those four:
When all things are completely permeated by a single thought-moment, each world possesses four directions; these four sets of three constitute the twelve.
Because they are interwoven in this manner, it is called "revolving. Initially, a single thought-moment constitutes one layer, totaling only twelve.
When deluded thoughts undergo further transformation, the preceding thought has already ceased while the succeeding thought continues to arise. This is the ultimate...

It is extremely subtle. Because the first arising of a single thought-moment has no origin, and because this single thought-moment already encompasses the three periods of time and flows through the four directions, it constitutes twelve. This is the first layer. As for the second layer:
within each of the three periods of time in the eastern direction, there is one fundamental [thought] for each period, totaling thirty; thus, the four directions together total one hundred.
Twenty times [ten] makes one hundred; this is the second layer. As for the third layer, taking those one hundred and twenty and adding ten to each, one reaches one thousand two hundred;
this is the third layer. By applying the worldly analogy of spatial dimensions, these boundaries can be understood.
As for the initial single thought-moment not establishing a fundamental basis, it is because it arises from the "basis of non-abiding" to establish that one.
Because all phenomena are thus. Nevertheless, the subtle flow of deluded thoughts of arising and ceasing continues:

it is said that within one thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) there are ninety *kṣaṇas*, and within one *kṣaṇa* there are nine hundred instances of arising and ceasing. In reality, these moments continue inexhaustibly throughout kalpas.
Now, I speak of them merely by way of three cycles, referring to the natural transition of phenomena within a single moment of arising and ceasing.
The "flows" (āsrava) encompass all three periods of time; even if one were to exhaust an entire kalpa, they would still only be described as the three periods of time.

Therefore, by taking the root-body of arising and ceasing as the basis, the functional activities of the six sense organs are clarified. Each of these fundamentally possesses a capacity of twelve hundred functions.
It is simply by way of whether the sense-faculties are pervasive or non-pervasive, and whether they are complete or incomplete, that their relative strength and function are determined.
If the eye-faculty sees what is before it but cannot see what is behind it—due to its functional inability to reach those areas—it lacks one-third and possesses only eight hundred [units].
The ear, however, hears completely throughout the ten directions; thus, it is fully endowed with twelve hundred. As for the nose, it is distinguished by its inhalation and exhalation...
When the breath is deficient in its middle function, it likewise amounts to only eight hundred; when the tongue proclaims the wondrous principles, it is complete with one thousand two hundred.
When the body is separated from objects, it does not perceive them and thus likewise amounts to only eight hundred;
