He exerted himself so intensely that he lost his sight from lack of sleep. By practicing according to the instructions, he subsequently attained the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

As for "not seeing the ten directions by means of the eyes," this refers to clarity not following the sense-faculties. When clarity arises spontaneously, then all appearances of darkness can never again obscure it.
[△@○] Second, the faculty of the nose.
Cūḍapanthaka rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I lack the capacity for recitation and retention, and am devoid of the nature of great learning.
Yet, when I first encountered the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and left the household life, I was able to remember and maintain even a single verse of the Tathāgata."

“...Dharmatrāta. For one hundred days, I was able to leave the former behind when grasping the latter, and leave the latter behind when grasping the former. The Buddha, out of compassion for my folly, instructed me to dwell in retreat and regulate the inhalation and exhalation.

At that time, I contemplated the breath until it became subtle and reached its limit; I perceived the moments (*kṣaṇa*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
My mind suddenly opened up and attained great non-obstruction. Eventually, with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), I became an Arhat and sat upon the Buddha’s seat.”

By forming the lower seal, one attains the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). When the Buddha inquired about the perfect penetration (*pariṇāmanā*), I replied that according to what I have realized, reversing the breath to follow emptiness is the foremost method.
The commentary states: this is entry by means of the faculty of the nose (*ghrāṇendriya*). Cūḍapanthaka is translated here as "Snake Slave."
He was also called Jidao (Successor of the Way) because he was born by the side of a road. His nature was extremely dull and obtuse;

because in a previous life he had been a Dharma Master who was stingy with the Buddha-dharma, he received this retribution of stupidity. When five hundred bhikṣus taught him a single verse together, he could not memorize it even after ninety days.
The World-Honored One instructed him to cease his distracted thoughts and observe the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, whereupon he finally attained the mind [of concentration].
"Open. [This refers to] returning the breath to follow emptiness, thereby departing from inhalation and exhalation.
[△@○] Third, the faculty of the tongue.
Kauṇḍinya immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I possess karmic activity of the mouth."
In past kalpas, I treated śramaṇas with contempt; consequently, in birth after birth and life after life, I suffered from the ailment of eructation (*go-mukha*).
The Tathāgata showed me the Dharma-gate of the Single Flavor of the Pure Mind-Ground. Having attained this, I extinguished the mind and entered *samādhi*.

I contemplated that the cognition of flavors is neither a substance nor a thing. Instantly, I transcended all worldly outflows (*āsrava*); internally, I was liberated from body and mind, and externally, I cast off the world.
I have distanced myself from the three realms of existence, like a bird escaping its cage. Free from defilement and with dust extinguished, my Dharma-eye is pure, and I have become an Arhat.

The Tathāgata personally certified me as having attained the path of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I replied: "As I have realized it, I turned back the sense of taste and returned to the faculty of cognition."
This is the first. The commentary says:
This enters through the faculty of the tongue. Kauṇḍinya (translated here as "ox-chewer") experienced a retribution corresponding to his habit of chewing like an ox.
When neither body nor object exists, then both faculty and sense-object are forgotten; thus, he was internally liberated.
The body and mind cast the external world aside.
[△@○] Fourth, the faculty of the body.
Pilinga-vatsa immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first set forth..."

My mind turned toward the Buddha and entered the Path. Having frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of the many things in the world that are not to be relished, I went into the city to beg for alms while contemplating the Dharma-gate.
Unaware of it, a poisonous thorn on the road pierced my foot, causing my entire body to ache.
I reflected: "I possess consciousness that knows this deep pain; though I am aware of the pain, the awareness is pure, and within the awareness there is no pain. I further reflected:
"Reflecting thus, how could there be two perceptions within this single body? Before long, having gathered his mindfulness, his body and mind suddenly became empty.

Within twenty-one days, all outflows were exhausted and he became an Arhat. Having received the personal seal of approval, he realized the state of No-more-learning. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied:
'According to what I have realized, pure awareness leaving the body—this is the foremost.'"

The commentary states: This enters through the faculty of the body. Pilinguṇavatsa—translated here as "residual habit"—formerly was a Brahmin and possessed many habits of pride, such as when he insulted the river deity, calling her a "little slave.
When he first entered the Path, hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the worldly dharmas of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, he said: "It cannot be..."
Pleasurable matters: when one contemplates the Dharma-gate with the mind, not realizing that a poisonous thorn has pierced the foot on the road is a painful matter.

I contemplate that the body possesses cognition and thus knows this deep pain; although there is cognitive awareness that perceives this deep pain, upon reflecting back, the cognizing mind is pure and devoid of pain—there is nothing that can cause pain to this cognizing mind. This is what is called "pure cognition" (*viśuddha-vijñāna*).
The relinquishing of the body. [△@○] The five faculties of the mind.
Subhūti then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "For kalpas as vast as the void, my mind..."
He attained unimpededness and recollected his own births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. From the moment he was first in his mother’s womb, he knew emptiness and stillness;
thus it continued until the ten directions became empty, and he also enabled sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness.

Having been inspired by the Tathāgata to awaken to the true emptiness of their nature, and through the perfect clarity of this emptiness, they attained arhatship. They suddenly entered the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness, becoming one with it.

The Buddha’s seal of knowledge and vision achieves the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Liberation is the emptiness of intrinsic nature; I am supreme. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, that which I have realized is this:
all phenomena enter into non-existence, and as even that "non-existence" is exhausted, the dharmas revolve back to the ultimate non-being. This is the foremost.
The commentary says: This enters through the faculty of mind (*manas*). Subhūti is here called "Born of Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-ja*) and also "Well-Appeared" (*Sujāta*);
at the time of his birth, all storehouses were empty, and he took the understanding of emptiness as supreme.

Because he had long known the quiescence of emptiness, upon hearing from the Buddha that the nature of awareness is true emptiness, he attained awakening. To say that he shares the same knowledge and vision as the Buddha refers to this.

The principle of emptiness as observed by the Buddha is partially shared [with other beings], yet it is not entirely identical. "The negation of the object of negation is exhausted" means that even the negation directed toward that which is to be negated is itself exhausted.
[Symbol] The three [realms] and six consciousnesses are divided into six. [Symbol] First, visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind and vision have been pure.

I have taken birth as many times as there are sands in the Ganges River; whether worldly or supramundane, all manner of transformations I have seen have been understood at once, and I have attained freedom from obstruction.
On the road, I encountered the brothers Kāśyapa, who were traveling together and proclaiming..."

He explained the causal conditions: having awakened to the boundlessness of the mind, he left the household life under the Buddha. Perceiving that enlightened clarity was perfect and complete, he attained great fearlessness and became an Arhat.
He was the eldest son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by birth from the Dharma. When the Buddha asked about the most perfect penetration, he replied:
"As I have realized it, the mind and vision emit light, and this light reaches the ultimate limit of knowing and seeing; this is the foremost."
The commentary states: This enters through the eye-consciousness. Śāriputra—here translated as "Sparrow Son"—is a name derived from his mother’s surname.
Since vast eons past, his mental vision has been pure, indicating that his past causes were already profound.

The various transformations of the mundane and supramundane realms refer to the dharmas of arising and ceasing within the Four Noble Truths. When his mental vision emits light, that light reaches the ultimate limit of knowing and seeing.
That is to say, it is not a cognition or vision arising from the objects of the preceding sense-fields.
[△@○] Second, the Ear-consciousness.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have already, in the past, together with..."

The Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are my Dharma princes. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct those bodhisattvas among their disciples who possess the requisite faculties to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra, and it is from me that they receive their names.
World-Honored One, with my mental hearing, I discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings.
If, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, there is a single sentient being who brings forth the illumination of Samantabhadra within their mind—
"O Practitioner, at that time I mounted a six-tusked elephant and manifested hundreds of thousands of bodies, all arriving at that place.
Even if their obstructions were so deep they could not see me, I would secretly stroke their heads and provide protection and consolation, causing them to achieve success.
The Buddha asks about the perfection of penetration; I speak of its fundamental cause: the illumination of the mind-hearing, through which discernment becomes sovereign. This is it."
First, the commentary says:

This enters through the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). To traverse the entire Dharma-realm is called "Universal" (*pu*); to occupy a station adjacent to the ultimate sages is called "Worthy" (*xian*).
If it were the ear-consciousness making distinctions, there would be limits; now, because one hears with the mind, the mind is all-pervading.
It is heard throughout the ten directions and pervades the entire Dharma-realm. This is because all the knowledge and views of sentient beings do not transcend this mind;
therefore, one is able to discern each and every thing. However, anyone whose mind accords with the practice of Samantabhadra is immediately embraced and protected.
Because hearing occurs through the mind, such discernment is sovereign and free.
[△@○] Second, regarding nose-consciousness:
Sundarananda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first left home and followed the Buddha into the Way, although I was fully possessed of the precepts, my mind was constantly distracted and agitated within samādhi, and I had not yet attained [liberation]."
"Leakage! The World-Honored One taught me and Cūḍapanthaka to contemplate the white [light] at the tip of the nose.

When I first contemplated it earnestly for twenty-one days, I saw the breath entering and exiting the nostrils like smoke. My body and mind became inwardly luminous, and the world became a transparent void, as pure and clear as lapis lazuli.

As the appearance of smoke gradually vanished, the breath in the nostrils became white. My mind opened and the outflows were exhausted. Thus he spoke regarding the various inhalations and exhalations.
The breath transformed into radiance that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, and I attained Arhatship. The World-Honored One prophesied that I would attain Bodhi.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied: "By means of the cessation and emergence of breath, after a long time of stillness, luminosity arose; this luminosity became perfectly pervasive and extinguished all outflows. This is the foremost."
The commentary states: This [practice] enters through the nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*). Sundarananda—translated here as "Glorious Joy"—was so named after his wife;

he was the Buddha’s own younger brother. At the beginning of his renunciation, because his mind was distracted and agitated, the Buddha instructed him to contemplate the white [spot] at the tip of the nose.
Thus, by fixing the mind there, it does not engage with external攀缘 (pān-yuan, objective conditions or attachments); for this reason, it relies upon the nose-consciousness.

Furthermore, the previous counting of breaths relied merely upon the sense faculties. Now, as the various inhalations and exhalations are transformed into radiance because they have detached from consciousness, the light of the mind surges forth, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
[△@○] Fourth, the tongue-consciousness.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Since the distant past, my eloquence has been unimpeded. I have proclaimed suffering and emptiness, profoundly penetrating the true mark of reality.
Thus, even regarding the secret dharma-gates of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I am able to provide subtle and wondrous elucidations within the assembly, attaining fearlessness.
The World-Honored One knew that I possessed great eloquence; He instructed me with the wheel of sound to bring it forth.

In the presence of the Buddha, I assisted the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma, and through this lion’s roar, I attained arhatship. The World-Honored One certified my teaching of the Dharma as unsurpassed.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties. I replied, "By means of the sound of the Dharma, I subdue demonic adversaries and extinguish all outflows;
this is the foremost. The commentary states: This is one who enters through the consciousness of the tongue. Pūrṇa is translated here as "Full";
Maitrāyaṇī is translated as "Compassionate One," which was her mother's title. Having possessed unimpeded eloquence since remote kalpas, she—

Because their past causes were already profound, they were able to reach the true nature (*dharmatā*) upon hearing the teachings on suffering, emptiness, the Four Noble Truths, and the laws of arising and ceasing;
this is what is called a subtle and wondrous revelation. By proclaiming the sublime Dharma with their faculty of tongue-consciousness, they attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*);
this is what is called skillfully understanding the meaning of the Dharma and attaining realization in accordance with what is taught.
[△@○] Fifth, the consciousness of the body.
Upāli immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I personally followed the Buddha when he left the city to renounce the world;
I personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity; I personally saw the Tathāgata subdue all the māras and..."
All those non-Buddhists, having liberated themselves from worldly greed and the outflows (*āsrava*), received the Buddha’s teachings and precepts;

thus, they became pure in all three thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand subtle categories of both positive and prohibitive actions. With body and mind stilled, they attained the state of Arhat.
I am the leader of the Tathāgata’s assembly; my own mind has been personally sealed by him. Among the multitude who uphold the precepts and cultivate the person...
I rank this as supreme. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied: "By grasping the body, I attained mastery over the body;
by gradually grasping the mind, I attained thorough penetration of the mind. Thereafter, both body and mind became entirely unimpeded and sharp. This is why I consider it the foremost."

The commentary states: This refers to those who enter [the path] through body-consciousness. Upāli—here translated as "Close Associate"—was a minister who attended personally upon the Tathāgata when he was a prince.
It is said that killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are inherently sinful by their very nature;

they do not require external restraint for them to become karmic offenses once committed. Therefore, these are called "inherent offenses" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). All others arise only due to specific transgressions.

The Vinaya rules state that an offense committed prior to the establishment of the precepts is not considered a transgression; therefore, it is called "obstructive karma" (*vārita-karman*). Because these two types of karma are empty, body and mind are in a state of quiescence.
Since the precepts of the body are perfectly luminous, there is mastery over the body; since the precepts of the mind are perfectly luminous, there is mastery over the mind.
[△@○] Sixth, the mental consciousness.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I was first begging for food along the road, I encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa—and they proclaimed the Tathāgata..."

Regarding the profound meaning of causes and conditions, I suddenly attained realization and achieved great penetration. The Tathāgata bestowed upon me a *kāṣāya* robe, which I donned, and my beard and hair fell away of their own accord.
Wandering through the Ten Powers, I attained unimpeded mastery; my supernormal powers were so brilliant that I was ranked as supreme, becoming an Arhat.
Not only did the World-Honored One praise me, but the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have also extolled my spiritual power as perfect, bright, and pure.

I am sovereign and fearless. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: "By turning back the turbid flow of my mind until its luminosity was revealed, it became as clear and crystalline as water long settled; this is the foremost method."
The commentary states: This refers to those who enter by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Maudgalyāyana is here translated as "Bean-Gatherer.
Kullaṭa is translated as "Knotless Tree. Uruvilvā is translated as "Papaya" or "Tumor.
Gayā is translated as "City," and it is also the name of a mountain. Nadī is translated as "River. These are the places where the three Kāśyapas resided.

Furthermore, the profound meaning of these causal conditions refers to the dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) undergoes arising and ceasing, one now awakens to non-arising and thus the mind attains thorough penetration.
"Whirling in stillness" means not pursuing the arising and ceasing of external objects; therefore, the light of the mind is manifested and proclaimed.
Those who enter through awakening by means of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) and those who enter through awakening by means of the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*).
[Symbol] The four [sections on] the seven great elements are divided into seven parts. [Symbol] First, the fire element (*tejo-mahābhūta*).
Ucchuṣma, before the Tathāgata, joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I constantly recall that in the distant past, many kalpas ago, I was naturally full of lustful desires. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Śūnyarāja."
It was said that those of excessive lust become a mass of fierce fire. He taught me to contemplate throughout the hundred bones, the four limbs, and all the sensations of cold and warmth.
As the divine light coalesced within, it transformed my lustful mind into the fire of wisdom.
From then on, all Buddhas called me by the name Huotou (Fire-Head). By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, I became an Arhat and made a great vow.
"When the Buddhas attained the Way, I was a powerful Malla who personally subdued the demonic enemies. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied:

'By clearly observing that the warmth and touch of my body and mind flow through without obstruction, all outflows were extinguished, a great jewel-flame arose, and I ascended to unsurpassed enlightenment.
This is the foremost.'"
The commentary states: This enters by means of the fire element (*tejas*). Acala is here translated as "Fire-Head.
This fire element is not external fire; rather, one contemplates it within the fire of desire of one's own mind.

By transforming the manifold lustful mind into the fire of wisdom, it is what is called the "nature-fire" (*prakṛti-tejas*). Because the Tathāgatagarbha inherently possesses the nature-fire of true emptiness, all...
When the mechanism of lust is once activated, it assists in giving rise to the lustful mind; thus, one is born as the fire of desire and dies as the fire of karma.

Yet, since lustful desire is the root of birth and death, it is formed through the fire of nature. Now, if one observes throughout the hundred bones, the four limbs, and all sensations of cold and warmth, they are by their very nature empty.
Therefore, when the lustful mind is extinguished, the light of wisdom manifests before one. This is what is called "birth."
Great Jewel Flame. [△@○] Second Ground: Greatness.
The Bodhisattva Earth-Holding immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I recall the distant past..."

When the Tathāgata Samantaraśmi appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu who constantly leveled all dangerous roads, fords, and narrow passages in fields that were improper or obstructed the passage of carts and horses; or I constructed bridges over them.
Or I carried sand and earth; thus I underwent such diligent toil for immeasurable eons as Buddhas appeared in the world.

Or there were sentient beings in marketplaces who required someone to carry their goods for them; I would first carry them for them, and upon reaching their destination, I would set down the goods and depart without taking any payment.
During the time when Vipaśyin Buddha was present in the world, there was widespread famine; at that time, I served as a porter.
Regardless of distance, I take only a single coin. Or when oxen drawing carts are mired in the mud, I employ my supernatural power to push their wheels and deliver them from their suffering.
At that time, the Great King of the country invited the Buddha to a vegetarian feast; I then leveled the ground to await the Buddha.
Viśvabhū Tathāgata touched my head and said to me: "You shall level the ground of the mind, and then the ground of the world will be level."
Everything became level, and my mind was immediately opened. I saw that the minute particles of my own body and all the minute particles that constitute the world were equal and without distinction.
The intrinsic nature of these minute particles did not touch one another; even weapons could not come into contact with them.
I realized the patience of non-arising regarding the nature of phenomena and attained arhatship. Having turned my mind toward enlightenment, I now enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
Hearing the Tathāgatas proclaim the ground of the Buddhas' wondrous Lotus wisdom and vision, I was the first to bear witness and serve as their leader.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. I replied: "By contemplating with clarity that the two objects—the body and the realm—are equal and without distinction, I realized they are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha from which delusive dust arises.
When this dust is消 (dissolved) and wisdom becomes perfect, one achieves the Unsurpassed Way; this is the foremost."

The commentary says: This is one who has entered through the element of earth. Although the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra previously leveled the ground of the world, he had not yet realized that the nature of the atoms of dust is fundamentally empty.
Therefore, following the instruction of the Buddha Viśvabhū to level the "mind-ground," his mind was immediately opened.
Because the mind-ground is equal, all things are equal; thus, he perceived the atoms of his own body and...
External atoms and the like are without distinction; this is the realization that the nature of atoms is empty and fundamentally lacks both internal and external.
That their natures do not touch one another is because it is like joining space with space. Since the nature of atoms is empty, all things are empty;
therefore, even weapons and armies have nothing to touch. When the ancients placed their heads before the white blade, it was as if they were being severed.

The "spring breeze" refers to awakening to the fact that the nature of sensory objects is empty. When these objects are eliminated and wisdom becomes perfect, one returns to the original *tathāgatagarbha*.
[△@○] Section Three: Water is Great.
The youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall that in the past, as many eons ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Varuṇa. He taught various bodhisattvas to practice the contemplation of water (*āp-dhyāna*) to enter *samādhi*.
They contemplated the nature of water within the body as being indestructible, beginning with nasal mucus and saliva, and thus exhaustively investigating it."
Saliva, fluids, essence, blood, excrement, and urine circulate within the body; their watery nature is identical.
When one perceives this water, there is no difference between it and the various fragrant oceans of the Floating Banner King Lands outside the world.

At that time, when I first accomplished this contemplation, I saw only the water and had not yet attained the state of bodilessness. It was while I was practicing tranquil meditation in my chamber as a bhikṣu.
I had a disciple who peered through the window to observe the room; he saw nothing at all except clear water filling the entire space.
Being a child without understanding, he took a piece of tile or rubble and threw it into the water, causing the water to splash and make a sound as he looked back and walked away.
After emerging from samādhi, I suddenly felt pain in my heart, as if Śāriputra had encountered the malevolent ghost. I reflected to myself:
"I have now attained the path of Arhatship and have long been free from the conditions for illness; why has this heart pain suddenly arisen today?"
"I hope you have not lost [the water]. At that time, the boy quickly came before me and reported the matter as described above.
I then said to him, "If you see the water again, you may immediately open the door and enter this water to remove the tiles and debris. The boy followed my instructions.

Later, when I entered meditative concentration again, I once more saw the water and the rubble exactly as they were. Upon opening the door and emerging, my physical body was restored to its original state.

Thus I encountered immeasurable Buddhas, continuing in this manner until I reached the Tathāgata Sovereign King of Unhindered Penetrations of Mountains and Seas, where I finally attained the dissolution of the self.
My body became one with the nature of true emptiness within the fragrant water-seas of the worlds of the ten directions, non-dual and without distinction.
Now, having attained the name "Celibate Youth" under the Tathāgata and being admitted into the assembly of Bodhisattvas, when the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the Way, I reply:
through the single flavor of the nature of water flowing everywhere, I have attained the patience of non-arising and perfected Bodhi; this is the foremost.
The commentary says: This arises from entering through the water element (*āpas*). One should become a bhikṣu; at that time, one will certainly achieve the contemplation of water (*āpasmṛti*).
A disciple of his saw water filling an entire room. Thus, we know this is a transformation produced by consciousness alone (*vijñaptimātra*).

In the past, there was a monk who lived in the mountains and entered the contemplation of fire (*tejas-smṛti*); he then saw flames everywhere throughout the mountains from afar. Therefore, we know that this is the nature [of reality].

The nature of water is perfectly pervasive and complete; it merely manifests according to karma. Initially, one has not yet forgotten the body because there is still entry into and emergence from samādhi.

After the forgetting of the body, the sentiment of dualistic opposition is extinguished; thus, the water within the body and the water of the Fragrant Ocean merge with the nature of true emptiness, being non-dual and without distinction.
Only then is revealed that the water of the nature, as true emptiness, is fundamentally perfect and all-pervasive.
Because it is universally of one taste and its circulating nature is non-dual.
[△@○] Fourth, the element of wind.
The Dharma Prince Lapis Lazuli Radiance rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I recall..."
In the past, across kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Immeasurable Sound (*Amitaghoṣa*).

He revealed to the bodhisattvas the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), teaching that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all driven by the power of the wind of false conditions.
At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the realms, the movement of the world, the motion and stillness of the body, and the stirring thoughts of the mind—all such movements.
There is no duality and no distinction between them. At that time, I realized that this nature of universal movement comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
The deluded sentient beings, as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, are all equally false.

This extends even to all sentient beings within a single world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds; they are like hundreds of mosquitoes and gnats contained within a single vessel, buzzing and chirping together.
Chaos erupted; within the span of a mere inch, a frantic clamor broke out. Not long after meeting the Buddha, I attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

At that moment, my mind opened, and I beheld the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya in the eastern direction. Serving as a Dharma Prince for the Buddhas of the ten directions, my body and mind radiated light, penetrating all things without obstruction.
When the Buddha asked about the path of perfect penetration, I replied: "By observing that the power of wind has no basis, I awakened to Bodhi."
Focus the mind and enter *samādhi*. Unify the transmissions of the Buddhas of the ten directions into this one wondrous mind;
this is the foremost method. The commentary states: This enters by means of the wind-element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*).

One observes that the bodies of all sentient beings are merely driven by the power of illusory conditions of wind; therefore, all collective movements belong to illusory conditions. [Their] fundamental nature...

It is quiescent and extinguished; therefore, it is said that all movements are non-dual. Thus one knows that movement possesses no characteristics of coming or going, and that sentient beings, through their inversions, merely stir up madness and clamor within the nature of quiescent extinction. Movement is fundamentally without movement;
therefore, in the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya in the eastern direction, he is a Dharma Prince, whose body neither moves nor stops, and whose mind neither arises nor ceases. Therefore—
Body and mind emit light, penetrating through all things without obstruction.
[△@○] Fifth, the Great Emptiness.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I and the Tathāgata..."

When he came before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he attained the body of infinite extent. At that time, he held four great precious jewels in his hands, which illuminated the Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space.

Furthermore, from within his own mind, he manifested a great circular mirror, emitting ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-light that flowed and permeated the ten directions to the very limits of empty space. All the kingly banners and lands entered into this mirror.

Internally, it penetrates my body; the body becomes identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction. The body is able to skillfully enter lands as small as motes of dust to extensively perform Buddha-works, attaining great accordance.

This great supernormal power arises from my contemplation that the four elements have no basis, that they are born and perish through delusive thought, and that empty space is non-dual and the Buddha-lands are fundamentally the same. By illuminating this sameness, I have attained the state of non-arising.
"Endurance. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I attained samādhi by contemplating the boundlessness of space;
its wondrous power is perfectly clear and bright, and this is the foremost."

The commentary states: This is that which enters through the great element of space (*ākāśa*). Space is the substance of form; because one is deluded regarding true emptiness and falsely binds together the four great elements, one loses the nature of space.

Now, by using the precious jewels of the four great elements to illuminate the Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions and transform them into space, one contemplates that the perfect luminosity of the four great elements merges with true emptiness. This is it.

This is what is called attaining the boundless body. Because the Great Perfect Mirror is manifested from one's own mind, its light illumines the ten directions to the very limits of empty space; this mind merges with true emptiness.

Because the Wisdom of the Great Perfect Mirror manifests with equanimity, all lands enter within the mirror and penetrate my body; the body is identical to empty space, and thus they do not obstruct one another.

This is because the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) illuminates all with perfection, such that body and mind are quiescent, and the environment and its inhabitants (the dependent and the primary) are equal.
Thus, one skillfully enters the lands and extensively performs the Buddha-work. Those who attain great accordance enter each and every thing into the equal Dharma-realm.
[△@○] Section on the Six Consciousnesses.
Maitreya Bodhisattva immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, after the passage of atoms of kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. From that Buddha, I attained realization."

My family was one that placed great weight on worldly reputation; I delighted in frequenting the circles of the noble and well-born. At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to cultivate the samādhi of mind-only consciousness to enter into *samādhi*.
Throughout successive kalpas, I have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges through this samādhi, until the seeking of a heart for worldly fame ceased and vanished.
When Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world, I then attained the unsurpassed, wondrous [enlightenment].

The Samādhi of the Perfectly Round Consciousness-Mind: Even unto the exhaustion of empty space, whether the lands of the Tathāgatas be pure or impure, existent or non-existent, all are manifested as transformations of my own mind.
World-Honored One, because I have realized that all is but the mind and consciousness, from the nature of consciousness flow forth immeasurable Tathāgatas;

I have now received the prediction that I shall next succeed to the Buddha’s place. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration [of the faculties], I replied: "I have contemplated with clarity the ten..."

When one abides solely in consciousness-only, the mind of consciousness becomes perfectly luminous and enters the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Far removed from the dependent nature (*paratantra*) and the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is the foremost [stage].
The commentary states: This is because he entered through the gateway of *vijñāna-mahābhūta*. Maitreya has long cultivated the Dharma-gate of *Vijñapti-mātra* (Mind-Only).
Those who formerly left the household life with a mind heavy with worldly fame were those who, being deluded by wisdom, formed *vijñāna*, and thus became firmly attached to self-love;

hence their minds were heavy with worldly fame. Because they indulged in the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and dallied with the various faculties (*indriya*), they delighted in frequenting noble clans. Because of these faculties...
The conjunction of the sense object, consciousness, and the sense faculty constitutes a "realm" (*dhātu*). "Realm" carries the meaning of a lineage or seed-potential.

Because he has long cultivated the meditative concentration on mind-only and consciousness, and has encountered many Buddhas, he has realized that all phenomena are but consciousness; thus, his pursuit of worldly fame has ceased and is no longer present.
It was only upon reaching the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha that he perfected the wondrous and perfect samādhi of the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*).

Thereupon, he realized that the purity and defilement of all lands are manifestations of one's own mind, and that the infinite Tathāgatas all flow forth from the nature of consciousness. Consequently, he received the prediction of his future Buddhahood as the successor to the Buddha’s seat.

By contemplating *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), he attained the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), thereby becoming detached from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
[They] grasped it. Thus, they attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). [△@○] Seventh, the Great Vision:
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Dharma Prince, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, immediately rose from their seats. They bowed their heads...
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "I recall that in the past, during an eon as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared a Buddha named Immeasurable Light.
Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another throughout that eon, the last of whom was named Surpassing the Sun and Moon."
That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. It is like two people: one is single-mindedly mindful of another, while the other is single-mindedly forgetful of that person.

Thus, even if these two meet, they may not recognize one another; or even if they see each other, it is as if they do not see. Yet, because the two are mindful of one another and their mutual mindfulness is profound, [they truly perceive each other].
In this way, from birth to birth, they will remain like a form and its shadow, never diverging or differing.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child flees and wanders away, what can the mother’s remembrance do?

But if the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers him, then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall not be separated or distant. If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and recite the Buddha’s name...
In the present and in the future, you will certainly behold the Buddha; you are not far from him. Without relying on expedient means, you shall spontaneously attain the opening of the mind.
It is like a person who has been perfumed with incense, whose body carries a fragrant scent. This is called the Adornment of Fragrant Light.

In my original stage of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha; now, within this world, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.

When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I made no selection; by completely withdrawing the six sense faculties and maintaining a continuous flow of pure mindfulness, I attained samādhi—this is the foremost method.
The commentary states: "This is one who enters through the 'Great Seeing. This 'Great Seeing' is precisely the seeing of the eighth consciousness."
It is the division [of subject and object]. Because one is deluded regarding the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), it becomes ignorance (*avidyā*) and forms the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

Because it gives rise to false views, it constitutes the "seeing-division" (*darśana-bhāga*). Because the false views grasp at and defile the root-body, the vessel-world, and all sentient beings, they form the impure land.
Now, as one shall return from the false to the true, one employs the practice of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*) to gather and return to the pure [land].
When the soil is cleared, false views are shattered and all impurities are instantly eliminated; thus, mindfulness of the Buddha is the essential method for destroying false views.
Since these false views are fundamentally the light of wisdom, the Buddha who is the teacher of Mahāsthāmaprāpta is known as Amitābha (Immeasurable Light).
Because these views arise from the delusion of wisdom, they stand to it as a mother stands to her child. False views...

Because deluded beings flow along with their emotions and create karma, they are like children who have run away from home. Because the Buddhas’ wisdom and vows gather and transform sentient beings, they are like mothers who remember their children.
If there is a resolve to turn back from delusion and return to the truth, one is then like a child remembering its mother.

If mother and child remember one another, how could there not be a time for them to meet face-to-face? If sentient beings, in every thought-moment, turn the light back to reflect upon themselves, there are none who do not see the Buddha of their own mind.
This is like the person who is stained by incense, due to the power of transformative perfuming.
Therefore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta relies on this vision to gather all those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha and cause them all to return to the Pure Land. He universally gathers them all.
Regarding the six sense organs and so forth: because of false views, one grasps at sense objects moment by moment, becoming defiled in every thought and creating various karmas.
Consequently, at the time of death, one perceives the evil signs of the hells and falls into the cycle of birth and death.

Now, for those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, all that is seen, heard, sensed, and known through the gates of the six sense organs is a single pure mind; only the Buddha appears before them as they maintain this mindfulness.
Because mindfulness achieves purity, one sees the Buddha at the moment of death; thus it is said that the six sense faculties are fully gathered and pure mindfulness continues in succession.
This is precisely the power of inconceivable perfuming and transformation. That the Pure Land is "mind-only" is seen herein.
However, seeing is the root of birth and death. If one practices Chan meditation, it is said: "Do not seek the Truth; you need only cease seeing. If one [practices] mindfulness...

The Buddha then transforms defiled views into pure views; there is only one aspect of seeing that is either functional or non-functional—this is the distinction between meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and purity.

This is divided into three sections. [Symbol] First: An Exposition of the Origins of the Contemplative Practice.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Avalokiteśvara.
Under that Buddha, I gave rise to the bodhicitta; that Buddha taught me to enter through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.”
Samādhi. [□@(?(○/(○*○)))] Part Two: Describing the Attainment of Perfect Penetration through the Faculties, in three sections.
[△@○] First: This faculty is first understood, first realizing the emptiness of persons, in two parts.
First, the external objects perish.

Initially, within the faculty of hearing, one enters the stream and causes the objects of perception to vanish. Once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise.
[?×] Second, the internal faculties are exhausted.
Thus, as one gradually increases [in practice], what is heard and what is to be heard are both exhausted.
[△@○] Second, the perfect clarity of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is divided into two parts for the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
First, one dispatches the wisdom of observation;
hearing ceases entirely, and both the perceiving subject and the perceived object are empty.
Next, one dispatches the "repeated emptiness."
When the realization of emptiness is perfectly fulfilled, that which is emptied by emptiness ceases.
When these three are simultaneously empty and non-arising, one suddenly realizes the One Mind.
Since birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one.
[□@(?(○/(○*○)))] Third, the section on entering the stream and attaining perfect enlightenment, which has two parts.
[△@○] First, a general exposition of the instantaneous transcendence of the ten stages.
Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains perfect clarity throughout the ten directions and achieves two kinds of extraordinary excellence:
first, above, one harmonizes with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as the Tathāgatas;
second, below, one harmonizes with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful yearning as all those beings.

The commentary states: This refers to the Perfect Realization through the Ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara. To speak of "contemplation" (*guan*) in relation to sound implies that one no longer relies on the physical hearing of the ears.
The reason the Buddha whom he takes as his teacher is named Avalokiteśvara is to manifest that this Dharma has its source therein.
"Following hearing, reflection, and cultivation" means to reflect upon and cultivate within the state of hearing. Initially, one enters the stream of hearing and causes the objective realm to vanish.
The term "etc. refers to what was previously stated: "This faculty first understands and first attains the emptiness of persons.

Because the six faculties flow with the current toward objects, one creates karma according to one's emotions. Now, through contemplation and cultivation of the ear-faculty, one does not take external objects as conditions.
"Entering the stream" means reversing the flow; that is, to turn back from that karmic current and reflect upon the nature of hearing, thereby no longer relying on the sensory dusts.
When the knowledge and vision thus arise, the nature of hearing manifests before one, and the sensory objects consequently become empty; hence it is said that "the object is lost.
Furthermore, prior to observing the nature of hearing, because the objects possessed the characteristics of movement and stillness, the hearing could not transcend sound.

Now, as the nature of hearing is observed to be quiescent, the objects lack the marks of movement and stillness; hence it is said that "it is clearly non-arising. This refers to the loss of what was previously [perceived].

It is also a dust-sensory object (*viṣaya*). Regarding the phrase "thus gradually increasing" and so forth: because the objective realm has become quiescent, one further increases the contemplative practice (*bhāvanā-caryā*).
Since the sound-dust that was heard is now devoid of movement or stillness, this faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) also vanishes. Hence it is said, "hearing and what is heard are exhausted.
This exhaustion refers to the internal faculty. Regarding the phrase "exhausting hearing and not abiding," this luminous perfection of emptiness constitutes the liberation of the Dharma.

It means that the simultaneous vanishing of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) constitutes the "exhaustion of the locus of hearing. Yet, one does not dwell even in the awareness of this exhaustion of hearing, but further increases the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Since both the faculties and objects have vanished, this wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) also ceases; thus, the awareness of that which is to be known is also empty.

This is the wisdom of contemplation of emptiness. Regarding the phrase "the emptiness of the wisdom of contemplation reaches ultimate perfection," it means that the emptiness of the wisdom of contemplation reaches its limit.
At the point of ultimate perfection, even the emptiness that empties [all things] spontaneously ceases; hence it is said, "the emptiness that empties is extinguished.

This refers to the elimination of the superimposed emptiness through the principle of the truth of cessation. Regarding the phrase "when arising and ceasing have both ceased," this clarifies that when both are empty, there is no further production.
Thus, through these successive negations reaching a state where there is nothing further to negate, it is said: "When arising and ceasing have both ceased..."
Cessation and quiescence manifest before one; these sublime practices are now perfected. Thus, the three truths appear equally within a single mind, enabling a sudden transcendence.
Because of the instantaneous realization in a single thought-moment, it is called "sudden";

because the ten realms of existence—both the environment and its inhabitants—are all quiescent manifestations appearing from the single mind, it is called "transcendence. Perfectly fulfilling the ten directions, it is transparently pervasive.

Because it is unimpeded, it is called "perfectly luminous" (*yuanming*). This is what was previously described as the essence of the mark of luminosity being pure and refined, such that all transformations do not become afflictions, but rather accord with the pure and wondrous virtue of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it harmonizes above with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas.
Because one’s own mind is perfectly enlightened, there are no sentient beings whom one does not wish to deliver;
hence it is said that they share the same power of compassion (*maitrī*). Below, one shares a single *dharmakāya* with all sentient beings of the six realms.

Since the sorrowful yearning within the minds of sentient beings is itself the ground of awakening where the Buddhas extract suffering, it is said that they share the same sorrowful yearning (*karuṇā*). These two supreme qualities are attained simultaneously.
This is what is called attaining the "perfect penetration" that transcends all others.

From the ninth stage up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), there exists a body born of the same category as the innate [nature], produced through effortless mental attention (*anābhoga-manasikāra*).

World-Honored One, if bodhisattvas enter samādhi and advance in their cultivation until their untainted resolve (*anāsrava-adhimukti*) becomes fully perfected, I shall manifest [before them].
