yet, if the wondrous samādhi is awakened and the single mind is wondrously realized, one suddenly attests to the secret treasury of the three virtues.

This "wondrous permanence and stillness" is sequentially assigned to the three virtues of prajñā, dharmakāya, and liberation—the perfect realization of the single mind. When both existence and non-existence are absent, there is neither birth nor death.
When non-duality is also extinguished, that is not yet nirvana. This means that delusive causes are severed and delusive karma is suddenly emptied;
without this, one is insufficient to sever the cycle of saṃsāra.
[○@◇] Third, the response to the question: "Ānanda, the three karmas are not severed;
each has its own private cause. Because of these individual privacies, the collective class of these privacies has no lack of a fixed location.
They arise from one's own delusion; this arising of delusion is without cause and cannot be traced."
The commentary states: This concludes the response to the questions. It follows from the previous inquiry: "Is there a fixed location, or does it arise spontaneously?

Do they each individually initiate karma and receive its results privately? Therefore, this conclusion states: Because the three karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are not severed and are created separately by each person, it is said that "each has their own private [karma].
Since these individual karmas are collectively experienced, it is not the case that [the results] do not exist.
The locus of concentration: since delusion fundamentally has no cause, there is nothing to be sought or investigated.
[○@◇] Fourth, the exhortation for true cultivation: you must exhort yourself in practice;
if you wish to attain Bodhi, you must eliminate the three delusions. Even if you were to obtain supernatural powers, as long as the three delusions are not exhausted, [you have not attained it].

All these are worldly conditioned activities; because their habitual tendencies have not been extinguished, they fall into the path of Māra. Though they wish to eliminate delusion, they only redouble their falsehoods.
The Tathāgata says such people are to be pitied; you have falsely created this for yourself—it is no fault of Bodhi.
[○@◇] The fifth section: The Correct Teaching.
To speak in this manner is called the correct teaching; if one speaks otherwise, it is the teaching of Māra.
The commentary states: This is an exhortation to practice. As previously stated, "Because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise," then you...
The wild nature within the mind will naturally subside; when it subsides, that is bodhi. Therefore, it is said that one must eliminate the three delusions and so forth.
This means that only by necessarily severing them does one engage in true cultivation. This follows from the previous question: "Does this Way originally exist of its own accord?"
This arises from the deluded habitual tendencies of these sentient beings; therefore, this concluding statement says: "You have created this yourself through delusion; it is not the fault of Bodhi.
The preceding detailed investigation of the seven realms of existence, which specifically demonstrates the various distinctions within delusion, is now complete.
△ Section Two: A Detailed Exposition of the Skandha-māra, Subdividing the Characteristics of Realization.
[○@●] First, the section showing the five skandha-māra activities, divided into twelve parts. [□@◇] First, the World-Honored One’s spontaneous discourse without being questioned.
At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his session at the Dharma-seat, he took up a seven-jeweled armrest from his lion throne,
turned toward the Purple Gold Mountain, and leaned against it once more, addressing the great assembly and Ānanda, saying:
The commentary states: This section provides a detailed analysis of the "demonic māras" (*ātmabhāva-māra*) to demonstrate the distinctions among various stages of awakening.

It begins by stating that practitioners who fail to attain supreme *bodhi*, and instead become *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, or followers of external paths—such as various devas, māras, and their retinues—all do so because they...
Knowing that there are two kinds of fundamental delusions to be cultivated through practice, he first revealed the method for true cultivation:
namely, using the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama as the common path for the fifty-five stages of true Bodhi, thereby manifesting correct awakening.

However, within this state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because deviant practices and deviant awakenings have not yet been fully clarified, the previous classification of the seven destinies (*gati*)—

which explains how a single deluded thought manifests as the states of ascent and descent across the seven realms— is specifically intended to reveal the distinct characteristics within the midst of delusion. Now,
that there are fifty layers of the *skandha-māras* within this very concentration precisely reveals the distinctions within the midst of awakening.
This is their distinguishing characteristic. What was previously explained was the direct demonstration of true cultivation through the application of meditative concentration;

however, because those of the three vehicles had not yet undergone erroneous awakening, it was not something they could know. This, however, concerns the Tathāgata’s exhaustive experience of all realms.

Furthermore, these subtle demonic activities cannot be clearly understood except by one possessing all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), and there was no one capable of asking about them. Therefore, without being questioned, he spoke of his own accord. Thus far.
Having fully revealed the causes and effects of delusion and awakening, he was about to conclude his teaching on the Dharma seat.

Yet, with the intention that there was still something remaining unsaid, he once again leaned upon his precious lectern to address the great assembly. This most supreme and profound compassion constitutes his final instruction.
[□@◇] Second, a brief indication of the causes and conditions of demonic activities:

You who are still in training—whether pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas—who today have turned your minds toward great bodhi and supreme, wondrous enlightenment, I have now already taught you the method for true practice; yet you still do not recognize how to cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Subtle demonic activities and demonic realms manifest before you, yet you fail to recognize them. Your purification of mind is not authentic, and you fall into false views.

Whether it be the *skandha-māra*, the celestial *māra*, possession by ghosts and spirits, or encounters with malevolent demons, your mind lacks clarity, leading you to mistake a thief for your own son.
Furthermore, within this state, you consider a mere trifle to be sufficient, like the unlearned bhikṣu in the fourth dhyāna.
He falsely claimed to have realized the state of a sage. When his heavenly retribution was exhausted, the signs of decay appeared before him.
Having slandered an Arhat, he underwent further existence and fell into the Avīci Hell. You should listen attentively; I shall now explain this to you in detail for you. Ānanda rose from his seat.
Together with those fellow students present in the assembly, they joyfully prostrated and humbly awaited his compassionate instruction.
They deliberated, saying: "This has been a brief indication of the causes and conditions of demonic activities (*mārakarman*).

As previously explained, for those of the three vehicles who turn their minds toward Bodhi, this is the method of authentic practice. However, regarding the subtle demonic activities within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), you..."

Since [the practitioner] has not yet recognized this, it is necessary to provide a detailed analysis to prevent erroneous understanding. If one does not explain it thoroughly, there is a danger that demonic realms will manifest before them;

with the mind lacking clarity, they may mistakenly take these as real. This would be like an unlearned bhikṣu who falsely claims realization, slanders the Dharma, and thereby brings hell upon himself.
Therefore, I cannot help but distinguish these matters in great detail.
[□@◇] Third, demonstrating the root of delusion and awakening.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly: "You all should know that within the world of outflows, there are twelve classes of living beings."
The essence of the mind, which is the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment and the perfection of awakening, is non-dual and indistinguishable from that of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

It is due to your deluded thoughts that you mistake the principle, which is the fault; thus, ignorance and craving arise. Because these arise and develop into universal delusion, the nature of space appears.

As this delusive transformation does not cease, the world-systems come into being. Thus, these microdust-like lands of the ten directions that are not free from outflows are all merely products of deluded stubbornness.
These are established through false conceptualization; you should know that the empty space arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity of the great sky.

How much more so, then, are all worlds contained within this empty space? If even one among you awakens to the truth and returns to the source, this empty space of the ten directions will completely vanish and perish.
How could the lands existing within that space not be shattered and torn asunder?
The commentary states: To clarify the causes for the arousal of demons, it first demonstrates that the single reality is the foundation of both delusion and enlightenment.
Within the single reality of the Dharma-realm, there is no differentiation between mind, Buddha, and sentient beings; the transformations of delusion and enlightenment do not transcend this mind.
The world of empty space is established in dependence upon it. The mind is fundamentally wondrously luminous;

however, because of a single moment of ignorance and deluded thought that obscures the truth and turns away from principle, delusion and craving arise. This indicates that ignorance serves as the root of the four afflictions (*kleśas*).

Once the "phase of arising" (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*) has manifested, the entire substance is in a state of delusion; hence it is called "universal delusion. The nature of emptiness depends upon this [ignorance].

That which is manifested by clarity is what is called the void of delusion. Because deluded confusion transforms without ceasing, it is said that "the transformation of delusion being unceasing gives rise to the birth of worlds.
This means that darkness is congealed to form matter, and upon the void, worlds are established.
Thus, the lands of the ten directions are all established based on false imagination. Because the true mind is supremely great, [it is able to manifest all this].
Space arises from the wondrous mind like a single cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky; how infinitesimal it is!

How much more so, then, are the worlds within that space—not exceedingly minute? Therefore, when a practitioner today awakens to the truth and returns to the source, once ignorance is shattered, space itself vanishes, and the lands within that space do not fail to shatter and split asunder. For Māra relies upon darkness.
Obscurity constitutes its essence, and the world serves as its basis. Now that the land has quaked and split apart, the palace of Māra will surely collapse;
this is truly the cause for the agitation of Māra.
[This concludes the section on] fourfold demonstration of the causes for the agitation of Māra.

"You all cultivate dhyāna and adorn yourselves with samādhi. The minds of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the great Arhats free from outflows are profoundly attuned and remain serene in their respective states.

Yet, when the Māras, ghosts, spirits, and ordinary devas see their palaces suddenly collapse and shatter without cause, and the great earth tremble and split apart, causing all creatures of land, water, and air to be struck with terror and awe."

Ordinary beings are muddled and ignorant, failing to perceive their own transformations and errors. Although they all possess the five supernormal powers, they lack the power to exhaust outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Being attached to these worldly defilements, how could you cause them to shatter that place? For this reason, the ghosts, spirits, and various heavenly Māras—
"Mantles and spirits come in droves to harass you during your samādhi.
They deliberated and said, "These words will provoke the Māras and cause disturbance. The Superior replied, "If one awakens to the truth and returns to the source, then even empty space will vanish.
Now, practicing dhyāna-samādhi is precisely the practice of returning to the source. Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and those who can cultivate it [are all included]."
The mind becomes thoroughly proficient. This means that once deluded thoughts are shattered, the subjective mind and objective realm become one as a single reality;

because the essence of non-arising is revealed, one remains tranquil in that very place. As empty space dissolves, the palaces of Māra tremble of their own accord. This is truly the cause for shaking the demons.
Māra possesses the five supernatural powers and great spiritual might. Having gained his name through the harming of virtue, he is deeply attached to these sensual realms;
how could he willingly allow you to destroy them? Therefore, it is but natural that they all come to disturb you within this samādhi.
[□@◇] Fifth, as for the demonstration of awakening, it is superior to the heterodox.

Although those various māras may be filled with great rage within their realm of defilement, within your wondrous enlightenment, they are like wind blowing against light or a blade cutting through water;
they do not touch one another at all. You are like boiling water, while they are like solid ice; as the warmth gradually approaches, [the ice will surely melt].
They will not last long before they perish; you merely rely on their supernatural powers, becoming but their guest.
That they succeed in causing disruption is due to you, the master of the five aggregates within your own mind. If the master is deluded, the guests gain the advantage.

If, while in *dhyāna*, you awaken to the truth and remain free from confusion, then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you. As the aggregates dissolve and you enter into clarity, all those malevolent spirits will be reduced to mere obscure vapors.
Brightness can destroy darkness, yet even that which is close to it perishes; how then could [darkness] dare remain to disturb meditative concentration?
(6) This shows that when one is deluded, the heterodox prevails.
If you do not attain clear awakening and remain deluded by the *skandhas*, then you, Ānanda, will surely become a son of Māra and a perfected agent of Māra.
Even though Maṭaṅga was extremely lowly and inferior, he merely used incantations to destroy your monastic discipline; among the eighty thousand practices, he violated but a single precept.
Because your mind remained pure, you have not yet fallen into ruin. This [present situation], however, destroys your entire body of precious enlightenment.
It is like a high minister’s family suddenly encountering confiscation of their property; they fall into ruin and decay, with no means of rescue or relief. The commentary states:
These words mean that the heterodox cannot overcome the orthodox. Māra relies on darkness and obscurity, while the settled mind is empty and luminous.
Thus, it is like blowing upon light or cutting through water; the two characteristics of light and darkness do not reach one another, nor do they touch. Luminosity is able to...
It destroys darkness as hot water melts ice. Because it comes from without, it is like a guest; because the false cannot overcome the true, it cannot cause destruction.
It is because your mind is deluded that the demon finds its opportunity. If you simply illuminate with the wisdom of *dhyāna*, the māra will find no place to enter.
As the power of concentration becomes firmer, the māra cannot disturb you. Through awakening, you triumph over the false. If...
Because you are deluded by your own aggregates (*skandhas*), you bring about the works of Māra. Through such delusion, the heterodox triumphs.
Consider, for instance, how Mātanga was utterly inferior; yet, relying on the power of incantations, he managed to destroy but a single precept.

How much more so when Māra possesses great supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to annihilate the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body and destroy the royal house of the Dharma? You must certainly guard yourself deeply against this and not allow him any opportunity.
[□@◇] Section Seven: The Detailed Exposition of the Deeds of Māra, divided into five parts. [○@◇] First, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), divided into three.
[△@△] First, when the aggregate has not yet been destroyed.
Ānanda, you should know this: when you sit at the site of enlightenment, you must dissolve all thoughts.

When those thoughts are exhausted, then all that is luminous and penetrating, free from thought, remains unmoved by motion or stillness, and recollection and forgetfulness become one. You should abide in this state and enter samādhi.

It is like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness; though the essence of the mind is wondrously pure, its light has not yet emerged. This is called the domain of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
If the eyes become bright and clear so that the ten directions open wide and there is no longer any darkness, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa. One should observe its origin, which takes solidified delusive thought as its root. The commentary says:

This demonstrates the characteristics of delusion and awakening regarding the five aggregates (*skandhas*) in order to discern the realms of Māra. Māra has "dark obscurity" as his nature; the aggregates have "concealment and obstruction" as their meaning.
It is through delusion regarding the one true reality that the five aggregates of form and mind are formed. Indeed...

This conceals the true mind; it is the universal transformation of the field of enlightenment into a den of demons. For this reason, the world of sentient beings serves as the dwelling place for demons.
Now, if one turns back from delusion to return to truth, one must necessarily dissolve these five aggregates of body and mind to restore the single, true essence of awakening.
It is because of the delusion or enlightenment of the one mind that the distinction between demon and Buddha is thereby made.

Now, when one uses contemplation to investigate the five aggregates (skandhas) at the very moment they are about to be destroyed but have not yet been destroyed, the objective realm of the aggregates transforms according to the mind.
Because of the habitual tendencies accumulated over kalpas, these transform into various kinds of realms; this is what is called "the ceaseless transformation of delusion.
Since these are manifested solely by the mind, there is no fault in awakening to them. Within the pure mind, there is not even a speck of dust.
Do not stand [in conceptualization]. As soon as a single thought arises and clings, one falls into the ranks of Māra.

When you sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and cause all thoughts to subside and vanish, this is the time when you first gain power through the practice of meditative observation. You should abide in this state and enter *samādhi*;
for a straightforward mind and right mindfulness constitute the foundation of concentration. Then, within that concentration, you will be like a person with clear vision standing in a place...
Obscurity is the characteristic of being shrouded by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); it signifies confinement and limitation. "Universe" (*yu*) means to be covered.

If the aggregate of form were exhausted, the ten directions would open up clearly, and there would be no further darkness. The preceding turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) exists in dependence upon the aggregate of form.

A *kalpa* (劫) is time. Space (*ākāśa*) constitutes the initial state of time and serves as the substance of form (*rūpa*). Once the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is shattered, the three temporal dimensions are suddenly emptied;

thus, one is able to transcend the turbidity of the *kalpa*. Within the obscurity of space, darkness coagulates into form; therefore, solidified false discrimination (*dṛḍhābhiniveśa-vikalpa*) is taken as the root of form.
[△@△] Second, showing the distinctions of the meditative objects in the following ten sections:
"Ānanda, within this state, you should investigate the wondrous clarity until the four great elements no longer interweave. In a brief moment, the body will be able to pass through obstructions.
This is called the overflow of refined spirit into the external realm; it is merely a temporary attainment through the power of practice and is not [the ultimate state]."
"Sacred realization. To not conceive of it as sacred realization is called a "wholesome state"; if one conceives of it as sacred realization, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
The commentary says: This refers to the ten successive stages that occur when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is about to be destroyed.

That is to say, within the state of brilliant clarity where thought has been abandoned, one contemplates and investigates with precision the essence of the wondrously luminous mind-body, whereby all deluded thoughts dissolve and permeate the four great elements.
Therefore, they are interwoven and do not disperse. Now, as you investigate the mind and detach from form, delusive thoughts no longer arise;
thus, the four great elements are no longer woven together. "A short while" refers to a brief moment. When they are no longer woven, the four great elements become separated from one another.

Consequently, the body no longer constrains the mind, and the mind is able to pass through obstructions. However, this is merely the overflowing of refined spirit into the objective realm; the aggregate of form has not yet truly been shattered.
Such is the temporary attainment through effort. If one does not give rise to the mind of holiness (*ārya-citta*), it remains a wholesome state produced by effort.
However, if one forms a conception of holiness, one will immediately be possessed by demonic influences.
Ānanda, if one further uses this mind to investigate its wondrous clarity until it penetrates deep within the body, that person will suddenly, within that—
One may extract intestinal worms from within the body, yet the physical form remains intact without any injury or damage. This is called the overflowing of refined essence through the physical body;
it is merely a temporary attainment resulting from refined practice and is not a realization of the Sage.
To regard this as the state of a Sage is a "good realm," but to interpret it as the realization of a Sage is to fall prey to various demonic influences.

The commentary says: This is the second stage of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Furthermore, through the previous contemplation and investigation, the essence of the mind and its luminosity penetrate inwardly;
the four great elements become empty and harmonious, transparent and unobstructed. Thus, one may extract worms such as *ārma* from within the body without the physical form being destroyed.
Although the aggregate of form has not yet been shattered, its material substance is already void. This is specifically...
Vitality and intelligence overflow from the physical form; this is a temporary function and not a realization of the sages.

Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate both internally and externally, at that time the *po*, *hun*, *yi*, and *shen* spirits—excluding the body they sustain—all interpenetrate and act as guest and host to one another.
Suddenly, one hears the sound of preaching the Dharma in mid-air, or hears it coming from the ten directions.

We shall likewise expound the meaning of the Esoteric Teachings. This is called the mutual separation and union of the vital essence (*śukra*) and the spirit (*ojas*), which accomplishes the seeds of goodness.

To temporarily attain such a state does not constitute the realization of a sage. If one does not conceive of it as being the state of a sage, it is called a "wholesome realm"; however, if one interprets it as the realization of a sage, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

The commentary states: This is the third stage of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). It concerns the body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) which is appropriated by the *ālayavijñāna*.

Within the five viscera (*pañca-kukṣi*), each has its own presiding function and thus receives its respective name: in the liver it is called the *hun* (soul); in the lungs it is called the *po* (spirit);

in the spleen it is called the *yi* (thought/intention); in the kidneys it is called the *zhi* (will/volition); and in the heart it is called the *shenjing* (spiritual essence). Now, let us observe this through contemplation.
He illuminates and investigates until the four elements are exhausted and the five viscera are fused; even the *hun* and *po* souls are transformed and find no reliance.

Thus, he departs from his body and enters into various states, alternating between being guest and host. This arises because seeds previously perfumed by hearing are stimulated by meditative concentration, whereby the spirit and soul manifest to produce the sound of preaching the Dharma.
This is merely the successive separation and union of the vital spirits; it is not a realization of the holy path.

Furthermore, when this mind is clear, luminous, and transparent, its internal radiance becomes manifest, causing the ten directions to appear everywhere as the color of Jambūnada gold and all species to transform into Tathāgatas.
At that moment, one suddenly beholds Vairocana seated upon the Terrace of Celestial Light, surrounded by a thousand Buddhas;
a billion lands and lotus flowers appear simultaneously. This is called the "soul of the mind" (cittātman).
When one is colored by spiritual awakening, the light of the mind becomes refined and bright, illuminating all worlds. To briefly attain such a state does not constitute a realization of sainthood.
If you do not conceive of it as a state of sainthood, it is called a "wholesome realm"; if you interpret it as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately succumb to various delusions.

The commentary states: This is the fourth stage of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Because one previously observed the mind and investigated the body and mind until they were luminously transparent, the aggregate of form has been dissolved;
as the light of the mind thus becomes manifest, the objects of experience appear.

The phenomena manifested throughout the ten directions are seen because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of names and phrases from the sacred teachings, accumulated through hearing over many lifetimes, are stimulated by meditative concentration. Therefore, the world is perceived.

The appearances of golden-colored realms, transformation Buddhas preaching the Dharma, lotus flowers, and so forth, are called "spiritual awakening" because they arise from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of cultivated wholesome seeds.
Through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the light of the mind investigates and thoroughly understands, clearly illuminating all worlds;
one may temporarily attain such states, yet these are not the realization of a sage (*ārya*).
Furthermore, with this mind, one investigates the wondrous clarity with ceaseless observation, suppressing, subduing, restraining, and transcending it.
At that time, suddenly the empty space of the ten directions becomes the color of seven treasures or a hundred treasures, simultaneously filling all space without mutual obstruction;
blue, yellow, red, and white each appear in their pure forms. This is called the power of suppression exceeding its proper measure.

To temporarily attain such a state does not constitute a realization of the holy; if one does not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm. If, however, one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately be possessed by various demonic influences.

The commentary states: This is the fifth stage of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Furthermore, with the concentrated mind of prior meditative absorption, one minutely investigates the wondrous clarity.
When the substance of the mind observes without ceasing, suddenly empty space takes on the color of the seven treasures.

When these five colors appear purely, this is called the luminous mind of precious awakening. Because ignorance has not yet been exhausted, it is stimulated by meditative concentration, and thus this phenomenon manifests.
This is called "the power of effort exceeding one's limits" resulting in a temporary attainment; it is not a realization of the noble ones (*ārya*).

Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate until it becomes clear, translucent, and its refined radiance is undisturbed, suddenly at midnight within a dark room one sees various objects no different from those seen in broad daylight, yet the objects in the dark room do not vanish. This is called "refinement of the mind."
If you can clarify your vision so that what you behold penetrates the profound darkness, and you momentarily attain such a state, it does not constitute a holy realization.
To refrain from conceiving of it as a holy attainment is called a "wholesome realm"; if you instead interpret it as a holy realization, you will immediately succumb to various forms of delusion.

The commentary states: This is the sixth stage of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). By means of the concentrated mind of prior meditative absorption, one investigates until the mind becomes clear and translucent, and a refined spirit emits light.
Because this light issues forth from within meditative concentration, it is not subject to distraction; thus, in a dark room at night, one perceives various objects.
This is not the mind’s luminosity penetrating and illuminating; rather, it is because the mind is subtle, dense, and its vision is clarified that one is able to see through to the profound darkness.
This is not a realization of the Sage.
Furthermore, when this mind enters completely into emptiness and fusion, the four limbs suddenly become like grass and wood, such that even if burned by fire or hacked with a sword—
One has never experienced such awakening. Furthermore, the firelight cannot burn or scorch; even if one cuts one's flesh, it is like shaving wood.

This is called the simultaneous merging of the sensory objects and the exclusive entry of the nature of the four great elements into purity. To temporarily attain such a state is not a realization of the holy ones.
To not give rise to the thought of being a sage is called a wholesome state; if one forms a conception of being a sage, one immediately succumbs to various delusions.
The commentary says: This is the seventh stage of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Previously, one used a concentrated mind to make the four great elements empty and harmonious;

now, through the observing mind, one enters completely into this emptiness and harmony. Furthermore, because one is detached from grasping and receiving [the body], one suddenly becomes like grass or trees, devoid of cognition.
Even when burned by fire or cut by a blade, there is no sensation whatsoever. This is called "expelling the nature of the four great elements" and entering purely into emptiness and fusion;
it is a temporary attainment of such a state that is not yet a realization of the noble ones.

Furthermore, as this mind achieves purity and the power of the pure mind reaches its peak, one suddenly sees that the great earth, the mountains, and the rivers of the ten directions all become Buddha-lands, replete with the seven treasures and filled with pervasive radiance.

One also sees Buddhas and Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges filling the void of space, their towers and palaces magnificent and ornate. Looking down, one perceives the hells; looking up, one contemplates the celestial palaces, attaining unimpeded vision.

This is called the deepening of focused contemplation through the alternation of joy and aversion; after long practice, it becomes transformed. It is not a holy realization. If one does not regard it as a state of sainthood, it is a wholesome state;
however, if one interprets it as a holy attainment, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

The commentary states: This is the eighth stage of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Because one has previously used a concentrated mind to investigate and exhaust the habitual tendencies of attraction and aversion until they are internally integrated, purity is achieved.
Once the internal mind is pure, the external vessel-world becomes void and luminous, manifesting the colors of the seven treasures.
All Buddhas fill it, and one simultaneously perceives both the hells and the celestial palaces without any obstruction. This is called...
When joy and aversion cause one’s concentrated visualization to deepen daily, things manifest in accordance with those thoughts; this is not a holy realization.

Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate the profound and far-reaching, suddenly in the middle of the night one may see from afar the markets, streets, and alleys, or the relatives and kinsmen, or hear their voices.
This is called the "pressing of the mind," where it is so intensely constrained that it flies out, and thus many things are seen across distances.
This is not a sign of saintly realization. To regard it as such without forming the thought of being a sage is called a "wholesome state";

however, if one interprets it as saintly realization, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences. The commentary states: This is the ninth stage of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Previously, although the concentrated mind investigated deeply and far, because the true mind—which is fundamentally all-pervasive—was obstructed by form, one could not see at a distance. Now, through the power of concentration, one investigates the aggregate with refined precision.
Although it has not yet been broken through, the mind is able to see and hear from afar; relatives and kin all appear according to habitual tendencies.
This is called "the mind being pressured and forced to fly out," whereby one sees many things at a distance; it is not the realization of an Arhat.
Furthermore, if you investigate with this mind to the utmost degree of refinement, you may see the physical form of the spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra) undergo transformations;
in a brief moment, it shifts and changes in various ways without apparent cause. This is called the evil mind harboring malevolent spirits (chimei).

Or, you may encounter a celestial Māra entering your heart and belly, preaching the Dharma and penetrating subtle meanings without cause. These are not signs of saintly realization. If you do not regard them as such, the demonic activities will subside.
If one interprets this as a realization of the holy, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

The commentary states: This is the tenth stage of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Because one has previously used a concentrated mind to investigate matters to the ultimate degree, and because of the seeds of false cultivation planted by hearing from a false teacher in the past, the concentrated investigation undergoes a transformation, causing one to see the physical form of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
These transformations arise because the mind harbors heterodox influences or because celestial Māras enter the mind and preach the Dharma without cause;
this is not the realization of a sage. As the power of meditative concentration deepens, the activities of Māra likewise increase in intensity;
therefore, it is a natural principle that the latter four aggregates gradually penetrate deeper.
[△@△] Third, the admonition for profound prevention:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states that appear during *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a state of mutual interaction with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
When sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, they fail to reflect upon themselves; encountering these conditions, they remain confused and do not recognize them for what they are, saying:"
To claim sainthood is a great falsehood that leads to falling into the Avīci Hell.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, you should proclaim this meaning so that celestial Māras do not find an opportunity to exploit you. Maintain and protect it so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
The commentary states: This refers to the breaking of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the manifestation of the ten kinds of signs within the stages of *dhyāna*.

Therefore, it is summarized by saying that these are all instances where the mind’s application toward the aggregate of form becomes mutually conflicted. If one were to suddenly break through fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) in a single thought-moment such that the five aggregates were simultaneously eliminated, this situation would not occur.
It is because habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are now sequentially investigated and provoked that this is said.
The mind and its objects interact with one another. If one is deluded and fails to recognize this, claiming instead that one has realized sainthood, one falls into a great falsehood.
I now instruct you to proclaim and identify these demonic activities, so that you may protect yourself and achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
[○@◇] The second, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), is divided into three parts. [△@△] First, when the aggregate has not yet been destroyed:

Ānanda, when that virtuous son practices *samādhi*, and within *śamatha* the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, he perceives the minds of all Buddhas appearing like reflections manifested in a clear mirror. Although there is something attained, it cannot yet be utilized; it is just as...

When a person experiences nightmares, their hands and feet remain perfectly functional, and their senses of sight and hearing are not confused; yet, because their mind has been contacted by external deviant influences, they are unable to move.
This is called the realm of the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation).

The commentary states: "This demonstrates the signs that the *vedanā-skandha* has not yet been destroyed. One for whom the *rūpa-skandha* (the aggregate of form) is exhausted is one whose four great elements have already dissolved."

Do not harbor further doubts. Because the contemplation of the mind becomes increasingly luminous, the Buddha-mind appears within the midst of contemplative observation, like images appearing in a mirror.
However, although the Buddha-mind is signless (*animitta*), that which appears as an image is merely a reflected shadow (*pratibimba*) transformed by the contemplating mind;
it is not the true mind itself. That one has attained something yet is unable to employ it is because there is still a state of grasping and containment.
Because of this grasping, one is like a person in a nightmare; this is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

If the affliction of the nightmare ceases, the mind departs from the body and turns back to observe its own face; when going and staying are free and there is no further obstruction, it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Observing its origin, one sees it is but empty, luminous, and delusory.
This is taken as its basis. The commentary says:
This is a preliminary indication of the signs of the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha). When sensation is exhausted, there is no longer any grasping or appropriation;

therefore, the mind is able to detach from the body. Because the body resides within the mind, one can look back at one's own face. As the four great elements have already dissolved, there is nothing left to grasp or appropriate.
Therefore, there is no longer any further obstruction. The turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) exists in dependence upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*);

because one perceives that there is a root-body (*mūla-kāya*) which can be felt, received, and grasped, it constitutes the turbidity of views. Now, because the aggregate of sensation is exhausted, one is able to transcend it.
Because it contains the characteristic of empty luminosity (*śūnyatva-prakāśa*), it is called the deluded thought of empty luminosity (*śūnyatva-vikalpa*).
[△@△] Second, showing the distinctions within the meditative objects in the following ten sections:
"Ānanda, when that virtuous man is within this state, he attains great radiance and his mind becomes luminous.

If he suppresses his internal thoughts to an excessive degree, he will suddenly give rise to inexhaustible compassion toward that object. This continues until he perceives even mosquitoes and gadflies as if they were..."
Upon seeing an infant, his heart gave rise to compassion and he involuntarily shed tears. This is called the suppression and overcoming of excessive emotions through effortful application;
if one realizes this for what it is, there is no fault. It is not a sign of saintly realization. If one awakens to its nature and remains undeluded, it will naturally dissipate over time.

If, however, one mistakes this for a state of sainthood, the demon of sorrow will enter one’s heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, one will weep and wail boundlessly, losing right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*); such a person must follow [the instructions for correction].
[The mind] sinks and falls.

The commentary says: This is the first stage of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Because one previously used the contemplation of the mind to investigate and dissolve the *skandha* of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the mind became luminous;
however, as the perception of form was being dissolved, the application of the mind was too urgent and internal suppression was excessive, and thus [this state] arose.
Boundless compassion arises; this is because one possesses the seeds of compassion from past lives, which are now stimulated by the power of contemplation.

Consequently, one views even mosquitoes and gnats as if they were one's own infants. This, however, is an excessive suppression and crushing through meditative effort; it is not a true realization of the holy state.
Failing to realize its error, the demon of compassion enters the mind and one loses right concentration (*samādhi*).
Ānanda, furthermore, within that state of concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear.
As superior signs manifest before them, they are moved by an excess of emotion and suddenly give rise to boundless courage within that state.

Their minds become fierce and sharp, their resolve equaling that of all Buddhas, and they claim that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment. This is called "the overstepping of functional effort through rashness. If they awaken [to this], then...
There is no fault; this is not a sign of saintly realization. When one awakens to this truth and is no longer deluded, [the afflictions] will naturally dissipate over time.
If you mistake this for saintly realization, then mad demons will enter your heart and entrails. Upon meeting others, you will boast that your self-importance is peerless.
Your mind will reach such a state that you look neither up to the Buddhas nor down to other men. You will lose right concentration and fall into ruin.

The commentary states: This is the second stage of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Within meditative concentration, one perceives that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved, and thus the aggregate of sensation becomes clear.

Seeing this superior sign, a sense of inspiration arises in the mind. If this inspiration becomes excessive, then within concentration, a great courage and vigor arise, such that one’s will equals that of the Buddhas.
One claims that what took three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can now be transcended in a single thought-moment. This is called...

"Exertion that is overbearing and transgressive": "overbearing" (*ling*) means to treat others with contempt; "transgressive" (*shuai*) means to be self-aggrandizing. This is not the realization of a sage.
Failing to realize its error, demons of madness enter the mind and great *asmimāna* (conceit) arises.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanāskandha) become clear.
Having no new realization before them and having lost their former abode, their power of wisdom declines and they enter a state of collapse, seeing nothing at all in the distance.
Suddenly, a great parching thirst arises within their minds, which sinks into constant recollection without dispersing; they take this to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called "cultivating the mind while lacking wisdom, thereby losing oneself. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a realization of the holy.

If one takes this to be a holy attainment, then the demon of recollection will enter one's heart and viscera. Morning and evening, one will clutch the mind and suspend it in a single place; one will lose right concentration and shall surely fall into ruin.
The commentary says: This is the third stage of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Because the aggregate of sensation is not yet exhausted, there is no new realization;

because the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already been exhausted, one loses the former dwelling place. In this interval between advancing and retreating, where both are difficult, wisdom and power decline and the path collapses midway.
With no recourse for the mind, a great parching thirst arises; thus, one takes deep recollection as the essence.

This is the characteristic of progress. It is called "losing oneself through a lack of wisdom"; it is not the realization of a sage. If one does not realize its falsity, then the demon of recollection enters the mind;
the mind is like a suspended net, and one loses right concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear.

Because the power of their wisdom exceeds the concentration, they lose its sharp intensity; yet, harboring various superior qualities within their minds, they themselves suspect they are Vairocana, taking little as sufficient.
This is called losing constant discernment through the application of the mind and being submerged in mere intellectual views. If they awaken to this, there is no fault.
This is not a sign of saintly realization. If you mistake this for such realization, then the demon of inferiority and easy contentment will enter your heart and mind.
You will see others and say of yourself, "I have attained the unsurpassed ultimate truth," thereby losing right concentration and falling into ruin.

The commentary says: This is the fourth stage of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Because the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) exceeds that of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one loses its sharp intensity.
Due to the emergence of a superior nature, one suspects within one's own mind that one is Vairocana; deludedly considering this sufficient, one no longer advances.

This is called using the mind with too little concentration and too much wisdom; thus, one loses constant discernment and becomes submerged in mere intellectual views. This is not the state of a sage.

This is realization. If one does not awaken to its falsity, the demon of inferiority and easy contentment will enter one's heart and viscera, leading one to claim that one has already attained the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, in Zen practice, it is essential that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) be equalized in order to skillfully employ the mind.
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) has become clear;

yet, because they have not yet attained a new realization, their former mind has already perished. As they survey these two boundaries, difficulties arise spontaneously within them, and suddenly an inexhaustible anxiety takes birth in their hearts.
It is as if sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison; the mind has no desire to live and constantly seeks someone to end its life so that it may quickly attain liberation.
This is called practicing while losing the skillful means. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a state of saintly realization.
If one forms a noble understanding [of these experiences], then a portion of the demon of constant sorrow will enter their heart and viscera.

Grasping a sword or blade in hand, they will cut their own flesh, rejoicing in the relinquishing of their life-span. Or, being constantly sorrowful, they will flee into mountain forests, unable to bear the sight of people.
If one loses right concentration (*samādhi*), one shall fall into ruin.

The commentary states: This is the fifth stage of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). When the dissolution of form and the manifestation of sensation lie between two boundaries, the former state of mind has already been lost and no new realization has yet been attained.
It is like treading upon a precipice where danger arises spontaneously; it is the seed of sorrow.
If a practitioner, spurred by intense concentration, suddenly gives rise to anxiety and distress, desiring early liberation, this is called failing in the skillful means of cultivation;

it is not a noble realization. Failing to recognize this as erroneous, one will be constantly beset by sorrow, and the Māra will enter one’s heart and viscera, causing the loss of right meditative absorption (*samyaksamādhi*).
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becoming clear and bright.
While dwelling in this purity, their minds become tranquil; thereafter, suddenly and spontaneously, an infinite joy arises within them, such that they cannot restrain their own heart’s rapture.
This is called "light ease" (praśrabdhi) without wisdom, a form of self-restraint. If one awakens to its true nature, there is no fault; it is not a realization of the holy state.
If one mistakes this for a holy attainment, a demon of partial delight and pleasure will enter one's heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, one laughs;
by the side of the road, one sings and dances alone, claiming to have attained unimpeded liberation. Having lost right concentration (samādhi), one shall surely fall into ruin.

The commentary says: This is the sixth stage of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one investigates until form (*rūpa*) dissolves and sensation becomes luminous;
consequently, body and mind become tranquil and secure, and a sudden joy arises that one cannot restrain. This is called "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*);

if one lacks wisdom and maintains this state, it is not a realization of the holy ones (*ārya*). Failing to realize its error, the demon of delight (*nandi-māra*) enters one’s heart and viscera. This is wisdom.
This is the fault of having little stability and much imbalance.
Furthermore, within that state of concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear;

they consider themselves sufficient and suddenly experience groundless great conceit (māna). Thus it extends even to conceit (māna), excessive conceit (atimāna), and conceit beyond the measure (mānātimāna).

Either the pride of superiority or the pride of inferiority may arise simultaneously; in such a state, one holds even the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt, let alone those of lower rank, such as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is called "viewing oneself as superior while lacking the wisdom to save oneself. Should one awaken to this, there will be no fault.
This is not a sign of saintly realization. If one takes this to be such realization, then a portion of the great demon of self-conceit will enter their heart and viscera.
They will fail to pay homage at stupas and temples and will destroy scriptures and images, telling donors: "These are merely gold and copper, or perhaps clay and wood."
The sutra is written on tree leaves or *karpāsa* flowers. To fail to respect one's own physical body—which is truly eternal—and instead revere earthenwood is a profound perversion.
Those with deep faith should take such [images], break them into pieces, and bury them in the ground; those who harbor doubts and mislead sentient beings will enter the Avīci Hell.
Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), they shall surely fall into ruin.

The commentary says: This is the seventh stage of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). As physical form dissolves and the clarity of sensation is revealed, the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) probes and investigates, thereby stimulating latent tendencies toward arrogance (*māna-vāsanā*).
Consequently, various forms of pride arise. To rely on oneself and look down upon others, characterized by loftiness of spirit, is generally termed *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am").

There are seven types of such pride. When one weighs oneself against others and compares one's own virtues with those of equals, it is simply called *māna* (pride). That is to say, regarding oneself as...

To consider oneself superior to those who are truly superior is called *abhimāna* (overweening pride). To contend for superiority over those who are already superior is called *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride).
To claim one has attained what one has not attained is called *adhimāna* (conceit). To look back with self-congratulation despite being inferior is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride).

To revile the scriptures and images is called *mithyāmāna* (false pride); all these arise from the habitual tendencies of pride. Thus, to treat the Buddha, the Tathāgata, with contempt is called the view of "being superior" (*śreyas-dṛṣṭi*).

Using wisdom to save oneself is not yet the realization of a sage. If one does not realize this error, the demon of great conceit will enter the heart and viscera, causing one to lose right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).

Furthermore, within that state of meditative absorption, those good men who see the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) become clear, amidst their refined spirit—
When Yuanwu refines his principles and attains great compliance, his mind suddenly gives rise to immeasurable lightness and ease. He then says, "I have become a sage and attained great mastery.
This is called obtaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom; if he recognizes this as such, there is no fault, for it is not yet a realization of sainthood.
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, then a portion of the "light-and-pure" māra will enter their heart and inner organs.
They will consider themselves satisfied and no longer seek further progress. Such people mostly become unlearned bhikṣus who mislead sentient beings and cause them to fall into the Avīci Hell.
If one loses right concentration (*samādhi*), one shall fall into ruin.

The commentary states: This is the eighth stage of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). By investigating the aggregate of sensation through meditative stability until it is found to be empty and thin, the mind of concentration becomes brilliant and pure.
Within this concentration, one perfectly awakens to the subtle principle; as the principle manifests in accordance with contemplation, sensation can no longer act as an obstruction.
Therefore, it is said that one attains great conformity. Because body and mind are harmonized and relaxed, a sudden sense of lightness and ease (*praśrabdhi*) arises.
One then imagines that one has become a sage and attained great mastery; this is called obtaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom, yet it is not the realization of a sage.
Failing to realize its falsity, a demon of "delightful lightness and purity" enters one's heart and viscera, leading one to claim self-sufficiency and cease further pursuit of progress.
The "unlearned bhikṣu" refers to one who lacks the wisdom of extensive learning, does not penetrate the factors of dhyāna, and falsely gives rise to a sense of contentment.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within that state of concentration, when the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes clear, they attain a nature of empty luminosity within that clear awakening.
Suddenly, they turn toward eternal extinction, repudiating cause and effect and entering exclusively into emptiness.

When the realization of emptiness manifests before one, even to the point that a mind arises with the understanding of perpetual cessation and extinction, there is no fault if this is merely an intellectual awakening; it does not constitute a holy realization.

However, if one takes this to be a holy realization, then the "emptiness-demon" (śūnyatā-māra) will enter one's heart and viscera, leading one to slander those who uphold the precepts as being followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Since a Bodhisattva has realized emptiness, what is there to be maintained or transgressed? Such a person constantly consumes alcohol and meat and engages extensively in sexual misconduct before faithful lay donors (*dānapati*).
By means of demonic power, they cause those before them to harbor no suspicion or slander. Having long been possessed by a ghostly mind, they may even eat excrement and urine;
for them, wine, meat, and such things are all equally empty. Thus, they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code and lead others into sin.
One will lose right concentration and fall into ruin.

The commentary states: This is the ninth stage of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Because the power of prior meditative concentration causes the wisdom of emptiness to manifest before one, as the aggregate of sensation is about to end, one attains great enlightenment.
Yet, suddenly giving rise to a view of emptiness, one turns toward eternal extinction and denies the existence of causes.
Consequently, he develops and grows in the view of annihilationism; this is not the realization of a noble one. Failing to realize his error, the demon of emptiness enters his heart and inner organs.

He then slanders the observance of precepts and violates the Buddha’s disciplinary code. Because internal meditative power stirs up false views while external forces draw in the demon of emptiness, he loses right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
Furthermore, within that meditative state, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becoming clear and bright.

They savor this empty luminosity, which penetrates deeply into the marrow of their hearts. Suddenly, an infinite craving arises within their minds; when this craving reaches its peak, it becomes madness, resulting in lustful desire.

This is called the state of meditative concentration where the mind enters with ease and compliance; however, if one lacks wisdom and maintains this through self-will, one may mistakenly enter into various desires.

Awakening to this brings no fault, for it is not a realization of the holy. If one interprets this as a holy attainment, then the demon of desire will enter their heart and viscera, leading them to invariably claim that desire is the path to Bodhi.
They will transform laypeople to practice desire equally, asserting that those who engage in sexual intercourse are "sons of the Dharma" who uphold the teaching.
By the power of divine spirits, they gather ordinary and foolish people during the final age, numbering as many as one hundred;
thus it may reach two hundred, five or six hundred, or even fill a thousand or ten million. When the demons become weary and detached, their physical bodies vanish.

Since their majestic power has vanished, they fall into the calamities of kingship; they mislead sentient beings into the Avīci Hell; having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), they shall surely undergo a downward plunge.

The commentary says: This is the tenth stage of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). As the aggregate of sensation is about to end, the internal and external become empty and luminous. By means of this—

This empty luminosity is taken as a superior realm; through greedy attachment, craving arises and penetrates deep into the marrow of the heart. When craving reaches its peak, madness ensues, and one becomes a prey to lustful desire.
By means of meditative power (*samādhi*), the seeds of habitual tendencies for greed are stimulated, thereby causing this madness.

This is called the "realm of concentration" (*samādhigocara*) which, being peaceful and compliant, enters the mind; yet because it is not shattered by the illumination of wisdom (*prajñā*), one erroneously falls into various desires. This is not the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
This is the realization. If one does not awaken to their falsity, the demon of desire will enter the mind; seized by the ghosts of lust, one will engage extensively in sexual misconduct.
When afflicted by the demons and encountering calamities, one will inevitably fall into ruin.
[△@△] Third, the earnest admonition for profound prevention:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifest states in *dhyāna* all appear because the mind is applied in a conflicting manner within the *vedanā-skandha*.
Beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to reflect upon themselves; encountering these conditions, they are confused and fail to recognize them for what they are, saying:"
To claim sainthood is a great falsehood that leads to rebirth in the Avīci Hell.

You all should likewise take these words of the Tathāgata and transmit them after my parinirvāṇa during the Final Dharma age, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find an opportunity;
maintain and protect [these teachings] so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

The commentary states: This is a profound admonition for diligent prevention. Because the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is refined and strict, yet ignorance (*avidyā*) has not been fully exhausted, residual habits (*vāsanā*) manifest along with that concentration;
thus, these phenomena are manifested through transformation. Because wisdom and principle have not yet been distinguished, it is said that "the mind and its objects interact.
If one is deluded and fails to recognize this, one falls into great falsehood. Therefore, he exhorts that the words of the Tathāgata be proclaimed to all practitioners in the Dharma-ending age.
The practitioner should realize its characteristics early; do not allow the celestial Māra to find an opportunity.
[○@◇] Third, the division of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) into three parts. [△@△] First, when the aggregate has not yet been broken.

Ānanda, when that son of good family has cultivated samādhi and exhausted the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), although his outflows (āsrava) are not yet exhausted, his mind is detached from its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage.

He is already able to achieve this: from this ordinary body, he ascends through the sixty saintly stages of a bodhisattva and attains the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya), proceeding everywhere without obstruction. It is, for example, as if a person were sleeping soundly and speaking in their sleep; this person...
Although there is no distinct object of cognition, the words they utter already possess rhythmic cadence and sequential order, causing those who do not sleep to fully comprehend their speech.
This is what is called the domain of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).

The commentary states: These words describe the manifestation of the perception of the exhaustion of experience (*pari-kṣaya-saṃjñā*). Once the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) have been shattered, the mind is free from obstruction;

thus, it is like a bird escaping from a cage. From this point, as the ordinary person ascends through the sixty stages of the bodhisattvas, such as the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), when the craving for desire (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*) has withered and the faculties and their objects no longer meet, one is able to abide securely therein.
One establishes the stage of the sages (*ārya*). Although the latter three aggregates (*skandha*) have not yet been destroyed, form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) are already exhausted;

thus, one may pass through the stage of the sages while still possessing ignorance (*avidyā*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The mention of "sixty" refers to the continuous progression through the three gradual stages up to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Having attained the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), one passes straight through mountains and walls like an Arhat, moving with the speed of a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). Therefore, it is called swift.

It is called "unimpeded," yet it is not the three kinds of mind-made bodies (manomayakāya) attained on the stages (bhūmi). Because the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) has not yet been shattered, it is like a person in deep sleep who utters gibberish.
Although one has awakened to and clearly realized the perfect principle, because this has not yet been truly realized through direct proof, it is like words already formed into sound.

Those who hear that nowadays there are few who attain awakening through Zen meditation but have not yet reached great penetration, therefore know only the Zen of intellectual understanding. Thus it is said by the listener.

Although you have attained awakening, you have not yet truly realized it; because you remain trapped within the nest of recollective thought (*smṛti-saṃkalpa*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not been shattered—this is precisely what that refers to.

If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating imaginings are eliminated, then the mind of awakened clarity will be like a mirror with dust and grime removed. This constitutes one cycle of birth and death.

When the beginning and end are illuminated all around, it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
One should observe its origin: pervasive delusion (*vyāmiśra-vikalpa*) serves as its root.

The commentary states: This is a preliminary indication of the signs of the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of perception). Since the characteristics of perception (*saṃjñā*) constitute the dust and the consciousness-emotions constitute the grime, when perception is eliminated, it is like removing dust and grime.

Because perception is exhausted, mental formations (*saṃskāra*) manifest; thus, one is able to perfectly illuminate the beginning and end of the cycle of birth and death within a single category of existence.
The turbidity of afflictions exists in dependence upon the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), arising from the confusion of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, when the aggregate of perception is eliminated, one transcends the turbidity of afflictions. Because perception can integrate the mind to give rise to mental forms and grasping, it is called "integrative deluded conceptualization."
[△@○] Second, showing the distinctions among the objects of concentration in the following ten sections:

"Ānanda, when that good man’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts as his perfect concentration becomes luminous, within this samādhi his mind comes to love its perfect clarity.
He sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks out skillful methods. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity."

He then uses his supernatural power to cause his essence to enter another person’s mouth, who speaks the Dharma and the scriptures. That person, unaware that they are possessed by a demon, claims for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
He comes to the place of that son of good family who seeks skillful means, spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma.
For a brief moment, his form may appear as a bhikṣu so that the person may see him; or he may become Śakra, or a woman, or a [lay] brother.
A bhikṣuṇī may sleep in a dark room while her body emits light; such a person, deluded by folly, falsely claims to be a bodhisattva.

Trusting in his teachings, they allow their minds to be shaken and they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code, secretly indulging in lustful desires. They take pleasure in speaking of calamities, auspicious omens, and supernatural transformations;
they may claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in a certain place, or speak of the kalpa-ending fires, or describe the terrors of war.
Regarding humans, it causes their family wealth to dissipate without cause. This is called the "Strange Ghost," which becomes a demon as it grows old and torments such a person.
Once it has become satiated and its mind turns away, it leaves the person's body; both the disciple and the master then fall into royal peril.
You should perceive this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
The commentary states: This is the first stage of the *saṃjñā-skandha*. Because the *vedanā-skandha* has already been exhausted, one does not encounter perverse deliberations;

that is to say, one has already departed from the ten previous stages of perception. Consequently, the power of meditative concentration becomes perfectly luminous, which excites latent habits of greed.
Because the mind craves this perfect luminosity, it is said to "seek skillfulness. Thus, one sharpens one's thoughts and greedily seeks out clever techniques. Since the inner mind is thus attached—

Therefore, external demons find an opportunity and send their spirits to first attach themselves to others, coming to seek out those skilled in speech to manifest various signs before them while preaching the Dharma.
Those who are skillful in speech believe [the demon] to be a Bodhisattva; such is the nature of the matters they speak.
These strange ghosts originate from the habit of greed; having thus attached themselves to people, they create obstacles when they depart.
If one awakens to this, there will be no fault.

Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts as his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination, yet within this samādhi his mind loves to wander;
he flits about with his refined reflections, greedily seeking out experiences. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for such an opportunity.
He then uses his spiritual power to attach his essence to a person’s mouth, causing them to recite the sutras and the Dharma. That person is unaware that they are possessed by a demon;
they claim for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. He comes to the place of the good man who seeks to travel [the path], spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma.
His own form undergoes no change. Those listening to the Dharma suddenly see themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers, their entire bodies transformed into purple-gold.
In this assembly of gathered light, each listener individually attained such an unprecedented realization. This person was deluded by folly and took himself to be a bodhisattva;
his mind was licentious and dissolute, and he violated the Buddha’s code of discipline while secretly practicing greed and desire.

He was fond of saying that various Buddhas had appeared in the world, claiming that "a certain person in a certain place must be the emanation-body of a certain Buddha come here," or that "a certain person is indeed a certain bodhisattva."

When figures such as these come to transform human beings, those people, upon seeing them, develop a heart of longing and thirst. Consequently, false views arise secretly and the Wisdom of All Modes (sarvajñajñāna) is extinguished.
This is called the *pūtana* ghost, who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb such a person. Once his heart has become satiated, he departs from that person’s body;
yet both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter into the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) through delusion.
Unaware that they were falling into the Avīci Hell, they deliberated, saying:
"This is the second stage of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Through the power of meditative concentration, one investigates and probes until sexual habits are aroused.
Because the mind of lust is vast and turbulent, it agitates both body and mind; thus, one greedily seeks out experiences and delights in wandering about. Therefore, [one becomes] a *pūtana*."
Ghosts originate from the habituation of lustful practice; they thereby attach themselves to humans to bring about ruin and destruction.

Furthermore, O son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts as perfect concentration (samādhi) brings forth illumination, the mind within this *samādhi* may become attached to a lingering, continuous state.
One clarifies their refined contemplation and greedily seeks a point of resonance. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for such an opportunity.

A flying spirit takes possession of a person who speaks of the Dharma and its methods. That person is actually unaware that they are possessed by a māra, yet they claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place where a seeker of the Way—a son of good family—resides, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma.
Their form and those listening to the Dharma undergo no outward change; yet they cause the listeners to experience an internal awakening of mind even before hearing the Dharma.
From moment to moment their states shifted and changed. Some attained the knowledge of past lives; some possessed the power of knowing others' minds; some beheld the hells;
some knew all manner of good and evil affairs among humans; some spoke verses aloud, while others recited sutras themselves. Each was filled with joy, experiencing things they had never known before.

Such people are deluded and confused; some may even claim to be bodhisattvas. Their hearts are permeated with attachment, and they violate the Buddha’s precepts while secretly indulging in lustful desires.

They take pleasure in saying that there are great and small Buddhas—that such-and-such a Buddha was a former Buddha and such-and-such a Buddha was a later Buddha—and that among them there are true Buddhas and false Buddhas, male Buddhas and female Buddhas; they say the same for bodhisattvas as well. Because these people see such things, they wash away their original minds.

It is easy to enter into deviant awakening. This is called a *māyā* ghost that, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb this person. Once it has become satiated and its mind turns away, it leaves the person’s body;
yet both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and unaware, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
The commentary states: "This is the third stage of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

Because the power of meditative concentration probes deeply and excites deceptive habits, the mind becomes entangled in affection and greedily seeks conformity. By using fraud and hypocrisy to deceive others while desiring to achieve harmony, one becomes possessed by demons."
Demons are fundamentally rooted in the habit of deception. Now that you have grown old, they become māras who destroy the concentrated mind.

Furthermore, when a good man’s *skandha* of sensation becomes empty and subtle, escaping perverse thoughts and illuminating the perfected concentration, within this *samādhi* he may come to love the fundamental source.
He exhaustively surveys the beginning and end of the transformation of things, refining his spirit and mind as he greedily seeks to analyze and discern them.
At that time, a celestial Māra, waiting for an opportunity, sent his refined essence to possess a person who then spoke the Dharma and the sutras.

That person was unaware beforehand that he was possessed by a Māra, and he claimed for himself that he had attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. He came to the place of that seeker of the source, a good man, where he spread out a seat and preached the Dharma.
His body possessed majestic spiritual power, which subdued those seeking instruction; thus, even before they had heard the Dharma, those beneath his seat were already overwhelmed.
Their minds were naturally subdued. These people took the Buddha’s nirvana and dharma-body to be none other than their own present physical bodies;
they saw that fathers and sons, generation after generation, mutually producing one another, was itself the eternally abiding and uninterrupted dharma-body.
They all point to the present as being the Buddha-land; there is no separate Pure Abode, nor is there the golden-hued mark. Those people, having accepted this with faith, lose their former resolve;
they offer up their bodies and lives in refuge and attain what they have never had before. Such deluded ones are mistaken for Bodhisattvas.
Investigating their minds, they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code and secretly practice lust.
