They are fond of saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all pure lands, and that the male and female organs are the true locus of Bodhi and Nirvana.
Those ignorant ones believe these defiled words; this is known as the evil ghosts of *gudu* and *yan-sheng*, who have become demons in old age to harass and disturb such people.
When a sense of satiety arises, the spirit departs from the person's body; both the disciple and the master will then fall into royal calamity.
You should attain prior awareness so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

The commentary states: This is the fourth stage of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception). Through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one investigates and exhausts the *saṃjñā-skandha*, which gradually dissolves, and the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of mental formations) is about to manifest.
Consequently, within this state of concentration, one may crave to investigate the fundamental source of things, seeking to analyze their transformations from beginning to end.

Malevolent spirits and poisonous ghosts originate from the habit-energy of resentment; because the root of resentment is deep, they now attach themselves to humans to destroy their concentration. Indeed, there are such cases.
This is the cause.

Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by deviant thoughts as his perfect concentration (*samādhi*) gives rise to illumination, he may within that *samādhi* come to love the response of distant spirits.
He circulates through them with refined investigation, greedily seeking their dark resonance. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for his opportunity.

A flying spirit may possess a person and speak of the Dharma and its methods. That person, originally unaware that they are possessed by a demon, claims for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place of a virtuous man who seeks a response, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma.
They can cause the audience to perceive their form as if it had been there for hundreds of thousands of years; the listeners develop a deep attachment and are unable to let go, becoming their slaves.
They provide the four kinds of offerings without feeling weary, each causing those in their retinue to realize that he was originally their own teacher and good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
They develop a distinct dharma-love that adheres like glue or lacquer, attaining what they have never experienced before. These people are deluded by folly and mistake him for a bodhisattva;
they draw near to his mind, violating the Buddha’s disciplinary code (*vinaya*) while secretly practicing greed and desire. In their mouths, they love to speak of—
"In a previous life, during such-and-such an existence, I first delivered such-and-such a person. At that time, they were my wife, concubine, or brother;
now they have come to deliver me. Accompanying you, we shall return to such-and-such a world to make offerings to such-and-such a Buddha.
Or it may say: "There is another Great Radiant Heaven where a Buddha dwells; it is the place where all Tathāgatas take up residence. Those who do not know this..."
Faith is deceptive and causes one to lose their original mind. This is called a fierce ghost who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb this person.
Once it has become satiated and its mind turns away, it leaves the person's body; yet both the disciple and the teacher will fall into the king’s calamity.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

The commentary states: This is the fifth stage of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Because one has brought forth illumination through perfect concentration, a mind that anticipates a responsive resonance arises.

Consequently, one greedily seeks mysterious response, thereby inviting demons into the heart. While malevolent ghosts are rooted in the habit-energy of anger and thus differ from the state of meditative concentration, their attachment must necessarily have its cause.

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and he has not encountered perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes luminous.
Within this *samādhi*, his mind loves to penetrate deeply; he disciplines himself with diligent toil, delights in dwelling in the stillness of the aggregates, and greedily seeks quietude.

At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity and sends forth his essence to possess a person, who then speaks the teachings of the sūtras. That person originally does not realize they have been possessed by a Māra.

He also claimed to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. He would come to the dwellings of those seeking the aggregates (*skandha*)—good men—and spread out his seat to preach the Dharma, causing each listener to recognize their own past karma.

Or, at such a place, he would say to one person, "Though you are not yet dead, you have already become an animal," and then command another person to step on the [first one's] tail from behind, suddenly making it impossible for that person to stand up.
Thereupon, the entire assembly bowed their hearts in reverence and submission. As soon as someone gave rise to a thought, [the Buddha] already knew its inception.

Beyond the Buddhist rules of discipline, he imposed upon himself further ascetic rigor. He slandered bhikṣus and reviled his followers; he exposed the private affairs of others without avoiding censure or reproach.
He delights in speaking of future calamities and blessings; when the time comes, not even a hair’s breadth of his predictions misses the mark.

This powerful ghost has grown old and become a demon, who harasses and confuses this person. Once he becomes satiated, he leaves the person's body, and both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal peril.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

The commentary states: This is the sixth stage of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Because the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) gradually deepens, the mind loves to enter further.
As the agitation of the aggregate of perception now gradually subsides, one takes pleasure in the stillness of the aggregates and craves profound tranquility—*mì* (謐) meaning deep stillness.
When perverse thoughts arise within, external demons secretly manifest; thus, they take advantage of the opportunity to attach themselves to people, speaking of "the Great [Vehicle]."
The "Force-Demon" (*bala-piśāca*) is precisely a hungry ghost (*preta*). It originates from the habitual practice of arrogance.

Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts as his perfect concentration (*samādhi*) gives rise to illumination, he may within this *samādhi* come to cherish knowledge and views.
He diligently and painfully investigates and seeks after past lives. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to exploit him.
A flying spirit enters a person’s mouth and speaks of the Dharma; that person is utterly unaware they are possessed by a māra, and likewise claims to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
This spirit comes to the place of a seeker of the Good—where a son of good family resides—and spreads out a seat to preach the Dharma.
Without cause, this person obtains a great precious jewel at the site of the preaching. At times, the māra transforms himself into an animal and holds the jewel in its mouth.
Furthermore, he would first bestow upon those people various rare treasures, scrolls, official documents, and diverse exotic objects before finally wearing them himself.
Or, he would entice listeners by hiding bright moon pearls beneath the ground that illuminated the spot; these listeners experienced what they had never known before.
He consumed many medicinal herbs rather than fine delicacies, and at times ate only a single grain of hemp and a single grain of wheat per day.
Their forms are plump and robust because they are sustained by demonic power. They slander bhikṣus and revile their assemblies, showing no regard for censure or reproach.
Their mouths are fond of speaking of hidden treasures in other regions and the secret abodes of sages and worthies throughout the ten directions;
those who follow them often encounter strange and extraordinary persons. These are known as the ghosts and spirits of mountain forests, lands, city walls, rivers, and peaks.
When they grow old, they become demons. Some may preach licentiousness to violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly indulging in the five desires with those who serve them;

others may practice asceticism by eating only grasses and trees. They cause confusion and distress to these people until they become weary and satisfied, at which point the demon leaves the person's body.
Both the disciples and the teacher often fall into royal punishment. You should recognize this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and unaware, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
The commentary states: "This is the seventh stage of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

Because a single thought of a mind that delights in knowledge and views suddenly arises within meditative concentration, and because one greedily seeks past lives, the Māra finds his opportunity. All such instances involve forgetting and losing oneself through the vain pursuit of desires."
Because one practices correctly, demonic disturbances are summoned. That is to say, to cultivate various roots of goodness while forgetting the bodhicitta is what is called a demonic activity;

all such instances belong to this category. Deities of the mountains, forests, and so forth are fundamentally habituated to deception. When they encounter a secluded place, they manifest forms and are termed "hypnotizing ghosts" (yān-ghosts).

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) has become empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by perverse thoughts as his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination, he may within this samādhi come to love various supernatural transformations and powers.
He investigates the source of these transformations and greedily seeks to grasp such spiritual power.

At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity and sends a refined spirit to possess a person, who then speaks of sūtras and dharmas. That person is truly unaware that they have been possessed by a demon.
He also declares that he has personally attained unsurpassed nirvana, and comes to the place where those seeking supernatural powers reside; there he spreads his seat and preaches the Dharma.
This person may even hold a flame in his hand and, grasping that light with his hand, distribute it over the heads of the fourfold assembly who are listening.
The flames atop the heads of all these listeners were several feet long, yet they lacked the quality of heat and never burned.
Some walked upon water as if treading on level ground; some sat motionless in mid-air; and some entered into jars.
Sometimes he was inside a sack; passing through windows and penetrating walls, he encountered no obstacles. Only with respect to weapons did he lack mastery.
He claimed to be a Buddha, wearing white robes and receiving the prostrations of bhikṣus; he slandered dhyāna and the Vinaya, and reviled his followers.

He exposed the private affairs of others without avoiding censure or suspicion; he constantly spoke of his supernatural powers and mastery while in their presence, or even caused people to see Buddha-lands from the side.
His demonic power deluded people and possessed no truth; he praised sexual misconduct and did not condemn coarse behavior.
To take such vulgar and lewd things as the transmission of the Dharma—these are known as the mountain spirits, sea spirits, wind spirits, river spirits, and earth spirits of heaven and earth;
the accumulated essences and phantoms of plants and trees over many kalpas; or perhaps dragon phantoms; or immortals who have reached the end of their lifespan and returned to life as phantoms;
or those whose time with the immortals has ended and whose years dictate they should die, yet their forms do not decay because they are possessed by other monsters.

When they grow old, they become demons who harass and disturb these people; once their desires are satisfied, they leave the person's body. Both the disciples and the teacher often fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
The commentary states: This is the eighth stage of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

Because one suddenly gives rise within meditative concentration to a mind that craves supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and greedily seeks to grasp such spiritual might, a demon seizes the opportunity to attach itself to a person to bring about ruin.

Due to this craving for supernatural powers, the manifestation of such powers occurs. Mountain spirits and the like originally stem from the habit-energy of views (*dṛṣṭi-vāsanā*); when they encounter an essence and take form, they are called *māng* (goblins).
Liang-ghosts.

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts as his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination, he may within this samādhi come to love entering extinction.
He researches birth by transformation and greedily seeks the profound emptiness. At that time, a celestial Māra awaits for his opportunity.
A flying spirit takes possession of a person and speaks of the Dharma; that person never realizes they are possessed by a demon, yet claims for themselves the attainment of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the dwelling of a son of good family who seeks emptiness, where they arrange seats and preach the Dharma.
Within the great assembly, their form suddenly vanishes so that the multitude sees nothing; then, from the void, they suddenly reappear, appearing and disappearing with total mastery.
Sometimes they manifest their bodies as transparent as lapis lazuli; sometimes they let their hands and feet hang down, emitting the fragrance of sandalwood;

or their excrement and urine are like thick rock honey. They revile the precepts and hold those who have left the household life in contempt, constantly speaking of the non-existence of cause and effect.

They claim that upon one death there is eternal extinction, with no further rebirth for either ordinary beings or sages. Although they have attained emptiness and stillness, they secretly indulge in lustful desires;
those who receive such desire also attain a "mind of emptiness. They deny cause and effect.

These are called the sun, moon, eclipses, vital energies, gold, jade, cinnabar plants, qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes—which do not die for thousands of ten-thousands of years and thus become spirits born within the lands.

When they grow old, they become demons who harass and disturb these people; once their desires are satisfied, they leave the person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher often fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

The commentary states: This is the ninth stage of the *saṃjñā-skandha*. Because the *saṃjñā-skandha* is gradually being shattered and the *saṃskāra-skandha* is about to manifest, within meditative concentration one develops an attachment to entering cessation (*nirodha*).
Since the *saṃskāra-skandha* serves as the basis for rebirth, one investigates the nature of transformation and greedily seeks profound emptiness (*gambhīra-śūnyatā*).
Consequently, demons manifest empty phenomena to destroy this state; these auspicious signs originate from the habitual tendencies of perversion.
Attachment to Clarity. Now, the auspicious omens of the qilin and the phoenix arise because of such spiritual practices.

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by deviant thoughts as his perfect concentration (*samādhi*) brings forth illumination, he may within this *samādhi* develop a fondness for longevity.

He laboriously investigates the subtlest points, greedily seeking eternal years, and abandons the birth of segmented existence (*vipākaja*) in order to suddenly hope for the transformational birth (*nairmāṇika*).
He contemplates the permanence of the subtle mind. At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity to send his essence to possess a person, who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma.
That person remains entirely unaware they are possessed by a Māra, yet claims for himself the attainment of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

He comes to the dwelling of the son of good family seeking the Path, spreads out his seat, and preaches the Dharma. He delights in speaking of traveling to and from other lands without obstruction, even across ten thousand *li*.
In an instant they return, having obtained those objects from that very place;

or, within a single location inside a house, across a distance of only a few paces, they cause a person to go from the eastern wall to the western wall, such that even if the person were to walk with great haste for many years, they would not arrive.

Therefore, with a mind of faith, one should believe that the Buddha appears before them. One should constantly say with one's own mouth: "The sentient beings of the ten directions are all my children.
I give birth to all Buddhas; I produce the worlds. I am the primordial Buddha; appearing in the world spontaneously, I did not attain this through cultivation."

This is called "Abiding in the World with Sovereignty. There, the celestial Māras cause their retinues—such as Cāmuṇḍā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Piśāca youths who have not yet resolved for enlightenment—to take advantage of one’s empty clarity and consume one’s vital essence.
Or, without relying on a teacher, the practitioner may personally behold Mañjuśrī Vajrapāṇi granting them long life, manifesting in the form of a beautiful woman.

They are preoccupied with greed; before even a year has passed, their livers and brains are withered away. They speak to themselves alone, and their voices sound like those of demons or malevolent spirits.
Those who do not recognize them for what they are often fall into royal calamities; they die of dehydration before even facing execution. They torment others until the victims perish.
You should perceive this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

The commentary states: This is the tenth stage of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Because within meditative concentration a mind that cherishes long life suddenly arises, one greedily seeks eternal years.
Having already departed from the fragmented existence (*bhedya-bhava*) of the desire realm, to suddenly long for the transformed existence (*pariṇāma-bhava*) is a false conceptualization.
The "subtle characteristics" (*sūkṣma-nimitta*) are said to be eternal because they take the subtle mind of arising and ceasing as their permanence. Thus, Māra finds an opportunity to destroy them.
The *Piśāca* youth refers to the *piśāca*, a spirit that consumes vital essence; *Cchaman* is also of this class.
"Listening" (*śṛṇoti*) refers to either a *yakṣa* or a *māra*. "That person" (*sa puruṣaḥ*) refers to a person who has been possessed by such beings.
[△@△] Third, the admonition for profound prevention:
Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of māras will, during the final age, leave the household life to practice the Way within my Dharma.
Some attach themselves to human bodies, while others manifest their own forms; all claim to have already attained the perfectly complete enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbuddha*).

They praise sexual desire and advocate the breaking of the Buddha’s disciplinary rules (*vinaya*). Originally, evil demonic teachers and their disciples transmitted these practices from one to another through sexual intercourse.

Thus, such perverse spirits bewitch the mind and the inner organs. In the near term, they affect nine lifetimes; in the long term, they persist for more than a hundred generations, causing those who truly practice cultivation to become entirely part of the demonic retinue.
"After their lives end, they will surely become subjects of Māra. Having lost the Right Universal Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), they shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
The commentary states: "These are the ten kinds of demonic affairs (*mārakarman*) pertaining to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

Formerly, when the Buddha dwelt in the world, although various Māras sought to destroy the Dharma, they were unable to do so due to the Buddha’s spiritual power. Māra then made this vow: 'After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, I shall rely upon...'"
He taught those who had left the household life to destroy the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha then shed tears and said, "There is nothing that can be done for you.
It is like worms within the body of a lion devouring the flesh of the lion itself. Thus we know that the bhikṣus who destroy the Dharma in the final age are all the retinue of Māra.
Nine lifetimes remain, and nine hundred years; this is the time when the One Thousand Years of the True Dharma (Saddharma) is about to end.
One kalpa consists of three thousand years. At the beginning of the Final Dharma (mofa), it is a time when the power of demons is strong and the Dharma is weak.
You need not first attain parinirvāṇa now; even if you have attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), you should remain by your vow within that period of the Final Dharma.
Arouse great compassion to rescue and deliver those sentient beings who possess a correct mind and deep faith, causing them not to cling to demons and to attain right knowledge and vision.
I have now delivered you from birth and death; if you follow the Buddha’s words, that shall be called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
The commentary states: This is an exhortation to remain and propagate the teachings in order to save the Dharma in the final age. The Buddha’s grace is difficult to repay;
even if one were to carry it upon one's head for aeons as numerous as motes of dust and offer one's body as a seat, one could never fully repay it.
If one does not propagate the Dharma, there will ultimately be no way to repay that grace. Therefore, proclaiming the Buddha’s words is what is called repaying the Buddha’s grace.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of meditative states that appear before you all manifest because the mind is applied in a state of mutual interaction within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not examine themselves. Encountering such conditions, they fail to recognize their own confusion and claim to have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You must take the words of the Tathāgata as my [instruction].

After my parinirvāṇa, transmit and reveal this to the age of the Dharma’s decay, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity;
maintain and protect them so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
The commentary states: This section on binding Māra is intended as a solemn admonition. By reverently following the Buddha’s words, one will not fall into the net of Māra;
therefore, it is fitting that these teachings be widely proclaimed to protect practitioners.

[○@◇] The fourth section, the Aggregate of Consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), is divided into three parts. [△@△] First, when the aggregate has not yet been broken through.

Ānanda, when that good man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, his ordinary dreams and fantasies vanish, and he remains constant in both waking and sleeping.
His awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky; there are no longer any coarse or heavy shadows of external objects.
He observes the great earth, mountains, and rivers of the world as if in a clear mirror: they come without sticking, and pass away without...

Traces. Receiving illumination in emptiness, all habitual patterns are utterly extinguished; there remains only the singular, pure reality. From this point, the root-source of birth and death is revealed.
One perceives the twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category.

Although one has not yet penetrated the individual origins of their respective destinies, one sees their common basis of birth as shimmering and turbid like a mirage in the wilds, serving as the ultimate ground for the floating sense organs and their objects.
The Pivot-Acupuncture Point. This is what is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. The commentary states:

This demonstrates the signs of the exhaustion of *saṃjñā* (perception) and the manifestation of *saṃskāra* (volitional formations). During the day, it constitutes the mind of perception; at night, it takes form in various dreams.
Therefore, when conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is dissolved, dreams cease. Thus, waking and sleeping are always one. The substance of the mind is fundamentally perfect and luminous;

it was previously obscured by floating thoughts and afflictions (*kleśa*). Now that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, its perfect luminosity and empty stillness are like a cloudless sky.
As afflictions vanish, the coarse and heavy phenomena that are but shadows of external objects disappear, and the essence of the eight consciousnesses shines with clarity.
All the mountains, rivers, and great earth of the world are merely like reflections in a mirror, without any separate analysis.

It is only because they are obscured by the delusive thoughts of the six consciousnesses that it is said: "the characteristics of thought become dust, and the emotional intellect becomes defilement," and thus one lacks clarity.
Now that the aggregate of thought has been shattered and the six consciousnesses have already dissolved, the essence of empty luminosity is like a mirror reflecting all things without being stained.

As for the traces: although there is the root-source of the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), there are no floating thoughts or habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the preceding six consciousnesses that can enter it;

therefore, it is said that "one realizes the absence of accumulated habits. "Realizes" (*liǎo*) means to sever; "absence" (*wǎng*) means non-existence; "accumulated" (*chén*) is synonymous with "arrayed" (*liè*).

This means there are no habits to be arrayed, and thus the eight consciousnesses are solely a single, pure reality. Furthermore, the subtle arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāra-skandha* is also stripped away.

It is revealed. This is the manifestation of the downward movement of arising and ceasing. The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) serves as the basis for the production of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Because formations manifest while perception (*saṃjñā*) has ceased, the twelve classes of sentient beings exhaust their respective categories; "exhaust" here means to reach the limit.

The individual threads of life are the seeds of karmic maturation (*vipāka-bīja*); because their substance is profound and subtle, they cannot be known, yet they are precisely the basis for the production of the homogeneous class.

The characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) have now been revealed; thus it is like a shimmering, turbid mirage. A "mirage" (*marīci*) is the solar vapor in a marshy place.

"Shimmering" (*yi yi*) refers to its flickering appearance. "Turbid" (*qing rao*) describes the characteristic of the aggregate of formations. It is called "turbid" because one has already departed from the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Because external floating sense organs and objects serve as the pivot and mechanism [for these formations], it is so described.
The Pivot Cavity: The pivot is the turning axis; the cavity is the socket of the door. This below indicates the signs of the completion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

If this clarity is undisturbed, the radiant original nature enters into the fundamental lucidity; once the fundamental state is clarified, the habitual tendencies of the original nature vanish. When the waves have subsided and transformed into still water, it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations.

Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings. Observe its origin: *Note: The term "original nature" (*yuan xing*) here refers to the fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), while "fundamental lucidity" (*yuan cheng*) refers to the cessation of that consciousness’s delusive activity.*
"Obscure and hidden delusive thoughts constitute its foundation.
The commentary states: This is a pre-indication of the signs of the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Because the *saṃskāra-skandha* is the phenomenon of arising and ceasing upon the substance of the eight consciousnesses, it is called "original nature. The eight consciousnesses are the substance of the profound abyss; they are solely a single, brilliant clarity.

It is called "clarity" and it is called "oneness. Now, when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) returns to its original nature, the eight consciousnesses are entirely devoid of arising and ceasing;
thus, the nature enters the primordial clarity. It is like water without ripples, being only still water—this is called the extinction of the aggregate of formations.

Since the turbidity of sentient beings exists in dependence upon the aggregate of formations, once this aggregate is extinguished, one is able to transcend it. This is why this aggregate [does not arise].
That which is "exhausted" takes obscure and hidden delusive conceptualization as its basis. The seventh consciousness is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness;
because it is profound and difficult to know, it is called "obscure and hidden."
[△@△] Second, showing the distinctions among the objects of concentration in the following ten sections:
Ānanda, you should know that within this *śamatha* attained through right knowledge, those sons of good family possess a concentrated, luminous, and upright mind.
The ten classes of celestial Māras will find no opportunity to harm them. Only then can they refine their study and exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

Within that fundamental class, when the origin of life is revealed, they observe that profound, pure, and perfectly turbulent source of movement. If, within this perfect source, they give rise to speculative calculations, such a person falls into the two theories of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).
The commentary states: This demonstrates the first false calculation regarding the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), namely the two [views] of causelessness.

Here, the name is first designated: because concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) abide firmly, it is called "concentrated clarity and a rectified mind. This is the sign of the cessation of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception).

While the celestial Māras exist based on the *saṃjñā-skandha*, it is within the *saṃskāra-skandha* that one actually perceives them. Once the *saṃjñā-skandha* has dissolved, one attains the ability to scrutinize the *saṃskāra-skandha* thoroughly.

This is the fundamental source of all living beings. Once the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has manifested, the primal source of birth is revealed. However, because this primal source universally relies upon the seven consciousnesses, it is called the "perfect source.

If one merely perceives the aggregate of formations and gives rise to false conceptualization, one falls into the two types of "causeless theories" (theories of causelessness regarding the self and the world).
Thus, we know that the non-Buddhist practitioners of India all possess the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); they simply do not understand the eighth [consciousness].
It is merely because of consciousness that false conceptualization arises.

First, this person perceives that there is no fundamental cause. Why is this? Because this person has already attained the complete destruction of the life-faculty (*janman-indriya*) and, by virtue of the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), sees all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas; they see the winding currents of karma and their deaths.
They see beings being born here and there, cycling through those realms; yet beyond eighty thousand kalpas, it is dark and nothing can be perceived.
They then form this understanding: "The sentient beings of the ten directions in these worlds have existed spontaneously for eighty thousand kalpas, without cause.
By such conceptualization, they lose right and universal knowledge, falling into the ways of external paths and becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
The commentary states: This demonstrates that there is fundamentally no cause. "This person" refers to one who practices dhyāna.
Because the source of the manifestation of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) has been revealed, it is said that the "vital mechanism of birth is completely shattered.

Consequently, by means of the eight hundred merits of the visual faculty, one merely perceives the circling, winding, and meandering flow of karma among sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas as they transmigrate.
One clearly understands each and every aspect of the states of birth and death; yet, for eighty thousand kalpas prior, one remains in darkness, unable to discern them.
Consequently, one falsely calculates that sentient beings have existed spontaneously without cause since eighty thousand kalpas past.

Because one has not seen the seeds of maturation (*vipāka-bīja*) within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), one falsely calculates that sentient beings are fundamentally without cause. Thus, one falls into the delusions of external paths regarding Bodhi.
Regarding nature:

secondly, there are those who see that the end has no cause. Why is this? Because these people, having already seen its root in birth, know that humans produce humans and realize that birds produce birds;
they see that crows have always been black and cranes have always been white, and that humans and devas are originally upright while animals are horizontal.
Birth is fundamentally horizontal. White is not made black by washing, nor is black created by dyeing; for eighty thousand kalpas it has remained unchanged and unshakable.
Now, at the end of this physical form, it is likewise so. Since I have never seen Bodhi from the very beginning, how could there be any further matter of attaining Bodhi?
You should know that today all phenomena are fundamentally without cause. From this reckoning, [all conceptualization] perishes.
The Samyaksaṃbuddha [said]: "Falling into the delusions of external paths regarding the nature of Bodhi—this is called the first type of external path that establishes the doctrine of causelessness.
The commentary states: This demonstrates the ultimate state of causelessness. Such a person, through meditative concentration, investigates thoroughly until they perceive the root of birth.
Originally, one sees that for all beings there is a beginning when they receive a physical form. Throughout eighty thousand kalpas, this has never changed.

One falsely claims that because it did not change before, it will not change later; asserting that humans must always produce humans and birds must always produce birds, without changing into other species.
Since I fundamentally do not see the existence of bodhi, how could there be any more of it at the end?

Regarding the accomplishment of the matter of *bodhi*: because one clings to the idea that the root cause is non-existent, one likewise clings to the idea that the derivative effects are also causeless.
Therefore, it is concluded that "all are fundamentally causeless. Furthermore, these derivative causes themselves serve as the basis for subsequent causes. This is the first calculation (*kalpa*).
Ānanda, when these good sons within this samādhi concentrate their clarity and align their minds, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure source which is yet constantly subject to agitation. Those who give rise to speculative calculations within this perfect and eternal reality fall into the four theories of universal permanence.
The commentary states: This demonstrates the second of the four theories of universal permanence regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Since the aggregate of formations consists of the subtle marks of arising and ceasing within the substance of the eight consciousnesses, one now uses the power of meditative concentration to investigate and perceive that these marks of arising and ceasing continue in succession without interruption.
Consequently, one gives rise to the discourse on the four types of universal permanence within the context of perfect permanence; this is indeed a false conceptualization.
First, this person exhaustively investigates the nature of the mind and its objects, finding no cause for either.

Through cultivation, they are able to know all the births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within twenty thousand kalpas; seeing that these all circulate in a cycle without ever being lost, they reckon them to be permanent.
The commentary states: This demonstrates the first type of pervasive eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*).

Because the practitioner, within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), exhaustively investigates the two phenomena of mind and objects, they are able to maintain that sentient beings undergo birth and death in cycles for up to twenty thousand kalpas without their essence being lost.
Since they do not emerge from this cycle of arising and ceasing, they reckon it to be eternal.
Second, this person exhaustively investigates the source of the four great elements and their four natures as being eternally abiding.

Through cultivation, they are able to know all births and deaths among sentient beings throughout the ten directions within forty thousand kalpas; they reckon that these are all essentially constant and never dispersed or lost, and thus take them to be permanent.

The commentary states: This demonstrates two types of pervasive eternalism. Because the practitioner, within meditative concentration, contemplates only the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they are able to know that the essence of the birth and death of sentient beings throughout forty thousand kalpas is eternal.

Since the four great elements are the objective aspects (*nimittabhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses, and the eight consciousnesses have not yet been destroyed, the four great elements have not yet dissolved. Sentient beings all take these four great elements as [their basis].
First, because the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are eternal, sentient beings are also eternal.

Third, because this person has exhausted the six sense faculties and realized that within the *manas*, the *ādāna-vijñāna*, and the *citta-vijñāna-manovijñāna*, the fundamental source and locus of nature are eternally constant;
thus, through cultivation, they are able to know that all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas circulate in saṃsāra without losing their continuity.
"Originally and eternally abiding; even in its ultimate state, it does not lose its nature, and thus it is reckoned as permanent.
The commentary states: "This demonstrates the three types of pervasive permanence-reckonings. In Sanskrit, this is called *kliṣṭa-manas*, which translates as 'defiled mind';
it refers to the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*). That which 'appropriates' (*upādāna*) refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Now, the practitioner, by means of...
Through the power of meditative concentration, one investigates the six sense faculties up to the *manas* that grasps and sustains;

since this refers collectively to the eight consciousnesses, it is called "the place where mind, intellect, and consciousness fundamentally originate. At this stage, although practice is not yet complete, the nature of consciousness has already been revealed, and thus it is called "the place where the nature is eternally constant.
Consequently, one is able to know that sentient beings have been fundamentally abiding from the beginning throughout eighty thousand kalpas.
Since each and every sentient being possesses the eight consciousnesses, and since the substance of these eight consciousnesses is eternal, sentient beings are likewise eternal;
this is because their fundamental nature is never lost.
Fourth, once this person has exhausted the source of conceptualization, the functioning of the mind no longer flows, ceases, or revolves, and the mind of birth-and-death ceases.
Now that [the mind] has been eternally extinguished, it naturally becomes non-arising and non-ceasing within the principle. Because they are measured by the mind, they reckon it to be permanent;
due to this reckoning of permanence, they lose right universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths, deluding their nature of bodhi.
This is called the second type of external path: the doctrine of the established perfect permanence.
The commentary states: This demonstrates the four types of views regarding permanence. The principle of "arising" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

When a practitioner is in meditative concentration, they single-mindedly investigate only deluded thoughts as being in a state of flowing and ceasing, arising and perishing. Now, the coarse and floating aggregate of perceptions (*vijñāna-skandha*) has already been extinguished.
However, the subtle aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) continues as a single stream without interruption.

Consequently, one falsely claims that once birth and cessation have ceased, this aggregate of formations naturally becomes non-arising and non-ceasing. Because one takes what is subject to arising and cessation to be non-arising and non-ceasing, one falsely calculates it to be permanent.
Due to this, one forgets bodhi and thus falls into the four heterodox theories of permanence and roundness.
Furthermore, when those good sons within samādhi maintain a firm and concentrated right mind, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. If, amidst the distinction between self and others, they give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons fall into the four inverted views, specifically the doctrine that one part is impermanent while another part is permanent.

The commentary states: This demonstrates the third calculation regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which is a partial theory of the four inversions concerning impermanence and permanence.

Because the seven consciousnesses grasp the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as a self, they may either grasp that "I" can produce others, whereby "I" am permanent and others are impermanent;
or they may grasp that "I" arise from others, whereby others are permanent and "I" am impermanent. Therefore.
It is said that among those who give rise to calculations regarding self and others, there is one class who holds [the view] that some parts are eternal and some parts are impermanent.
This refers to a person who contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions, and taking its profound stillness to be the ultimate divine self (*ātman*).
From this, one calculates that the self pervades the ten directions, concentrated and luminous, unmoving; that all sentient beings are born and die within my own mind.
Thus, my own mind-nature is called "constant," while those who undergo birth and death possess a truly impermanent nature.

The commentary states: This demonstrates the first of the four inverted views. When the wisdom of contemplation thoroughly investigates and eliminates false conceptualization, the eight consciousnesses become refined and luminous, pervading the ten directions.
Because one does not realize that this is the inherent luminosity of the essence of consciousness, one instead clings to it as a divine self (*ātman*).
From this, one calculates that the self pervades the ten directions, and all sentient beings exist within my mind.
If one dies and is reborn within this very place, then my own mind-nature is permanent, while those who undergo birth and death possess a truly impermanent nature.
This is the first method: observing only oneself.

Second, if a person does not observe their own mind, but instead observes everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and sees places where kalpas have been destroyed.
That which is called the "ultimate impermanent nature" refers to the kalpa of destruction. That which is the indestructible place is called "ultimate permanence.

The commentary states: This demonstrates the second of the four inverted views. This person, within meditative concentration, does not contemplate their own mind, but contemplates only the lands of the ten directions.
Seeing the places where the kalpas are destroyed, they designate them as "ultimately impermanent," while the places where the kalpas are not destroyed... [are designated as ultimately permanent].
This state is called "Ultimate Permanence. This refers solely to the contemplation of the other.
Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind as being subtle, refined, and extremely dense, like a minute particle.

It transmigrates through the ten directions without its nature ever changing or altering. It can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant; that indestructible nature is called the permanence of the self-nature.
"All birth and death flow forth from me; this is called the nature of impermanence. The commentary states:

This demonstrates the third of the four inverted views. This person, while in meditative concentration, contemplates that the subtle and secret flow of their own mind pervading the ten directions is unchanging in nature; therefore, they designate it as "self. Now, regarding the aggregate of form...
This [faculty] is able to cause this body to arise and perish in that very moment. That which does not harbor [such change] is my mind-nature, called the "permanence of my nature.

All birth and death flow forth from me; this is called the "nature of impermanence. This is the view based on the joint contemplation of self and other, calculating the self to be permanent and the other to be impermanent.
Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and perceives the flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Because they reckon this constant flow to be eternally abiding, whereas they regard form, sensation, and perception—which have now ceased—as impermanent, they fall into the error of reckoning one part as impermanent and one part as eternal.
Thus, they fall among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), deluding their nature of Bodhi. This is called the third type of non-Buddhist.

Regarding the "Partial Eternalist" (Ekadeśa-śāśvatika-vāda), the commentary states: This demonstrates the fourth of the four inverted views. Within meditative concentration, one observes the sequence of the four aggregates (*skandhas*);

now, seeing that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) flows and continues without interruption, one conceives of it as having an eternal nature. One observes the three [aggregates] of form, sensation, and perception...

The cessation of the aggregates (skandhas) is termed impermanence. This combined contemplation of the arising of the four aggregates leads to the conceptualization that one part is permanent and one part is impermanent.
Because all of this fails to understand the wondrous clarity, it is said that the nature of bodhi is deluded.
Furthermore, when those sons of good family within samādhi maintain a firm and concentrated right mind, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. If, within these various states, they give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons fall into the four theories of finitude.

The commentary states: This is the fourth calculation within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), concerning the theory of the four limits. By means of meditative concentration, one investigates the point where the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted;
as the aggregate of formations manifests, there are four stages which are calculated as being either finite or infinite.
First, these people calculate that the source of life’s functioning flows without ceasing; calculating the past and future, they call it "having limits";
calculating the continuous mind, they call it "having no limits."

The commentary states: This is the first calculation regarding the four limits and the middle within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Within meditative concentration, one investigates and scrutinizes the aggregate of formations, seeing that its present flow continues without ceasing.
Not perceiving the past or the future is termed "having a limit" (*sānta*); the present mind in its continuous succession is termed "without limit" (*ananta*).
This is distinguished according to the temporal positions of the three periods.
Second, this person observes eighty thousand kalpas and perceives sentient beings; prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, there is silence with nothing heard or seen.
That place where nothing is heard or seen is called "boundless," while that place where sentient beings exist is called "bounded."
The commentary states: These two views—of finitude and infinity—pertain to the four types of calculations regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Within meditative concentration, one observes that for eighty thousand kalpas prior, there was no place where seeing or hearing occurred; this is termed "infinite. To see a place where sentient beings exist is termed "finite.
This is a calculation based on the stages of seeing and hearing.
Third, this person calculates that their own self possesses universal knowledge and attains the nature of boundlessness.

Yet, all those people appear within the scope of their own knowledge, while they themselves have never known the nature of those others' cognitions. Thus, it is said that they do not attain a mind of boundlessness, but possess only a finite nature.
The commentary states: This concerns the four views regarding the finitude or infinitude of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

During meditative concentration, one perceives that the knowledge of the self pervades all places, and that all sentient beings appear within the scope of one’s own knowledge; thus, one concludes that the self possesses an infinite nature.
However, the knowledge of those sentient beings does not appear within the scope of one’s own knowledge, because they have not yet attained an infinite mind. But...
It is merely the nature of having limits. This refers to the false conceptualization based on the respective states of "this" and "that.

Fourth, this person, having exhausted the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), uses the mental pathways they perceive to calculate that within the single body of every sentient being, all things are reckoned as half-born and half-extinguished, thereby clarifying everything that exists within the world.
"Half has limits and half is limitless; by such conceptualization of being limited and limitless, one falls into the ranks of the externalists and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the fourth externalist doctrine that establishes the existence of limits."
The commentary states: This refers to the four views concerning finitude and infinity within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
By investigating and scrutinizing the aggregate of formations to realize its emptiness, one takes the state of emptiness as "cessation" and the locus of perception as "arising.

Consequently, one calculates that within the bodies of all sentient beings, half is arising and half is ceasing; the same applies to the world. Thus, the presently perceived locus is reckoned as having a limit.
That which cannot be seen is called "boundless. This is a calculation based on the stages of arising and ceasing.

Furthermore, within samādhi, those sons of good family who maintain a firm, concentrated, and upright mind will not be given an opportunity by Māra; they exhaustively investigate the fundamental source of all living beings.
If one contemplates that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source and gives rise to conceptual calculations within that knowing and seeing,
such a person falls into four kinds of inverted, undying, and evasive sophistry, which are pervasive, false speculations.
The commentary states: This demonstrates the fifth calculation within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), namely the four types of "immortal equivocation" (*amarā-vikṣepa*).
Changshui cites the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which says that non-Buddhists calculate that the heavens are eternal and thus name them "immortal.

They calculate that by answering without equivocation, one will be reborn in those heavens; however, if one answers recklessly when not truly knowing the answer, they fear it will constitute equivocation. Therefore, when there is a question...
At that time, he would answer with secrecy, saying that not everything should be spoken; or he would give an evasive reply. The Buddha criticized this, saying:

"This is truly deceptive equivocation (*sammoha-vyākarana*). Because one cannot exercise discernment regarding knowledge and vision, when questioned, one uses deceptive intelligence to give confused answers."
Therefore, it is called "immortal evasive confusion.
First, this person contemplates the source of transformation: seeing where things shift and flow, they call it "change";
seeing where there is continuity, they call it "permanence"; seeing where there is that which is seen, they call it "arising"; and not seeing the locus of seeing, they call it "cessation."
The state in which the causal nature of the continuity is uninterrupted is called "increase. The point within the midst of that very continuity where it is severed is called "decrease.
The place where each [phenomenon] arises individually is called "existence. The place where they mutually cease is called "non-existence."
While observing with reason as a whole, his mental application sees things individually.

When seekers of the Dharma come to ask about its meaning, he replies, "I am now both arising and ceasing, both existent and non-existent, both increasing and decreasing," thus confusing his speech at all times.
This causes the former person to lose the essential passages of the text.
The commentary states: "This is the first calculation among the four types of deceptive confusion within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Because one contemplates and investigates the root source of arising and ceasing, it is called 'observing the source of transformation. Within the arising and ceasing of the single aggregate of formations, one separately perceives eight meanings, namely:"
Regarding permanence and change, arising and ceasing, increase and decrease, existence and non-existence: not seeing that which sees is called "seeing the place where there is no seeing.
One observes the mind of transformation as a whole through principle, yet employs the mind to specifically perceive the eight meanings such as arising and ceasing;
thus, these are taken as the fundamental tenets. When someone comes to question this, one answers by saying it is both arising and ceasing, and so forth, based upon these eight meanings.
Answer: Because there is no definitive view, he stands between the two pillars, causing the questioner to find no logical ground;
since there is no settled view, it is said that he has "lost the chapter and its verses."
Second, this person contemplates the mind and finds that it has no fixed location whatsoever; because there is nothing to be found, they realize the truth.
When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying simply "non-existence" (*wu*). Apart from this non-existence, they have nothing further to say.
The commentary states: This is the second of the four types of deceptive confusion regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), namely "single-mindedly investigating non-existence.
By examining and scrutinizing the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations, one perceives only that each moment ceases; this state of mutual non-existence is then reckoned as "non-existent.

One concludes that all phenomena are likewise so, and thus it is said: "One attains realization because of non-existence. Consequently, when someone comes to question them, they simply reply, "It is non-existent."
It is but a single word.
As for the three types of people, they each contemplate their own minds and find that each has its own locus; through this, they attain realization.
When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying simply "it is so. Apart from this, they have nothing further to say.
The commentary states: This is the third of the four types of deceptive confusion regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), namely the solitary reckoning of existence.

By investigating and scrutinizing the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations, one perceives that each and every place of arising is individually existent. Based on this, one concludes that all things exist.
Therefore, when someone comes to question them, they simply answer, "Yes. Although they observe the places of arising as being existent, furthermore—
Because he perceives cessation, he does not dare speak directly of existence, but merely answers with the single word "is" (*asti*) to prevent error.

Fourth, as for the person who perceives both existence and non-existence: because their object is bifurcated, their mind is likewise distracted. When someone comes to question them, [they respond thus].
He replied, "It is both existent and non-existent; yet within that which is non-existent, it is not existent. This was entirely evasive and beyond the reach of rigorous inquiry.
By such speculative and deceptive sophistry regarding emptiness, he fell into the ranks of the external paths and became deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the fifth heterodox school’s nature of the four perversions: the futile, evasive discourse of the "Immortal" (Amarāvikṣepa). The commentary states:
Among these four types of evasive discourse regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), this fourth type involves dualistically calculating both existence and non-existence.

Because one investigates and exhaustively analyzes the two aspects of arising and ceasing within the aggregate of formations, one dualistically calculates both existence and non-existence; this is because the objects of perception are manifold and not uniform.
Their minds are likewise confused. When someone comes and asks, they answer, "It both exists and does not exist.
This means that within "both existing," they implicitly admit the presence of non-existence, because they perceive that arising is itself cessation.

As for their claim that "within non-existence, it is not also existence," this is because they perceive that at the point of cessation, they do not allow for arising; that is, they dare not say there is existence within non-existence.
Because existence and non-existence thus mutually negate and exclude one another, it is said that there is no room for further inquiry or refutation.
All of this is merely false conceptualization, lacking any definitive principle; therefore, it is called "deceptive confusion" and "universal conceptualization of empty discourse."
Furthermore, when those good sons within samādhi maintain a firm and concentrated right mind, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. Those who, amidst this inexhaustible flow, give rise to speculative calculations will fall into the inverted resolve of perceiving signs after death.
The commentary states: This demonstrates the sixth calculation regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which consists of sixteen views concerning the arising of signs after death.

It is the inexhaustible flow of the aggregate of formations. Now, seeing that formations shift without ceasing, one universally clings to the existence of signs after death, because one takes these formations to be the self.

Some fixate upon their own bodies, saying "form is the self" (i.e., form is the self); some perceive the self as encompassing and pervading the entire realm, saying "the self possesses form" (the self is large and form is small, with the self within it);
some regard the preceding objects of perception as following the movements of the self, saying "form belongs to the self" (the self apart from form);

or again, they perceive the self as persisting through the continuity of mental formations, saying "the self is in form" (form is large and the self is small, with the self within form)—all of which are conceptual constructions.
"There is a mark after death. Thus, there are sixteen such marks in this cycle. The commentary states:

This view arises because one perceives the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as inexhaustible, and thus clings to the notion that there is a mark after death; this is the original fundamental calculation.

From the firm physical form (*rūpa*) being taken as "self" and so forth, there are four [such views]; subsequently, the same applies to the other three aggregates. Now, observing the aggregate of formations...

The "inexhaustible flow" (ananta-srotas). By analogy, observing the preceding three [categories] also results in inexhaustibility. Thus, calculating the post-mortem existence of signs constitutes sixteen signs.

Since the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has already been refuted, one likewise proceeds with the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) as inexhaustible; therefore, one clings to the body as solid. This calculation is that "form itself is the self" (rūpam eva ātmā).
Alternatively, one calculates that the self is pervasive and complete, thinking, "I possess form" (rūpavān ātmā), meaning the self is larger than the form.
"Small form is within me": the preceding object is the form currently before one's eyes. "Form belongs to me" means that apart from form, there is a self distinct from it.
Regarding the continuity within the formations (*saṃskāra*), one thinks, "I am in form," meaning that while form is large and the self is small, the self is within form.
One makes these four reckonings regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); and it is the same for the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
Thus it is. The four aggregates together constitute sixteen aspects.
From this, some may reckon that affliction and enlightenment are ultimately two distinct natures that proceed side by side, each remaining untouched by the other.
Because they speculate that there is existence after death, they fall into the ranks of the external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the sixth external path’s inverted theory of mind which establishes the characteristics of existence after death within the five aggregates.
The commentary states: This is because [the opponent] calculates that the four aggregates (*skandha*) persist after death and possess characteristics;

therefore, they separately calculate that afflictions (*kleśa*) and bodhi do not supplant one another, and that these two natures proceed together until a future existence ultimately arises, just like the four aggregates. This is, in fact, a discourse based on inversion.
Furthermore, when those sons of good family within samādhi maintain a firm, concentrated, and upright mind, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings, observing that which is profound, pure, and yet the constant source of agitation. If they conceive speculative calculations regarding the prior cessation of form, sensation, perception, and volition, such persons fall into the inverted resolve of asserting that there is no appearance after death.
The commentary states: This is the seventh false conceptualization within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), namely the reckoning that there is no appearance after death.

Through contemplative investigation, one perceives that the first three aggregates have already ceased; seeing this, one then realizes that the aggregate of formations has likewise ceased. Therefore, one reckons that there is no appearance after death.

Seeing that form has ceased, one finds no basis for its manifestation. Contemplating that perception has ceased, the mind is no longer bound. Knowing that sensation has ceased, there is no further connection.
The nature of the aggregates dissolves; even if the processes of life persist, being devoid of sensation and perception, they are the same as grass and trees.

If this physical basis cannot be found even while present before one, how could there be any further characteristics after death? Examining this, one finds that the characteristics after death do not exist;
thus, the cycle ceases and the eight [bases] become signless (the four aggregates perish, so cause and effect are lost).

From this, one may speculate that the causes and effects of *nirvāṇa* are all empty, existing merely as names and ultimately subject to total annihilation. It is from such reckoning that one concludes regarding death.
Because there is nothing after death, they fall into the heretical views that delude the nature of Bodhi. This is called the seventh heretical doctrine:
the inverted theory of mind which posits the non-existence of signs after death within the five aggregates.
The commentary states: This [argument] asserts that because the present causes of the four aggregates perish and the future fruits are lost, eight kinds of signlessness are established.
This, however, reckons the causes and fruits of nirvana as entirely empty; it constitutes a nihilistic view and a perverted doctrine.

Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi*, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māra finds no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure source which is yet constantly subject to agitation.

While abiding in the stage of "activity" (*saṃskāra*), they simultaneously suppress "perception" (*saṃjñā*) and "feeling" (*vedanā*), dualistically calculating existence and non-existence until their own conceptual frameworks cancel each other out.
Such a person falls into the nihilistic view that there is neither existence nor non-existence after death, giving rise to perverse theories.

The commentary states: This is the eighth false conceptualization regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), concerning the state after death as being neither existent nor non-existent.

While within the persistence of the formations, one simultaneously experiences the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā* and *saṃjñā*) and dualistically calculates both existence and non-existence; that is, one uses the three aggregates already ceased as an analogy for the currently existing aggregate of formations.

One constructs four propositions of "non-existence" (*abhāva*). Furthermore, taking the presently existing aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as an example for the three aggregates that have already ceased, one constructs four propositions of "non-non-existence" (*anabhāva*).

When these preceding and succeeding [propositions] are compared, each aggregate possesses both non-existence and non-non-existence, thus forming four propositions of "neither-existence-nor-non-existence.
Since it is so for the present, it is likewise after death; therefore, eight propositions of "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" are established.
Within form, sensation, and perception, one perceives both existence and non-existence; within the flux of mental formations, one internally contemplates neither existence nor non-existence.

Thus, through this cyclic progression, one exhaustively investigates the aggregates, elements, and bases, finding them all to be characterized by "neither-both-nor. Upon encountering any given object, one invariably asserts that after death there are both signs and signlessness.
The commentary states: This arises from the fact that none of the eight characteristics apply here. The three aggregates of form and so forth existed previously but now do not;

the same principle applies to the other [aggregates]. Thus, these four are non-existent. As for the statement that within the flux of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one observes through internal contemplation that there is neither existence nor non-existence:

this means that if one were to apply the same logic as before to the aggregate of formations and conclude it is non-existent, it would contradict what is currently perceived—namely, that the flux continues without interruption. Therefore, it is also not [the case that it is non-existent].
There is no [existence]. Since conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) is not non-existent, the same applies to the preceding three; these four are not non-existent either.

Thus, "cycling through until the aggregates and elements are exhausted" means that one currently cycles through the four aggregates by examining their characteristics and examples, seeing that each is neither existent nor non-existent;

hence it is called "cycling. It is only upon reaching after death that one speaks of "exhausting the aggregates and elements," which refers to the eightfold characteristic of being neither [existent nor non-existent].
"Whichever single condition is encountered" means that whichever aggregate (skandha) is cited, after death, all are neither existent nor non-existent.
That which has characteristics is not non-existent; that which lacks characteristics is not existent.

Furthermore, because they calculate that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is subject to change and distortion, their minds give rise to a penetrating realization that both existence and non-existence are neither true.

Being unable to determine whether things are empty or real, they speculate that after death one is neither of these two states; thus, the future limit (*aparānta*) is shrouded in darkness and beyond description.

Consequently, they fall into the ways of external paths (*tīrthika*), deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the eighth external path, which posits that within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) there is a state of being "neither" after death.
The Discourse on the Perversion of Mind.
The commentary states: These four views are specific reckonings within the "neither-nor" [position].

Because one contemplates that the four aggregates are neither existent nor non-existent, one reckons that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is subject to change and transformation; thus, one universally realizes that all things are neither existent nor non-existent. Because they are neither...

Because existence and non-existence, reality and unreality are indeterminate, it is said that one loses one's bearings. Since existence and non-existence are already indeterminate in the present, how much more so after death, when one is in a state of confusion;
what can possibly be said then? It is merely a matter of inverted views.
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure source which is yet constantly subject to agitation. If they subsequently engage in speculative calculations regarding non-arising, such persons fall into the seven theories of annihilationism.
These include: calculating that the body is annihilated; or that desire is annihilated; or that suffering is annihilated; or that extreme bliss is annihilated.
Or there is the ultimate abandonment and extinction. Thus, through such cycles, one exhausts the seven limits until they manifest and are extinguished;

once extinguished, nothing remains. Based on this calculation, one concludes that after death there is annihilation. Falling into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), one becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the ninth heterodox doctrine: the inverted theory of mind within the five aggregates which asserts annihilation after death.

The commentary states: This refers to the ninth false conceptualization within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), namely the seven types of annihilationism. It consists of observing that at the point where the aggregate of formations arises and perishes moment by moment, there is "non-existence" in each subsequent instant.

It further posits that even if one were born in seven specific locations, one would subsequently undergo total annihilation. These seven locations are: (1) the cessation of the body in the human or heavenly realms; (2) the exhaustion of desire in the first dhyāna;

(3) the exhaustion of suffering in the second dhyāna; and (4) extreme bliss in the third dhyāna. [The remaining three are the cessation of perception in the fourth dhyāna, the realm of infinite space, and the realm of nothingness.]

This refers to the ultimate relinquishment of the four dhyānas and the formless realms; this is called the "seven limits. It means that in these seven locations, all [defilements] are completely severed and extinguished, such that after death one is no longer reborn.
Furthermore, within samādhi, those sons of good family who maintain a firm and concentrated right mind cannot be exploited by Māra; they exhaust the very root of all classes of living beings.

Observing that profound stillness which is constantly subject to the movement of its source, if one subsequently engages in speculative calculations regarding rebirth, such a person falls into the "Discourse on the Five Nirvanas. The commentary states:
This refers to the tenth false calculation within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), wherein one observes the cessation of the aggregate of formations and—
Furthermore, they give rise to what is called "subsequent existence," falsely calculating the five stations as the fruit of nirvana.
This is because they may take the desire realm as the true basis of transformation due to perceiving its clarity and brightness and thus conceiving a longing for it;

or because they take the nature of the first dhyāna to be free from sorrow; or because they take the mind of the second dhyāna to be free from suffering; or because they take the third dhyāna to be accompanied by extreme joy.

Alternatively, because both suffering and pleasure have perished in the four dhyānas and one does not undergo the nature of birth and death within saṃsāra, one becomes deluded regarding the tainted heavens and conceives the notion that they are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Taking the five voids as peaceful and secure, one regards them as the supreme pure refuge. Thus, one revolves through these five locations until reaching their ultimate limit.
Based on this speculative reckoning, they conceive of five kinds of present nirvana; thus they fall among the heterodox paths and become deluded regarding the nature of bodhi.
This is called the tenth heterodox doctrine: the inverted theory of establishing five kinds of present nirvana within the five aggregates.

The commentary states: This refers to the five characteristics of *nirvāṇa*. "Transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) means transforming the basis of birth and death into the basis of *nirvāṇa*.

When one has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), one perceives the mark of perfect luminosity within the mind of contemplation, and thus takes that very realm of desire as the locus of transformation.

Alternatively, in the first dhyāna, one has already abandoned the defilement of desire and no longer possesses a mind of sorrow; in the second dhyāna, one is free from suffering; and in the third dhyāna...
Extreme joy (*prāmodya*). When both suffering and pleasure have ceased in the fourth dhyāna, it is called extreme equanimity (*upekṣā*).

These five stages are precisely the bases for the transformation of the support (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), namely, the five [types of] manifest nirvāṇa. Due to practicing meditative concentration, one attains a slight degree of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*);
not realizing that these are present outflows (*sāsrava*), one falsely clings to them as being nirvāṇa.
[△@△] Third, the exhortation to guard deeply:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of delusive understandings regarding *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) in a state of mutual interaction.
Beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. When these states appear before them, they mistake their confusion for understanding and say:"
To claim sainthood through such great false speech constitutes falling into the Avīci Hell.
The commentary states: these constitute the ten kinds of delusory understandings within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). All ten of the above are, in fact, wrong views.
