Because one gives rise to false views while practicing meditative concentration, it is called "mad understanding. Because one falsely engages in conceptual calculations amidst arising and ceasing, failing to clarify the contemplation of principle, it is called "intermingling."
"You must certainly transmit these words of the Tathāgata to the final age after my parinirvāṇa, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning.
Do not allow the demons of the mind to give rise to deep afflictions within themselves; maintain and protect them so that false views may be extinguished."
Instruct them so that their body and mind may awaken to the true meaning, ensuring they do not encounter byways on the unsurpassed path;
do not allow their minds to seek the small and consider it sufficient, but act as the pure guiding finger of the Great Awakened King.

The commentary states: This is an exhortation to propagate and proclaim [the teachings]. In the preceding section on the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate), external māras were cited; therefore, they are called "celestial māras" (*deva-māra*).
In this *saṃskāra-skandha* (volitional formations aggregate), the phenomena are subtle and all arise as false views within the concentrated mind itself;

therefore, they are called "mental māras" (*citta-māra*). These are calamities and misfortunes created by oneself, not something that comes from without. Therefore, one must propagate and proclaim [the teachings] to protect them, maintaining foreknowledge and vigilance so as not to fall [into error].
Because of wrong views, it is said that one does not encounter "branches and forks. Branches are not the root, and forks are not the correct path;
by departing from these, one may reach the place of ultimate peace and security.
[○@◇] The fifth aggregate of consciousness is divided into three parts. [△@△] First, when the aggregate has not yet been destroyed:

Ānanda, when that virtuous man practices *samādhi* and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the subtle, pure, and restless commonality of all worldly natures and the generative impulses of living beings suddenly collapse and shatter;
the subtle, underlying tendencies and the *pudgala*’s retribution for karma [are likewise dissolved].

The profound resonance of the channels was suspended and severed. As the dawn approached in the heaven of Nirvana, he was about to achieve great awakening; like a rooster crowing at daybreak, he looked toward the east and saw that it already possessed a refined radiance.
The six sense faculties were empty and still, no longer wandering or dissipated. Internally and externally, they were limpid and bright, entering a state of non-entry.

He profoundly penetrated the fundamental source of life for the twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions. Observing the origins of these various classes through their attachments to the root...
Without being summoned, one has already attained identity with all within the realms of the ten directions; its refined radiance does not sink away, but reveals what is obscure and secret.
This is called the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

The commentary states: This clarifies the manifestation of consciousness when formations (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted. "The nature of the world" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) as the substance of worldly birth and death.
Because the birth and death of sentient beings all depend upon the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations, it constitutes the "vital mechanism" (*jī*) of shared existence (*sabhāgatā*).
What was previously called the "foundation" (*ji*) refers to its root; what is now called the "mechanism" (*ji*) refers to its pivotal function. This means that...
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the most profoundly deep and subtle, acting as a net that ensnares all realms of existence and forms knots that cannot be untied;

thus it is called a "mainstay and tie. Now, through the power of meditative concentration, one investigates and exhaustively penetrates it, suddenly shattering it; thus it is said to be "suddenly torn asunder. A *pudgala* is translated as "one who repeatedly takes up [existence].
The twelve classes of beings are grasped by means of this aggregate of formations; now that it has been shattered, the cause...

Since the fruits of existence have perished and one no longer undergoes future rebirths, it is said that the profound channels through which karma is repaid and the resonance between cause and effect are suspended.

Thus, we know that if one can extinguish the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one will forever be liberated from the birth and death of the segmented realm (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*). This is the exhaustion of the *skandha* of formations.

The darkness of the five *skandhas* covers the heaven of *nirvāṇa*, creating the long night of birth and death; now that the four *skandhas* have been shattered, it is like the opening of the heavens.

"Approaching dawn": when the rooster crows after midnight, it is the time approaching dawn. Because the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is pure and brilliant, it is like the brilliant color of the eastern sky.

Once the formation-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has ended and the faculty of mind (*manas*) has been dissolved, the six consciousnesses have no substance; thus, the six sense faculties become empty and still, no longer racing outward.
Internally illuminating the essence of consciousness, there is a pervasive, singular, and profound clarity. This profound entry merges with the profound, such that there is nothing further to enter.

Therefore it is said: "Internally and externally serene and luminous, one enters that which has no place of entry. The consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is the fundamental source from which the twelve classes of beings receive their life-force.

Upon reaching this stage, one profoundly penetrates [this truth] and observes only the nature of consciousness as it sustains the root of the sense organs. Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) no longer function, and new karma does not arise;
thus, there is no further portion for rebirth. Therefore it is said: "The various classes do not summon [them]; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the twelve classes..."

The worlds of body, mind, and environment arise as the manifestation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Now, because one contemplates that they return to the nature of consciousness, it is said that "one has attained their sameness.
Because the essence of consciousness is present before one without obscuration, it is said that "the subtle color does not sink.

Because the substance of consciousness is profound and secret, and is now investigated and penetrated through the power of contemplation so that it clearly enters the sphere of observation, it is said to be "revealed. This is called the "confined region of the aggregate of consciousness" (*vijñānaskandha-vyavasthāna*).
The term "universe" (*yǔ*) refers to the fact that although the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) has manifested, it has not yet been destroyed;

hence it is called the "realm" (*qūyǔ*). If, within the collective invocation, one has already attained the dissolution of the six sense-gates within the state of sameness, such that their opening and closing are perfected, and seeing and hearing interpenetrate so that their mutual functions are pure, then the ten directions of the world, as well as one's own body and mind, will be as transparently clear inside and out as *vaiḍūrya* crystal.
This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness. Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life. One should observe its origin:
it is rooted in the insubstantial, the void, and inverted false imaginings.

The commentary says: This clarifies the characteristic of the exhaustion of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*). "Amidst the collective summons" refers to the midst of the essence of consciousness itself.
If one investigates and exhaustively analyzes within this midst through the power of contemplation, then that which was previously obstructed by the six sense organs will now be worn away;
the six gates will merge into a single entity, and their obstructions will open. Thus, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing will function interchangeably for one another. Then...

The six sense organs are purified, and the dull [state] becomes one of perfect, bright, and pure awakened awareness. Thus, the body, mind, and world are as clear and transparent inside and out as vaidūrya;

this is called the exhaustion of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate). Since the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kāluṣya*) is established upon consciousness, now that the *vijñāna-skandha* is shattered, one transcends the turbidity of life.
"Vague and void" means it appears as if existent yet as if non-existent; this is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The "shadow of clarity" refers to taking the initial phase of ignorance (*avidyā*) as the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
[△@△] Second, "showing the distinctions of the meditative objects" comprises the following ten sections.

Ānanda, you should know that when these good men have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and returned to the source within consciousness, they have extinguished arising and ceasing;

yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, they have not yet perfected it. They are able to cause their own physical sense organs to merge or open at will, and they can communicate with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions.
Their awareness is universally pervasive, enabling them to enter the perfect source. If, however, they establish a cause of true permanence based upon this state to which they have returned—

One who gives rise to such resolute conviction falls into the attachment to causes and their underlying reasons. Such a person becomes an associate of the followers of Śāṃkara who take refuge in the obscure principle (tattva).

They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the first instance of establishing a mind that seeks attainment and forming a fruit toward which one returns.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvāṇa, giving rise to the seeds of external paths.

The commentary says: This is the initial false conceptualization within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Because the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has already been emptied, one returns to consciousness to revert to the source.
However, as ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet exhausted, there remains a subtle, continuous flow; thus, the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected.

Through the perfect clarity of contemplative observation, one is able to cause the six sense organs of one’s own body to shift from being mutually exclusive to now becoming integrated and opened. Yet, they have not yet attained complete mutual functioning.

Observing that all categories of beings in the ten directions are manifestations of consciousness-only, one awakens to the knowledge that they universally flow into the perfect, fundamental nature of enlightenment (*bodhi*).

However, this power of contemplative observation alone is not yet ultimate. If, regarding the ground to which one returns, one falsely establishes it as the cause of true permanence and develops a definitive understanding based upon this, such a person falls into the "cause-as-effect" [error].

Attachment to cause (*hetu-grāha*) means that because one clings to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as being truly eternal and as the cause of all phenomena, it is called "the cause of causes.
Since the myriad phenomena of the world arise from delusion, and delusion itself has no fundamental cause, they are said to be "unborn" (*anutpāda*).
Now, if one insists that this consciousness can produce all phenomena, it is no different from the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) clung to by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Because the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists cling to the principle of the Primal Darkness (*avyakta*) as the sovereign truth, asserting that from this darkness arise the twenty-five principles, such as Intellect (*buddhi*), they take the Truth of Darkness to be the cause of all produced phenomena.
Since they conceive what is not a cause to be a cause, this erroneous view arises, causing them to lose right knowledge and vision.
All of these reckonings are based on the mind that grasps at existence as its point of refuge; therefore, they contradict *nirvāṇa*.

One thus becomes a follower of the non-Buddhist paths. Therefore, for a practitioner of Chan, if even the slightest trace of intellectual views remains undestroyed, they will fall into the heterodox views of external paths;
how much more so if they engage in false conceptualization?

Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth and death, yet regarding that subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction—

It is not yet perfected. If one regards that which is taken as refuge as being one's own self, and develops the conviction that all sentient beings within the twelve categories throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space are but a single class of beings born from within one's own body, such a person falls into the attachment to "the capable" and "the incapable.
Maheśvara will manifest boundless bodies to become their companion; they will lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and fall into delusion.
This is called the second establishment of the capacity for the mind to accomplish its functional fruit. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana;
it gives rise to the seeds of the "all-pervading self" among the deities of great arrogance.
The commentary says: This is the second false conceptualization within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Although one has investigated the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) through contemplative insight and realized its emptiness, one has not yet attained complete awakening to the single mind of quiescent extinction. Consequently, one takes the nature of the returning consciousness as one's own self.
Seeing that the nature of consciousness is perfect and pervasive throughout the realm of empty space, one then conceives that the twelve classes of living beings proceed from this "self."
To claim that a certain class of things within the body flows forth as something fixed is to fall into the dualistic grasping of "the capable" and "the incapable.
In reality, they are incapable, yet they falsely conceive them to be capable; thus it is called "the capable and the incapable.
Maheśvara is Mahādeva. Non-Buddhists reckon Mahādeva to be eternal and capable of producing all phenomena, manifesting boundlessly.
The "body" refers to the grasping at one's own body as being able to manifest for immeasurable sentient beings.
Since this cause cannot accomplish the functional efficacy of the fruit, it is not right knowledge or vision; thus, it contravenes Nirvana and constitutes the seed of the pervasive and perfect self.

Furthermore, a good man may have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet his subtle and wondrous state of cessation has not yet reached full perfection. If, regarding that to which he returns,
he takes it as a place of refuge and suspects that his own body and mind flow forth from it, and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it— then,
regarding the very ground from which all these things arise and flow forth, he will conceive the understanding that it is a true, eternal body free from birth and death.
Within the midst of arising and ceasing, they prematurely reckon it to be eternally abiding; thus, they are deluded regarding non-arising and likewise confused about arising and ceasing.

Those who dwell securely in this deep-seated delusion while forming a resolute conviction [of permanence] fall into the dualistic attachment of permanence and impermanence, reckoning the Lord (Īśvara) as their companion.
They have lost the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeited their true knowledge and vision. This is called the third stage: establishing causes based on the mind to produce deluded calculations of results;
it is to be far removed from perfect penetration, to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana, and to give rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.

The commentary states: This is the third false conceptualization within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). That which is "returned to" is the very substance of consciousness itself. Previously, one perceived that which is returned to as one's own substance;
now, one identifies that which is returned to as an alien substance. Consequently, one suspects that one’s own body and all phenomena arise from that [alien source].
Thus, one regards consciousness as the universal ground of flux, calculating it to be eternally real and devoid of arising or ceasing.
Commentary: While still dwelling within birth and cessation, they prematurely reckon it to be true permanence (*nityatā*), failing to realize the meaning of true non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Since they take birth and cessation to be non-arising, it is said: "Being deluded regarding non-arising, they are also deluded regarding birth and cessation.

Because they recognize neither and stubbornly cling to them without relinquishing them, they abide in deep-seated delusion. Because they reckon the impermanent to be permanent, it is said: "The permanent is not permanent."
[The Master] said: "Since you reckon that he can produce me, this is of the same category as reckoning that the Lord (Īśvara) can produce me.

Because one relies on the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*)—which is a cause—and falsely reckons it to be an effect, it is called 'false reckoning of the effect. Because one reckons that which is subject to arising and ceasing to be non-arising, it is called 'perverted perfection.'"

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) has already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), he has not yet perfected it.

If, regarding that which is known, his knowledge is universally pervasive, he establishes a view based on that knowledge: that all plants and trees in the ten directions are called sentient beings and are no different from humans;
that plants and trees become humans, and when humans die, they return to becoming plants and trees in the ten directions—possessing a universal knowledge that makes no distinction.
One who gives rise to such superior understanding falls into the attachment of knowing non-knowing. Paṭācārī and Śākya-bhadra take all forms of awakening as their companions;
they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fourth calculation: reckoning the perfect mind to result in false and erroneous fruits.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of inverted cognition.

The commentary states: This is the fourth false discrimination within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). That which is known is precisely the aggregate of consciousness being observed.

By contemplating that the substance of consciousness is perfectly pervasive, one realizes that all grasses and trees throughout the ten directions are manifestations of consciousness alone. Failing to comprehend this principle—

Consequently, they falsely calculate that plants and trees possess consciousness and are of the same substance as humans. Because they do not distinguish between sentient and insentient beings, it is said that their "omniscience" is indiscriminate.
Taking this as a certainty, these individuals fall into the attachment of regarding consciousness as non-consciousness.

*Pāṭa* and *Sainika* are the names of two such heterodox teachers. They maintain that all that is conscious is identical to the consciousness found in plants and trees; thus, they are categorized as such.
Because they falsely conceive that insentient things possess cognition, they produce false and erroneous results, which serve as the seeds for inverted knowledge.

Furthermore, good son, one who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished arising and ceasing, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected—
If one has already attained conformity within the interfused mutual functioning of the sense organs, then all things will arise through circular transformation:
one seeks the light of fire, delights in the purity of water, craves the circulation of wind, and contemplates the perfection of sensory objects, each revering and serving their respective domain.
Using these various sensory objects as the primary cause for their manifestation, they establish a view of permanence. Such people fall into the attachment to birth and non-birth;
they become companions to those Kāśyapas and Brahmins who diligently exert themselves physically to serve fire and revere water, seeking to transcend birth and death.
They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true insight. This is called the fifth form of attachment: the devotion to ritual service.

The deluded mind follows external objects to establish false seeking; because of this seeking, it falsely hopes for results. Thus, it becomes remote from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of perverted transformations.

The commentary states: This is the fifth false discrimination within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Although one has investigated and scrutinized the six sense faculties through contemplative illumination, [it remains...]

Having mutually employed them, they attain a state of conformity. As the four great elements gradually dissolve, they falsely claim that all things are transformed through this perfect integration and thus arise.

Consequently, they reckon the four great elements to be permanent and capable of producing the fruits of sagehood; therefore, each person reveres and serves them. Taking the four great elements to be eternally abiding, they believe they can produce superior fruits;
yet the nature of these four great elements is in fact incapable of producing anything—it is only through false calculation that they are reckoned as being able to produce.
Therefore, it is said that they give rise to the grasping for birth within non-birth. The three Kāśyapas were among those non-Buddhist practitioners who worshipped fire;

having become deluded regarding mind-only, they falsely established cause and effect based on external objects. Because they perverted the principle of transformation, they are called the "seed of inverted transformation."

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*) is not yet perfected:

if he reckons that within this perfect luminosity there is a voidness of clarity and is not the extinction of the manifold transformations, and thus takes this eternal extinction as his refuge and gives rise to a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), such a person falls into the attachment of "taking refuge in that which is no refuge.
This refers to the various *śūnyatā* beings among the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).

They become its companions, deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the sixth fruit of emptiness and loss, achieved through a mind that is perfectly void and heartless.
It violates and distances itself from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of nihilism.

The commentary says: This is the sixth false discrimination within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). By means of contemplative observation and thorough investigation, one perceives that the nature of consciousness is empty and luminous;

thus, within this state, one sees that the preceding four aggregates have already ceased, and since all things are eternally extinguished therein, it is said that "the manifold transformations are not extinguished," meaning they are not utterly annihilated.
One then takes this eternal extinction as the place of refuge and clings to this view of certainty.
This person falls into the attachment to "non-return as a refuge. Because annihilation is not a ground of refuge, it is called the attachment to non-return as a refuge.
This is the same category as the non-conceptualizing (asaṃjñika) non-Buddhists and those who have attained the four formless absorptions (ārūpya). Śunyatā is emptiness.
This attachment takes the voidness of emptiness and the cessation of the mind as its cause; therefore, it results in the fruit of empty extinction and serves as the seed for annihilationism.

Furthermore, O son of good family, you have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and have already extinguished birth and death, yet regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, you have not yet perfected it.

If one develops a resolute conviction that the body is perfect, eternal, and solid, remaining forever without changing or passing away—being like a refined essence that is circular, long-lasting, and never tilting or perishing—such a person falls into the attachment of grasping at both desire and non-desire. They become companions to those Āsuras who seek longevity.

They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the seventh: clinging to the source of life to establish a cause of solid delusion, which leads to the fruit of long-lasting toil.
It is to be far removed from perfect penetration and to turn one's back on the city of nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of delusory prolongation.
The commentary states: This is the seventh false discrimination within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Because one contemplates the aggregate of consciousness as perfect and eternal, one desires to solidify the physical body so that it becomes identical to the aggregate of consciousness; thus, one falsely seeks longevity, which is why it says, "long and not subject to decline.

It is improper to be covetous. Asita, meaning "Incomparable," was a long-lived ṛṣi. He stubbornly clung to false consciousness as the cause, thereby pursuing the fruit of prolonged toil.
In the traditional interpretation, "toil" (láo) is taken to mean "firm confinement" (láo). Because he falsely clung to extending his years, he is called one who sows the seeds of false prolongation.

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*) is not yet perfected, may perceive that life-force is interpenetrating.

Fearing that its residual momentum might be exhausted, he remains at this juncture within a Lotus Palace, extensively transforming the seven treasures and increasing his retinue of precious women, indulging his mind at will. One who generates such superior resolve shall fall [into the realm of demons].
Truly non-existent yet truly grasped; Ṭakkirāja becomes their companion. They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their wisdom and insight.

This is called the eighth: giving rise to the cause of perverse thinking and establishing the fruit of blazing dust. It violates and distances one from perfect penetration, turns one's back on the city of Nirvana, and gives birth to the seeds of celestial Māras.

The commentary states: This is the eighth false discrimination within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The aggregate of consciousness serves as the fundamental source of life for the twelve classes of sentient beings.
Now, by observing this consciousness, one perceives that the lives of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions are mutually interconnected.
From this, a false discrimination arises, leading one to claim: "If my life should end, then the lives of all sentient beings would also end. This is the teaching.
Who has realized the true and eternal? Who transforms sentient beings? Therefore, they remain amidst the dust and toil of saṃsāra, greatly increasing their desires and seeking to prolong their lives.

Because they claim to have realized the truth to transform others, they give rise to delusions and indulge in lust; yet in reality, they have not realized the truth—thus it is said that what is "true" is not truly true.
This refers to the *Ṭakkirāja*, whose ancient explanation was previously unclear; its meaning must be the name of a Māra deity. This is certain.
In the midst of this, he suddenly gives rise to perverse thoughts; because these serve as the cause for establishing the fruit of blazing dust, he is born into the lineage of celestial Māras.

Furthermore, O son of good family, one who has exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to their emptiness has already extinguished birth and death, yet regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), it is not yet perfected.
Within the *jīvitajñāna* (knowledge of life), they distinguish between the refined and the coarse, and resolve upon the true and the false.

They seek only a response through the retribution of cause and effect, turning their backs on the path of purity—namely, the vision of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path.

Having settled into cessation and ceased further progress, those who fail to generate superior resolve fall into the category of the Śrāvaka of fixed nature. This increases the number of monks who have not heard the true Dharma.

Pride becomes its companion; one becomes deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and loses right knowledge and vision. This is called the ninth fruit, the "Perfectly Pure Essence Responding to the Mind," which achieves a state of quiescence.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to seeds that entangle one in emptiness.
The commentary states: This is the ninth false discrimination within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
By means of contemplation and inquiry, one regards the essence of consciousness as subtle and true, while regarding afflictions and karma as coarse and false.

Since these two types—subtle and coarse—constitute a correspondence between cause and effect, one cultivates the cause of subtle truth in order to seek the fruit of a subtle response. Thus, one perceives suffering, abandons its origin, aspires toward cessation, and cultivates the path.
Now, having attained cessation, they consider it an end in itself; satisfied with a mere trifle, they no longer advance.

Such persons fall into the category of the śrāvakas of fixed nature, or those among the four dhyānas who lack learning; claiming what they have not attained to be attained, they are characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Because they employ perfect refinement to accord with the mind, they achieve the minor fruit of quiescence; as they sink into emptiness and stagnate in stillness, it is said: [as above].
This is the seed of being entangled in emptiness.

Furthermore, a good son may exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena until he has extinguished both arising and ceasing; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, he has not yet perfected it.
If, within this perfectly fused, pure, and luminous awakening, he investigates its profound subtlety and establishes himself in *nirvāṇa* without proceeding further, [he remains stuck].

One who gives rise to such a superior resolve falls into the fixed nature of a pratyekabuddha. Those of the solitary class who do not turn their minds back [toward the Great Vehicle] become his companions.

They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the tenth stage: the "mind of the *huǒ* (obscuration) of Perfect Enlightenment" which achieves the fruit of profound clarity.

It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana; though it produces a sense of awakened perfection and brilliance, it cannot plant the seeds of universal enlightenment.

The commentary states: This is the tenth false conceptualization within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). "Awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*) refers to the perfect luminosity of the essence of consciousness;

yet, as the four aggregates have already been eliminated, this essence of consciousness is also about to be destroyed and is no longer subject to coarse defilements, hence it is described as "perfectly fused, pure, and clear.
To investigate and exhaustively analyze this state and establish it as *nirvāṇa* is a false conceptualization. Such a person...

Thus, one falls into the fixed nature of a pratyekabuddha; such as the various classes of pratyekabuddhas and solitary awakeners (dujue), they perceive the aggregates (skandhas) as perfect enlightenment (yuanjue).
They conjoin false conceptualization to form the "surging" mind. Because they remain silent and unmoving yet have not yet shattered ignorance, it is called the fruit of profound clarity.
Because they abandon sentient beings to seek their own liberation, they do not bring the seeds of the Perfectly Awakened One to fruition. [△@△] Third, the Precepts Exhorting Deep Prevention:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* become causes for madness midway through the path, based on delusion within that which is not yet sufficient."
The arising of the realization of satisfaction occurs because the mind of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) interacts with its objects; thus, this stage is produced.
Beings, stubborn and deluded, fail to reflect upon themselves. When this state appears before them, each rests according to their own cherished habitual patterns and their deluded minds.
They will claim that they have attained the ultimate state of refuge and that they have fulfilled unsurpassed Bodhi;

yet, having committed this great falsehood, they will be influenced by external paths and malevolent spirits, and at the end of their karma, they will fall into the Avīci Hell. Furthermore, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas will fail to make further progress.

The commentary states: This passage generally refutes false conceptualizations. Because one is about to break through the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate) but has not yet reached the ultimate wondrous perfection, and because false conceptualizations arise while what appears to be awakening is not yet true awakening, it is said that "one becomes mad midway.

Because one fails to understand the *vijñāna-skandha* and falsely gives rise to a sense of contentment, it is said that "one relies on delusion as a cause. Those who are shallow become the seed of external paths and malevolent spirits; those who are deep fall [into the hells].
Regarding the stages of the two vehicles:
[I] command you eight times to propagate and proclaim [this].
You all must keep this in mind and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata; after my parinirvāṇa, transmit this Dharma-gate to the final age.

May all sentient beings universally awaken to and understand this meaning. May they not allow Māra to cause them to sink into calamity; may they be comforted, protected, and rescued, and may their deviant conditions be quelled.
May their bodies and minds enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that from their initial accomplishment they shall never encounter divergent paths.

The commentary states: This edict is for the purpose of wide dissemination. It is called "demons of views" because all demons within the *vijñānaskandha* (consciousness-aggregate) rely upon false views.
It is called "creating one's own submerged calamity" because grasping and attachment within one's own mind destroy true cultivation.

Were it not for this Dharma-gate, one could not provide protection, offer compassionate rescue, or pacify and eliminate evil conditions to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. [This applies to] grasping outside of the mind...
Because it is the Dharma, it is called "the diverging paths. [Symbol] Nine: All Buddhas realize this in common.
Such a Dharma-gate was previously realized by Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms within the sands of the Ganges throughout kalpas of the past, who, by means of this mind, attained awakening.
They attain the Unsurpassed Way.

The commentary states: This demonstrates that all Buddhas realize the same truth; it means there is not a single Buddha who attains Bodhi without shattering the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).
[□@◇] When the ten aggregates are exhausted, merit is perfected.

If the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, then your present sense faculties will function interchangeably. From this mutual functioning, you can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*).
Within this state, the perfectly luminous and refined mind manifests its transformations, like a pure lapis lazuli gem containing a precious moon within.
In this way, one transcends the stages of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and the four preparatory minds;
surpassing the conduct of Bodhisattvas through the diamond-like ten grounds and the perfect clarity of Equal Enlightenment, one enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment,
fulfilling Bodhi and returning to the state of non-attainment.

The commentary states: This demonstrates the function of the perfect realization upon the exhaustion of the *ālaya-vijñāna* (the shadow). Regarding "immediately entering the Vajra-dry-wisdom from within the mutual functioning":

this means that once the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) is shattered, one does not pass through the various stages but transcends them directly to enter the perfect realization of the Buddha-fruit.
The reason for this is that the *tathāgatagarbha*, the pure true mind, is fundamentally devoid of delusion or enlightenment.

However, because of a single moment of deluded movement, this constitutes the ignorance of the characteristic of arising. The union of the non-arising and non-ceasing with the arising and ceasing forms the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
This transforms and gives rise to all phenomena of form and mind, thereby forming sentient beings composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Now, returning from delusion to the truth, one employs the Vajra-like Illusory Samādhi to directly contemplate the root of the eight consciousnesses.
Fundamental ignorance is itself the transformation of birth-and-death into nirvāṇa; therefore, without passing through the various stages, one suddenly and instantaneously realizes unexcelled bodhi.
This is the case for those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, such as Avalokiteśvara, whose faculty of hearing is perfectly penetrating.

Once birth and death have ceased and quiescent extinction has manifested, they suddenly transcend both the mundane and supramundane worlds. Thus, regarding the present consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha):

Once [the fundamental ignorance] is shattered, the six sense organs function interchangeably. From this state of mutual functioning, one immediately enters the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*).
Thus, by merely shattering the ignorance of the characteristic of birth (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*), one attains the fruit of Buddhahood; it is not necessary to pass through all the successive stages.

One should know that the sequence of the five aggregates does not necessarily require passing through each one individually; rather, they are presented one by one merely as a general method for contemplating the mind.
Therefore, when the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, the perfectly luminous and subtle mind manifests and transforms within it.
This is precisely to align upward with the compassionate power of all Buddhas and to harmonize downward with the sorrowful longing of sentient beings.
By manifesting through the Universal Gate (Pumen) to benefit sentient beings, it is called "emerging through transformation.

Because the body, mind, world, Buddhas, and sentient beings are perfectly interfused and mutually penetrating, it is like a pure lapis lazuli gem containing a precious moon within; thus, one is able to suddenly transcend all stages and enter the fruition.
Returning to the ocean, there is nothing to be gained; this is what is called the ultimate pinnacle.
[Symbol] Eleven: The Transmission of Previous Buddhas.
This is the discernment of the luminous awareness through *vipaśyanā* within the *śamatha* of the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
Subtle demonic activities and the realms of Māra appear before you; you are able to recognize them. The defilements of the mind are washed away so that you do not fall into false views.
The skandha-māras are extinguished, and the deva-māras are shattered. Powerful spirits and ghosts lose heart and flee, while *chi-mei* and *wang-liang* demons can no longer arise.
Until you reach Bodhi, you shall lack nothing; those of inferior capacity will advance toward Great Nirvāṇa.
His mind was not confused or distressed.
He deliberated, saying: "These words concern the transmission of the mind-dharma from one Buddha to another to instruct practitioners.

For the three contemplations are the very foundation upon which every Buddha attains enlightenment. That demonic obstacles occur within meditative concentration is something experienced by previous Buddhas; it is not something being taught for the first time now."
Therefore, one must have firm faith. By causing one to recognize demonic activities in advance, one will not fall into false views when demonic realms manifest before them.
When the demonic influence is extinguished, one can proceed directly to Bodhi without the mind becoming deluded or distressed. Such great benefits exist.
Therefore, it must be widely proclaimed.
[This concludes the] twelfth section showing the secret cultivation.
If there are sentient beings in the final age who are dull-witted and ignorant, who do not yet recognize *dhyāna* nor know how to preach the Dharma, yet delight in practicing *samādhi*:
Fearing that you might fall into heterodoxy, I wholeheartedly urge you to uphold this Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī.
If you are not yet able to recite it, write it down in your meditation hall or carry it upon your person; then no māras whatsoever will be able to move you.
You should reverently honor this as the final instruction left behind by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions upon their ultimate cultivation and advancement.
The commentary states: This is a further demonstration of the efficacy of secret cultivation.

When dull-witted sentient beings do not understand the preaching of the Dharma, and there are those who practice dhyāna who fear being disturbed by māras, they are taught to single-mindedly uphold this Buddha-Usnīṣa Divine Mantra.
This is the heart-seal of all Buddhas; by relying on the power of this mantra, māras cannot move them. Beyond this, there is nothing else that can subdue māras.
This Dharma-gate alone is that which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have ultimately cultivated and realized; it is the secret cause for transcending the world.
It is truly the final model bequeathed by the Tathāgata. You should reverently honor and proclaim it to benefit those of the future and bring great benefit to the Great Dharma.

[②] Second, showing the delusive conceptualization of the five aggregates, which is divided into two parts. [◇] First, the question posed by the appropriate recipient (the disciple).
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat. Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, he prostrated himself in reverence and respectfully received it, memorizing it without loss.

In the midst of the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more: "As the Buddha has said, among the characteristics of the five aggregates, the five kinds of delusion constitute the fundamental source of thought.
We have not previously received such subtle and detailed instruction from the Tathāgata regarding this. Furthermore, as for these five aggregates, do they..."
Their dissolution occurs in successive order until they are entirely exhausted. Thus, regarding these five stages, what constitutes their ultimate limit?
We pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion and clarify the minds and eyes of this great assembly, thereby serving as a guiding eye for all sentient beings of the future age.

The deliberation states: Ānanda, having heard the previous teaching that the five aggregates (skandhas) are all established based upon deluded thought (vikalpa), he did not yet know what constitutes the root of that deluded thought.
Above, it was stated that the characteristics of the five aggregates were to be destroyed;

however, the sequence of sudden or gradual [realization] regarding these characteristics was unknown, as was the boundary (sīmā) by which the five aggregates are defined. Thus, three questions were raised in their entirety, hoping for the Buddha’s [response].
This is the final revelation.
[□@◇] Part Five: The World-Honored One’s Detailed Explanation. [○@◇] First, a general indication of the source of delusion.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The subtle, true, wondrous clarity of original enlightenment is perfectly pure; it does not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements.

Even empty space arises solely from deluded thoughts. This originally fundamental, wondrously clear, and true essence of enlightenment gives rise to the various vessel-worlds through delusion—just as Yajñadatta, in his confusion, mistook his own head for a reflection. Delusion has no cause."
Within delusive conceptualization, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions; those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions call it spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
That nature of space is likewise truly born from illusion. Both causes and conditions and spontaneity are merely the conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings.

Ānanda, when one knows that which gives rise to delusion, one speaks of the causes and conditions of delusion; if delusion were fundamentally non-existent, then the causes and conditions of delusion would fundamentally not exist at all—how much less so [the nature of space]?
Because you do not know how to infer the nature of spontaneity, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the original cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but delusive thought (*vikalpa*).
The commentary states: This is a general demonstration that all five aggregates take delusive thought as their root. Before proceeding to clarify delusive thought, [the text first...]
Because the single true Dharma-realm is established as the basis of delusion, it is said that "the essence of reality, wondrously luminous, is the originally awakened, perfectly pure mind.
This means that the essence of reality, the wondrously luminous, originally awakened true mind is fundamentally complete and pure; within it, nothing else remains.
Therefore, it is said that neither birth-and-death nor any defilements are retained; it is stated that from the beginning, not a single dharma is established.

How, then, could there be the differentiated characteristics of the five aggregates? Such matters as the empty space, the world, sentient beings, karma, and its fruits all arise due to deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
they originally issue forth falsely from the wondrously luminous, true essence of the fundamental awakening mind.
The various marks of the world arise like the case of Yanruo, who, deluded about his own head, mistook a reflection for it and ran about wildly;

thus it is said that their false origin has no cause. Because one’s own deluded thoughts arise and serve as seeds for one another, to establish the nature of causes and conditions within these deluded thoughts is already a state of confusion.
Furthermore, those who are confused about causes and conditions also refer to them as "spontaneous" (svabhāva).
Is this not further delusion? Therefore it is said that all these are the conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings and are fundamentally non-existent.
If one knew the place where delusive existence arises, one could speak of causes and conditions; but since delusion is originally non-existent, causes and conditions do not exist.
How much more so when you further attribute it to spontaneity? Your delusion is profound indeed.
It is for this reason that I have clarified with you that the five aggregates are equally but false imaginings, wishing to lead you to realize that they are fundamentally non-existent.
[○@◇] Part Two: A Detailed Exposition of the Fundamental Causes of the Five Aggregates, divided into two sections. [△@△] First, the enumeration, divided into five parts.
[□@○] First, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Your body was originally produced through the conceptualization of your parents; if your mind were not conceptualizing, it could not have come into this state of thought to transmit life.
As I previously said, when the mind conceives of the taste of vinegar, saliva arises in the mouth; when the mind conceives of climbing a high place, a sourness arises in the soles of the feet.

Since there are no sour objects on the precipice and none have yet arrived, your substance must certainly not be of the same category as the saliva produced by the mouth through the power of conceptualization.
Therefore, you should know that this manifested physical body of yours is called the first false discrimination of solidity.
The commentary says: This demonstrates the false root of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Your body does not truly exist; it originated initially from the deluded union of your parents.
Your mind, riding upon this, conceived the thought that became the embryo, marking the beginning of the physical body.
If your mind were not conceptualizing, how could this life-root (*jīvitendriya*) have been transmitted through such thought? Thus, your body is indeed produced by the parents and yourself.
It is formed through the conjunction of the three bases and deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Although conceptualization is empty and false, it is capable of producing effects.
As I previously explained, by thinking of plums or imagining the water at the edge of a precipice, saliva flows from the mouth and the legs become numb;
thus, although the deluded conceptualization is empty, there is actually acid water produced. Know that your body exists because of deluded conceptualization, and it is just like this. Therefore—
This body is formed by the congealing of false conceptualization; it is called the first false conceptualization, that of solidity.
[2] Second is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

This refers to what was previously described as the thought of being on a high precipice, which can cause your physical form to truly experience aching and bitterness. This arises because sensation is produced from causes.
The capacity to move the substance of form—this present state of being driven by the two manifest conditions of benefit and harm—is called the second delusive thought, "empty luminosity.

The commentary states: This demonstrates the delusive root of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Your sensation does not truly exist; it arises merely from empty conceptions confronting height.
Furthermore, since it is evident that the sensations of sourness and astringency can move the physical body, one can verify through this that both the two types of sensation—
those of pain and pleasure arising from adverse and favorable conditions, and those resulting in loss or gain— are all produced by empty, luminous delusion.
[□@○] Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
It is by means of your thoughts and deliberations that you cause your physical body to act. The body is not of the same category as thought;

for what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought to grasp various forms? The mind gives rise to formal grasping in correspondence with thought. When awake, this is the perceiving mind; when asleep, it becomes various dreams.
Thus, the movement of your conceptual thoughts and deluded sentiments is called the third false imagination, "interfusion.
The commentary states: This demonstrates the false root of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The body, composed of the four great elements, is inherently devoid of cognition;
yet, because it is driven by deluded conceptualization and deliberation, the mind gives rise to forms and grasps them in correspondence with thought—whether waking, sleeping, or dreaming.
Realize that all these are the agitation of deluded sentiments arising from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). These are all false conceptualizations that permeate the entire body;
therefore, the body takes false conceptualization as its master.
[Section on] Four: The Aggregate of Formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
The principle of transformation does not abide; it shifts and moves in secret. Nails grow and hair sprouts, while vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles.

Day and night they replace one another, yet there is never any awakening to this. Ānanda, if this were not you, how could your physical form undergo change? If it were truly you, why would you have no awareness of it?
Thus, these formations of yours that ceaselessly flow from moment to moment are called the fourth subtle and hidden deluded thought.
The commentary states: This demonstrates the false foundation of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. The *saṃskāra-skandha* is fundamentally non-existent;

it is only because your mind undergoes incessant arising and ceasing that your body flows and migrates without rest. The six phrases beginning with "The principle of transformation" generally describe the subtle, profound, and hidden characteristics of the *saṃskāra-skandha* that are difficult to know.
The four phrases beginning with "If this were not you" distinguish that the delusion has no substantial essence.
Furthermore, if conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were not you, how could they cause the shifting of your substance? If they were truly you, why would you not perceive them?
Since they cannot be found when sought, one knows that these conditioned phenomena—which arise and perish in every thought-moment without ceasing—are called "subtle and hidden delusive thoughts."
[□@○] The five aggregates of consciousness.

Furthermore, that which you call "constant"—the place where your essence is bright and profoundly still, unmoving—is no different from the functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within the body.
If this true essence were incapable of admitting the cultivation of delusion, for what reason did you all once, in years past, behold a strange object?
Though many years have passed, there is neither memory nor forgetting; yet later, when suddenly beholding that former anomaly again, the memory is vivid and clear, not lost at all.
Thus, within this pure, lucid, and unshakable essence, how could one calculate the moments of being perfumed by thoughts from moment to moment?

Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not the true reality. It is like a rapid current that appears tranquil from a distance; because the flow is so swift, it is not perceived, yet it does not mean there is no flow.

If this were not the source of perception, how could one ever undergo the habitual tendencies of delusion? These false thoughts—the mutual functioning and the opening and closing of your six sense faculties—can never be extinguished.
Therefore, within your present seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, these habitual patterns have been reinforced for a long time.
Then there is the profound clarity within which is formless and void, the fifth inverted state of subtle and refined conceptualization.
The commentary says: This demonstrates the deluded root of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*). The consciousness aggregate is fundamentally not existent;

its original nature is the essence of the true, wondrously luminous mind-body. However, because it is permeated and shrouded by the habituation of false thoughts, it is called "consciousness. Nevertheless...
The substance of this consciousness is fundamentally the true, exquisite, and unshakable state. Within this body, nothing escapes its scope;
seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all functions of this consciousness. If the substance of this consciousness were truly real, it would not tolerate the cultivation of delusion.
Only by being unsullied by perfuming can it be called "true. How could it be that having once beheld a wondrous object in years past, after a long time...

It is not forgotten; is this not caused by perfuming (*vāsanā*)? Inferring from this, what calculation can there be regarding the fact that within that which you point to as "subtle, lucid, and unmoving," there is moment-to-moment reception of perfuming? How, then, could such a state be considered eternal?
Therefore, the "stillness" you cling to is not true stillness and quiescence; it is merely a subtle flow of arising and ceasing.
You do not perceive this. It is like a rushing torrent that appears calm at a glance; because the current is so swift, it is not seen, yet this does not mean there is no flow.
Thus, if the substance of your consciousness were not fundamentally conceptual, how could it ever receive deluded habit-energies?
Now, since it receives the permeation of delusion, it cannot be truly eternal, constant, or unitary. If this consciousness were pure and true, your six sense organs would function interchangeably.
Thus, these deluded thoughts can never be extinguished. How could the consciousness perfumed by such deluded thoughts be taken as real?
Therefore, while your current seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing manifest grossly to the exterior, within them there are subtle traces of habitual patterns of arising and ceasing;
amidst this profound clarity, they seem to exist yet are as if non-existent, impossible to fully investigate.
This is precisely the non-conceptual, void, subtle, and refined ideation that constitutes the essence of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Viewed from this perspective, all five aggregates take deluded thought as their essence; since deluded thought has no essence, the aggregates do not exist.
[△@△] Second, the summary: "Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by five kinds of false imaginings.
The commentary says: This section shows that the five aggregates are all formed by false imaginings. These five are precisely what sentient beings experience.

Because they are the ground for the ripening [of karma], they are collectively termed the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), also known as the five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādānakkhandha*), since they are repeatedly grasped by the *pudgala*.
The above has answered the fundamental cause of the five aggregates.
[○@◇] Third, showing the limits of the aggregates and elements:
If you now wish to know the depth and shallowness of the causal elements, know that only form and emptiness are the limits of form; only contact and separation are the limits of feeling;
only recollection and forgetfulness are the limits of perception; and only cessation and arising are the limits of mental formations.
"The profound entry merges with the profound to return to the limit of consciousness.

The commentary states: This answers two questions regarding the depth and shallowness of the causal realms (*dhātu*). "Cause" (*yin*) has the meaning of "realm" (*dhātu*), and it also carries the meaning of "division" (*bhāga*).
Because they are distinguished by their respective causal bases, supports, elements, and limits, they are called "causal elements" (*dhātu*).

"Form" refers to shape; "space" refers to color. Both are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Only form and space constitute the limit of form. Regarding contact, there are those that are disagreeable and those that are agreeable;

when free from both, there is only the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). These three feelings constitute the limit of feeling (*vedanā*). Memory and forgetfulness constitute perception (*saṃjñā*).
The "limit" (*paryanta*). The four phases of arising and ceasing constitute the limit of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).
As for "the tranquil enters and merges with the tranquil," "tranquility" (*zhan*) refers to the essence of the eight consciousnesses, what is called "tranquil and yet seemingly existent.

Since arising and ceasing flow forth from this tranquility, and now one turns back to merge with this wondrous tranquility, it is said that "the tranquil enters and merges with the tranquil" constitutes the limit of consciousness.
[○@◇] Fourth, the demonstration of delusion and enlightenment, sudden and gradual.
These five aggregates originally arise in a layered succession; their arising is due to consciousness, and their cessation proceeds from the elimination of form.

In principle, there is sudden enlightenment, whereby one attains awakening and eliminates them all at once. In practice, they are not suddenly removed, but are exhausted through successive stages. I have already shown you the knots in the *kalpavṛkṣa* cloth.
What is it that you do not understand such that you inquire about this again?
The commentary states: This answers the three questions regarding the sudden and gradual [teachings].

According to this, when these five aggregates first arise, they evolve from the *ālaya-vijñāna* as the two divisions of the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving (*darśana-bhāga*). These two factors—form and mind—combine to constitute [the aggregates].

Sentient beings are composed of the five aggregates; therefore, it is said that birth arises from consciousness. Now, returning from delusion to truth, one first destroys the aggregate of form and subsequently destroys the aggregate of consciousness;

thus, it is said that cessation proceeds by removing [delusions] starting with form. If one relies on the perfect principle and attains sudden enlightenment in a single thought-moment, one ascends directly to the stage of Buddhahood without passing through gradual stages;
thus, it is said that through awakening, all is simultaneously eliminated. However, as for the ignorance accumulated over kalpas...
Habitual tendencies must be investigated one by one; therefore, it is said that they are gradually eliminated and exhausted through a sequential process.
As previously demonstrated, the similarities and differences between the knots in the cloth and the sequence of their tying and untying—what is there that is not clear? Why do you ask again?
This is a reprimand for your questioning.
[○@◇] Fifth, the exhortation to practice and uphold:
You should take these roots of delusive thought and cause your mind to attain clarity;

you must transmit this to all practitioners in the future age of the Dharma’s decay, so that they may recognize the nature of their falsehoods, develop a profound weariness with themselves, realize the existence of Nirvana, and no longer cling to the three realms.
The commentary states: This is an exhortation. All worlds are sustained by deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).
Now, if one knows that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), body, and mind are all one and the same deluded thought, then everything is nothing other than established by deluded thought.

If one realizes that deluded thought has no inherent nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), then body, mind, and the world vanish instantly. What difficulty could there be in realizing *nirvāṇa*, and what further [need would there be]?

How deeply one may be attached to the three realms! Therefore, this root of delusive thought is transmitted and shown to those at the end of the path, so that they may know the essentials of practice.
The preceding section on the Correct Teaching is hereby concluded.

"Ānanda, suppose there were a person who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures, and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are atoms of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a sincere heart that never wasted its purpose. "By means of this causal condition of giving to the Buddha, would one not obtain much merit?

The commentary states: This exhortation to circulate [the teaching] first compares merits to inspire faith and reverence. Throughout the vast expanse of the empty space of the ten directions, one might fill it with the seven treasures;
such is the magnitude of what could be given. Yet, even more than that is the offering made to the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust.
O assembly, to have no empty passage of the mind and to establish the mind with such firmness—how inconceivable is the merit obtained through such excellence!
[□@(?╳)] Second, the excellence of the merit obtained.

Ānanda replied, "Space is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless. In the past, there were sentient beings who gave the Buddha seven coins and, by relinquishing their bodies, still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King;
how much more so now, when space itself is exhausted and Buddha-lands are filled to overflowing with precious jewels?
Even if one were to contemplate this for an entire kalpa, it could not be fully grasped. How could such merit have any limit?"
The commentary states: This response concerns the extraordinary excellence of the merit obtained from making offerings to the Buddha.
By giving seven coins, one receives the retribution of becoming a Wheel-Turning King; thus, what was given was small, yet the reward received is vast.
How much more so when one offers the seven treasures, as inexhaustible as the entirety of space, to the Tathāgata, who is the ultimate pinnacle—how could such merit ever be fathomed by thought?
[□@(?╳)] Third, a general manifestation of the supreme benefits.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "The speech of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is not false. If there should be a person who has committed the four grave offenses and the ten pārājikas, they would immediately pass through the Avīci hells of this region and other regions in a mere instant, until they have reached their ultimate end."

There is nowhere throughout the ten directions that they have not traversed. If one can, with a single thought, take up this Dharma-door and reveal it to those who have not yet studied during the final kalpa, that person’s karmic obstacles will be extinguished at that very moment.
The causes for the suffering of the hells they were to undergo will be transformed into a Land of Peace and Bliss.
The merit they shall attain will surpass that of the previous donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten million, or even a hundred billionfold.
Thus it continues until it reaches a point beyond the reach of calculation or analogy. Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra—
as I have explained at length, which would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon— and who follow my instructions and practice the Way according to the teaching,
they will directly attain Bodhi without further demonic interference.
The commentary states: If one were to compare the merit of generous giving with the gravity of extreme offenses, the former would not equal the superior benefits of propagating the Dharma.

Offenses as grave as the four pārājikas and the ten heavy transgressions, and the suffering of the Avīci hell, even if they were to exhaust the vastness of the ten directions—such offenses and such suffering are truly inconceivable.
Yet, if one can, through this Dharma-gate, for even a single thought-moment...

By revealing this teaching for the Dharma-ending age, it causes previously accumulated grave offenses to be instantly extinguished and the instruments of suffering to be transformed into a land of bliss.
One can thus know the supreme benefits of this Dharma. It not only eradicates offenses but also secures merit;
that it exceeds the merit of those who practice mere giving by incalculable multiples—how extraordinary is the excellence of this Dharma! This is truly because it is perfect and sudden.
In this Dharma-gate, through a single moment of cultivation, one immediately attains the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi.
Therefore, this sutra teaches that the merits of the Tathāgatagarbha nature are inexhaustible. Mantras are the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas; they are held fast without end.

The simultaneous cultivation of both Exoteric and Esoteric teachings is the essential requirement for attaining Buddhahood; thus, they cannot be fully described. If one practices according to these instructions, one will directly achieve Bodhi.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* comprehensively encompasses the teachings of the various periods throughout the entire dispensation, integrating the causes and effects of delusion and awakening, as well as cultivation and realization. It directly severs...

This constitutes the supreme One Vehicle Dharma-gate of sudden and perfect realization, which directly reveals the one true Dharma-realm, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. It is called...
