Due to this nature of the storehouse (ālaya), it is deluded as the *ālayavijñāna*, which transforms to give rise to the two divisions of the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving (*darśana-bhāga*).

When this nature of the storehouse exists within consciousness, it is called the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). Because its fundamental nature is undefiled, it is termed the "white-pure consciousness" (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) and serves as the verifying-of-self-verifying division (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga*).
According to the treatise on the two gates of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), this self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is precisely True Suchness.

This self-witnessing division is the fundamental awakening (*mūla-ajñāna*) within delusion; the seeing division (*darśana-bhāga*) consists of the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); and the image division (*nimitta-bhāga*) consists of space and the four great elements.
Externally, these manifest as the world, mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the objects of the five sensory realms; internally, they manifest as the sense organs.
The body consists of the five appropriated aggregates (*upātta-skandha*) and the two [appropriating] aggregates of sensation (*vedanā*). "View" refers to the seven consciousnesses:

the mind-faculty (*manas*), the six mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*), and the five sensory consciousnesses, along with their simultaneous discriminative mental consciousnesses. Now, the primary aim of cultivating the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama is to directly penetrate and shatter these eight consciousnesses.
However, the substance of these consciousnesses has long been deluded, bound by the two divisions of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*) and seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).

The five aggregates, the sense organs and the body, as well as the external world and its five objects, give rise to the two types of grasping—discriminated and innate, coarse and subtle—toward self and phenomena.
Grasping the five aggregates, the sense organs, and the body as a self constitutes the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).

Craving the external five objects as things to be enjoyed by the self, and reckoning them as having functional activity, constitutes the grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). Because of these two graspings, one is entangled in the cycle of birth and death. Therefore...
Now, the vow to transcend birth and death must first break through the two attachments as its primary expedient.
Therefore, Ānanda specifically requested the sublime *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* as the essentials for attaining Buddhahood.

The Buddha specifically granted this *samādhi*, naming it the Great Buddha-Crown *Śūraṅgama-rāja*. This was because [Ānanda] had requested them individually, whereas the Buddha relied upon a single [principle].

This is spoken from the perspective of the Great Samādhi of the Perfect Fusion of the Mind. Thus, one knows that this sutra, from beginning to end, does not transcend the three contemplations (sanzhuan), ultimately not departing from the single mind.
Although the sutra’s text does not explicitly state its ultimate aim, the passages concerning refutation and revelation are crystal clear;
it is only that those who circulate it have failed to investigate them. Regarding these three contemplations, the sutra is subtle...

Śamatha corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā); samādhi corresponds to the contemplation of the provisional (upāya-vipaśyanā); and dhyāna corresponds to the contemplation of the Middle Way (madhyamā-pratipad-vipaśyanā).

That all are termed "wondrous" (miao) intends to reveal that the three contemplations are perfectly interfused and wondrously accord with the one mind. To mention one is to include the three; to speak of the three is to include the one.
Transcending both identity and difference, they stand far beyond the reach of conceptual thought. Now, we shall discuss this scripture in its entirety.
Regarding the indication by means of essence (*tī*), characteristic (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*): the intention is that awakening comes first and cultivation follows.

Therefore, the essence is indicated at the outset so as to cause one to first awaken to the principle-essence of the three truths within the *tathāgatagarbha*, upon which the characteristics of contemplation are established. This refers to first awakening to the *Vairocana* Dharma-realm.
Next, the characteristics of contemplation are shown; the meaning is that the true mind, which is devoid of marks, is currently entirely deluded.

Because consciousness binds together the five aggregates, the physical body, and the objective world—all phenomena possessing characteristics—it is essential to practice by means of these very characteristics.

Therefore, in the section on the cultivation of the path, the text specifically points to the five aggregates and the six sense organs, followed by the three categories and the seven elements, each of which serves as a gateway for awakening and entry.
That the section on the realization of the fruit uses "contemplative function" (*guan-yong*) as its heading precisely reveals this.

The three contemplations one cultivates possess the power and function to sever [delusions] and to realize [enlightenment]. Therefore, what I, the fool, mean by saying that from beginning to end there is nothing that does not fall within the three contemplations is precisely this.
Question: Why are the three contemplations divided according to essence (ti), characteristic (xiang), and function (yong)? Answer: Although they are designated as three, [they are ultimately one].
Contemplation. This means that regarding the principle of the three truths of the *tathāgatagarbha*, one must realize them through the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).
In reality, these are all but a single mind; therefore, the Buddha granted him the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama. The intent is that the three contemplations are not separate from the single mind.
According to the *Awakening of Faith*, there is a dharma capable of giving rise to the root of faith in Mahāyāna, which is said to be...
The Dharma refers to the mind of sentient beings. This mind universally encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas; therefore, it is not called "mind" but is named "Dharma.
Yet, for there to be a dharma, there must necessarily be its meaning. The meaning of the one mind is established through its essence (*tǐ*), characteristics (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*).
These are what are known as the three greats (*sāndà*). Because the essence of this true mind is vast and great, it is so described.

Its substance is great because it is originally without marks; yet now, the phenomenal appearances of the ten dharma-realms—the environment and its inhabitants, causes and effects—are all dharmas with marks, and thus its marks are also great.

Because delusion regarding this mind results in the six realms of ordinary beings, while awakening to this mind results in the four classes of sages, these are all the wondrous functions of the transformation of the one mind; therefore, its function is also great.
This means that one first causes [the practitioner] to awaken to the substance of this mind. The Buddha spoke of "opening and showing" this substance so as to facilitate its cultivation;

therefore, the substance is clarified at the outset. Once this substance is awakened to, one understands that all delusive appearances—the faculties, the body, and the environment—are established based upon the single mind.
Now, one shall use the substance thus awakened to illuminate and shatter each of these delusive appearances to reveal their original nature.

This is the wondrous, luminous true mind; therefore, cultivation relies solely upon delusive appearances. Thus it is called "contemplating appearances," which precisely constitutes the essential core of the path of cultivation.

All fifty-five stages are established based on contemplating the mind, primarily to reveal that these three contemplations possess the great function of severing delusions and realizing the truth; hence, they are termed the "functions of the three contemplations. By means of...
Having examined the scriptures, it is clear that the text is manifest and perfectly accords with the Buddha’s mind;
therefore, I have categorized it without hesitation so as to reveal the Tathāgata’s fundamental intent in preaching the Dharma and to facilitate the practitioner’s entry.

Question: Within the substance of the Three Contemplations (*san guan*), three and a half fascicles of the sutra are subsumed. Indeed, a single section on the contemplation of emptiness (*kong guan*) already encompasses the text of all three fascicles.

As for the three sections and seven chapters, which fundamentally reveal the *tathāgatagarbha* and seem to manifest the principle of emptiness—the initial portion, beginning with the inquiry into the mind and the discernment of vision, unfolds through the manifestation of two kinds of false views and various further inquiries and discernments—how is this to be understood?
"What is the Master’s intention? He replied, "This sutra purely encompasses the five teachings.

Thus, this very essence of the contemplation of emptiness fully contains the principle of emptiness across the five teachings, penetrating the discourse of the entire era. Its text is concise while its meaning is profound; it is exceptionally difficult to comprehend."
Therefore, I have compiled this General Discourse (Tongyi), listing exhaustively the titles and outlines to make known the essential points.

As for the refutation of the false and the revelation of the true, the scriptural text consists of no more than half a fascicle; yet its meaning already encompasses the doctrines I have expounded over the past forty years—it is by no means a shallow matter.
For my Buddha appeared in the world and preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, discoursing upon the sutras three hundred times.
Other assemblies were held solely to shatter the sentient beings' dual attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).
Once these two attachments are shattered, one realizes *nirvāṇa*. *Nirvāṇa* is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha, the quiescent single mind.

Because sentient beings are deluded regarding this Tathāgatagarbha mind—which is neither arising nor ceasing—it combines with the arising-and-ceasing [mind] to form the *ālayavijñāna*. This consciousness...
It possesses four divisions: first, the *svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga* (the division of self-cognition of cognition), which is the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the one mind;

second, the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (the division of self-cognition), which is the original enlightenment (*mūlabodhi*) within delusion—this shall be discussed in the context of the meanings of "enlightenment" and "non-enlightenment"; third, the *darśana-bhāga* (the division of seeing), which consists of the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*);
and fourth, the *nimitta-bhāga* (the division of appearances), which consists of the external vessel-world. In the sutras, earth, water, fire, wind, and space constitute the five external [elements].
The great refers to the world. That which is internal—the root body—is the sentient being composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

Because sentient beings are deluded regarding this true mind, they recognize only the illusory and false body of the five aggregates as their own body and mind; this false attachment to it as "self" is called the "discriminative attachment to self.
The external world of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) is that which is experienced and enjoyed by them; this is called the "discriminative attachment to phenomena" (*dharma-grāha*). This...

The two types of conceptual grasping (vikalpita-grāha) are both reckoned by the six consciousnesses; since the seventh consciousness is the root of the six, it functions in dependence on the internal and external gates, and in reality, these two consciousnesses reckon together.
Furthermore, there is innate grasping of self and phenomena (sahaja-ātma-dharma-grāha), which belongs exclusively to the seventh consciousness;
it takes the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness as its own internal essence, which is called "grasping of self. This is what is falsely perceived during cultivation.
Realizing [them] constitutes attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). These two subtle types are called the two innate attachments (*sahaja-grāha*).
Only when these two kinds of dual attachments are completely destroyed can one realize entry into the source of the One Mind; this is what is termed "Buddhahood.
Since Ānanda was deluded regarding the True Mind and was precisely ensnared by these two obstacles, he must destroy them entirely; this alone is the true path to Bodhi. Therefore—
The three contemplations are the instruments for shattering the two types of grasping, both coarse and subtle.
In this sutra, the investigation of the mind and the discernment of the seeing-faculty comprehensively shatter the two types of self-grasping and the two types of deluded views;

furthermore, the subsequent refutation of the "harmonious conjunction" comprehensively shatters the two types of dharma-grasping, both coarse and subtle. By means of this Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama, one completely severs the afflictions of the five abodes.
The two types of birth and death discussed in the *Nàozhì* are not comparable to the sequence of before and after found in other sutras;
because it comprehensively subsumes the five teachings and realizes the one mind all at once, it does not establish a sequence of before and after.

Question: Various teachings state separately that one first abandons the two types of conceptual grasping (*vikalpita-grāha*) and subsequently abandons the two types of innate grasping (*sahaja-grāha*).
What is meant by this statement that they are abandoned collectively? Answer: The seventh consciousness is the root of the two types of grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).
It evolves through internal and external modes. If it evolves through the external mode, serving as the root for the six consciousnesses, then there is conceptual grasping of the two types.
If one relies on the internal door, then grasping the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses as the self constitutes innate self-grasping (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*).

This grasping is severed upon reaching the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). As for the fact that innate grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) still persists from the eighth stage upward, it is because the seventh consciousness possesses the dual meaning of both defiled and pure aspects; thus, what is severed at the seventh stage is the defiled aspect of the manas.

Regarding those who grasp at the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses as the self: now, once this defiled portion is severed, one abandons the name "store-consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

These eight consciousnesses, which are the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the evolving consciousnesses, are called the "pure white consciousness. Yet, there still remains the pure portion of the manas that grasps this true suchness, claiming, "This is what I have realized as my own.
This constitutes a subtle attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*). As the subsequent sutra states:
The arising of the bodhicitta and the ceasing of the mind of birth-and-death still belong to the realm of arising and ceasing.

Because one clings to *tathatā* (suchness) as something to be realized, the subject-object duality has not been forgotten and the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) has not yet dissolved; this remains a subtle form of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

Only when this attachment is severed does one enter wondrous enlightenment and realize the source of the one mind. This meaning accords perfectly with the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith), as can be clearly verified. Therefore:
It is said that [delusion] is suddenly severed and [enlightenment] is suddenly realized. A question is raised: "The passages in this sutra that refute attachment have not been clarified previously;

those who have transmitted it from of old have only spoken of 'investigating the mind' and 'discerning the seeing. As for the two kinds of false views, it is also unknown for what purpose they were taught."

Now, although the "Section on Clarifying and Refuting" in the *Tongyi* clearly sets forth the principle of refuting attachments, the sequence of its preceding and succeeding stages remains unclarified.

I request that you explain this in detail. The answer is as follows: The two attachments of the refined and the coarse pertain to the two paths of the Real and the False, and in total do not transcend the eight consciousnesses and the five aggregates. These are what are to be refuted throughout the various teachings of one lifetime.
This is all there is. Because one is deluded regarding the single mind, the *ālayavijñāna* is formed. This consciousness possesses four divisions (*caturbhāga*).

Its first three divisions are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the body-and-mind, and the world. Its "witnessing-of-the-witnessing" division (*sākṣin-sākṣin-bhāga*) is the *tathatā* (suchness) that is realized.

Now, the two attachments—the coarse and the subtle—are merely the refutation of the fourfold consciousness-only (*caturbhāga-vijñaptimātra*) and the subsumption [of all phenomena] back into the single mind.

This is the limit. Therefore, having established the scriptural text, one refutes [the self] according to this. First, one refutes the five aggregates as belonging to the conceptual grasping at a self;
in refuting the aggregate of consciousness, the innate grasping at a self is simultaneously included therein.

As for the two kinds of false views, these refute the conceptual grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which is that which is commonly clung to by both ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles. Thus, they are refuted.
Following the second delusion, the original awakening of the true mind is revealed. For this reason, it is known that the innate grasping at a self has already been undermined and set aside.

When the next chapter states, "Although you have previously awakened to the luminous mind of original awakening, you have not yet clarified that such an awakening-source is neither produced through combination nor produced without combination," this is precisely the refutation of the innate [grasping].

One gives rise to the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). This very sutra later states that while the bodhicitta arises and the mind of arising-and-ceasing ceases, these still pertain to arising-and-ceasing.
Therefore, once this attachment is shattered, one immediately returns to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

Thus, the subsequent passage clarifying that "each and every thing is the Tathāgatagarbha" intends to show that what was previously revealed through negation was merely emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Below, the three [vehicles] are reconciled...
The text of the "Seven Great Divisions" (Qidai) reveals the meaning of the wondrous existence (*miaoyou*) as the true mark of reality (*shixiang*) and ultimate emptiness (*zhenkong*).
This is truly the master key for shattering delusion; one must contemplate it with a refined mind to perceive its subtlety.
Question: Although the sections of the text for refuting the adherence to dharmas have been divided, the general sequence of the argument is not yet clear.
Please explain this in detail. Answer: The differentiation of the two types of adherence refers to the five aggregates (skandhas), body and mind, and the world to which all sentient beings adhere;
these belong to the two divisions of the "perceived" (nimitta-bhāga) and the "perceiving" (darśana-bhāga) of the eight consciousnesses. As for the innate self-...
"Grasping" refers to the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses, which has previously been internally grasped by the seventh consciousness as a self.

This "self" is the essence of the self-verifying portion—the fundamental awakening of Buddha-nature within delusion. Therefore, once the two kinds of delusions are destroyed according to the sutras, this fundamentally awakened true mind is revealed.
This belongs to the Buddha-nature of the condition (*pratyaya-hetu*), which is manifested through the severing [of delusions].

This is not yet the *tathatā* (suchness) that is free from obstacles. Because the purified manas still clings to this awakening as something realized by a self, it constitutes a subtle form of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
This is what is meant by "attachment to phenomena that does not forget its own views still persists.

Thus, even Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* remain deluded regarding the principle of *tathatā*; they must await the three empowerments and seven exhortations before they can [attain it].
Regarding "abandonment": it is shown to be the most difficult to sever because its karmic maturation has not yet been exhausted.
This refers to the transition from the eighth stage into Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Following the examination of these two delusions in the sutra text, the Buddha says:

"Although you have previously awakened to the luminous mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), you have not yet clarified that this source of awakening is neither produced through combination nor through non-combination. The intent of this is to dismantle [the remaining misconceptions].

The "harmonious awakening" (*sāṃyogika-bodhi*) refers to the initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*) harmonizing with the original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), which is termed "ultimate awakening" (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*); yet this still belongs to the realm of harmonization and relative opposition.
Therefore, once this harmony is shattered, the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is revealed, and one suddenly realizes the source of the single mind.

Thus, it should be understood that from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one merely shatters the innate clinging to dharmas (*sahaja-dharma-abhiniveśa*). The treatise states that the Buddha possesses purity...

The meaning of the "dividing manas" lies herein. The passage refuting the two types of conceptual grasping begins from the initial request for clarification and extends through the refutation of the seeing-essence, subsequently refuting the five aggregates, the body, and the mind as a whole;
within this, the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) is also included among what is refuted.
The passage concerning the two delusions refutes only the conceptual grasping at phenomena (*parikalpita-dharma-grāha*). The intent of these texts is very clear.

Question: Previously, you refuted the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Now, the Tathāgata first addresses the investigation of the mind, yet the topical outline states that this section refutes the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*).

This still leaves me unclear; please explain it directly. Answer: Regarding the two divisions of the eight consciousnesses—the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*)—the objective aspect consists of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), while the subjective aspect consists of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). This is because the subjective aspect initially grasps and consolidates the four great elements.
A small portion [of the aggregate] constitutes my own root-body (*mūlakāya*). What is indicated in the treatise is that which is the locus of appropriation;

thus, it becomes a sentient being of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Therefore, the Sūtra says: "When deluded once, it becomes the mind; one is inevitably confused, taking it to be within the physical body. This refers to this very point.
For the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) are precisely the locus upon which appropriation depends. Although the names are distinct, they refer to the mind and consciousness.
This demonstrates that this root-body is fundamentally empty and not a locus upon which to rely. One who wishes to cultivate the Great Samādhi must first internally liberate body and mind;

therefore, one first destroys the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*). Once the physical body is destroyed, there is nothing to be grasped or sustained, and thus the deluded mind has no basis.
Consequently, one subsequently proceeds to destroy the six consciousnesses, which constitute the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā*).
Question: After the inquiry into the mind, Ānanda again requested the path of *śamatha*. The Tathāgata then emitted light and further interrogated him regarding his mind.
Why is this section categorized as "Destroying the Aggregate of Perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) of the Six Consciousnesses"? Answer:

The initial inquiry into the mind was intended to destroy the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), thereby directly refuting the "view of a self" (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) of the Śrāvakas. Its underlying intent is to reveal that one who wishes to cultivate the Great Samādhi must necessarily...

One must internally liberate the sense-faculties and the body. This is because ordinary people merely recognize deluded thoughts as the mind; non-Buddhists rely on this to engage in false conceptualization;
those of the Small Vehicle merely sever the six consciousnesses; and the devas and humans of the two upper realms merely suppress the six consciousnesses. Therefore, the Buddha first stated:
"All sentient beings, due to grasping at these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistakenly take them to be real."
True. Although it is said that practicing [this meditation] does not result in the fruit of sainthood, one must first shatter it when cultivating the Great Samādhi.

Because this deluded thought has consistently clung to this physical body as its locus of dependence, and because this clinging mind was pointed out as being within the body, it was subjected to the Buddha’s interrogation;
thus, there arose the sevenfold shifting attachments, all of which have now been shattered and revealed.
Since the four great elements are fundamentally empty, the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) are already empty.

Because this deluded thought alone is the root of birth and death, it is next destroyed. This is intended to show that this thought is not something that can be resolved through the contemplation of emptiness alone;
thus, Ānanda again requests instruction on the path of *śamatha*. Before the destruction [of the thought] occurs, the Buddha emits radiance, intending thereby—
This light is the very substance of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). To realize this light is, needless to say, the immediate shattering of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).
This is because sentient beings are obscured by this light and instead employ various inverted deluded thoughts.
Therefore, the two kinds of inversion are first set forth as the fundamental basis for what is to be destroyed. That is to say, the non-arising of inversion is itself suchness (*tathatā*).
This is because he has come to the True Samādhi. Therefore, what is to be refuted below are merely the two types of inversion;

yet, when his mind is interrogated, it is precisely the mind of correct inversion that is addressed. Since inverted minds give rise to inverted views, [the Buddha] raises his fist to test both the eyes and the mind as to where they reside.
Ānanda merely clings to the deluded thought that performs the act of discernment as being the mind; therefore, the Buddha rebukes and scolds him.

"It is not mind. The concluding statement, "all arise from clinging to these deluded thoughts of birth and death," correctly refutes the six consciousnesses as they pertain to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

The subsequent passages proceed to refute inverted views accordingly. Therefore, when Ānanda again requests that the wondrous mind be revealed to open his "Dharma-eye," his intention lies solely in the refutation of deluded vision.
Question: I do not understand where the passage on "refuting views" leads; please explain it in detail. Answer:

"View" refers to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of the eight consciousnesses, which serves as the basis for the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). These seven consciousnesses constitute the mental faculty (*manas*) of the seven consciousnesses;

therefore, they evolve according to internal and external gates. When evolving externally, they function as the discriminating view within the six consciousnesses; when evolving internally, they grasp the eighth consciousness as...
I [teach that] what is called "speculative view" (*tarka-dṛṣṭi*) consists merely of differences in coarseness and subtlety.

First, the common person’s view of permanence, the two vehicles’ view of impermanence, and the externalists’ view of annihilationism are all refutations of the view of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*).

These belong to the first inversion and are still connected to the six consciousnesses. Therefore, the subsequent text belongs to the seventh consciousness; within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it refutes speculative view.

The second is the inversion. However, the view of discrimination (*vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*) is the discriminating grasping at a self (*parikalpita-ātmagrāha*), while the view of speculative reasoning (*tarka-dṛṣṭi*) is the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātmagrāha*).
One must proceed until the innate grasping at a self within the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-sāra*) is destroyed for it to be fully eliminated.

Those two types of views and delusions destroy the discriminating grasping at phenomena (*parikalpita-dharmagrāha*); following those two delusions, the chapter on "Harmonization" destroys the innate [grasping].

This is attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). Because, although one has realized *tathatā*, the subject and object have not yet been extinguished, and there remains something attained; this is called subtle attachment to dharmas.
The title of this section, "Wiping Away Traces to Enter the Profound," intends to extinguish the contemplative mind so that it becomes absolute and free from all relativity.
However, once these two attachments are shattered, one immediately returns to the single mind. Therefore, in the following text, each of the three categories and seven elements...
All are fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha*. A question is asked:
"In the section analyzing the views, the text from the sixth to the seventh consciousness seems to be entangled; it is difficult for students to distinguish them.
We would be grateful for your guidance. The answer is: "The eight consciousnesses and their three parts each possess [all aspects]. By means of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part)..."
Because they serve as the basis for the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses, the treatise states that they "can manifest, can see, and can grasp objects.

Therefore, both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess the faculty of seeing (*darśana*). As for the views of ordinary beings, *śrāvakas*, and non-Buddhists residing within the six consciousnesses—those which are precisely what grasp objects—they are termed "discriminative seeing" (*vikalpa-darśana*).
The treatise explains this as the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the [seventh] consciousness. Its...

Regarding the analysis of the seven consciousnesses by means of the "eight returns": this specifically refers to the "seeing faculty" (*darśana-bhāga*), meaning the capacity for discernment and investigation.

It is precisely directed toward that which faces the "object-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*). As for the refutation of "perceptual cognition" (*pramāṇa*), this is conducted in terms of the "manifesting capacity.

Since it is the manifesting capacity that gives rise to the seeing of the object-part, it still belongs to the seventh consciousness. Only when this cognition is refuted do the two parts vanish, returning [to the source].
It is merely the seeing-essence. The Buddha’s intent is exceedingly profound and subtle; it cannot be understood without subtle and secret contemplation.
Since this occurs within the section on "Destroying Falsity," it must be investigated and elucidated in detail; it is by no means a matter of entangling discourse.
Question: In the section on "Refuting Views," the analysis first employs the "eight returns" to distinguish the conditions (*ālambana*), which is titled "Distinguishing Conditions.

Later, when revealing the essence of seeing (*darśana-sāra*), it likewise uses the title "Distinguishing Conditions. Why is it that while the scriptural meanings differ, the headings are the same? Answer:

Although the headings for "distinguishing conditions" are the same, their meanings are indeed distinct. The former "distinguishing conditions" refers to the confusion of the visual faculty (*darśana-bhāga*) with its objects.

Within the conditions of sensory objects, the subject and object are invariably undifferentiated; therefore, these seven types of conditions are excluded as they are merely the objective spheres of perception.
Because the condition of discrimination specifically differentiates subject and object, each has its own source from which it returns; yet, the nature of seeing remains non-deficient.
This means that all things which can be turned back are not the seeing; it is only that which does not turn back that is the nature of seeing.
This merely distinguishes between the subject and the object for the time being, and has not yet specifically designated the nature of seeing as the "seeing-essence" (*jijing*).

Next, in manifesting the seeing-essence and distinguishing it from conditions, one single-pointedly distinguishes the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect), which is the reflected image of conditions manifested by the eight consciousnesses. It is not...
Regarding the term "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*): the meaning is that all various objects and images are manifested within the substance of the eight consciousnesses.

Just as the reflections and the mirror in a mirror are not separate, one eliminates the conditions of the immediate object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), and the seeing-part naturally dissolves while the substance of consciousness remains;
therefore, it is called the essence of seeing, which is the perfect luminosity of the essence of consciousness. This pertains to the general [explanation].
By eliminating the two aspects of subject and object, one points exclusively to the essence of consciousness as the "seeing-essence" (*jijing*). This meaning is profound and subtle;
it cannot be grasped by a coarse mind and must be observed with meticulous care.
Question: Since the extent of this seeing seems to belong to the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the eighth consciousness, why does this initial refutation immediately speak of "body and mind"?
If the perfectly luminous and immovable Way is manifested at the tip of a single hair, it can already contain and receive the lands of the ten directions;
this has reached the ultimate limit. Why, then, does the subsequent text further employ the analysis of the eight consciousnesses to refute the notion of a self? The answer is:

Although the "seeing-measure" (*darśana-māna*) resembles the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the eight consciousnesses, since it is the consciousness that can directly perceive the two divisions of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*) and seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), the treatises state that it is the "directly perceived object-condition" (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*).
However, as long as the appearance and seeing have not been extinguished and their mutual opposition has not been forgotten, it must belong to the seven [evolving] consciousnesses.

Regarding the passage concerning the manifestation of truth—wherein body and mind are perfectly luminous (*pariśuddha-prabhāsvara*)—this specifically refers to the destruction of defiled ignorance; thus, it does not [apply here].

Because it grasps at body and mind, it is called "perfectly luminous" (*yuanming*). That a single hair can contain the lands of the ten directions clearly demonstrates that it is free from measure and thus unobstructed.
This, however, is but a partial vision of the True Principle; in reality, it is not yet the ultimate limit.
The commentary on the *Shu* is very clear; one should examine it carefully.

Question: The Buddha points to the essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddhi*) as being like a second moon, saying that although it is not the wondrously pure and luminous mind (*amala-vijñāna*), it is nonetheless like a second moon.
Why, then, does he use the essence of seeing as a standard of comparison when the eight consciousnesses have not yet been destroyed? Furthermore, the Sūtra immediately states:
"If one can transform objects, one is identical to the Tathāgata; within the tip of a single hair, one can contain the lands of the ten directions. This—
If the principle has already been fully revealed, how is it that one can achieve this while the eight consciousnesses have not yet been destroyed? The answer is:

This is not something that can be known by those of shallow intelligence. Consider, for instance, that as soon as a Bodhisattva of the First Ground (Prathamā-bhūmi) destroys the two types of conceptual grasping (*vikalpa-grāha*), the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) remains entirely present, and they are immediately able to perceive a hundred Buddha-worlds. From this point on, there is further progress in each successive ground.
Seeing it gradually expand and broaden—could this not mean that a single hair contains the lands of the ten directions?
Furthermore, the substance of this consciousness is fundamentally True Suchness (tathatā); it is merely obstructed by the two divisions of subject and object.

Now that these two divisions have dissolved, the essence of consciousness is perfectly luminous, and the lands of the ten directions appear vividly pure. How can there be any further doubt that a single hair contains the ten directions?
Question: Is the transformation of objects identical to or different from the transformation of consciousness into wisdom?
Answer: Although the transformation is the same, the reason for the transformation is vastly different.

The transformation of consciousness into wisdom refers to each of the eight consciousnesses having its own specific transformation, occurring in a sequential order; this is explained solely in terms of the consciousnesses themselves. This sutra...

Regarding the "transformation of objects," this does not refer to the transformation of consciousnesses (*vijñāna-parāvṛtti*), but rather to the transformation of objects. When objects are transformed, the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) also vanishes.
Once the subjective aspect has vanished, the first seven consciousnesses are all transformed simultaneously and instantaneously; there is originally no sequence of before and after.

Because "seeing" (darśana) is the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the discernment (*vijñapti*) of the eight consciousnesses, the first seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are established based upon this seeing.
Therefore, when seeing ceases, the seven consciousnesses turn together. This is because, in the Dharma-character school (*lakṣaṇa-yāna*), consciousness is taken as the fundamental basis.
This sutra assembly brings the characteristics back to their fundamental nature, specifically manifesting the realm of Mind-Only, taking the true source of the one mind as its basis.

Because one is deluded regarding the true suchness (tathatā) of the one mind, it becomes the ālayavijñāna; thus, there arise the two divisions of the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiver (darśana-bhāga).
Since the perceived division is established, the perceiving division grasps that perceived division and constitutes sentient beings—what is called "the self-mind grasping."
One's own mind is not illusory, yet it manifests as illusory phenomena. Now, since the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*) has dissolved, one is free from grasping;
thus, all phenomena are fundamentally true, each and every one being the Tathāgatagarbha. Without waiting for transformation, they transform of themselves.

As it is said: "There is no need to seek the Truth; one need only cease false views. Once the perceived aspect dissolves, the objective aspect (*grāhyabhāga*) spontaneously transforms into the single mind of True Suchness.
As it was before, so it is identical to the Tathāgata. That which is called "non-apprehension" is not non-illusion;
since even illusion does not arise, how could illusory phenomena be established? This meaning is profound, hidden, subtle, and secret; only through contemplative insight can one know it.
Question: We have already understood the intent behind the refutation of [false] views. Regarding the passage that refutes the eight consciousnesses:
first, it states that in refuting the self (*ātman*), one should investigate by taking objects as they are; furthermore, it instructs Mañjuśrī to discern [the truth] by means of right and wrong.

In refuting self-validation (*svasaṃvitti*), it refutes it by means of spontaneity and dependent origination. In refuting the essence of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*), it further relies on light and darkness.
Form is empty—this is used to distinguish it. Furthermore, all the sections state that this is "to reveal the one true reality. Is this not redundant?
The answer is: it is not redundant. This is because the Tathāgata’s teaching was specifically intended to shatter the false attachments of sentient beings.
It was stated previously that various forms of perversion mean that the deluded conceptualizations of sentient beings are not of a single kind.

This teaching does not compare to the Chan school’s approach of attaining immediate realization through a single awakening. Within the teachings, one must necessarily investigate and expound with thorough detail;

because there are inherently various types of deluded conceptualizations within delusion itself, it is necessary to refute them one by one. To refute the notion of self, these eight [points] are used.

The two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) grasp this consciousness as the self of nirvāṇa; when they have not yet awakened, they further reckon that the aggregates are either identical to or separate from the self.
Non-Buddhists reckon it as the divine self (puruṣa-ātman); when they have not yet attained penetration, they reckon it as the self of saṃsāra.

Therefore, because one now wishes to destroy this consciousness, one first destroys its view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). This is precisely the innate grasping of self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*). However, by means of the object itself, one causes...

Regarding the investigation of right and wrong: since this substance of consciousness has completely transformed into the delusive thoughts of the sense organs, the body, and the physical world—originally being no two distinct dharmas—one must now investigate right and wrong by means of these very objects to reveal that they are fundamentally one true reality.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī was commissioned to expound this in order to sever the views of "is" and "is not," so that one might awaken to the principle of the single reality.
As for his refutation of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) by means of both causes-and-conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*):

it is because non-Buddhists do not understand this consciousness; they falsely calculate that all phenomena arise spontaneously, asserting that they are self-generated or produced without cause. Furthermore, they calculate...
All phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; this is called "co-arising" or "arising from another.

Yet none realize that the self-substance of the eight consciousnesses is fundamentally the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind. Therefore, [the teaching] refutes them by means of natural causes and conditions.

Once this calculation is refuted, the essential awareness will manifest of itself. This refutation of the seeing-essence is precisely the original luminosity of the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-dhātu*)—the capacity to give rise to all conditions—which was overlooked among the two types of inversion previously established. Therefore, it is only upon reaching this point that the various delusions are finally refuted.
Furthermore, by means of the analysis of light, darkness, form, and space, it is precisely revealed that this consciousness-essence is capable of giving rise [to them].
That which is left behind by all conditions (*pratyaya*) is therefore distinguished from conditions in order to refute them;
one must transcend conditions to reveal the true mind (*tathatā*). This is indeed the ultimate principle for refuting consciousness.

Furthermore, as each section is titled "Revealing the True," it means that by refuting those false conceptualizations, the truth is revealed—this is a partial revelation, not the manifestation of the whole. The Buddha said, "Ādāna..."
That consciousness is extremely subtle; therefore, it cannot be easily understood by the coarse mind. One should contemplate it deeply. Question:
In the section refuting the "seeing-essence" (*jien-jing*), you again used the preceding objects—light, darkness, form, and emptiness—to refute it, stating, "I say that I am able to see.
Furthermore, in the section clarifying the "initial awakening" (*shijue*), you again distinguished away from conditions. Thus, this and...

Question: Regarding the previous refutation of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), how does its selection of objects differ? Answer: This passage appears similar [in wording] but differs widely in meaning;

it is profoundly difficult to clarify. Please explain this in detail. The previous refutation of the seeing-part regarding the selection of objects was because the seeing-part grasps its perceived object (*ālambana*) in a manner that is entirely conflated and undifferentiated; therefore, in order to now refute the seeing-part, one must—
First, eliminate delusive conditions. Once delusive conditions are removed, there is nothing for the vision to grasp; this vision does not vanish, yet it vanishes of its own accord.

This is because one regards the characteristics [of objects] as existence and the arising of those characteristics as non-existence. When these two divisions have vanished, the essence of vision alone remains.
Therefore, he specifically refutes it, saying: "At the moment of seeing the seeing, that seeing is not [the true] seeing; even seeing is something to be transcended."
The seeing of seeing cannot reach it; yet the commentary states that this reveals the initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*).
This is because this essence of seeing is precisely fundamental ignorance (*mūlavidyā*). When one says that true seeing sees this essence of seeing, true seeing is not the essence of seeing.
The meaning is this: when true wisdom illuminates this ignorance, that ignorance is not itself true wisdom. Furthermore, this ignorance is a transformation of true wisdom;
though it is intimately close to the truth, wisdom still remains distinct from it. Hence it is said, "even seeing is still to be left behind by seeing.
How could that deluded view of grasping and attachment ever reach it? Therefore, it is said, "seeing cannot reach it."
When this wisdom arises, delusion perishes; therefore, the commentary designates it as the "manifestation of initial enlightenment" (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*).

However, when one refutes the essence of seeing while still distinguishing its conditions, this is to distinguish the essence of seeing from those conditions. As stated previously: "The essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous and is able to give rise to all conditions."

Therefore, now that one is separated from conditions, the essence of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is revealed. These conditions are the immediate objective conditions (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*), serving as the direct objective part (*sabhāga-bhāga*) for the eight consciousnesses.

The conditions distinguished by the aforementioned seeing-part are the remote objective conditions (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*). The former involves transformation and carrying along (*pariṇāma-ādāna*);
the latter involves grasping and carrying along (*upādāna-ādāna*). If one understands this school of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vāda*), the principles herein will become perfectly clear.

Question: Since the essence of seeing has already been shattered, the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-jñāna*) has manifested, and both the five aggregates and the eight consciousnesses have been destroyed so that all delusions are abandoned, why does Ānanda’s mind still not open up regarding the calculations of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and their combination?

Why does he further increase his confusion and distress by focusing on "seeing the seeing"? For this reason, he makes a repeated request, leading to the following section where the World-Honored One [responds].

To speak directly, these two types of views are explained as delusions without answering according to the specific question asked; yet the topical outline (*kośa*) states that this is "to refute the attachment to dharmas" (*dharma-grāha*).

This meaning is profound and subtle, and is indeed difficult to comprehend. I request a detailed exposition of it. The answer is: The hidden intent (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) herein has never been understood from the past.

For the teachings state that among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), there are both those that exist as mere designations (*prajñapti-sat*) and those that exist as substantial dharmas (*dravya-sat*). As mentioned previously...

The five aggregates of body and mind that were previously refuted merely refer to the refutation of the clinging mind that grasps at the aggregates; what was refuted there was but a provisional designation.

However, since these five aggregates as substantial dharmas still remain, one continues to harbor doubts regarding their being produced by causes and conditions, arising spontaneously, or through combination, and thus has not yet opened the eye of wisdom.
Consequently, when encountering the teaching that "seeing is non-seeing," confusion and distress increase all the more.
This is because the essence of seeing (*darśana-vijñāna*) is the very substance of the eight consciousnesses, acting as the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Therefore it is said:
"The subtle *ālayavijñāna* (dāna-vijñāna), whose habitual tendencies form a torrential stream; fearing that the true might be mistaken for the untrue, I have never openly expounded it.

This is why the World-Honored One has consistently refrained from speaking lightly of it, and why those of the Two Vehicles have been perpetually deluded regarding it. Now, [the text] speaks of "seeing" (*darśana*).
"Seeing is not seeing" means that true seeing perceives this essence of seeing; it is true wisdom illuminating this ignorance.
How could this be known by those of the Two Vehicles? For instance, when light comes, darkness departs; when wisdom arises, delusion perishes.
Truth and falsehood cannot coexist. As the Sūtra says: "This ignorance has no real substance. How could there be a truly real ignorance?
How appropriate his wisdom was! Ānanda thought that there must truly be a "seeing-essence" (*dṛṣṭi-sāra*) distinct from the true seeing, which could now be perceived;
yet, since he sought this seeing-essence and could not find it, he became bewildered and distressed.

Moreover, as this ultimate state is by no means the realm of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, how could he help but harbor doubts in a state of mental desolation? Below, the World-Honored One’s reply does not follow [his expectations].

Regarding the direct explanation of the two kinds of deluded views concerning what was doubted: because Ānanda did not yet understand fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), his attachment to the five aggregates as real dharmas had not been eliminated.
As long as the five aggregates persist, the world, mountains, rivers, and the great earth will obstruct the eyes;
this is simply because his attachment to the true dharma has not perished and his own views still remain. If one were to consider ignorance alone, it would merely be...
The World-Honored One’s statement that this ignorance has no real substantial entity can be understood through a single phrase.

However, the present intention lies in destroying the attachment to the dharmas of body, mind, and world; thus, he employs the metaphor of hair-nets on a lamp to illustrate that the five aggregates are merely provisional.
This is because what is seen arises from a cataract in the eye. Now, there is no need to inquire whether the hair-nets actually exist or not.
If one simply knows that this is merely an optical aberration, then there is no longer the affliction of seeing.

This is a metaphor for the fact that if one contemplates the five aggregates of body and mind as being provisional—existing only due to the deluded vision caused by ignorance—and realizes that ignorance is fundamentally empty, then body and mind naturally dissolve.
Therefore, in the analogy, it is said that if one knows it is an aberration, then there is no fault in seeing; this refers to these very words.
This resolves the doubt regarding the seeing of seeing through the destruction of [false] views.
If one realizes that body and mind are fundamentally empty, then one may analogously observe that the world is likewise like body and mind—both being merely the response to deluded karma.

How, then, could there remain any doubt concerning the seeing of seeing as being caused by conditions or occurring spontaneously? This is why there is the teaching of advancing and retreating to achieve mutual clarification. Thus, these two delusions...
Once [the delusions] are shattered, the true mind of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āveśa*) is suddenly revealed. Therefore, the Sūtra concludes:

"If one can remain far removed from all conditions of conjunction and non-conjunction, then one further eliminates the causes of birth and death; the pure fundamental mind, original enlightenment, is eternally abiding. The topical outline states:
"Original enlightenment, detached from conditions, is True Suchness emerging from its entanglements. How could this not be profound? This is the intention of the Buddha.
This is very clear; it is simply that the wisdom of the observer is dim, making it difficult to comprehend.
A question is raised: "Regarding the subsequent chapters of the scripture, commentators have always said they repeatedly refute the 'conjunction' (of subject and object).

Yet this section speaks of 'brushing away traces to enter the profound. Moreover, the scripture still employs the term 'seeing-essence' (jien-jing) in its discussion. Is there not a direct path here?"

I requested in the courtyard for an exposition of its essentials. He replied: "It is very clear within the treatise. Herein, it is precisely because initial awakening (*ādikṣa-bodhi*) exerts its function that fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) becomes manifest.

The *Śāstra* states: 'When initial awakening accords with fundamental awakening, it is called ultimate awakening (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*). Now, you wish to manifest the true source of the one mind, which transcends all dualistic oppositions.
You must simply allow both contemplation and wisdom to subside and let both subject and object be forgotten. Therefore, when [this state] is reached...

This is the consciousness that breaks up the harmony [of the aggregates]. This is precisely the subtle, co-emergent clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), which is termed the ignorance of the "mark of arising" (*utpattilakṣaṇāvidyā*).
The treatise states: "This ignorance can only be understood by a Buddha; it is not the domain of others. Therefore, the Buddha spoke of it spontaneously without being asked.
However, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* says: "Although you have previously awakened to the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment (*mūlapratibhāsa*)," thereby acknowledging what preceded it.
"You have already awakened. Next, it says, "You still do not clearly understand that such an awakened source is neither a composite nor [the like]"; this meaning is extremely explicit.
Below, it says, "You still use worldly delusions to harbor doubts within yourself regarding the realization of the bodhicitta.
This specifically refutes the habitual tendencies of linguistic convention; therefore, it says, "one uses worldly delusions to doubt bodhi. Regarding this:
This means that if one uses a mind subject to arising and ceasing to discern Perfect Enlightenment, the nature of Perfect Enlightenment will likewise flow along with it.
Therefore, one must extinguish such cognitive views in order to enter the source of the single-mind aspect. For the true mind and true wisdom are difficult to express in words.

This was merely a provisional borrowing of the concept of "seeing-essence" as an illustration for refutation. Since the notion of a composite [perception] has been refuted, Ānanda then posits a non-composite seeing;

therefore, he again doubts, saying: "As I contemplate it, this wondrous source of awakening is neither a composite of the various objective conditions, sensory objects, and mental deliberations, is it?
To observe this, one must simply forget both mind and object, so that the paths of speech and thought are cut off.
This is simply entering the subtlety of single-mindedness.
A question is asked: "In the previous assembly on the five aggregates (*skandhas*), you first raised the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as existing based on deluded vision;

thus you said that the eyes, due to fatigue, falsely perceive flowers in the sky. Now, in discussing the six sense bases (*āyatana*), you again take up the previous point regarding the eyes and their resulting fatigue."
Regarding the sense-base of the eye, what is its underlying meaning? The answer is: it is most extremely subtle and cannot be compared to the previous metaphors.

This is because herein is explained the origin of the initial six faculties; due to the seeing-part’s grasping of signs and the subsequent accumulation of habit-energy, they return to a state of harmony and combine to form the five pure material faculties (*pañca-viśuddha-rūpa-indriya*), which serve as the support for the physical organs (*tuccha-kāya*). Originally, these do not exist.

Entering [into this state], it only now begins to exist. Furthermore, "the eyes" refers to the present eye-faculty as the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), while "fatigue" (*láo*) refers to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect).
Since these two aspects fundamentally do not exist, they are both equally the appearance of fatigue produced by the staring of Bodhi.

This intends to reveal that the essence of consciousness is deluded because it relies upon awakening; thus it is said that "Bodhi produces fatigue. These two aspects manifest in dependence upon consciousness and serve as the [objects] of consciousness.
Regarding their modes of activity (*ākāra*), they do not depart from self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) and originally possess no dual nature; thus it is said they are "identical.

Therefore, they are used as a metaphor for the formation of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) as their own essential substance. This implies that fundamentally there are no six sense-faculties, but rather that through the initial conjunction of seeing and its object, pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) is formed.
Thus, both are cited together to clarify the beginning of the six faculties' first formation. Consequently, this is difficult to comprehend.

[The text continues with] "Ear. [The interlocutor] asks: "What is the meaning of 'basis' (*āyatana*)? [The respondent] answers: "A basis refers to that which, according to the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), exists as a real entity;

it is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of form that serves as the locus upon which the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) relies. It functions as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) regardless of whether the relationship is direct or indirect, because all such things exist."

Regarding those that possess both [subjective and objective] supports: it is now stated that both are without substantiality and are solely True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, this is the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha. Question:

In the *Awakening of Faith*, the three subtle states are said to follow the sequence of karma, transformation, and manifestation. In this sutra, however, the three subtle states are— [The text ends here.]
Seeing (*darśana*) is listed as the "transforming characteristic" (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*) third; this means that manifestation (*darśana*) occurs first, followed by transformation (*pariṇāma*).

Does this not contradict the intent of the treatise? The answer is: it does not contradict the intent of the treatise, for each [characteristic] has its own specific domain. The intent of the treatise is to speak simply of the arising of mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).

That is to say, within the true realm (*tattva-viṣaya*), when there is initially a single moment of deluded movement, one immediately transforms the perfectly luminous true mind (*pariśuddha-cittatā*).
This constitutes ignorance (*avidyā*). Due to this ignorance, the characteristics of manifest discrimination and continuity arise.

If one can depart from discursive thought (*vikalpa*), one immediately realizes the single mind (*ekacitta*). Since this sutra emphasizes the source from which sentient beings arise, it explains that because of the initial movement of a single deluded thought, the signless true mind (*animitta-tathatā-citta*) is suddenly transformed into the deluded appearances of conditioned phenomena. Therefore, [it is like] empty space...
The four great elements take form from this; this constitutes the characteristic of "having something.
Because there is the characteristic of having something, the originally existing light of wisdom is transformed into deluded vision, becoming the deluded cognition that grasps at characteristics.

Consequently, these perceived characteristics are seen as identical to the single essence of primordial awakening; now, being muddled and undifferentiated, they become sentient beings—what are called the physical form and the mind.

These combine to form the sentient beings of the five aggregates. The emphasis here lies on deluded views and grasping, which constitute the root of the disease of birth and death—namely, the "pudgala" (the one who goes from existence to existence).
Thus it is said: "The self-mind grasps the self-mind; what is not illusory becomes an illusory dharma.
If one does not grasp, there is nothing that is not non-illusory. Therefore, the Patriarch said: "Do not seek the Truth; you need only cease [deluded] views."

Since this treatise discusses the mind that functions alone, true cultivation lies precisely in the departure from discursive thought (*nirvikalpa*). Since this sutra discusses the transformation of objects, it says:
"If one can transform objects, then one is identical to the Tathāgata. Therefore, true cultivation lies precisely in non-grasping; this is the severing of the very root of birth and death.

Therefore, while the Sūtra refutes delusion by focusing exclusively on the selection of objects (*ālambana*), it emphasizes the "grasped" (*grāhya*) and thus treats "characteristics" (*nimitta*) first;

whereas the Śāstra emphasizes the "grasper" (*grāhaka*) and thus treats "views" (*dṛṣṭi*) first. Consequently, because their approaches differ, the cultivation and abandonment [of afflictions] are also distinct. One should contemplate this deeply.
Supplement to the General Discourse on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra (Lengyan Tongyi)
